====================================================================================================

Why the 'great Aussie summer' may become a thing of the past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:34:39 UTC
05:34:39 KST

Last summer, Paris Brooke watched in horror as a bushfire blazed through the national park across the lake from her township of Mallacoota in north-east Victoria.
The town wasn't directly at risk, but she knew what the impact would be.
"The camp park emptied out overnight, leaving businesses that depend on summer tourism stuck with unused supplies and staff, but no more tourists," Brooke tells SBS News.
The exodus was reminiscent of the summer of 2019-20, when Australia's Black Summer bushfires swept through and devastated the beachside town.
Mallacoota was among the hardest-hit areas. Apocalyptic-looking scenes of residents and holidaymakers sheltering in boats off the coast, under a red sky thick with smoke, were broadcast around the world.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
While Brooke hasn't necessarily seen a slowdown in holidaymakers to the town since, she believes stays are shortening and worries the increased likelihood of extreme weather will hit summer trade long-term.
It's why she set up the Wilderness Collective, a community not-for-profit aimed at helping locals build new skills and businesses to reduce reliance on summer tourism.
"People are much more aware of natural disasters such as bushfires or droughts," she says.
On the same day last summer, climate scientist Linden Ashcroft was on the beach in Mallacoota. She recalls her kids playing in the water as embers and burnt leaves fell around them.
"It was pretty heartbreaking and terrifying. Everyone was really creeped out, and the town was covered in smoke," she says.
It left her with a lasting sense of cognitive dissonance — this is not how summer is supposed to feel.
That feeling is now rippling around the country, reaching far beyond places like Mallacoota that are historically prone to bushfires.
"Black Summer 2019–2020 was a real step change; it made people face the reality that summer can't just be carefree anymore," Ashcroft says.
You could call it the end of summer as we know it — or an evolution.
Climate Council director and academic Lesley Hughes says the changing climate is reshaping Australians' notion of summer: instead of looking forward to it, people increasingly feel apprehensive.
"They dread the heatwaves, the bushfires, not being able to do the things they used to. Climate change is stealing the part of the year Australians looked forward to most."
With higher temperatures and more extreme weather events becoming a fixture of the holiday season in parts of the country, could this signal the end of 'great Aussie summer'?
How our summers are changing
Australia is now 1.5C warmer on average than it was a century ago, according to the National Climate Risk Assessment. It's driving more extreme heatwaves and dangerous fire weather.
Monash climate scientist Andrew Watkins, former head of the Bureau of Meteorology's long-range forecast team, says the expected shifts will likely be dramatic.
"Heatwaves will cover larger areas, happen more frequently and grow more intense, with longer fire seasons stretching into autumn and spring. Rainfall will be less frequent but more intense, raising flash flood risk. Tropical cyclones may become less frequent but more severe," he tells SBS News.
Rising humidity is also driving up "wet-bulb temperature" — a combined heat-and-humidity measure that determines how well sweat can cool the body. Watkins says high readings — when sweat stops evaporating because the humidity is too high — put children and the elderly at particular risk.
"The temperature might only be 35, but if the wet-bulb is up to 25, you're going to put your body under a huge amount of stress."
Looking ahead to this summer, the Bureau of Meteorology has forecast a strong El Niño — generally meaning hotter, drier conditions — which it expects will mainly affect parts of Australia's east and south-east, raising the risk of drought and bushfires.
As extreme heat becomes more commonplace in Australia, other countries face similar conditions. Los Angeles was hit by raging wildfires last January, and Europe endured one of its worst summers on record for fire and heat this year.
It's a trend that is unlikely to shift without major and rapid structural changes, shifting global energy use to renewables and divesting from fossil fuels to limit further global warming.
New data published this week by the UN Environment Programme showed the world has lost the fight to limit warming to 1.5C. Even the most optimistic projections now point to warming of at least 1.8C — locking in more extreme weather, ecosystem loss and sea-level rise.
Reorganising the year
As projections worsen, experts are turning their attention to health risks.
Hughes at the Climate Council says the impacts of excess heat on the body can creep up slowly, and are especially dangerous for the elderly, the young, and those with heart or respiratory conditions.
She suggests more public awareness of the risks associated with heat stress is needed, but she's also calling for something more radical: reframing the calendar year to keep more of us inside during the country's hottest months.
Maybe a lot of summer would be better spent indoors, in air-conditioning, working, and leisure time moved to spring and autumn.
"Maybe our biggest school holidays shouldn't be in January," she says, adding "that would be an enormous social change for Australia".
Not everyone can escape the heat during their workday either. Professions such as tradies, farmhands, park rangers, delivery riders and some hospitality and event workers, for example, have no choice but to endure it.
A Spanish study published in 2023 offers another perspective, instead proposing to shift the country's national holidays to align with its hottest weeks to boost productivity and reduce industrial electricity consumption. Researchers found moving Spain's traditional holiday period from August to late July — the point of peak heat damage — would cut heat-driven electricity demand by 3 per cent, lost work hours by 25 per cent, and ozone pollution by 4 per cent.
Whether holidaying or working over summer, the general advice is to find ways to stay cool, and limit outdoor time to early mornings or evenings.
Although now, some Australians are reconsidering how they spend the season altogether.
The rise of the 'coolcation'
Research suggests people are already adapting to climate change without realising it, as evidenced by the rise in 'coolcations' — holidays to cool-climate destinations.
For Australians, this might include escapes to parts of northern Europe instead of southern Europe; visiting the tropics in winter instead of summer; venturing south to New Zealand or Tasmania for a mid-summer break; or snowy escapes to the Arctic, Antarctica or Alpine villages.
Trip.com data shows a 74 per cent year-on-year jump in searches for cooler destinations since the start of 2026, spiking 237 per cent across the June–August northern hemisphere summer. Searches for flights to Iceland rose 85 per cent, as travellers favoured northern Europe over traditionally popular Mediterranean spots. In Asia, cooler destinations such as Inner Mongolia, Yunnan in China and Sapporo in Japan saw similar gains.
Holidaygoers are also increasingly considering extreme weather events when making travel plans. Booking.com's 2026 Travel & Sustainability Report found 74 per cent of travellers now factor extreme weather into where and when they travel, and 31 per cent have cancelled a trip because of it.
In Australia, the Climate Council found 61 per cent of people are concerned about extreme weather disrupting summer holidays and are adapting — shifting from inland bush locations to the coast or travelling in cooler months.
Climate scientist Watkins is a coolcationer and spends his summers camping in Victoria's cooler high country.
"[It's about] beach holidays in spring, camping in autumn, taking more advantage of Easter. Getting up into cooler places over summer is a joy."
Travelling in cooler months isn't just about comfort, of course; it often also means fewer crowds and protecting destinations from over-tourism in mid-summer.
If you're holidaying in summer
However, travelling to far-flung places to access cooler weather may not be viable for some people. Distance and cost can be prohibitive, even for domestic travel.
Simply avoiding regional or bushfire-prone areas isn't necessarily a silver bullet either.
Ashcroft warns that heat risk in major cities can be just as dangerous.
"Urban areas get hotter due to the heat-island effect, so vulnerable people may not be better off in cities."
No matter where you spend the summer months, the advice is familiar by now: watch the forecasts, have a fire or heat plan, know when to leave early if conditions turn catastrophic, and avoid driving through floodwaters or bushfire smoke, which can be as thick as fog. Sometimes that means a detour, or staying put overnight until the danger passes.
Ashcroft thinks the language around summer should change altogether to help people prepare and understand the risks.
"Seasons are baked into how we talk about our year, but they're changing, so the way we talk about them has to change too. The Bureau's new term 'severe weather season' is more honest," she says.
"Being real helps us plan and prepare."
Rethinking summer sport
As our summers become more brutal, outdoor events such as music festivals and sport events may also become more challenging.
Ashcroft questions whether it still makes sense to push elite athletes to compete in extreme heat, conditions that are "not healthy and not safe".
Joanne Bowen is CEO of Cricket for Climate, a player-led movement that aims to build resilience for community clubs and the game. She calls cricket "the canary in the coal mine" for how climate change is disrupting outdoor activities.
Grassroots clubs are already cancelling junior games on hot days, with many lacking the infrastructure and budgets to adequately light night matches.
At the elite level, players have also struggled to perform in the heat, adds Bowen.
"But it's not just about the players; fans in concrete stadiums are exposed as well."
Increasing rainfall during summer is a growing problem too, she adds.
"If there's rain, you simply can't play, and there are commercial consequences for partners and fans."
She expects more games to move to nighttime and says shifting the cricket season to winter or spring is possible, though it would clash with other codes.
Another staple of Australian summer is the Australian Open.
Tennis Australia declined to discuss the long-term viability of tennis as a summer sport or moving the Australian Open from its midsummer slot, but a spokesperson said in a statement the organisation "continues to introduce strategies to protect the safety of players in hot conditions".
These include shading, misting fans, science-based heat guidelines with real-time monitoring, and heat acclimatisation education for players arriving from overseas.
The organisation's response to heat also appears to be shifting. Back in 2014, tournament director Craig Tiley defended playing through 40C conditions, saying "we are, at the end of the day, an outdoor event", even as players required medical attention.
By contrast, this year organisers suspended play after defending champion Jannik Sinner cramped mid-match under 40C conditions, with play resuming under a closed roof.
Planning for future summers
Beyond the challenge of adjusting our summer holiday plans to increasingly extreme weather, a deeper issue persists: how to curb climate change.
The best way to protect Australian summers, experts say, is to stop burning fossil fuels.
"We have to address the root cause of the problem, and Australia has a big responsibility to do that," says the Climate Council's Hughes.
Experts say adaptation can't wait: retrofitting homes with renewable energy, better resourcing emergency services and warning systems, investing in coastal protection, and upgrading infrastructure — from power grids to more public cooling and green spaces — all matter now more than ever.
Climate scientist Watkins wants to see more rigorous climate risk assessments underpin a genuine national adaptation plan, backed by coordination across all levels of government.
"The most important thing is coordinated efforts — talking with communities, business sectors, and the public to find out locally what adaptation is possible," he says.
I think we'll still have fun [in summer]. We'll just need to do things a little differently.
Back in Mallacoota, Brooke’s Wilderness Collective is helping locals to build off-season opportunities.
"We're working hard to broaden the economy, so visitors come throughout the year. Winter is actually the best time to visit; it's less crowded and the weather's beautiful," she says.
"We're starting to see visitors spread across the year, which is great, but we need more of it."
Even as Australians adapt to the new realities of summer, a trade-off is occurring.
For Watkins, adapting also means facing loss.
"There's a kind of grief that doesn't get talked about enough — grief for a place," he says.
"Many of us return to the same spots every summer, hoping our kids will see them the way we first did. But those places are changing. The National Climate Risk Assessment confirms it: huge numbers of plant and animal species are already shifting, with more change ahead.
"That sense of loss is real, and it deserves to be taken seriously."

Poland extends asylum restrictions at Belarus border for another 60 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:34:04 UTC
05:34:04 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Poland’s parliament on Friday approved another 60-day suspension of the right to apply for asylum for migrants illegally crossing the country’s border with Belarus, TVP World reported.
A total of 418 lawmakers voted in favor of the extension, while 16 opposed it.
The measure, which will take effect Sept. 18, marks the ninth consecutive renewal.
Poland first suspended the right to claim asylum at the Belarus border in March 2025, following what Polish officials described as an influx of mostly Middle Eastern and African migrants entering the EU through Belarus.
In a motion submitted to parliament, the government said “dangerous incidents have regularly occurred in which aggressive foreign nationals attacked Polish patrols.”
It said migrants had thrown stones, bottles, bricks and other objects at Polish personnel and damaged sections of border barriers.
The government also accused Belarusian state services of participating in attacks on Polish soldiers, police officers and border guards.
It said border guards had prevented attempts supported by Belarusian state services to build and use tunnels beneath the frontier to move groups of foreign nationals into Poland.
Between March 2025 and Aug. 16, Polish authorities rejected 492 asylum applications and accepted 178 from migrants in vulnerable groups, according to government figures.
Meanwhile, attempted illegal crossings have fallen sharply.
Polish Interior Ministry figures showed 235 attempts during the first half of this year, compared with more than 15,500 during the same period in 2025.
Polish and EU authorities have linked the influx to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, while human rights groups have accused Polish authorities of pushing some migrants back to Belarus without allowing them to seek asylum.
Dozens of migrants are believed to have died in the border area since 2021.

More than 900 families displaced in 2 days as fighting intensifies in Yemen’s Taiz

Mohammed Sameai and Mohammad Sio
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
More than 900 families have been displaced in two days as fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis intensified in the western province of Taiz, local authorities said Friday.
Preliminary figures show that 917 families fled their homes Thursday and Friday amid renewed fighting in Maqbanah district and nearby areas, particularly Jabal Habashi, according to the Taiz office of Yemen’s Planning and International Cooperation Ministry.
The office said the escalation had forced residents to evacuate several communities and displacement camps, while residential areas and sites sheltering displaced people had also come under attack.
Families fled parts of Maqbanah, including Ozul Al-Yaman, Al-Abdalah and Al-Ashmalah, as well as Al-Jubb camp. Others were displaced from Al-Rahbah and Al-Rajhi camps in Jabal Habashi.
They moved to safer areas, including parts of Jabal Habashi and Al-Ma’afer districts, the statement said.
Authorities warned that the displacement figure was likely to rise if the fighting continued.
The ministry office said many families had fled with little warning, leaving behind belongings and basic necessities, and were now facing “extremely difficult” humanitarian conditions.
It appealed to local and international relief organizations for emergency shelter, food, drinking water and sanitation services, calling for an “urgent, multisectoral humanitarian intervention” before the crisis expands further.
The displacement comes amid heavy clashes since early Thursday on several fronts in Taiz and neighboring Hodeidah province, near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Local media, citing military sources, have reported dozens of government troops and Houthi fighters killed or wounded since the fighting intensified.
Civilians have also been killed and wounded in shelling, but no consolidated official casualty toll has been announced as clashes continue.
The latest violence is part of a series of exchanges that began in July and ended a period of relative calm that had largely prevailed along Yemen’s front lines since a UN-brokered truce in April 2022.
The Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa and several other cities since September 2014, while the internationally recognized government and allied forces control large areas of southern, eastern and western Yemen.

Tate brothers indicted in Romania over sex crimes involving minors
Romanian authorities have indicted social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate in absentia on charges including human trafficking, sex offenses involving minors, money laundering and witness tampering. The brothers have been held in a US jail since mid-July while fighting a separate British extradition request.
Both have strongly denied wrongdoing.
Andrew Tate, a former professional kickboxer and dual British-US citizen, built a global following promoting wealth, hyper-masculinity and traditional gender roles. His online content has attracted millions of followers while drawing widespread criticism over remarks about women.
Romania’s Directorate for the Investigation of Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) announced on Friday that Andrew had been charged with human trafficking, having sex with a minor, money laundering and influencing witnesses. Tristan is accused of aiding and abetting him.
Prosecutors allege that in 2012 Andrew recruited a 15-year-old girl in the UK by falsely claiming he wanted a romantic relationship with her before taking her to Romania. She was then allegedly forced to produce pornographic content for a webcam business, with the brothers controlling her through threats, emotional blackmail and physical violence.
Tristan allegedly managed proceeds from the operation totaling around $1.25 million. DIICOT is seeking the confiscation of four luxury cars allegedly bought with the money and registered in the names of associates.
Prosecutors have separately accused Andrew of having sex with another 15-year-old girl.
The case has been referred to the Bucharest Tribunal, where preliminary proceedings are expected to take at least two months.
Eugen Vidineac, the brothers’ Romanian lawyer, said the defense would challenge the indictment. Andrew and Tristan, who moved to Romania in 2016, were arrested there in December 2022 in a separate case involving similar allegations. An appeals court later returned that case to prosecutors after finding some evidence inadmissible. The charges were not dismissed, but travel restrictions were lifted in February 2025, allowing the brothers to fly to Florida.
In July, Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service announced additional charges against the Tates, bringing the British case to seven alleged victims and 59 charges combined, including rape, sexual assault and trafficking-related offenses.
The brothers were subsequently arrested in Florida following a British extradition request.
Their lawyer, Joseph McBride, has said Andrew and Tristan will vigorously fight extradition, describing the British case as politically motivated because his clients have repeatedly criticized the UK authorities and political establishment.

Watchdog report alleges misconduct by Trump’s former labour secretary
Lori Chavez-DeRemer reportedly used staff for personal tasks, drank at work and violated ethics regulations.
A federal watchdog in the United States has published a report detailing allegations of misconduct involving former US Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, who resigned in April.
On Thursday night, the Department of Labor’s Office of Inspector General released 44 pages detailing incidents where Chavez-DeRemer reportedly blurred the line between her public office and personal life.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3US intelligence director pick refuses to acknowledge Trump loss in 2020
- list 3 of 3Karoline Leavitt to step down as White House press secretary
The report drew from 500 documents and interviews with 53 current and former Labor Department employees, as well as one employee from another federal agency.
It said 38 of the interviewees described the secretary’s office as a “toxic, intimidating and humiliating” workplace.
It also accuses Chavez-DeRemer of using government employees for private errands, drinking alcohol in her office during working hours and developing an “inappropriate relationship” with a member of her security detail.
The rumours of misconduct ultimately forced Chavez-DeRemer to leave her post on April 20.
She became the third cabinet secretary to leave the second administration of President Donald Trump, after the departures of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Attorney General Pam Bondi earlier this year.
A ‘toxic’ environment
Chavez-DeRemer, a former Republican Congress member from Oregon, was sworn in on March 11, 2025. Her position lasted just over a year.
The final months of her tenure saw the resignations of several high-level staff members. One, Melissa Robey, claimed in media reports that she was fired under pressure from the White House after sitting down with the inspector general’s office.
Thursday’s report alleged that Chavez-DeRemer oversaw a hostile workplace, with senior staff having “routinely engaged in threatening, demeaning, and abusive verbal and written communication” towards their colleagues.
It cited incidents of Labor Department employees being berated in front of colleagues and threatened with termination.
Some of the episodes involved Chavez-DeRemer’s chief of staff, Rebecca Wright. She allegedly relocated one employee’s desk to avoid having a “fat person” seen in the front office, and she reportedly advised another employee not to cut her hair too short to avoid looking like a “lesbian”.
The report alleges that Chavez-DeRemer was aware of such incidents but failed to take action to prevent them from happening.
Allegations of inappropriate requests
Investigators also found that Chavez-DeRemer herself directed government employees to perform personal tasks during official time.
A personal aide and executive assistant were reportedly sent to her residence to organise her closet, hang laundry and arrange her clothing and purses.
Investigators said another employee, who was Hispanic, was directed to oversee workers at Chavez-DeRemer’s home, including a moving crew.
Employees were also tasked with buying personal items, including gifts, picture frames, holiday decorations and alcohol, according to the report.
Chavez-DeRemer, Wright and her deputy chief of staff also regularly drank alcohol in the secretary’s study during duty hours, according to witness reports. Some employees said they felt pressured or ridiculed when they declined to participate.
Department of Labor policy requires advance written authorisation for alcohol on federal property. Investigators found no record that the required approval had been obtained.
Relationship with security detail
The watchdog also zeroed in on aspects of Chavez-DeRemer’s personal behaviour that violated government ethics standards.
Regulations prohibit government employees from using their office “to coerce or induce another person, including a subordinate, to provide” them with “any financial or other benefit”.
It also bars officials from requesting subordinates to use government time for activities that fall outside their job’s official duties.
But the report determined that Chavez-DeRemer developed an “inappropriately close and unprofessional” relationship with a senior agent on her protective detail.
Witnesses reported seeing Chavez-DeRemer massaging the agent’s shoulder, golfing and gambling with him, and leaving an event walking arm-in-arm.
The report, however, did not find “sufficient” evidence to conclude the relationship was sexual.
Still, investigators documented conduct where the relationship between Chavez-DeRemer and the agent created conflicts of interest or inappropriate work situations.
The report describes an April 2025 incident in which Chavez-DeRemer was taking a personal trip to Oregon and asked her security detail to make an off-the-record stop at a club featuring partially nude dancers.
The senior agent she was involved with was also on the trip. A limousine driver objected to her requests to drop money onto a performer, but the senior agent reportedly instructed him to comply.
The agent occasionally reduced the number of officers covering Chavez-DeRemer or assumed sole responsibility for her protection.
Investigators obtained electronic hotel door lock records suggesting the two spent time overnight in each other’s rooms and reviewed video footage that documented his visits to her home.
Unreported gifts and excess spending
The report also found travel policy violations involving excessive spending.
In November 2025, for instance, Chavez-DeRemer and two other officials reportedly stayed at hotels in Palm Beach, Florida, to attend an America First Policy Institute gala.
The cost for their lodging approached or exceeded three times the government reimbursement rate, despite there being no documentation showing the required approval for the increased costs.
Investigators further found that Chavez-DeRemer failed to report several gifts to the government, including rodeo tickets, an alligator-hide wallet and cowboy hats given to her and her husband.
Federal government officials are required to report gifts they receive as part of their official duties, to avoid conflicts of interest.
In its conclusion, the watchdog report recommends structural changes to the Labor Department, including removing the protective units from the secretary’s oversight.
Such agents, it suggested, could instead work under the inspector general’s office.
The report also called for independent travel audits, stronger whistleblower protections and annual training for senior leaders.
Since resigning her cabinet post, Chavez-DeRemer has announced she has taken up a senior adviser position at Think Big, a public affairs firm.
According to the company’s website, the former secretary heads a practice dedicated to labour and national infrastructure.

Ayhan Simsek

Far-right AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund said Friday he will become premier of Saxony-Anhalt only if his party wins an absolute majority and can govern alone.
Siegmund told ZDF’s Morgenmagazin that the AfD is not seeking a coalition in Sunday’s closely watched election in the eastern German state. He said he would take the top job only if he can carry out the program he put before voters.
“If someone wants to tackle the basic problems in the state such as migration, crazy energy policy, all the gender nonsense and so on — then I will gladly do that. But is there this partner? There isn’t in this state.”
He said other parties have shut the AfD out for a decade. “For 10 years people have wanted to ban us, for 10 years they have excluded us, for 10 years they vote our committee chairs out and deny us deputy speakers of the state parliament.”
“And we have accepted the realities and say: Fine, if no one wants to do it with us, then we just have to do it alone.”
Public broadcaster ZDF put the AfD at 41% in its latest poll, well ahead of its rivals. The current premier, Sven Schulze of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), was second at 23%.
In the same poll, the socialist Left Party stood at 11.5%, the Social Democratic Party (SPD) at 8.5% and the Greens at 6%. The newer left-populist BSW was at 4%, and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) at 3%.
The state parliament normally has 83 seats, meaning 42 are needed to govern alone. If the AfD falls short, Magdeburg could face weeks of negotiations over who becomes premier.
Saxony-Anhalt’s domestic intelligence service has classified the AfD’s state branch as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization, citing anti-democratic aims and members’ ties to far-right groups. Mainstream parties have ruled out coalition talks with the AfD.
Speaking on the same program, CDU lead candidate Schulze ruled out formal coalitions not only with the AfD but also with the Left Party.
“There will be no coalition with the Left Party, there will be no coalition with the AfD. I would ideally like to lead the state from the centre,” he said. “I know the poll numbers. So please let us wait for the election result.”
If the AfD falls short, the scenario most often discussed is a CDU-led minority government with the SPD and possibly the Greens, surviving vote by vote. Even then, such an arrangement would likely still need Left Party support to command a majority in the state parliament called Landtag.

====================================================================================================

Why the Falklands Is a Pressure Point For the U.K.—and How Milei, Trump Are Stoking Tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:13:05 UTC
05:13:05 KST

Argentina’s President Javier Milei has escalated his country’s claim over the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory, warning he will place economic pressure by sanctioning oil companies with operations in the area.
The Falkland Islands are "Argentine, by history and by right, there is no debate about it,” he said in a nationally televised address Thursday evening.
Milei argued the “winds of change blowing around the world” are favorable to Argentina’s long-claimed sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago, citing remarks made by his ally, U.S. President Donald Trump, who recently suggested the U.S. would be reviewing its neutrality on the dispute.
The Argentine President flagged a planned oil project in the area as a cause for concern. Within the next 18 months, two companies—one British and the other Israeli—are set to start extractions from the Sea Lion oilfield, which lies north of the islands and holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
Milei described the project as an urgent threat to Argentina’s sovereignty. "If we do not act swiftly, in a few months they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea—something that has never happened before,” he said.
The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as “Islas Malvinas,” sit roughly 300 miles from the Argentine coast, and have been a British territory for almost two centuries, but Argentina has never accepted British sovereignty over the area.
Vowing to take action, Milei said he plans to send a bill to Congress to strengthen Argentina’s response to what he views as attacks on its sovereignty.
Responding to the economic threats, the U.K. government reasserted its “unshakeable” commitment to the archipelago on Friday, with British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting insisting: “Milei’s statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands.”
“The U.K. supports the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources for their own economic benefit, and this is an integral part of their right to self-determination,” a spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham told TIME. “We continue to have a diplomatic relationship with Argentina, and from our perspective we want to continue to strengthen that.”
Here’s what to know about the contentious history of the Falkland Islands and why Milei and Trump’s remarks have sparked concern amid mounting geopolitical tensions.
Do the Falklands belong to Britain or Argentina?
The Falklands' defense and foreign policy is handled by the U.K., but otherwise it has an internal government of its own. The territory has its own constitution and as of 1983, residents of the islands have been British citizens.
In a 2013 referendum, Falkland residents voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining under British rule. The referendum saw 92% of all eligible voters turn out, with 99.8% of votes being “yes.”
“The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” Streeting said Friday, pointing to the will of the voters.
The first recorded landing on the island was made in 1690 by English naval captain John Strong. Britain took possession of West Falkland in 1765. France and Spain each had settlements on the islands at different times, but Britain re-established control in 1833 and has since administered the islands.
“Argentina claims the U.K. took the islands as an act of imperialism in the 1830s, but the remedy to colonial acquisition would be self-determination,” says Marc Weller, programme director of the international law programme at U.K.-based think tank Chatham House.
Given the British government’s insistence on Falklanders deciding their future, “it is therefore acting in accordance with the principle of self-determination,” he tells TIME.
Under the rule of military dictator Leopoldo Galtieri, Argentine forces attempted to stake a territorial claim in April 1982, sparking a 74-day war that Britain won.
Argentina has since continued to claim sovereignty over the islands and the rhetoric has become a unifying issue in the country, experts tell TIME.
The issue recently reared its head during Argentina’s victory over England in the semi-finals of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with some Argentine players holding up a banner reading "Las Malvinas son Argentinas,” which translates to "The Falklands are Argentine.”
“The Argentinian nation is easily united behind this claim through the Falkland Islands. It's a rallying point, and it's perhaps no accident that as the present Argentinean government is in a little bit of trouble, that they have rediscovered the issue,” says Weller, pointing towards Milei’s controversial fiscal policies and falling popularity among the public.
Milei steps up claim over British territory with sanctions threat
Milei has previously ruled out using force to claim the islands, instead pushing for a diplomatic resolution. Still, his newly-announced plans to impose sanctions against oil companies with operations in the area pose an economic threat.
The two petroleum firms heading the Sea Lion oil drilling project have already felt the impact of Milei’s proposed sanctions.
British company Rockhopper Exploration’s stock value fell by around 10% on Friday morning, with Israeli firm Navitas Petroleum stock value falling by at least 4.5%.
“It's an attempt to add some uncertainty, perhaps to inhibit investment,” suggests Weller, adding he’s doubtful any such threats will impact Downing Street’s position on the sovereignty dispute.
Trump says U.S. position on Falklands is under review
The dispute over sovereignty remains a tense geopolitical issue. China, for example, has been vocal in its support of Argentina’s claim, encouraging negotiations to take place on the matter.
The U.S., meanwhile, has historically recognized the U.K.’s “administration of the islands,” but has maintained a neutral position regarding sovereignty.
However, Trump has indicated that the U.S. may be open to reversing that position.
The Falklands sovereignty became a talking point in April as the U.S. and Europe drifted on account of Trump lambasting European leaders for refusing to get actively involved in the Iran war.
A leaked Pentagon email, which reportedly suggested various ways the Administration could punish NATO allies it believes let the U.S. down, suggested a review of the U.S. position on Britain’s claim to the Falkland Islands, according to Reuters.
Earlier this week, when asked if the U.S. position on the islands was under review, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: “I always review every position. That's just one of many."
In an interview with a British broadcast channel that aired on Thursday, Trump did not directly respond when asked if the U.S. would come to the U.K’s aid if Argentina claimed the Falklands.
Trump instead pivoted to discuss the Iran war, repeating his claims that the U.K. let him down. “Your country was not there to help me,” he insisted.
When approached by TIME, a spokesperson for Burnham said such comments “are a matter for the U.S. President.”
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Andrew Gawthorpe, a lecturer at Leiden University and an expert in the foreign policy of the U.S., tells TIME a Washington reversal on the issue “would be an enormous defeat for the U.K. diplomatically and a huge blow” to the special U.K.-U.S. relationship.
Weller agrees, adding that if any U.S. policy were to go against the territorial integrity of the U.K., then “Britain would have to respond quite strongly.”
Trump’s remarks on the Falklands this week could prove difficult for Burnham, who inherited a splintered Washington-London relationship upon replacing Keir Starmer as Prime Minister in July.
“On the one hand, Burnham needs to appear like a strong leader,” says Gawthorpe. “But on the other hand, I think he's very aware that he needs to not annoy Trump any more than is strictly necessary.”

SC awards pension to Mumbai engineer who forged ST certificate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:09:18 UTC
05:09:18 KST

SC allowed him to superannuate in peace with retirement benefits
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court has rewarded a wrongdoer - a man who got appointed as a junior civil engineer in Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM) by producing a forged ST certificate, and, subsequently, stalled the scrutiny of his eligibility for quota for more than a decade - by allowing him to superannuate in peace with retirement benefits.Shirish P Patil got a certificate in 1984 by identifying himself as belonging to the 'Tokre Koli' Scheduled Tribe community. Based on the certificate, he was appointed a junior civil engineer in MCGM in 1994. He misplaced the original ST certificate but managed to secure a fresh one from the sub-divisional magistrate, Bhusawal division, in Oct 2000.Following scrutiny initiated by MCGM, the Police Vigilance Cell traced Patil's family history and found that his ancestors had been recorded as 'Koli', 'Hindu Koli' and 'Hindu Suryawanshi Koli', none of which belonged to the ST category. In July 2009, MCGM issued a show cause notice to Patil.He successfully dodged and delayed proceedings before the scrutiny committee until Jan 2020, when the panel rejected his plea that his lawyer and elderly family members were not available, and invalidated the ST certificate. HC dismissed his appeal against cancellation of ST status.
SC, however, stayed Patil's dismissal from service through an interim order on Nov 18, 2021.
As a result, the engineer continued to serve until June 30, 2025, when he retired after being employed with MCGM for more than three decades based on a forged ST certificate.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi Thursday upheld the cancellation of Patil's ST certificate and Bombay HC order. However, it took a lenient view given his undertaking that he or any of his family members "shall (not) be entitled to claim any future benefit on the basis of the invalidated ST certificate".The ruling contrasts with SC's consistent rulings against benefits accruing to people who forge SC or ST certificates to gain admission or employment.

The cost of repairing the damaged infrastructure, locomotive, and crossing equipment was estimated at approximately 140,000 zlotys. PKP PLK plans to seek compensation for these costs from the person responsible for the accident through the courts.

Ivanov is believed to have been in command of the military intelligence unit involved in the clash and is now accused of attempted murder of a government official. An SBU operative, whose identity has not been officially disclosed, has also been detained and is now accused of exceeding official powers.
Several dozen masked men, some wearing camouflage, gathered outside the Pechersky Court to support Ivanov. The court held the hearing behind closed doors, determining whether the suspect should be taken into pre-trial custody. Ivanov was ultimately released on personal recognizance, the mildest possible pre-trial restriction in Ukraine. He was ordered not to contact witnesses, leave his place of residence, and surrender his passport.
Later in the day, the same court heard the case of the SBU operative involved in the skirmish. The court also convened behind closed doors and handed the operative the same restrictive measure of release on personal recognizance.
The shootout between the HUR and the SBU has sent shockwaves across the Ukrainian political landscape, further reinforcing rumors of a longstanding rivalry between the two security services. The Ukrainian authorities and the agencies themselves have provided highly contradictory accounts of events, at first attempting to portray the incident as a joint operation to thwart some alleged Russian intelligence plot.
The standoff apparently revolved around Stepan Kaplunov, a reported white supremacist and senior officer with the so-called Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), a paramilitary unit under the HUR patronage. While the SBU claimed Kaplunov participated in a Russian government plot to assassinate a “leader of the Russian opposition movement” on Ukraine’s Independence Day, the militants accused the service of kidnapping him and holding him at a black site for about ten days.
Kaplunov, who was released from SBU custody following the shootout, blamed the “historic competition” between the SBU and HUR, claiming his kidnapping was an attempt by the agency to get to his superiors.

Individuals with psychotic spectrum disorder are less successful in recognizing the emotions of others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:00:50 UTC
05:00:50 KST

A study conducted in Sweden found that individuals with psychotic spectrum disorder were less accurate in recognizing the emotions of others compared to healthy controls. Moreover, among participants with psychotic spectrum disorder, those with a history of interpersonal aggression tended to be less accurate than those without such a history. The paper was published in Schizophrenia.
Emotion recognition is a basic part of human social interaction, helping people understand what others are feeling from facial expressions, tone of voice, and body movements. When this ability is impaired, social situations become harder to interpret and misunderstandings become more likely.
Such difficulties are especially relevant in psychotic spectrum disorders. Psychotic spectrum disorders are a group of mental disorders characterized by symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking or behavior, and impaired reality testing. These include schizophrenia and related conditions. The emotion recognition impairments found in individuals suffering from these disorders are not limited to static facial expressions, but can also appear when people interpret changing facial expressions, body movements, or other dynamic social signals.
Difficulties in recognizing emotions in these individuals tend to be particularly pronounced for negative emotions, although positive emotions can also be misidentified. People with schizophrenia may, for example, confuse one negative emotion with another or sometimes interpret neutral or positive expressions as negative. These problems usually reflect broader disturbances in perception, memory, attention, language, and other cognitive processes that contribute to understanding social information.
Study author Gabriela Gavalova and her colleagues wanted to compare the emotion recognition abilities of healthy individuals and those suffering from psychotic spectrum disorders. They also wanted to compare individuals with psychotic spectrum disorders who have a history of interpersonal aggression with individuals without such a history. Additionally, they wanted to see whether their recognition abilities depend on the way emotions are presented. With this in mind, they conducted a study in which they used three modes of presenting emotions to be recognized: visual (videos presented without sound), auditory (sound only), and multimodal (videos presented with sound).
Study participants were 79 individuals suffering from psychotic spectrum disorders and a history of interpersonal aggression (recruited from Forensic Psychiatry Stockholm, Sweden), 72 participants with psychotic spectrum disorders but without a history of interpersonal aggression (recruited from psychiatric outpatient clinics in Stockholm), and 86 healthy individuals (recruited via the State Person Address Registry in Sweden). The study authors note that the healthy control group had a higher level of education than the two psychotic spectrum disorder groups.
All participants underwent a short semi-structured demographic interview and were asked about the presence of the studied psychiatric disorders in first- and second-degree relatives, prior interpersonal aggression, as well as prior alcohol and substance abuse. Healthy participants and those without a history of interpersonal aggression also completed assessments of alcohol and drug use disorder symptoms.
The study authors collected data about the type and number of aggressive acts for the group with a history of interpersonal aggression from crime reports, forensic psychiatric assessments, hospital case reports, and participants’ own self-reports. Participants completed an intelligence test to measure fluid intelligence, which is the ability to reason and solve novel problems, a psychomotor speed test to measure the physical speed of responses to cognitive processing, and an assessment of their semantic understanding, or knowledge of the meaning, of emotion words using a synonym test.
Finally, participants completed a series of emotion recognition tasks called the Emotion Recognition Assessment in Multiple modalities test. These tasks contained 72 unique emotional stimuli displaying 12 different emotions. The participants’ task was to select the emotion being presented in the stimulus.
Results showed that participants from all three groups were able to recognize emotions in the emotion recognition task better than chance, meaning their responses were not random guessing. All three groups tended to misclassify some emotions. For example, they all tended to misclassify pride as happiness or interest, happiness as relief or as fear and despair, irritation as anxiety, and anger as irritation. Some other misclassifications were common as well.
Participants with a history of interpersonal aggression tended to also uniquely misclassify happiness as anxiety. The psychotic spectrum disorder group without a history of interpersonal aggression tended to misclassify pride as irritation, while healthy participants tended to mistake interest for anxiety. Crucially, the researchers found an unexpected and clinically significant pattern: participants with a history of interpersonal aggression were much more likely to misclassify negative emotions as positive emotions compared to both the non-aggressive psychotic spectrum group and the healthy controls. The authors suggest this could lead these individuals to miss negative social cues and fail to withdraw from escalating situations.
Healthy participants were much more accurate in recognizing emotions compared to the two other groups. In particular, participants with psychotic spectrum disorder and a history of interpersonal aggression were much less accurate in recognizing emotions than participants with psychotic spectrum disorder but without a history of interpersonal aggression.
Other than this, participants were more successful in recognizing emotions when they were presented with both video and sound compared to situations when one of these was missing. Overall, among individuals with psychotic spectrum disorder, participants with higher fluid intelligence, those who knew more words for emotions, and those who had better education tended to be better at recognizing emotions. Within this group, women and those without a history of interpersonal aggression tended to be better at recognizing emotions. Interestingly, when controlling for other factors, those with a history of alcohol or substance use disorder in remission also tended to score higher. However, the researchers caution that this might be a statistical anomaly known as a suppression effect, rather than proof that past substance abuse improves emotion recognition.
“In summary, individuals with PSD [psychotic spectrum disorders] and a history of interpersonal aggression exhibit more pronounced deficits in emotion recognition than those with PSD alone. This underscores the potential value of incorporating emotion recognition assessment and training into clinical interventions to reduce aggression risk and improve social functioning in individuals with PSD,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the psychological specificities of individuals with psychotic spectrum disorders. However, it should be noted that all participants with these disorders were recruited from Stockholm, Sweden. Results in other cultural groups might differ.
The paper, “Emotion recognition misclassification patterns in individuals with psychotic spectrum disorders and history of interpersonal aggression,” was authored by Gabriela Gavalova, Petri Laukka, Lennart Högman, Malin V. Källman, Marianne Kristiansson, Märta Wallinius, Håkan Fischer, and Anette G. M. Johansson.

Appreciation: Gloria Steinem was a rock star of revolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:59:59 UTC
04:59:59 KST

Appreciation: Gloria Steinem was a rock star of revolution
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Ten years ago, I went with my older daughter and a group of her classmates to see Gloria Steinem speak. Though they were part of a feminist group recently formed at their all-girls Catholic high school, some were not quite sure who Gloria was, exactly. My daughter knew her mostly as my former “boss”; my first job out of college had been as an editorial assistant at Ms. magazine. That was back in the ‘80s — ancient history.
I was a tiny bit nervous about how the evening would go. Gloria herself was in her 80’s by then; how would she connect with a group of teenagers who had come of age post-post-everything in a social media world of makeup tutorials, fit checks, and so much rage bait?
By being precisely herself, as it turned out. Calm and witty, impassioned and informed, clear-eyed yet hopeful, Gloria enthralled them — and the entire audience — for almost two hours. By the time we left, the girls were ready to follow her anywhere.
“She’s a rock star,” my daughter breathed.
That she was. Gloria Steinem did not invent feminism, not even its second wave, but for many years she was its most recognizable frontwoman. Tall, slender, with (for many years) aviator glasses framed by her signature long, straight hair, she was the Jackie Kennedy of the women’s movement: a physical dismissal of all those childish critics who deride feminists as an army of unlovely and unloved women, devoid of humor and, most likely, surrounded by far too many cats.
Column: Ms. Magazine helped millions become feminists. Its workplace helped me become an adult
Attending the 50th anniversary of Ms. last week, I thought I would find anger and regret. Instead I found memories of an anti-toxic office culture.
Even so, how she looked was beside the point. No feminist I know ever wanted to look like Gloria; we all wanted to be like her. Smart, funny, incisive, generous and, perhaps above all, unflappable.
For an activist organizer, she had a low center of gravity. Her speech was measured, her tone was mellow — even when calling out the most outrageous hypocrisies, the most sinister forms of oppression, she rarely if ever raised it. Though by her own admission she was often furious about many things, her sharpest weapon was always a deadly talent for stating the obvious. “If women could sleep their way to the top, there‘d be a lot more women at the top.” “I have yet to hear a man ask for advice on how to combine marriage and a career. ” “A pedestal is as much a prison as any small, confined space.” “This is what 40 [or 50] looks like.”
She believed in shaping the future by being fearlessly frank about the present and the past. For more than seven decades, she helped millions strip away the veils of hierarchy, patriarchy and all the stories spun about gendered expectations to confront the actual experience of women’s lives. “If the shoe doesn’t fit, must we change the foot?”
She never incited anger; she simply pointed out the facts as she saw them and let human nature take its course. “The truth will set you free, but first it will piss you off.”
Gloria listened as much as she spoke, and with great attention and democracy. When I worked at Ms., she was always running late, invariably having been pulled into some conversation or other. Her assistant groaned over her calendar; Gloria would say “yes” when asked for help, even if it meant being two places at once.
She often came in for staff meetings to which everyone was invited and, when discussing ideas for future issues, would ask for, and attentively listen to, the opinions of even a lowly editorial assistant like me. Her interest was sincere, astonishing and made for very long meetings. Wherever she went, it was the same. She needed to know what all manner of women thought about a wide variety of topics. More important, she wanted them to learn the habit of speaking up. In a private meeting or a public forum, to colleagues, politicians, friends, the boss or even a feminist icon, she wanted women to be unafraid of saying what they thought.
The feminist icon, who died Wednesday at 92, never stopped advocating for equal rights.
When I worked at Ms., and for many years after, people would invariably ask me: “What’s Gloria Steinem like?” and it was, and remains, impossible to describe. She was kind when she didn’t need to be, generous with her attention when no one expected it. She didn’t want laws and social constructs to be fairer, less dangerous, more fulfilling for women as a concept; she wanted it for you, for me, for the lady in the back row.
She gave aura but also advice about where to find discount shoes. She instantly claimed any room she entered and then made sure there were snacks. She believed that the world could change, that with work, we could change it. But she also believed in having fun; otherwise why bother?
On the day Gloria Steinem died at 92, I awoke to a text from one of the friends I made all those years ago at Ms.; soon there were four of us on the thread. I had just arrived in New York to take my youngest daughter back to college, and we had planned to meet one of those friends in Union Square at noon. Instead, we met at Gloria’s brownstone and laid flowers along the fence outside her door. It seemed the least we could do.
My youngest never got to hear Gloria speak and, at 19, she is too young to know who Gloria was, exactly. Which was always the point of all that Gloria did. She didn’t want the future to feel beholden to the past; she just wanted it to be better. And despite the recent setbacks, particularly in reproductive rights, and all the work that still has to be done, it is.
There stood my daughter. Like her sister, she never doubts for one minute that she is a first-class citizen, entitled to equal rights, bodily autonomy, basic respect and a life of her choosing. God help the poor souls who try to tell them different.
“She’s a big part of why you are here,” I tell her. “Of why your life at 19 is so better than mine was, and why mine, at 19, was so much better than hers.”
That’s not just a rock star; that’s a revolutionary.

====================================================================================================

Trouble brewing in global bond markets: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:55:33 UTC
04:55:33 KST

Trouble brewing in global bond markets: What to know
A storm is gathering in bond markets across the globe as yields on government debt are in many cases near multi-decade highs.
High and rising government debt levels pose a problem for bond markets for which no solution seems imminent. The rising deficits, meanwhile, are colliding with diminished demand for government debt.
On top of this, renewed fighting in the Middle East earlier this week pushed oil prices higher and elicited concerns of what one Wall Street analyst called an “inflation monster.”
RT takes a look at the rumbling in global bond markets and what to look for in the coming days and weeks.
What happened and what caused it
After fighting between the US and Iran restarted earlier this week, oil jumped more than $4 a barrel on Tuesday, settling at a five-week high of $94.65 per barrel Brent. Prices retreated somewhat later in the week, but oil is still set for a roughly 9% gain on the week. US diesel futures, meanwhile, surged to a 52-month high earlier in the week.
Bonds sold off sharply across the board on both Tuesday and Wednesday before stabilizing on Thursday.
More broadly, the volatility comes as major economies have flooded the market with debt, demand for which has been tepid. In particular, the pool of price-insensitive institutional buyers is shrinking in what is a larger structural shift. All things being equal, investors want higher yields to absorb the quantity and also to protect themselves against rising inflationary risks.
Perhaps most concerning are what seem to be permanently expanding budget deficits in numerous countries, particularly given the apparent lack of political will to stem the profligacy. The US recently passed the $40 trillion debt mark with no sign of slowing down. Debt as a share of economic output is at or above 100% across the G7, except Germany, which seems determined to catch up.
Heavy borrowing by AI companies – which are in many cases unable to fund growth out of cash flow – is also contributing to the rising rates. According to a blog post by the European Central Bank, US tech giants are flooding European bond markets to fund AI investment, potentially reaching $1 trillion by 2028, thus crowding out other borrowers – including governments.
Meanwhile, higher energy prices are having a direct feed-through to inflation. Consumer prices in the Eurozone climbed 3.3% in August year-on-year, the fastest pace of inflation in nearly three years. The recent move higher in oil prices will only make this worse.
What it all adds up to is that yields on government bonds across major economies are in many cases trading at levels not seen in years or even decades.
• The UK’s 30-year bond yield hit its highest level since 1998.
• Japan’s 10-year yield has broken through the 3% mark for the first time in three decades.
• Yields in Germany and France are also trading at their highest levels in a decade.
• The yield on the US 10-year, the single most important interest rate in the world, is at a level last seen in 2023.
“It’s becoming harder and harder to disentangle” all the factors behind the moves in bond markets, said Ed Al-Hussainy, a portfolio manager at Columbia Threadneedle. “The only thing we can say right now is that they’re all pointing in the same direction, and that’s in the direction of higher rates, and they’re doing it globally.”
10y government bond yields of select major economies
War and the bond market
US yields are currently sitting at or near multi-decade highs across much of the curve and have edged higher since hostilities with Iran resumed. With the war now in its seventh month, many analysts are wondering whether the bond market might end up being the major constraint on US military ambitions.
It wouldn’t be the first time Treasures put a damper on moves by the administration of US President Donald Trump.
A few months into his new term, Trump introduced his Liberation Day tariffs, thus opening a trade war against the whole world from the White House lawn. It would take exactly three trading days for the 10-year yield to chalk up a gain of around 50 basis points, putting it on pace for its biggest weekly rise in a quarter century. The administration beat a humiliating retreat by canceling or postponing most of the tariffs.
Many analysts believe the specter of inflation, and downstream from that, Treasury market turbulence, has already limited the scope of what Washington can do in the Middle East. With yields rising aggressively now, the administration may well end up being even more constrained.
Meanwhile, the worsening inflation climate is not lost on the Fed. New Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh delivered a hawkish message at last week’s Jackson Hole Symposium – an implicit acknowledgement of the war-related risks. The market is now pricing in a 70% chance of a rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting in September.
A hike would push Treasury yields higher, but mostly at the short end. This is essentially what the market gave Warsh after Jackson Hole: the 2-year jumped while the long end was much calmer, producing what is called a bear flattening, when short-term yields rise faster than long-term yields. This can be interpreted as a vote of confidence that the Fed is going to deal with inflation.
But if the war in Iran is raging and inflation is surging, a Fed hike might not convince the market. If the Fed hikes and long-term rates rise anyway, it would be a very ominous signal that the central bank might be losing control of the bond market.
France – the new sick man of Europe
France has emerged as the Eurozone’s biggest sovereign debt risk, which means that a problem once confined to the southern periphery of the union has moved to one of the two political pillars of the entire European project.
France’s finances are a mess. The country’s public budget deficit stood at 5.1% of GDP in 2025, while its debt-to-GDP ratios hit 115%. Both figures are well above EU limits and both are highly unusual for a country that is neither at war nor in a deep recession.
France has accumulated more than €3.5 trillion in public debt, which is becoming more expensive to finance as the yields on its bonds have risen dramatically over the past year. As a result, the French 10-year is trading above its Greek and Italian counterparts, a state of affairs that few previously would have imagined.
Meanwhile, Paris has committed to billions in increased defense spending in the coming years. A major update to the country’s defense budget authorizing an additional €36 billion for 2026–2030 was signed off on by lawmakers in June.
Where Europe and the US meet
France, with its political deadlock and fiscal profligacy, may have emerged as the most acute source of potential stress in the EU, but the trend of higher yields is visible across the bloc. German Bunds, the benchmark for the bloc, have also moved sharply higher, hitting 15-year highs.
The surge in European yields is potentially bad news for the US. Japan recently off-loaded some US Treasuries to defend its beleaguered currency. The move elicited a rare joint US-Japanese intervention, ostensibly aimed at stabilizing the currency but almost certainly with the deeper goal of preventing a weak yen from forcing Japan to unload Treasuries to defend it.
Given that Europe is a large holder of Treasuries, there are two ways this can become a problem for Washington. First, higher yields across the bloc make European bonds relatively more attractive, thus potentially steering yield-hungry investors toward Europe. Second, if European financial conditions deteriorate badly enough, banks and other institutions may need to raise cash. Selling Treasuries would be a natural source of funding. Either way, US yields would rise.
What to watch for in the coming days and weeks
Any prolonged resumption in hostilities in the Middle East could easily push oil prices back over $100. With bond markets already strained, selling could pick up further. Any disorderly selling would be a signal in itself. But short of that, inflation is the key transmission mechanism to watch. A new wave of price growth would push investors to demand more compensation for holding long-dated liabilities and would likely force the hand of central banks, who may still be reluctant to tighten.
Meanwhile, with politicians reluctant to impose fiscal discipline, the bond market might have to do it for them. If yields continue to rise, governments will eventually have to choose between higher taxes, lower spending, and still greater borrowing costs. Policy-wise, what invariably prevails are options to kick the can further down the road, but any substantial change in rhetoric toward fiscal responsibility would suggest that the bond market’s message is beginning to be heard.

Food has returned to Gaza’s markets, but most people still cannot afford to eat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:54:55 UTC
04:54:55 KST

In a tent in Tal al-Hawa, west of Gaza City, 39-year-old Iman Abdel Karim, a mother of six, hands pieces of bread to her hungry children, some of whom are too young to have grown their teeth. Around her are a few empty cooking pots. At the entrance to the tent, the stove has not been lit either yesterday or today.
Abdel Karim and her family live on a single meal a day, usually eaten around noon. When available, it comes from a communal kitchen. When there is no food from the kitchens, they eat bread alone. Sometimes they manage to get a meal from a neighboring tent, or they cook lentils – long among the cheapest foods in Gaza, though even lentil prices have risen beyond what some families can afford.
“My children see some vegetables and fruit with the neighbors, and they start asking me for some,” Abdel Karim says. “But even though some fruit, vegetables, and other foods are available in the markets, we cannot buy anything. We have been living in tents for more than two years. We have spent all our money trying to stay alive, and we have nothing left.”
Food is visible in Gaza’s markets for the first time in years, but hunger is not gone. According to the August 2026 IPC report, more than 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza’s population, are projected to face Crisis conditions or worse through December 2026. The presence of goods on shelves has not translated into food security for the majority of Gaza’s population, whose purchasing power has been destroyed by more than two years of war, displacement, and economic collapse.
Prices have fallen noticeably compared with last year, when famine was ravaging the population. At the peak of the crisis in mid-2025, a kilogram of flour could cost around 250 to 300 shekels ($70 to $90) in some parts of the Strip. According to a WFP report, wheat flour was being sold at a price 4,900 percent higher than pre-October 2023 tags. Today, a 25-kilogram bag of flour costs around 30 shekels ($10).
Tomato prices have fallen by approximately 81 percent since the ceasefire, potatoes by around 70 percent, and rice by approximately 73 percent, according to a UNICEF humanitarian situation report covering the period from October 2025 to June 2026. Accumulating humanitarian supplies – including commodities such as legumes and flour, which can spoil when stored for long periods in Gaza’s summer heat- drives merchants to sell them fast.
But falling prices have not reached all goods equally. Milk, protein, and fish, which people need, remain difficult to obtain. Cooking gas is regulated by Gaza’s Ministry of Economy, with families allocated an estimated eight kilograms of cooking gas every six months — a quantity far below weekly household needs. And electricity remains unavailable across much of the Strip, making food storage nearly impossible for families and merchants alike.
Abdel Karim remembers the famine with particular pain.
“During the famine last year, I could hear my children crying from hunger day and night, moaning, and there was nothing I could do for them. I could not go to the aid trucks that they described as the road to death. My husband could not either. He has had an injury to his foot since the beginning of the war.
“So instead, I sold my jewelry so I could bring bread to my children. And I was not alone. Many women did the same.”
‘A political game’
Rami Oweis, 56, a father of eight and a retired employee, sees the gap between what is visible and what is accessible as deliberate — part of what he calls “a political game” in which Israel has become highly adept at creating the appearance of normality.
“You see the markets filled with fruit and vegetables in every color and shape,” Oweis says. “But who can afford to buy them every day? Who can bring enough food for himself and his family back to a tent that becomes like an oven in the summer?”
Storage is its own problem. “There are no refrigerators in the tents. Even if there were, there is no electricity to run them.” Cooking what can be brought, he explains, requires firewood, which takes hours to gather and fills the tents with smoke.
“All of this is part of the policy,” Oweis told Mondoweiss. “You see the pictures, but only those who live among the people of Gaza and under the conditions of Gaza know the hell they are living through.”
In Gaza, Oweis says, the markets reflect these contradictions.
A kilogram of meat, which during the Israeli-engineered famine could cost 400 or 500 shekels when it could be found at all, now sells for around 40 shekels.
Potatoes cost around six shekels per kilogram, tomatoes eight, onions six, and cucumbers 12. By pre-war standards, these would be manageable prices. But purchasing power has collapsed.
More than one-third of Gaza’s bread needs are covered by WFP-supported bakeries, where bundles of eight to nine pitas are sold at a capped price of around $1. But the WFP has been forced to reduce flour supplies to bakeries due to Israel’s import restrictions, pushing many families who relied on these bakeries to look elsewhere.
“We no longer have money,” Oweis says. “We are no longer able to buy things the way we did before the war. This war drained everything we had saved for the future, and then destroyed the future itself.”
Permanent state of emergency
Merchants are caught in the same bind. They struggle to store what they buy, watching perishable goods deteriorate in the heat without electricity to refrigerate them, and find themselves forced to sell at reduced prices, sometimes at a loss, to move stock before it spoils..
Abdel Aziz, a small-scale merchant in Gaza who declined to give his full name, says that whenever vegetables and fruit become available, merchants rush to buy them – knowing these are foods Palestinians have deeply longed for. But demand remains limited, even at ordinary prices.
“People are afraid to buy,” Abdel Aziz says. “They always try to keep some cash in their hands in case of an emergency. And Gaza has become a permanent state of emergency.
When people do buy, they buy as little as possible. “Instead of buying two kilograms of potatoes, for example, a father might buy only two potatoes for the family to eat that day.” Families no longer cook full meals every day. They eat at aid kitchens or have sandwiches with cheese or jam instead of preparing a full meal, he adds.
On how the war has impacted Gazans’ eating behaviors, Abdel Aziz describes this as “politics”. “Deliberate politics, so that people remain in a state of need. Even if goods are available, people will not be able to buy them.”
 “The Israeli occupation tells the world that it is bringing food into Gaza,” Abdel Aziz says. “The world can see it. But the world does not know how those who survived in Gaza managed to survive, what exhausted them, or what they sacrificed to reach this point, where they can no longer afford to buy vegetables and fruit for their families.”

The UN General Assembly approved a resolution on a new world map: what makes it special
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:53:18 EEST

The UN General Assembly approved a resolution on a new world map: what makes it special
Kyiv • UNN
164 countries supported the use of Equal Earth maps, which more accurately represent the sizes of the continents. The United States voted against the resolution.
The UN General Assembly approved a reform of the use of world maps with more realistic proportions. The relevant resolution was supported by 164 countries on Friday; the United States voted against it, and six countries abstained, UNN reports, citing DW.
Details
The resolution was introduced by Togo and the African Union, calling on international organizations and states to use Equal Earth maps in the future. This type of world map reflects the actual sizes of the continents more accurately: Africa appears larger on it, while the United States is reduced in size.
This map is intended to replace the so-called Mercator map, which is associated with the cartographer Gerardus Mercator, who was born in Flanders in 1512. The Mercator map was developed for maritime navigation and artificially enlarged areas at high latitudes.
"Maps shape our understanding of the world," Togo's Foreign Minister Robert Dussey said at the UN General Assembly. "But they are never neutral." There is a risk that they "present a distorted picture of our planet and reinforce misconceptions passed down from generation to generation."
We would add
The Equal Earth map was created in 2018 by a group of geographers to ensure that the depiction of the continents corresponds as closely as possible to their actual sizes. As a result, Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania are shown as significantly larger than on conventional world maps.

- Political stability has improved Italy's financial reputation, lowering borrowing costs despite ongoing economic challenges.

AI generated
ROME – A record period of government stability has strengthened Italy, which is no longer viewed within the European Union as “a case to monitor”, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Sept 4 as her administration became the longest-serving of the postwar era.
In a country notorious for political volatility, Meloni’s right-wing coalition has surpassed Silvio Berlusconi’s 2005 record, passing more than 1,400 days in office since taking power in October 2022.
Speaking at an event in the southern city of Bari to mark the milestone, Meloni listed what she described as her government’s key achievements. Delivering lasting political stability in a country that had had 68 governments in 80 years was itself a major accomplishment, she said.
“Stability is the first major reform we have delivered to this nation. Thanks to that stability, Italy has stopped being a country under watch in Europe,” she told supporters.
Financial discipline
During a tumultuous global period of conflict and economic shockwaves, Italy has appeared steadier than some nearby countries, including France, which has had five prime ministers since autumn 2022, and Britain, which has had four.
Meloni said political stability had reassured financial markets about Italy’s handling of its public finances and high debt pile, helping soften borrowing costs on government bonds.
“Having the public accounts in order means fewer constraints. Those who keep their finances in order get to decide where to spend their money,” she said.
Analysts broadly agree that Meloni’s strongest achievement has been restoring confidence in Italy’s finances, but critics say little has been done to overhaul the inefficient public administration, healthcare and education systems.
The government’s main institutional reforms, including plans to strengthen the prime minister’s powers, have stalled, while voters this year rejected a government-backed referendum on judicial reform.
The centre-left opposition on Sept 4 accused the government of failing to address Italy’s longstanding problems.
“Four years of inactivity and inertia are not a badge of honour but an aggravating factor,” said Giuseppe Conte, a former prime minister and leader of the 5-Star Movement, pointing to the country’s persistently sluggish economic growth.
A demonstration was staged in Bari against the rally organised by Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party.
With elections due in 2027, Meloni is expected to lead her coalition into the campaign.
In opinion polls, the centre-left bloc holds a narrow lead over Meloni’s alliance, whose support has been eroded by Futuro Nazionale, a far-right movement that has tapped into concerns over immigration, security and cultural change. REUTERS
