Why political optimism has become scarce in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
'Afraid of change': political optimism now a rare commodity in Australia
What a despairing mob we've become.
This week's national accounts confirmed how stuck we are in a foul and pestilent congregation of vapours … to steal from English literature's greatest melancholy wobbler.
It's doubtful Hamlet ever dwelt on the state of Denmark's real net national disposable income (RNNDI) per capita.
But if he had he might have embraced what a downer it is.
RNNDI is one of those measures that helps explain why voters look desperate to try new and "dangerous" things, as the prime minister put it this week. He was referring to One Nation and its quickening political momentum around the country, where Pauline Hanson is eagerly harvesting the dark mood.
Prosperity heading in wrong direction
The Australian Bureau of Statistics says RNNDI estimates the income a person derives from the economy that they can spend and save after the pernicious impact of inflation is taken into account.
It renders what's left in people's pockets after cost-of-living increases.
"This is a broader measure of prosperity than the commonly cited measure of real GDP," the bureau explains on its website.
"It more accurately reflects the average lived experience and prosperity of Australians."
In the June quarter, it shrank by 0.4 per cent from the previous three months. And from the same period a year earlier it was unchanged.
Over the last two years it has been either falling outright or pretty much flat.
By contrast for most of the last half century this measure has enjoyed steady gains with brief exceptions such as the early 1990s recession and the post GFC "secular stagnation" of the early and mid-2010s.
In the real world, this reflects how pretty much every generation since federation has secured a better quality of life, greater opportunity and choice than their parents.
But now, living standards and prosperity are headed in the wrong direction.
Which is where a majority of Australians think the country is going.
Albanese government's performance judged harshly
Perceptions of the national economy, as well as state and territory economies, are at their lowest level, according to a nationwide poll in August by JWS Research that began testing views on this question in 2013 during the dying days of the Rudd-Gillard-Rudd turmoil.
And to the degree that governments are responsible for the gloomy sense of national direction, the JWS survey shows they're getting a good slab of blame.
Views of state and territory governments are at their lowest ebb since early 2017.
For the federal government it's particularly acute.
Judgements on the Albanese government's performance have never been this harsh.
It's worse, according to JWS, than at any time during Scott Morrison's oft-derided prime ministership.
And is now on par with levels of disillusionment that accompanied Malcolm Turnbull's time in office not long before his colleagues rolled him out the door.
War, bond markets and AI
These may turn out to be temporary miasmas of the public's mood.
But there was a creeping sense this week that the federal government hasn't yet figured out how to flip the script. And that time is starting to run out.
To be sure, some of what ails people and the economy that dictates their fortunes is externally driven.
There's a lengthening war in the Middle East.
Loading...
Bond market klaxon horns are blaring about the dangers of ballooning government debt and persistent global inflation. And AI is giving many the jitters.
Yet Labor is already well into its fifth year in office.
By the standards of Australian governments this is early middle age.
Well before the autumn of life, so to speak, but also when things start to get tired.
The old sparkle doesn't come so easy. There's no blaming youthful indiscretions when things go wrong. The last lot is long gone.
The buck is firmly in hand. And consequences from mistakes or omissions of the past begin to accrue.
While much of what ails people can be linked to a crazy world, voters often respond to two big drivers: a sense the government has a positive plan and knows where it wants to go.
And a belief that it's fighting for people rather than its own preservation.
The government claims it is embarking on the most thorough economic reform program in a generation with its changes to capital gains taxation of assets and overhaul of trusts.
Promoted as "fairness measures" they're mainly about collecting more tax.
For many critics in the business community — and voters more generally — they're a drag rather than an inspiration.
For economists they fall short of producing what used to be called a "growth agenda".
And Labor's opponents accuse it of running a redistributionist program rather than an expansionist platform.
At the same time, the progressive left is frustrated that the government isn't targeting the honey pots of billionaires and "greedy" foreign corporations.
Loading
A reminder that leadership matters
Paul Keating this week told an audience in Sydney that governments are "afraid of change".
And not-withstanding the adjustments to negative gearing and capital gains on housing that have been legislated to boost affordability, he warned the country needs to "manage capital accretion … more ambitiously than we have in recent times".
"We've gone 26 years without any structural change. And of course it shows [in] the lag in productivity and the lagging growth numbers."
A new history of Keating's prime ministership by historian James Curran published this week makes the case for boldness and bravery.
Keating's legacy — as recognised by both sides of fair-minded elements of the political divide — is that he delivered that in spades when it came to economic reform.
But Curran's book, Grand Ambition, is a reminder that he can flourish in other realms.
Keating became prime minister within days of the end of the Cold War and the collapse of the Soviet Union in late 1991, a geopolitical rupture that compares surely to anything happening today.
Grand Ambition details how the new prime minister didn't retreat into passivity in the face of that new global reality — the moment, in Keating's words, when the "electromagnets of the Cold War were switched off".
Others might have been content to merely describe the new world for Australian voters.
Keating, according to Curran, saw the juncture as an opening.
He pressed George HW Bush — just arrived in Sydney — to engage in the region, setting the stage for Keating to win support for turning APEC into a leaders' forum.
One that endures to this day.
Keating noted this week that the November APEC leaders meeting will allow Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to meet and "discuss their real matters".
"That's been going on now for 34 years. This was a gift to the West by Australian foreign policy and it made a very big difference," Keating said on Wednesday.
"And because we invented the show, we were in charge."
Whether you bought into Keating's story — one that fused foreign policy and domestic reform into one big "ball of wax" (as Keating's advisor Allan Gyngell told Curran) — or not, that's not the point.
It was a time when Australia aspired to be more than history's passenger. Or a fixed South Pacific aircraft carrier for a powerful friend.
A reminder that leadership matters.
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

Germany calls on the EU to restrict the issuance of tourist visas to Russians following acts of sabotage
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
21:59:28 EEST
03:59:28 KST

Germany calls on the EU to restrict the issuance of tourist visas to Russians following acts of sabotage
Kyiv • UNN
Berlin links the suspected attack on Leipzig Airport to Russian special services. Germany demands tougher visa restrictions for Russians.
Germany is calling on its European partners to tighten restrictions on the entry of Russian citizens into the EU for tourist visas following recent acts of sabotage, for which Berlin holds Moscow responsible, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
German authorities are investigating a Belarusian citizen who also holds a Russian passport in connection with an alleged attempt to attack Leipzig Airport using drones and explosives.
According to available information, the person entered the Schengen Area on a tourist visa issued by the Italian Embassy in Minsk (Belarus). Sources in the security services note that, apparently, he did not visit Italy.
Germany's Foreign Ministry has expressed dissatisfaction that too many visas are being issued to Russians.
"The number of visas issued to Russian citizens for holidays in the European Union is excessively high," a ministry representative said.
Sources close to the government claim that the significant number of visas issued to Russians contradicts the spirit of the sanctions imposed in connection with the war in Ukraine and makes it impossible to determine who is entering the EU and for what purpose.
Statistical data show that in 2025 Italy issued more Schengen visas than any other country in the bloc; according to Euractiv, Italy, France and Spain accounted for three-quarters of all visa applications from Russians.
Last year, Italy issued more visas to Belarusian citizens than any other EU country, with the number rising sharply after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to European Commission statistics analyzed by the Italian news outlet Linkiesta, in 2021 Italy issued Belarusian citizens only 2,968 visas, whereas last year the figure was 50,709.
A similar trend can be observed with regard to Russia. The number of Italian visas issued to Russian citizens rose from 63,894 in 2021 to more than 165,000 in 2025 — nearly a threefold increase despite the war.
This week, the German government announced measures in response to the Kremlin's actions, stating that Russian intelligence services were likely behind the alleged plot to attack Leipzig Airport. These measures include closing the Russian consulate in Bonn, summoning the Russian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry, and tightening controls on Russia's "shadow fleet" — illegal vessels transporting oil to the Baltic Sea. The EU also announced its 22nd package of sanctions and said it was expanding the list of Russians banned from entering the union's territory.
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani ordered an investigation into the visa issued to the Belarusian citizen suspected in the Leipzig sabotage case.
"There is a specific procedure for issuing visas, since established requirements must be observed," Tajani said. "If applicants meet these requirements and there are no particular concerns regarding them, the visa is issued. If that was indeed the situation, we will try to determine why this visa was issued."
Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and the Czech Republic have virtually stopped issuing visas to Russian citizens, introducing national restrictions that go beyond the pan-European measures. However, a number of other EU member states continue to issue visas in large numbers, and in some cases have even increased their numbers.

UN adopts new map: Africa bigger, North America and Europe smaller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:58:44 UTC
03:58:44 KST

UN adopts new map: Africa bigger, North America and Europe smaller
The US was the only vote against the resolution for a shift to the Equal Earth cartographic projection over the traditional Mercator map
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe.
Aimed at “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the US voted against it and six other states abstained.
The new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world”, the resolution said.
It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.
Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which drove the resolution, said maps “guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions”.
“They are therefore never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation.”

Iran has rebuilt a large portion of its oil and gas refining infrastructure damaged during US-Israeli attacks, with the country’s oil minister saying crude exports continued despite intense bombardment.
Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad told the Oil Ministry’s Shana news platform on Friday that reconstruction began within days of the attacks and that much of the work has now been completed.
He said the progress is expected to become increasingly visible over the coming months, while Iran also plans to boost its gas production capacity.
Oil exports continued under heavy bombardment
Paknejad said Iran’s main oil export hub on Kharg Island came under particularly intense attack during the conflict.
The island, which covers roughly 23 to 24 square kilometres, was struck more than 550 times, according to the minister.
Despite the attacks, workers continued loading crude oil onto tankers, he said.
“This island ... was subjected to more than 550 attacks, but our colleagues continued loading oil onto tankers even under bombardment,” Paknejad said.
Paknejad said reconstruction at damaged refineries began by clearing debris, with the process starting roughly two to three days after the attacks.
“A large portion of the reconstruction work has been completed,” he said.
The minister did not provide a detailed estimate of the facilities’ remaining damage or specify the full production capacity restored so far.
Tehran targets higher gas production
Paknejad said Iran’s focus in the coming months would include further rebuilding and increasing gas production, with the impact of the repairs expected to become clearer over time.
The comments come amid continuing tensions surrounding Iran’s energy infrastructure and regional trade routes following the conflict.
US-Israeli attacks on Iran began February 28, prompting Iranian missile and drone strikes against Israel and US interests across the region.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy shipments, but implementation has stalled over disagreements about security arrangements in the waterway.

The Trump administration is drawing up a post-war strategy for the Middle East aimed at curbing Iran’s regional influence while strengthening cooperation among U.S. partners and pursuing broader normalization between Israel and neighboring countries, Axios reported Friday.
The strategy remains in the early drafting stage and is intended to shape U.S. policy after the Iran war and during the final two years of Trump’s term, the report said, adding that planning is underway at both senior political and interagency levels.

The report said Israel’s Oct. 27 elections and the November U.S. midterms are important considerations. The administration hopes Israel’s next government will support the strategy, but officials reportedly said Trump intends to pursue it regardless of the election outcome, including in the event of political deadlock.
A source briefed on the process said drafting could take several more weeks. "They are cooking it but it is not yet cooked,” the source said.
"The idea is to tie a whole lot of things in the region together - how you create a regional alignment after the war. It is still unclear if all U.S. allies in the region will be on board,” the person added.

The proceedings followed a post-match confrontation after Fenerbahce defeated Lyon 2-1 in France to advance to the Champions League league phase with a 3-2 aggregate victory.

Five EU nations inch towards deal on migrant ‘return hubs’ by 2027
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands did not outline where the centres would be located.
Five European nations have agreed on concrete steps towards a deal with an unspecified non-European Union country to host migrant return facilities, senior officials said, in a sign of mounting determination to counter immigration.
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands, known as the Group of Five, aim to sign deals this year to send migrants without legal residency to countries outside the European Union. The nations expected to host return centres have not been named.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Spain’s PM says no evidence Morocco planned Ceuta border rush
- list 2 of 35 dead, dozens missing after migrant boat found after weeks at sea
- list 3 of 3Burnham, Macron talk border security and stronger Europe-UK ties
“Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union,” Danish Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov told reporters on Friday at a news conference in Copenhagen, without elaborating.

Danish Refugee Council Secretary-General Charlotte Slente said a better policy would be to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which focuses on stricter border screening, faster return procedures and expanded digital systems for managing asylum claims.

Brazilian Supreme Court roiled by dispute between justices

Brazilian Supreme Court roiled by dispute between justices
The country’s highest court is considering investigations into two judges who have accused each other of wrongdoing.
Brazil’s Supreme Court has found itself at the centre of a corruption scandal roiling the country, with the body considering investigations into two justices who have accused each other of wrongdoing.
The dispute centres on Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the case that convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro, and Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Lula holds slim lead over Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of Brazil election
- list 2 of 3Brazil: Lula, Bolsonaro return to strongholds to launch runs for president
- list 3 of 3Brazil sues chat platform Discord over failure to protect child users
Mendonca released a report this week showing alleged links between de Moraes and disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro, accused of a wide-reaching fraud scheme.
De Moraes subsequently accused Mendonca of abusing his authority by unsealing the documents.
Chief Justice Edson Fachin said on Friday that he would give Brazil’s attorney general five days to weigh the allegations against Mendonca.
The court is also set to decide next week whether to investigate de Moraes.
“This may be the most dramatic moment in the history of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court,” said Felipe Recondo, a journalist and researcher who is a longtime observer of the court.
The right has pounced on the allegations against de Moraes to cast doubt on the case against Bolsonaro, who is currently under house arrest after receiving a 27-year prison sentence for his involvement in a coup plot.
Following his loss to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in 2022, prosecutors say Bolsonaro and his far-right allies sought to subvert the election results and derail the transition of power.
Post-election tensions culminated in an attack on key government buildings in the capital Brasilia on January 8, 2023, led by Bolsonaro supporters who allegedly hoped to trigger a military uprising.
In November 2024, Brazil’s federal police recommended charges be brought against Bolsonaro and a group of his key allies.
Bolsonaro, however, has portrayed the case as a “witch hunt” orchestrated by the left. He has received support from high-profile figures, including United States President Donald Trump.
De Moraes oversaw the Bolsonaro case, putting him at the centre of a political firestorm.
Trump’s Treasury Department briefly sanctioned De Moraes for his involvement in the Bolsonaro trial, as well as his suspensions of online platforms like Rumble and X, the latter run by Trump ally Elon Musk.
De Moraes was appointed to the Supreme Court under the presidency of Michel Temer, a centre-right politician, and he has since become a target for Brazil’s far-right, due to his involvement in sensitive cases, including Bolsonaro’s.
Experts like Recondo say the Supreme Court has served as a intermediary in some of Brazil’s most heated political fights.
“The Supreme Court can provide some balance in that game,” said Recondo. “Remove the court from that position, and all that remains is conflict. And that is a problem.”
The Vorcaro fraud scandal, however, threatens to tarnish the court’s reputation. This week’s unsealed documents suggest that the banker Vorcaro may have reached out to de Moraes for advice.
Politicians have called for de Moraes to clarify his relationship with the disgraced banker, with some calling for his resignation.
Candidates on both the right and left have both sought to portray each other as corrupt in the run-up to the country’s contentious presidential election on October 4.
That race will see the left-wing Lula face off against Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
The right-wing candidate has sought to capitalise on the scandal, painting it as a conspiracy between de Moraes and the political left to dismantle his father’s legacy.
“Out with Lula! Out with Moraes! This duo has no place left in leading the Country,” Senator Bolsonaro said in a recent social media post. “It’s time for change! Brazil will win!”
The younger Bolsonaro, however, has also been tarnished by his connections to Vorcaro.
Earlier this year, the US investigative news website The Intercept Brasil published messages reportedly between Flavio Bolsonaro and Vorcaro, whom the senator was petitioning for funding.
The funding was slated to go to a film about his father, Jair Bolsonaro. Vorcaro reportedly pledged millions of dollars to back the film project. Senator Bolsonaro has denied any wrongdoing, calling it a private project.

Three possible priorities have reportedly emerged: building a regional alliance of US partners to contain Iran, with Washington serving as guarantor; addressing issues stemming from the Oct. 7 attacks, including the next phase of Trump’s ceasefire plan for Gaza, a security agreement between Israel and Syria, and implementation of the Israel-Lebanon agreement; and expanding the Abraham Accords through a potential Saudi-Israeli normalization deal.
The report said Israel’s Oct. 27 elections and the November US midterms are important considerations. The administration hopes Israel’s next government will support the strategy, but officials reportedly said Trump intends to pursue it regardless of the election outcome, including in the event of political deadlock.
A source briefed on the process said drafting could take several more weeks. “They are cooking it but it is not yet cooked,” the source said.
“The idea is to tie a whole lot of things in the region together — how you create a regional alignment after the war. It is still unclear if all U.S. allies in the region will be on board,” the person added.

Casio ‘CasioNaut’ G-Shock GMC-2500 GAC-2500 Series: Price, Specs, Availability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:41:47 UTC
03:41:47 KST

The high-end watch world has an understandable affection for Casio. You can easily rock an iconic, brightly colored F-91W in any meeting with a luxury brand, and you'll get nods of approval. It is, after all, the watch that has graced the wrists of Barack Obama and Napoleon Dynamite.
If not the F-91W, you'd be on similar safe ground sporting the famous “CasiOak” that many G-Shock fans love because of its more than passing resemblance to Audemars Piguet's Royal Oak, which was recently given a similarly affordable makeover by Swatch with the Royal Pop. First introduced in 2019, the wallet-friendly G-Shock GA-2100 earned the nickname largely because of its octagonal case shape, and it is considered by some the definition of attainable luxury.
Now, however, it appears Casio has something genuinely new for the G-Shock line. Leaked on Notebookcheck and Instagram, the upcoming GMC-2500 and GAC-2500 series echo the CasiOak's links to high-end brand AP with more than a passing resemblance to Patek Philippe's Nautilus thanks to prominent shoulders on either side of the case.
Casio did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.
In 1972, legendary watchmaker Gérald Genta suggested an angular stainless steel watch design to Audemars Piguet with a high-end movement inside that would, perversely, be more expensive than gold dress watches. The Royal Oak, and the idea of the luxury sports watch, was born. In 1976, Genta repeated the trick for AP's main competitor, Patek Philippe, to create the now equally famous Nautilus.
According to Notebookcheck, the GAC-2500 series is a resin analog lineup supposedly built from the DNA of the DW-5000C, the very first G-Shock made back in 1983. Stainless-steel versions will be labeled the GMC-2500 series. So far, nicknames like the “CasioNaut” and “CasioTilus” are already being thrown around on Instagram. The leaked four resin colorways in November are expected to be white, black, green, and yellow, and the price is estimated at 20,900 Japanese yen (about $134) each. The metal versions will supposedly retail for about $320.
Another striking aspect of the CasioNauts, one that helps the comparisons with Patek even further, is that the watches are fully analog, a rarity in a G-Shock. The brand has always had a digital display somewhere on its main ranges, just like the CasiOak does.
A two-eye dial layout means a small seconds subdial on the left and a date window on the right. A Shock Resist mark is on the tail of the seconds hand. These pieces apparently have Casio's Magnetic Holding Structure, so the hands aren't fixed to a shaft but are instead held magnetically in place. When the rugged watch takes a severe smack, the hands can absorb the impact and won't break.
The metal GMC-2500 dimensions are supposedly 46.7 x 43.8 x 12.9 mm (H x W x D), with the GAC-2500 a shade thinner at 46.7 x 44.5 x 12.7. It looks like the metal versions will offer a choice of colors, along with the bracelet or strap options. The rumored release date for all of the CasioNauts is November, so set your watch.
According to legend, the inspiration for the Nautilus shape was the portholes on transatlantic ocean liners, and the idea struck Genta while he was having dinner at a hotel. Genta supposedly saw Patek executives sitting in a corner on the opposite side of the restaurant. It took him just five minutes to sketch the watch that would later become an icon.

Housing affordability hits all-time low despite falling property prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:41:41 UTC
03:41:41 KST

Housing affordability hits lowest rate on record despite recent falls in property prices
In short:
Housing affordability rates are at a record low, with households earning $125,000 able to afford around one in every 10 homes sold.
Mortgage repayments as a share of household income are also at their highest rate since 1989.
What's next?
Economists say affordability will remain a significant challenge until there is a meaningful increase in housing supply.
Housing affordability has fallen to its lowest rate on record, with households earning a typical income only able to afford about one in every 10 homes sold across the country.
According to data from realestate.com.au, a household earning a median income of about $125,000 a year could afford just 12 per cent of all homes (houses and units combined) sold nationally in the last financial year.
Despite recent falls in property values, stronger prices last year and recent hikes in interest rates have powered the result and reversed the "marginal improvement" from the 2025 financial year.
The company's senior economist, Angus Moore, said housing affordability is "challenged" as the central bank has increased the cost of borrowing money and repayments on loans.
"The three RBA interest rate hikes made in February, March and May increased mortgage rates and further constrained household borrowing capacity amid an already difficult cost-of-living environment," he said.
"Looking ahead, affordability may improve marginally if home prices continue to soften, but this is unlikely to be a turning point for many buyers.
"Without a meaningful increase in housing supply, affordability will remain a significant challenge, particularly for lower-income households."
The figures included in the report were based on a household spending 30 per cent of their gross income on mortgage repayments, with a 2.5 per cent buffer, meaning a household earning just over $125,000 annually could afford to make loan repayments on just 12 per cent of homes sold in the past year.
The data also relies on the median household income instead of the average household income.
For example, if the nation was made up of 99 households ranked from lowest-earning to highest-earning, the amount earned by the 50th one would be the median.
An average figure, however, would add up the earnings of all the 99 and divide them by 99, meaning the result is skewed by some wealthy households. According to analysis of HILDA data by the Grattan Institute, the average Australian household earns $161,000.
Victoria the most affordable, but even it slides
The report found that affordability declined in every state in the last financial year, but did not examine the territories.
South Australia became the least affordable state with just 7 per cent of properties sold affordable for median households.
Victoria was the best performer for people seeking a home, with 16 per cent of properties affordable for median households — but even that has fallen.
Even for people not seeking to buy, the data is tough. Mortgage repayments, relative to incomes, are at the highest point since 1989.
That means they are taking up 35.5 per cent of average household income, higher than during the so-called Global Financial Crisis (GFC) when it was 33.3 per cent.
In 1989, the figure was 37.5 per cent.
Back then, interest rates on mortgages were about 15.5 per cent, compared to 6.3 per cent in June 2026. But they were being applied to much lower house prices and the ratio of "annual income to cost of a house" was much lower.
If home loan interest rates were at 1989 levels today, three quarters of an average household's income would go towards repayments on the average mortgage.
Pressure unlikely to subside soon
Economist Luc Redman said despite a recent fall in property prices, the pressure within the market remains.
"Home prices have remained elevated across the sales distribution — despite a softening in the back half of the financial year — combined with higher interest rates reducing households' borrowing capacity," he said.
The problem, however, is what he calls a "clear structural supply problem" when it comes to having enough places to live.
"The country does not have enough homes, particularly in well-located areas. Without meaningful reforms to address supply across levels of government, this will continue over the long term."
Maiy Azize is the national spokesperson for Everybody's Home, a coalition of welfare and homelessness organisations that work on the housing crisis.
She said changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts, which have made it less attractive to be a property investor, were a start.
"The government's tax reforms are a great step, but they will take time to work their way through the housing market. These numbers show we need action in the meantime," she said.
However, she said there needed to be more changes if the situation were to improve sooner.
"Governments should put limits on rent increases to give renters some breathing room. That will help people trying to save for a deposit, as well as the growing number of people who will rent for the long term," Ms Azize said.
"We can't rely on the private market to deliver the affordable homes. These numbers make that clear. That's why the federal government needs to dramatically boost social housing.
"Government can build affordable homes at the scale needed, in the places people need them. It also takes pressure off the rental market because fewer people will be competing for affordable rentals."
Borrowers are feeling the pinch
Nadia Harrison is the chief executive of Mortgage Stress Victoria, a legal service that deals with people struggling with housing debt.
She said the body has seen "significant growth in demand" for its services.
"From February 2026, the number of people reaching out for assistance increased by around 30 per cent compared to the monthly 2025 average, and that level of demand has remained steady since," she said.
Ms Harrison advised people who are struggling to meet mortgage repayments should contact their lender for support.
However, that isn't a blanket solution, because not all lenders are legally forced to provide assistance.
Mortgage Stress Victoria wants to see a charter — a broad agreement — that extends hardship provisions to all borrowers.
"At the moment, the rights and protections you have as a home owner in hardship vary depending on the lender you've borrowed from, and the industry code that they subscribe to," she said.
"A mandatory Mortgages Charter which lifts and harmonises hardship protections across the board would go a long way to making mortgages fairer."

German police hunt suspect over power grid sabotage attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:34:00 UTC
03:34:00 KST

German police launched a manhunt Friday for a suspect who claimed responsibility for a string of sabotage attacks targeting the country’s power grid this week, after authorities discovered suspected explosives at his home, officials said.
In the letters, sent to authorities and media, the 48-year-old man stated his opposition to fossil fuels as a motive for the attacks, the interior minister for the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, Herbert Reul, said on Friday evening.
Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, addressing the same press conference, said the evidence pointed to a case of "climate extremism".
Germany has been the focus of European fears about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure this week, ahead of a closely watched state election on Sunday where the far-right, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) leads the polls.
It also formally blamed Russia this week for a drone attack in August at Leipzig/Halle airport as part of hybrid warfare meant to intimidate and divide countries that have supported Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Russia has dismissed the allegations as baseless.
There are still unanswered questions about the sabotage on the power grid, including whether the wanted man actually carried out any of the attacks and whether he acted alone, Reul said. German authorities have also not ruled out that the attacks were sponsored by a foreign state or carried out by left-wing extremists.
"We are currently facing a range of different threats and risks simultaneously. Sabotage, cyberattacks, covert operations, extremism and state terrorism - we are currently under threat from all these dangers at the same time," Dobrindt said.
The threats facing Germany and the number of attacks have increased and will likely continue - both state terrorism and extremism, he said.
"It is possible that these two factors are interlinked," he said.
His ministry had earlier said it was "no coincidence" that such "hybrid attacks" were happening on the eve of Sunday's election.
SPATE OF ATTACKS
The suspect claimed responsibility for an attack on a substation in Bergheim near Cologne on Tuesday that knocked five power generation units offline after conductive material was apparently launched onto high-voltage infrastructure, causing a short circuit.
Police later found several launch devices near the site.
The second suspected sabotage attempt claimed by the wanted man was discovered on Thursday evening in Dormagen, south of Duesseldorf, where a passer-by spotted pipes fitted with cables and timers aimed at a substation. Police subsequently found two launch devices in the area.
Reul said the letters named additional targets, including a substation in Weisweiler near the city of Aachen in western Germany.
As the ministers were speaking, Bild reported that suspected explosives or incendiary devices had also been found on overhead power lines at two substations in Saxony's Goerlitz district, prompting a police operation at facilities linked to the Lusatian lignite mining and power generation region.
In another sabotage incident this week, devices carrying conductive material damaged power lines at one of the most critical high-voltage nodes in the eastern state of Brandenburg. Police have not ruled out links between this case and the ones the man claimed responsibility for.
A spokesperson for Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the number of attacks that had been foiled or been unsuccessful was "a sign of how our security measures work - and that they do work".
(Reporting by Ludwig Burger, Friederike Heine, Matthias Inverardi, Mathtias Williams; editing by Kirsti Knolle, Kevin Liffey, Aidan Lewis, Philippa Fletcher)

Villagers vow to rebuild despite devastating mass demolition in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:32:40 UTC

Villagers vow to rebuild despite devastating mass demolition in West Bank
Israeli forces’ demolition of 12 homes in Khirbet al-Tabban leaves villagers determined to stand firm on their land.
Khirbet al-Tabban, occupied West Bank – The signs of the mass demolition were visible everywhere in Khirbet al-Tabban: destroyed homes, scattered rubble, empty animal pens, and water tanks and essential facilities that were no longer there.
A woman sits beneath a tractor trailer, trying to shelter from the heat of the sun. Beside her are some of the belongings she had managed to save from the demolition.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UN raises ‘ethnic cleansing’ concerns over Israel’s West Bank operation
- list 2 of 3US rejects Israeli suggestions of removing Palestinians from Gaza
- list 3 of 3Advocates decry US House vote to defund universities that boycott Israel
On Wednesday, Israeli forces arrived unannounced in this small village in the southern West Bank’s Masafer Yatta region, and demolished all of its 12 homes, as well as most of the community’s other structures, leaving about 70 people homeless.
Nidal Younis, head of the Masafer Yatta Council, describes the demolition as “wiping the village off the face of the earth”. But he’s insistent that the villagers will not leave, despite repeated attempts by Israel to force Palestinians out across Masafer Yatta.
“The decision to remain and stand firm is the people’s own decision,” Younis says. “They see no alternative to this land.”
But in Khirbet al-Tabban, remaining means sleeping in the open.
With water sources and sanitation facilities destroyed, Younis says the residents’ immediate priorities are shelter, drinking water and sanitation facilities.
He warns that tents will not be sufficient against the strong winds and cold that will arrive in the next few months, especially for children, women, older people and the sick.
And he’s fearful that what happened in Khirbet al-Tabban is likely to be repeated in other Masafer Yatta villages, following a 2022 Israeli court decision to allow for the displacement of the residents from the area after Israel designated it a military firing zone decades earlier.
Israel justified Wednesday’s demolition by saying the buildings were unauthorised. It is almost impossible for Palestinians in Area C of the occupied West Bank – which Masafer Yatta lies in – to get authorisation, even outside of military firing zones. Demolitions have become regular occurrences.
“The goal, as we see it, is to displace Palestinians and change the reality of these areas,” Younis says.
‘We will rebuild’
Nasser Mahmoud Obeid, one of the Khirbet al-Tabban villagers, says that Israeli forces ordered the residents to “get out by force” when they arrived on Wednesday morning.
The order wasn’t entirely unfamiliar to Obeid – he remembers a major demolition that took place in 1999, and has had to endure years of attacks from the Israeli army and settlers since then.
Obeid set to work after the Israelis left this week to clear the rubble and prepare temporary places to sleep.
He insists to Al Jazeera that the villagers will ultimately rebuild everything. Obeid says he was born in Khirbet al-Tabban in 1977, and that his father and grandfather lived there before him.
“This is our land, and here we will build and rebuild,” he says. “You can see with your own eyes what we are doing. We have not lost hope, and we will not.”
Sewing machine in the rubble
Suad Mohammed Obeid, 48, stood among the remains of the place where she had lived for more than three decades.
She searched through the rubble for her belongings, stopping at objects that had been part of her daily life, including the sewing machine she used to make clothes for her husband, who works in a metalworking shop, as well as for her children and grandchildren.
Suad has lived in Khirbet al-Tabban for 32 years, moving to the village after she got married. Over the years, her life became closely tied to agriculture, livestock and the production of dairy products, including cheese and yoghurt.
That life has now come crashing down.
“They demolished all of Khirbet al-Tabban and wiped it off the face of the earth,” she says.
“The night after the demolition was very difficult for us, our children, and our grandchildren,” she says. “The children are not used to sleeping outside their rooms, and we are already afraid to sleep outdoors because of settler attacks.”
She says the children remained frightened and awake throughout the night.
“Today we are out in the open. There is nowhere for us to shelter.”
She believes that what happened is part of an attempt by Israel to make life impossible for Palestinians in the West Bank, through demolitions, preventing access to grazing land, and attacks by settlers.
But she insists: “God willing, organisations will help us and provide us with tents, and we will remain steadfast.”

“I’m Laying Out Colorful Rugs for You” – a song of love, farewell and heroism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:30:12 UTC
03:30:12 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
News
“I’m Laying Out Colorful Rugs for You” – a song of love, farewell and heroism
Friday 4 September 2026 20:00
Friday, 4 September 2026, 20:00
PHOTO archive
Font size
One of the most beautiful folk miniatures from the Pirin region, “Ya Ti Postilam Shareni Chergi” (I Am Laying Out Colorful Rugs for You) carries a powerful emotional charge. At first glance, the scene seems simple: a young woman prepares a bed for her beloved, laying out “colorful rugs” as a symbol of intimacy and comfort. But instead of staying with her, he saddles his horse and prepares to set off.
“Who are you leaving me to?” she cries. The man replies: to the two mothers — his own and hers. He chooses the mountains to become a haiduk and a hero. His choice is driven by a yearning for freedom and a heroic destiny, while the ending is already foreshadowed.
In Bulgarian folklore, nature is always a majestic presence, but it is also a language of the human soul. In this song, the fallen mist symbolizes sorrow, while the dew symbolizes tears.
“I Am Laying Out Colorful Rugs for You” exists in various versions. In some, the hero is identified as Manush Voyvoda, while in others, no specific name is given. What remains is the drama of a woman in love, left behind by her man in the name of duty and a heroic death.
Performed by many of Bulgaria’s most distinguished folk artists — from Gyurga Pindzhurova to Trio Bulgarka, and from the Bisserov Sisters to the vibrant Nusha Choir — the song is now best known in the arrangement by the renowned conductor and composer Kiril Stefanov.
Stefanov’s version of “I’m Laying Out Colorful Rugs for You” is among the signature pieces in the repertoire of the State Ensemble for Folk Songs and Dances “Pirin.”
The name of Prof. Kiril Stefanov, one of the most significant figures in the history of Bulgaria’s folk ensemble tradition, has become legendary. Born in Blagoevgrad, his life and professional career remained closely connected to his native Pirin region.
Prof. Kiril Stefanov (1933–2005)
PHOTO Facebook/Pirin.Ensemble.Blagoevgrad
After graduating from the Music Academy with a degree in choral conducting, he took over the leadership of the Pirin Folk Ensemble at just 23 and remained at its helm for nearly 50 years. Those 50 years marked the most important chapter in the ensemble’s history. Under the leadership of its chief artistic director, it established itself as a prestigious ensemble with a distinctive style and a strong international presence.
Kiril Stefanov’s approach to folklore is highly professional, intellectual and exceptionally artistic, grounded in an in-depth knowledge of local musical traditions and an aspiration to preserve their distinctive character. In his arrangements, the harmony deepens and highlights the beauty of the original folk source. A vivid and unconventional personality, Kiril Stefanov left a remarkable mark not only on the development of Bulgaria’s folk choirs and ensembles, but on Bulgarian music as a whole.
PHOTO Facebook/Pirin.Ensemble.Blagoevgrad
In 2012, Ruska Stoimenova, a renowned Bulgarian singer, founder and one of the most prominent soloists of the Pirin Folk Ensemble, said in an interview with the website struma.com that immediately after joining the ensemble, Kiril Stefanov introduced new techniques and a new approach to presenting folklore on stage: “He was so open to innovation that within a few weeks he completely transformed the ensemble… He created as he went, he had his own vision…”
Ruska Stoimenova described Kiril Stefanov as “a man blessed by fate, with colossal talent”, and said: “There are no irreplaceable people, but there are unique ones, and Prof. Stefanov is one of them… Prof. Stefanov is a phenomenon”, concluded the singer, who is a soloist in the arrangement of “I’m Laying Out Colorful Rugs for You.”
Decades after its creation, Kiril Stefanov’s version continues to reveal the enduring strength of the Bulgarian spirit and the irresistible magic of Bulgarian folklore.
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

How to keep your kids safe at petting zoos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

A three-year-old girl has died from a rare illness after visiting a petting zoo in Victoria. She had developed brain damage and kidney failure after spending weeks in intensive care.
The girl is confirmed to have had haemolytic uraemic syndrome, a rare but serious serious condition, caused by infection with a specific type of Escherichia coli bacteria (or E. coli for short). This can be transmitted in a variety of ways, including after contact with animals on a farm or at a petting zoo.
Fortunately, such tragic cases are rare. But they do shed light on bacterial infections harboured by some animals and the need to take hygiene precautions when visiting petting zoos.
I'm a microbiology lecturer, and I'm planning to visit a petting zoo next weekend with my family.
Here's what we know about the infection risk at petting zoos, and what parents can do to help keep their children safe.
What is haemolytic uraemic syndrome?
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome most commonly results from infection with types of E. coli that produce a specific toxin called the Shiga toxin.
Early symptomsof infection are nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea, which can contain blood.
Warning signs that need urgent medical assessment include bloody diarrhoea, markedly reduced urination, lethargy, pallor (looking pale), unexplained bruising or red-purple spots on the skin.
If a doctor suspects someone has haemolytic uraemic syndrome, they will ask about symptoms and examine the person. Hospitalisation as soon as possible will be necessary. Blood, stool and sometimes urine tests confirm the diagnosis.
The Shiga toxin can damage the lining of blood vessels, which leads to circulatory and kidney problems. This can progress to haemolytic uraemic syndrome, leading to kidney failure, high blood pressure, seizures and in some cases death.
So emergency medical treatment is essential, in a hospital intensive care unit, with dialysis and blood transfusions often needed.
The disease is more common in children.
How is it spread?
These bacteria can can spread to humans by contaminated food and water. Humans can also spread the bacteria to other humans, via faeces, such as when changing nappies.
But the situation most relevant here is the spread via some animals. Bacteria are present on animal fur and wool, so children can come into contact with it when patting or cuddling an animal. But that's not the only way.
Bacteria are also present on manure, bedding, soil, feed, enclosure floors and fences.
The risk lies when people's contaminated hands come into contact with their mouth.
Toddlers are particularly difficult to protect because they often put fingers, toys, food and dummies in their mouths and need help to wash their hands thoroughly.
Are some animals riskier than others?
Cattle and other ruminants, including sheep and goats, are recognised animal reservoirs for Shiga-producing E. coli, as well as some other pathogens.
For example, animal contact can also expose children to Salmonella, Campylobacter and Cryptosporidium, all of which can cause gastroenteritis.
While exposure to these can occur on farms, petting zoos and open zoos specifically have been identified as a risk for these microorganisms. Animals may not always show symptoms.
But petting zoos are great for kids, aren't they?
Petting zoos and farm experiences can provide children with educational experiences involving animals, farming, food production and animal welfare. They're also such a great family activity and educational resource.
The Australian Veterinary Association supports petting zoos where animal health, welfare, public safety and disease-transmission risks are appropriately managed.
Hygiene plans include clear communication about the risks of infection, readily accessible handwashing facilities, and physical separation between animal-contact and food areas.
Parents need to ensure their children are supervised. Most importantly, they need to ensure their children's hands are washed before coming into contact with anything that might go into a child's mouth — a dummy, or food, for instance. Hand sanitiser is not as effective as washing with soap and water for 20 seconds or more.
So when choosing a petting zoo, favour venues with handwashing stations immediately outside animal areas, with running water, soap, disposable towels and signs reminding visitors to wash before eating or drinking.
Thomas Jeffries is a senior lecturer in microbiology at Western Sydney University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

Efe Ozkan
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
FIFA released its International Transfer Snapshot on Thursday, highlighting the impact of the 2026 World Cup on transfers in men’s and women’s football.
According to FIFA, 267 players who featured at the 2026 World Cup, representing 47 nationalities, changed clubs during the mid-year transfer window, with their transfers accounting for more than $3.3 billion in combined fees.
Women’s football also set new transfer records, with spending more than doubling compared with 2025 to reach $28.6 million, while more than 1,400 transfers were registered.
Beyond World Cup players, more than 12,500 international transfers in men’s football reached a cumulative value of over $9.89 billion.
- Record growth in women’s football
Women’s professional football continued its growth, setting records for both the number of international transfers and transfer fees.
A total of 1,406 international transfers were registered in women’s professional football, the highest number ever recorded and a 19.2% increase from the previous record, according to FIFA.
Transfer fees also reached an all-time high, with $28.6 million spent on international transfers, more than double the amount recorded during the previous mid-year window.
English clubs led spending with $8 million, followed by clubs in Spain with $6.6 million, Germany with $4.9 million, the US with $2.9 million and Italy with $2.1 million.
Swedish clubs were the biggest recipients of transfer fees, receiving $4.2 million, ahead of clubs in England with $4 million, France and Germany with $3.6 million each, and the Netherlands with $2.9 million.
 
- Men’s market continues to grow
The men’s transfer market also recorded a significant window, with more than $9.89 billion spent on transfer fees across more than 12,500 international transfers, the highest amount ever recorded, according to FIFA.
English clubs led global spending with more than $3.02 billion in transfer fees, followed by clubs in Italy with $1.1 billion, Spain with $940 million, Germany with $904 million and France with $641 million.
English clubs also completed the highest number of incoming transfers, followed by clubs from Spain and Portugal.
French clubs received the highest total in transfer fees at $1.7 billion, followed by clubs in England with $1.43 billion, Germany with $1.02 billion, Spain with $773 million and Portugal with $642 million.

Breadcrumb
Clashes in southern Sudan leave at least 21 dead, medical group says
Clashes in southern Sudan have killed at least 21 people, including women and children, a doctors' group said Friday.
Sudan Doctors Network, which tracks violence throughout the war in Sudan, said that the rebel group Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, or SPLM-N, launched an attack on Thursday in the areas of Debi and Luweri in the town of Kauda in South Kordofan.
Rebel leader Abdel Aziz al-Hilu has aligned his fighters with the Sudanese paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which has been battling the Sudanese military since 2023. The war killed at least 59,000 people, displaced some 13 million and pushed parts of the country into famine.
Al-Hilu’s group has been active in South Kordofan and joined a local government set up by the RSF. The group is a breakaway faction of the SPLM, the ruling party of neighboring South Sudan.
Thursday's attack was part of clashes that erupted between SPLM-N and the Otoro tribe, a minority group in the Nuba Mountains of South Kordofan.
The fighting came despite a ceasefire initiative backed by the RSF last month. The medical group said the attacks by al-Hilu's forces “constitute a clear violation of the agreement, a resumption of hostilities, and the targeting of civilians on an ethnic basis.”
Al-Hilu didn’t commit to the ceasefire agreement, and his forces launched attacks on 10 Otoro villages, displacing hundreds of civilians between Aug. 20 and 26, the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, a think tank, said in an analysis last week. It added that SPLM-N claimed in a video that it took control of Kauda.
Ali Mahmoud Ali, the group's Sudan analyst, said that the latest clashes risk bringing in more Nuba clans into the fight and could increase divisions across South Kordofan, where communities are facing an already dire humanitarian situation.
The group said it has recorded the killings of at least 158 people since violence erupted in March over land disputes.

KINSHASA, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and its partners on Friday launched an updated 180-day multisectoral response plan to intensify efforts against the ongoing Ebola outbreak, with funding needs estimated at 1.3 billion U.S. dollars.
With support from the World Health Organization (WHO), the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other partners, the plan was intended to serve as the operational roadmap for the response over the next six months.
According to the WHO Regional Office for Africa, the outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus had reached 6,342 reported cases and 3,072 deaths as of Sept. 2. It has spread to 60 health zones across six provinces.
Health authorities are particularly concerned that a large proportion of deaths continue to occur in communities, often among people who had not previously been identified as contacts and had not reached health facilities before dying.
"Every case detected too late, every contact missed and every delay in mobilizing resources translates into lives lost," Anne Ancia, acting WHO representative in the DRC, said, calling for rapid and coordinated action on a larger scale.
DRC Health Minister Roger Kamba said containing the outbreak required efforts beyond the health sector, involving communities, government agencies, partners and donors. "The government is fully mobilized to protect every Congolese," Kamba said.
According to the WHO, full implementation of the revised plan would require an estimated 1.3 billion U.S. dollars.
Damien Mama, United Nations resident coordinator in the DRC, said the Ebola response needed to be integrated into the broader humanitarian effort and supported by sufficient, flexible and predictable funding.
The Africa CDC also pledged continued support for national response efforts, including resource mobilization, coordination with partners and greater involvement of communities.
The current outbreak, officially declared in May, has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak recorded in the DRC to date. ■

Costa Rica president says US ground forces would help national security
SAN JOSE, Sept 4 - Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez said on Friday that U.S. ground operations could strengthen national security in the Central American nation, while emphasizing that nothing concrete was in the works with Washington and any such move would require legislative approval.
"It would obviously be very good for national security if it were about pursuing a common objective against transnational crime, transnational drug trafficking, transnational terrorism," Fernandez told Reuters in an interview, when asked about the possibility of U.S. ground operations on Costa Rican soil.
Costa Rica and the U.S. have cooperated for years on security matters, including through joint maritime patrols. U.S. President Donald Trump invited Costa Rica to join his Shield of the Americas coalition, which is aimed at combating drug cartels.
A right-wing populist who took office in May, Fernandez campaigned on a tough anti-crime platform, vowing to restore order in Costa Rica, a country that has seen a spike in drug trafficking and violence in recent years. The homicide rate hit a record 17.2 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023, double the rate of a decade ago.
Fernandez said she is not considering requesting from Congress a state of emergency or suspending constitutional guarantees in order to address the wave of violence, noting that homicides are declining.
Court data shows that in the first half of 2026 homicides fell 14% compared to the same period in 2025.
Fernandez has been in a tense standoff with Costa Rica's courts, accusing the judiciary of being infiltrated by organized crime and blocking her tough-on-crime security policies.
"I've been very critical of how slow the courts are, very critical in specific cases where judges release convicted criminals long before their sentences are complete, and I've also been very critical of administrative failures and potential corruption in the judiciary," Fernandez said.
The dispute has increasingly centered on the judiciary's role and funding. Fernandez has backed significant budget cuts to the judicial branch and supports a legislative proposal to have Congress, rather than the Supreme Court, appoint the attorney general.
Judicial officials have denied corruption allegations, challenging Fernandez to provide evidence. They argue that budget cuts planned for 2026 and 2027 would weaken democratic checks and balances and undermine efforts to fight crime. REUTERS

Ladakh residents to get ownership rights over 60,000 acres of barren land
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:11:40 UTC
03:11:40 KST

Ladakh residents will now have rights over barren lands or wastelands owned by govt
SRINAGAR: Ladakh residents will now have rights over barren lands or wastelands owned by govt, with the administration Friday approving Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (Nautor Regularisation) Rules, 2026.The Rules provide a comprehensive framework for granting proprietary rights on up to 10 acres of eligible Nautor land holdings to the occupants across all seven districts of the Union Territory. For Nautor land beyond the 10-acre limit, the proprietary rights may be allotted on a leasehold basis, in accordance with the rules.Nautor land refers to barren or wasteland, owned by govt, which was earlier allotted to individuals for cultivation or other productive use. More than 60,000 acres of land in Ladakh is presently recorded in revenue records as Nautor holdings.The Rules offer a one-time regularisation mechanism for Nautor land, occupied before the repeal of J&K Tenancy Act-980, on Oct 27, 2020. Any possession of Nautor land after this cut-off date will be ineligible for regularisation.“The Nautor issue has a deep historical connection with the lives and livelihoods of the people of Ladakh.
For generations, our people have worked hard to bring barren and waste land under cultivation in one of the most challenging agricultural environments in the country. These Rules provide a transparent and uniform mechanism to address this long-pending issue and give legal certainty to genuine holders. It will also enable such land to be utilised as a financial asset, including for availing bank loans,” Ladakh LG Vinai Kumar Saxena said.
According to the Rules, the authority of allotting Nautor land will be vested in Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils in all seven districts.A govt spokesperson said the absence of a clear and uniform legal framework until now restricted the effective utilisation of Nautor land. “In particular, landholders with limited or non-proprietary rights, were unable to use the land as a financial asset, including for purposes such as obtaining loans against it. At the same time, the absence of uniform rules also posed a threat of claims and disputes over govt, council land,” the spokesperson said.

voids and vertical space reinterpret traditional japanese machiya on a compact site in tokyo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:10:39 UTC
03:10:39 KST

Takumi Wakui + Riho Wakui Architects’ House in Kagurazaka
Located on a compact 33 sqm site in Kagurazaka, Tokyo, this four-story woodenresidence reinterprets the traditional Japanese machiya as a vertical dwelling. Designed by Takumi Wakui + Riho Wakui Architects as a home for an architect couple, the project examines how daylight, natural ventilation, and spatial openness can be introduced within one of Tokyo’s densely built residential neighborhoods.
Research into the site’s history revealed its origins in Edo-period urban subdivisions, where narrow-fronted townhouses, or machiya, developed alongside samurai estates. Successive land divisions produced the compact parcels that characterize the area today. In response to the 33 sqm footprint, the architects organized the residence vertically, extending the spatial experience through height instead of increasing the building’s footprint. Each floor is assigned a distinct function, with the programs gradually transitioning from public to private toward the upper levels. This organization separates different activities without relying on conventional partition walls. A series of voids connects the floors visually and spatially, allowing the residence to operate as a continuous volume.
Wood, Light, and Air Shape the Contemporary Machiya in Tokyo
Large framed openings are positioned above the living room, facing the street, and within the top-floor bathroom. These openings incorporate views toward planted greenery while allowing natural light to penetrate deeper into the interior. Along the exterior, projecting side walls extend up to 800 mm from the building envelope. These elements provide environmental control by shielding the interiors from strong western sunlight while also capturing the prevailing southwesterly breeze.
The structural system combines a robust truss along the longitudinal exterior walls with a double-wall spine at the center of the building. Takumi Wakui + Riho Wakui Architects use this configuration to provide stability while maintaining flexibility in the arrangement of the floors and allowing for potential future expansion. Connections between the interior and exterior, as well as between the individual levels, are established through a series of carefully positioned openings and voids. The resulting configuration distributes different places for occupation throughout the house, allowing its use to respond to changing daylight, airflow, and seasonal conditions within a compact urban footprint.

Analysis: Lower Treasury yields could require a weaker economy. Trump won't fix them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:08:16 UTC
03:08:16 KST

Policies from President Donald Trump's administration are helping keep bond yields higher despite the White House's own attempts to lower them. With the 80-year-old president unlikely to change his spots, Americans may not like what it could take to provide interest-rate relief: a weaker economy that cools borrowing costs but undercuts U.S. growth.
The investor base for U.S. debt has become more price-sensitive over the years as central banks and reserve holders have stepped back as buyers relative to parts of the private sector. Some of those global investors are starting to shun U.S. debt because policy changes under Trump have had the effect of worsening the economics for them. That is an uncomfortable turn for markets that are already seeing signs of a competition for capital between the flood of deficit spending and the surge of debt issuance funding the buildout of artificial intelligence.
The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note has risen by roughly three-quarters of a percentage point in the past six months. Lately it has hovered near 4.8%, the highest yield of the second Trump administration, despite efforts to bring it down. The Treasury Department will start next week to increase its buybacks of some long-term U.S. debt, an effort designed to improve liquidity in the market. Investors have also raised interest rates as they try to infer how new Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh will react to inflation that remains above the Fed's 2% target.
"Of course, everybody wants to ask for a bit more price to lend money to the U.S.," Ludovic Subran, chief investment officer and chief economist for Allianz, a European insurer and asset manager, said in an interview.
That judgment isn't political — it's "pure economics," Subran said.
Subran ticked off a set of factors he says have come to add something resembling credit risk to U.S. debt: "soaring [federal budget and trade] deficits, Fed unfazed by inflation, Treasury tampering with markets." He doesn't necessarily believe the U.S. will default on its debts, but he said Allianz — like many other global investors — has had to pay more to hedge its bets in the U.S.
The U.S. is projected to hit its $41.1 trillion debt limit between late-winter and mid-summer 2027.
This year, "we also have decided not to find duration in the U.S. fixed-income market like before, because it's not interesting," Subran said.
After accounting for inflation and hedging, "we were not making money," he said.
The rise in yields is a source of aggravation for Americans already frustrated by affordability problems. Mortgage rates have risen to nearly 6.8%. Mortgage rates move with the 10-year Treasury yield. So do auto loans and other forms of consumer debt.
Political risks to yields persist
There is little sign of easing in the political factors pushing up yields. A fall in oil prices might bring some relief, but an end to the Iran war remains elusive. There is no appetite in Washington to make the political compromises that would ease deficit spending. A meeting of global finance ministers and central bankers in North Carolina this week produced political shots at Canada. Coordinated action to ease borrowing costs wasn't on the agenda.
Meanwhile, some large holders are looking to move out of Treasurys into higher-yielding debt. Norway's massive sovereign wealth fund is considering shifting roughly $80 billion of its portfolio now in government debt into other parts of the bond market such as mortgage-backed securities.
Meanwhile, U.S. government borrowing continues to rise. The Congressional Budget Office recently had to revise up its expectations for the deficit this fiscal year to $2.1 trillion, a figure that is likely to exceed 6% of gross domestic product. That is an enormous volume of borrowing outside crisis times.
AI is driving major new corporate borrowing, too. JP Morgan estimates that five major tech firms and Nvidia, along with special-purposes vehicles those companies use to backstop data-center leases, have issued about $320 billion in debt so far this year.
"Hyperscalers are issuing so much debt that they may be causing a supply-demand issue at the long end of the yield curve," Michael Cembalest, chairman of market and investment strategy for J.P. Morgan Asset Management, wrote to clients this week.
That isn't necessarily a bad thing. AI is a bright spot in a U.S. economy hurting for sources of growth. GDP grew by 1.5% in the second quarter, a weaker-than-expected figure that is likely being dragged down by the sharp slowdown in immigration into the U.S. after Trump's crackdown. The labor market has also shown unusual moves lately. Friday's report that payrolls grew by 162,000 comes against a longer-term environment where firms are reluctant to hire or fire.
Competition in the debt market could drive an innovation boom as firms vie for the market's favor. It's too early to make a definitive judgment, but the possibility of that kind of growth and productivity boom is one explanation for the rise in real yields, which adjust for inflation.
The yield on 10-year TIPS — a Treasury instrument that accounts for inflation — has risen by 67 basis points over just the past six months, to 2.43% on Thursday, according to FactSet data. Breakevens, which measure inflation, have been flat over the same period.
The rise in real yields is "more of a reflection of the strength of the economy," New York Federal Reserve President John Williams told CNBC Wednesday. Some people want to read the rise in yields as dragging on the economy, but that logic is backward, he said.
"It's not really about financial conditions affecting the economy. It's more about the economy affecting financial conditions," Williams said.
The flip side of Williams' analysis is that it may take an economic slowdown for borrowing costs to cool. But that isn't a solution anyone would want to root for.

Belarusian Nuns Collecting Money in French Churches Accused of Funding Russian Military
Nuns from the Saint Elisabeth Convent in Minsk, Belarus, have been touring French Catholic churches to sell religious icons and souvenirs purportedly for charity, despite mounting evidence that their convent supplies material aid to Russian forces in Ukraine, according to an investigation by Ouest-France, posted on September 2.
In the coastal town of Les Sables-d’Olonne, the nuns recently spent several weeks in August collecting cash donations under the guise of funding orphanages and psychiatric hospitals, a practice they have replicated across France for years, Ouest-France reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The convent’s leadership maintains deep, public ties to the Belarusian regime and openly champions the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Ouest-France revealed. Archpriest Andrei Lemeshonok, the monastery’s spiritual father, has repeatedly used his platform to support the war, declaring in a May 2025 message that the monastery operates as a “combat unit” and urging prayers for Russian “warriors.”
Ouest-France also noted that the self-proclaimed president of Belarus, Alexander Lukashenko, visited the convent in January 2023, specifically praising the facility for organizing collections to support Russian troops on the battlefield.
The financial and logistical pipeline to the front lines is coordinated through a dedicated project dubbed “Help for Brothers,” Ouest-France reported based on an analysis of the convent’s Telegram channels. Led by Sister Alexandra in Minsk and coordinated in Russia by Sister Evgenia of the Saint Mary Magdalene convent in Orel, the network has successfully delivered drones, military boots, medical supplies, and at least nine all-terrain vehicles directly to Russian combat units, according to the Ouest-France investigation.
The French newspaper highlighted video evidence showing a Russian soldier explicitly thanking Sister Alexandra for a drone donation, alongside photos of the nun posing with a Russian flag bearing the pro-war “Z” symbol.
Operating more like a corporate holding than a traditional monastery, the Saint Elisabeth Convent controls seven companies, employs roughly 1,600 people, and manages extensive agricultural and retail operations, according to independent Belarusian investigative media cited by Ouest-France.
When questioned by the French newspaper, the nuns vehemently denied that funds collected in France are used for military purposes, insisting their French revenue strictly finances homeless shelters and orphanages. However, Ouest-France pointed out that the cash-based nature of the church sales makes tracing the exact destination of the European donations virtually impossible.
The presence of the pro-Russian nuns has sparked controversy within the French Catholic Church, where local priests are left to navigate the geopolitical fallout without institutional guidance, Ouest-France observed.
Father Antoine Nouwavi, the parish priest in Les Sables-d’Olonne, told Ouest-France he had previously suspended the nuns' visits but allowed them back this summer after receiving a written assurance from the Mother Superior, noting that he would need concrete proof from the French Foreign Ministry to permanently ban them.
While the French government and the national bishops' conference declined to comment to Ouest-France, the publication highlighted that churches in the United Kingdom, Poland, Sweden, and Switzerland have already banned the Minsk nuns over their role in financing the Russian war effort.
In another demonstration of pro-Russian clergy aligning with the war effort, Metropolitan Mitrofan of Murmansk previously brought military priests and Russian war veterans to a church directly on the Norwegian border for a religious service.
Mitrofan—a vocal supporter of the invasion who has described the border with Nordic states as a “spiritual border” against evil—defended Russia’s military during the gathering while accompanied by veterans and priests with direct operational ties to Russian combat units in Ukraine.

Mere possession of books with “dispiriting titles” does not make a person a criminal the Jammu & Kashmir high court said
SRINAGAR: Mere possession of books with “dispiriting titles” does not make a person a criminal, the Jammu & Kashmir high court said, quashing an order for preventive detention of a man under the Public Safety Act (PSA) on charges of keeping and authoring books promoting separatist ideology.A single bench of Justice Moksha Khajuria Kazmi Thursday also observed that the PSA detention order passed by Kupwara district magistrate against the petitioner, Shafat Maqbool Wani, wrongly attributed to him the authorship of alleged anti-national literature seized from his house.Being a scholar, the petitioner could be expected to possess a variety of literary material, the court said, directing police to release Wani forthwith.Police claimed to have seized books with what they alleged were incriminating titles — ‘Construction of an Islamic Order in Hindutva Reimagination’ and ‘The Saffronization of occupied Kashmir, Demystifing Hindutva Settlers, Colonial Designers’ —from Wani’s house. They also attributed the authorship of the books to Wani.The court said the assertion that the detainee had inculcated a separatist ideology since his childhood as his father has been an ex-militant was “delusory”.
“...The preventive detention, ordered so conveniently on such imaginary belief, is nothing but an unmindful exercise of power,” it observed.Justice Kazmi noted that the respondents had not shown any subversive activity against the petitioner that compelled them to take recourse to preventive detention.
The HC ruling assumes significance as the home department banned the publication and circulation of 25 books on Kashmir, saying they promoted a “false narrative” and “secessionism”, on Aug 5, 2025, the sixth anniversary of abrogation of Article 370.The books include ‘Azadi’ by Arundhati Roy, ‘Kashmir: The Case for Freedom’, a collection of essays by Tariq Ali, Pankaj Mishra and others; ‘Confronting Terrorism’, also a collection of essays, edited by Maroof Raza; and ‘In Search of a Future’ by journalist and author David Devadas.The Kupwara DM ordered Wani’s detention under PSA on Sept 13, 2025, to prevent him from indulging in activities “detrimental to the security of the State”. The grounds cited included invitations he had received to attend some international conferences. The detention order came the same day he was granted bail by a Jammu NIA court in a UAPA case registered at Handwara police station.
