Israel’s Gaza expulsion plans, Nepal’s loss and damage test, and Syria’s $7 billion deal: The Cheat Sheet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:15:04 UTC
01:15:04 KST

Share & more
Our editors’ weekly take on humanitarian news, trends, and developments from around the globe.
On our radar
Israeli ministers push plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza
Two Israeli government ministers have said that Israel is seeking to forcibly expel Palestinians from the Gaza Strip en masse – which would be a war crime under international law. On 2 September, Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel was seeking Donald Trump’s permission to expel Palestinians from Gaza, adding there was “no real solution for Gaza without migration” and that the Israeli government was “organised and ready to get them out”. On 3 September, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir followed up by saying that Israel has a plan to forcibly expel all 2.1 million Palestinians from Gaza over the next six years, starting with 250,000 people in the first year. Ben-Gvir said there were countries willing to take in expelled Palestinians, but did not specify which ones. The comments come in the lead-up to tightly contested Israeli elections next month. However, the mass expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza is something Israeli leaders and government agencies have consistently mooted since 7 October 2023. According to reporting, Israel’s Intelligence Ministry proposed plans for the removal of Palestinians from Gaza as early as 13 October 2023. The vast majority of Palestinians are barred from entering the nearly 70% of Gaza currently under direct Israeli military occupation. Around 2.1 million Palestinians are crammed into the remaining territory, over which Israel also exerts significant control, including continuing to restrict aid access and the blocking of any reconstruction efforts.
Nepal flood puts loss and damage funding to the test
Nepal’s catastrophic Himalayan flood is rapidly becoming a test case for climate justice. On 26 August, a collapse of glacier, rock, and ice near the Nepal-China border sent a wall of material down the Bhoteloshi-Trishuli river system, killing more than 1,250 people in Nepal and leaving more than 4,200 people missing. Kathmandu formally asked the UN’s Loss and Damage Fund for an unspecified amount of emergency financing, arguing that the destruction exceeded its response capacity. On 3 September, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the government had sought an immediate $20 million from the fund, adding that this assistance alone was “definitely not adequate”. The appeal is unusually urgent: The fund has yet to make its first country payout, and its next board meeting is not until December. Khanal has also called on the US, China, and India – the world’s top greenhouse gas emitters – to contribute “climate compensation”. Officials have estimated Nepal’s direct losses at $2.56 billion, with recovery costs at $4-$7 billion. For more on how early warning systems were overwhelmed and on what can be done to prevent similar disasters in the future, read our in-depth analysis.
Somalia’s political fight is spilling onto the battlefield
Somalia’s insecurity is worsening. Federal forces this week beat off an attack on Baidoa, the largest city in South West State, by militia loyal to ousted governor Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. The government accused Laftagareen’s fighters of collaborating with al-Shabab insurgents in the assault. Türkiye has thrown its weight behind the President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s government. A Turkish drone was reportedly used in a strike on a pro-Laftagareen general, while Ankara’s F-16 fighter jets have also been in the air, reflecting a relationship that has evolved from “Islamic humanitarianism” to hardnosed strategic interest. Several federal states and regions oppose Mohamud, accusing him of centralising power, pushing electoral reforms to extend his rule, and ousting uncooperative regional leaders. Laftagareen suffered that fate in March, triggering repeated attacks on Baidoa by his militia. Meanwhile, the drawdown – and looming funding crisis – of the African Union's peacekeeping force is intensifying the power struggle between Mogadishu and the states. No unified security architecture exists, creating fertile ground for further fragmentation.
Algeria’s rare intervention betrays fears of a fracturing Sahel
A surprising outcome of the failed coup against Niger’s military junta on 29 August was the arrival, a day later, of an Algerian air detachment, including four SU-30 fighter jets. The powerful deployment was a clear signal that Algeria was breaking from its non-interventionist traditions and wanted its troubled southern neighbours in the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) – Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger – to take note. Algeria was not involved in the quashing of the putsch against General Abdourahamane Tchiani by disgruntled soldiers angered by command failings in the war against jihadist insurgents. That win was down to the presidential guard, backed by Russia’s Africa Corps. But Algeria does fear state collapse, triggered by Islamist insurgencies that have their roots in its own violence of the 1990s. Algeria’s new-found interest happens to coincide with the start of construction of a Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline that will stretch from Nigeria to the Mediterranean coast. While Algeria offers a strategic alternative to Russia’s military intervention in the AES, military backing alone will not resolve the political grievances that fuel armed opposition and leave Sahelian juntas vulnerable to coups.
Tech and rights collide as new Human Rights Council session begins
A new session of the Human Rights Council opens 7 September in Geneva, with a wide swathe of escalating crises in the foreground and the UN’s budget crunch overhead. New updates or sessions on genocide prevention, an updated database on businesses in Israeli settlements in Palestine, and examinations of rights in Sudan and Afghanistan, are among the many pressing issues on the schedule. Tech is colliding with human rights and that’s reflected on the agenda: There are sessions on technology-facilitated gender-based violence, protecting human rights defenders in the digital era, how mercenaries use tech, and how artificial intelligence affects cultural and development rights. As on any multilateral stage these days, money troubles are never far away. Rights experts mandated by the council will be reporting less often to the General Assembly, weakening oversight and political attention, the International Service for Human Rights warned. Meanwhile, the advocacy NGO is urging more scrutiny of a country where rights and the rule of law are eroding: the United States.
Weekend read
And finally…
The pressure to tell a story of suffering
In this relatively short New York Times essay, author David Treuer deftly weaves in so many themes that are likely of interest to Cheat Sheet readers. He writes of being Indian (his word of choice for Native American) and moving from the Leech Lake Ojibwe Reservation to the hallowed halls of Princeton University, and initially feeling driven to tell false tales of suffering because that’s what people expected of someone like him, not understanding that someone like him could be relatively happy, or complicated, or even mediocre. And the realisation that he had also been consuming lies about Princeton vs. his home, which were really about civilised vs. savage. Treuer’s piece offers plenty of food for thought about the expectations and narratives we place on marginalised groups – and, ultimately, on ourselves.

Iran shifting military doctrine toward preemptive attack: Army spokesman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:07:59 UTC
01:07:59 KST

Ahmet Dursun, Baybars Can, and Rania Abushamala
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Iran has been gradually shifting its military doctrine toward preemptive attack since the June 2025 war, an army spokesman said Friday.
“When we face an American threat, we defend ourselves, and international law allows us to defend ourselves preemptively,” Mohammad Akraminia said during a program broadcast by Iran’s state television.
Akraminia said Iranian forces targeted US bases stretching from Jordan to the United Arab Emirates in response to American attacks.
Iran also destroyed air defense systems at US bases across the region, he claimed, warning that Tehran would respond “faster and more forcefully” if it faced another Israeli attack.
“Some of these bases housed radar facilities and air defense systems, which were destroyed,” he said.
“With the destruction of these systems, targeting the occupied territories and the Zionist regime’s bases in the region has become much easier than in the past,” he added.
Commenting on Israeli threats against Iran, Akraminia said Israel was currently preoccupied with elections and that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was making domestically focused statements for electoral purposes.
He stressed that any Israeli attack would be met with strikes carried out “more easily, more quickly and more forcefully.”
On June 13-24, 2025, Israel, with US backing, carried out a military campaign against Iran targeting military infrastructure, missile launch sites and nuclear facilities, while also assassinating senior military commanders and nuclear scientists. Iran responded by launching more than 550 ballistic missiles and hundreds of drones at Israeli military and intelligence sites. The 12-day war ended with a ceasefire on June 24.
Regional tensions have escalated since US-Israeli attacks on Iran began on Feb. 28 this year, triggering Tehran's retaliatory missile and drone attacks against Israel and US interests in countries across the region. Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled amid disagreements over security arrangements in the strait.

Iran-Russia alliance grows despite US pressure
TEHRAN — Russia’s robust and uncompromising support for Iran in the face of US military adventurism and all-out economic warfare has made it abundantly clear that the strategic partnership between Tehran and Moscow will never be swayed, deterred, or disrupted by outside pressure.
Rather than achieving its intended goal of isolating Tehran, Washington’s aggressive, coercive policies and warmongering have produced the exact opposite effect, acting as a powerful catalyst that has brought Iran and Russia closer together than ever before.
Moscow has repeatedly and forcefully denounced the unprovoked US war on Iran, while flatly dismissing Washington’s economic pressure as an illegitimate tool of Western hegemony. The United States, meanwhile, has sought to aggressively tout the supposed impact of its unilateral sanctions in an obvious bid to distract global public opinion from the strategic failure of its joint military campaign with Israel against Iran, which began six months ago.
In an effort to tighten its economic siege, the administration of President Donald Trump has pressured other sovereign nations to unilaterally sever their legitimate trade and financial relations with Iran under the banner of what the White House has termed “Operation Economic Outcast.” In characteristic hyperbole, Washington went so far as to compare this sweeping sanctions blitz to the historic Allied invasion of Normandy in World War II, theatrically nicknaming it an “economic D-Day.”
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared that the European Union had formally joined Washington’s campaign to completely sever Iran from the global financial architecture. Furthermore, in an interview on Fox News on Wednesday, Bessent blatantly demanded that Russia “stay away” from Iran and abandon its ties with Tehran—a provocative demand that was promptly and decisively rejected by Moscow.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov affirmed that Russia will never give up its strategic relations with its long-standing partners to appease Washington. Peskov declared that it is entirely unrealistic for the United States to believe it can monopolize international relations or dictate terms to independent global powers, emphasizing that Russia has its own dependable partners and friends and will vigorously maintain, protect, and expand these friendly and partnership relations regardless of Western hostility.
Russian President Vladimir Putin also explicitly and unequivocally expressed Russia’s profound support for Iran during his high-profile meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
“As I have repeatedly said before, Russia is standing in full solidarity with the people of Iran. We admire your courage and resilience in your fight for your national interests,” Putin told Pezeshkian during their crucial meeting held on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan’s capital of Bishkek. He further noted that the friendly relations between Russia and Iran are developing steadily and dynamically across all areas, adhering strictly to the letter and the overarching spirit of the historic Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
Russia and Iran have significantly and systematically expanded their multifaceted cooperation in recent years, deepening their bonds across a wide and comprehensive range of vital areas, including bilateral trade, energy integration, strategic transportation corridors such as the International North–South Transport Corridor, and advanced defense cooperation. In January 2025, the two countries officially signed the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement, providing a rock-solid, institutionalized framework for further strengthening bilateral cooperation, neutralizing illegal Western sanctions, and consolidating their joint resistance against unilateralism across multiple strategic sectors.
Moscow’s principled and unyielding stance comes even as CIA Director John Ratcliffe reportedly attempted to intimidate the Kremlin during an unannounced, high-stakes trip to Moscow on Tuesday. Ratcliffe reportedly issued direct warnings demanding that Russia immediately scale down its support for Iran, backing the threat with Washington’s earlier vows to significantly expand extraterritorial secondary sanctions against sovereign countries that refuse to cut their economic ties with Tehran.
Yet, amid mounting Western threats, ultimatums, and economic blackmails, Russia’s position leaves no room for doubt that Moscow regards its strategic partnership with Iran as a permanent, non-negotiable, and long-term priority in the emerging multipolar world order. Rather than bowing to Western pressure or succumbing to Washington’s coercive tactics, Moscow and Tehran are digging in their heels, actively turning mounting Western hostility into an enduring catalyst for deeper, irreversible strategic cooperation. Washington’s desperate efforts to drive a wedge between the two nations have completely backfired, pushing both countries ever closer together on the geopolitical and economic chessboard.
The powerful statements delivered by Putin and Peskov carry immense strategic weight in the wider context of the two-day SCO summit that concluded on Tuesday. SCO leaders—including President Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif—collectively signed the “Bishkek Declaration,” which explicitly and unequivocally condemned the joint US and Israeli war of aggression against Iran.
In the joint declaration, the leaders of the Eurasian powers denounced the military aggression as a flagrant violation of the fundamental principles and norms of international law, state sovereignty, and the United Nations Charter, warning that such reckless unilateral actions create grave, unprecedented risks to international peace, regional security, and global stability.
The SCO heads of state also officially expressed their sincere and deepest condolences on the assassination of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, who was martyred on the first day of the joint US-Israeli war on February 28. In his SCO meeting with Pezeshkian, Putin specifically asked the Iranian president to convey his warmest regards and words of sincere, unwavering support to Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, who was elected Leader of the Islamic Revolution following the assassination of his father.
Putin’s message of support to Iran’s new Leader is significant in this context. It suggests that Moscow’s backing for Tehran is rooted not in short-term political calculations, but in a broader strategic relationship that Russia is determined to maintain.

An art exhibition dedicated to St. Francis is being held in Siedlce, Poland

As a guest of the Diocese of Siedlce, the Italian ambassador to Poland, Luca Franchetti Pardo, inaugurated the exhibition titled “Patron Saints of Everyday Life” at the Diocesan Museum, marking the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis. The exhibition features works by El Greco, Luca Signorelli, Luca Giordano, and other important masters, on loan from various Italian museums. In the presence of Apostolic Nuncio Monsignor Antonio Filipazzi, Regional President Adam Struzik, and representatives of civil and ecclesiastical authorities, Ambassador Franchetti Pardo first recalled the recent reinstatement of October 4—the feast day of St. Francis— “the holiest of Italians and the most Italian of saints”—as a National Holiday. The ambassador then emphasized that, for Italian diplomacy, promoting the legacy of St. Francis is not merely a cultural diplomacy initiative, but a way to highlight the inspiration that Italy’s foreign policy continues to draw from the saint’s message. “The pursuit of peace, respect for Creation, and the ability to foster dialogue among people of different faiths and backgrounds,” observed Franchetti Pardo, “are, in fact, universal Franciscan values that guide Italy’s international actions.” In addition to the local collection, the exhibition includes eleven masterpieces on loan from Italy’s most prestigious collections, such as the Vatican Museums, the Barberini Palace in Rome, and the Museum of San Marco in Florence. A unique feature of the project is the unusual juxtaposition of two works by El Greco. On loan directly from the Vatican, the painting *Resurrection* has been hung in close proximity to the *Ecstasy of Saint Francis*, a painting discovered by chance in a parish in the Siedlce area back in 1964 and, after verification, attributed in 1974 to the Spanish painter of Greek origin Dominikos Theotokopoulou, known as El Greco. It is his only work housed in Polish museums.

Singlehood is increasingly celebrated among women, but the pressure to couple up persists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:00:46 UTC
01:00:46 KST

“Single positivity” celebrates women’s independence, but that approval seems to fade as women age and face renewed pressure to find a partner, according to research published in Sociological Research Online.
Single women have historically been portrayed as lonely, undesirable, or personally deficient because couplehood is treated as the normal and preferable way to live. These judgments are particularly gendered. For example, women may be expected to reach milestones such as partnership, marriage, and motherhood in a prescribed order and within a socially acceptable timeframe. Although being single may be considered normal during young adulthood, previous research suggests that it becomes increasingly stigmatized as women age and their single status is seen as long-term.
More recently, popular culture has promoted “single positivity,” presenting singlehood as an empowering opportunity for independence, personal growth, and self-love. Yet these messages may also reflect a postfeminist and neoliberal culture in which women are encouraged to solve difficulties through confidence, positive thinking, and continual self-improvement.
Alicia Denby examined whether this newer, more celebratory portrayal had genuinely transformed attitudes toward single women in the United Kingdom or whether it continued to preserve the expectation that women should eventually couple.
The qualitative study included 19 single women between the ages of 21 and 52. Participants were recruited through a public advertisement posted on the author’s social-media profiles. Seventeen women responded directly, while two were recruited through referrals from existing participants. Eligibility participants were between ages 18-65 who identified as single; participants defined singlehood for themselves. The final sample included women who had never been partnered, women who were divorced, and women who were dating but not in committed relationships.
The sample was predominantly White British and disproportionately composed of heterosexual women in their twenties. Between June 2022 and April 2023, participants completed life-story interviews lasting from 30 minutes to two hours. Eleven interviews took place in person at locations chosen by participants, including university study spaces, cafés, restaurants, homes, and workplaces; six were conducted through Zoom and two through Microsoft Teams. With participants’ consent, interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, anonymized using pseudonyms, and examined through reflexive thematic analysis.
Women in their twenties and early thirties commonly described singlehood as a period of self-discovery, self-prioritization, and self-love. Being single gave them space to pursue careers, friendships, travel, hobbies, and personal interests without accommodating a partner. Some credited feminist self-help books, podcasts, and social-media content with helping them become more confident and accepting of single life.
Several had become “defiantly single”—rather than entering an unsatisfying relationship simply to avoid being alone, they would consider a partner only if that person added something meaningful to an already fulfilling life. Denby found that this seemingly empowering message presented another ideal women were expected to meet: the confident, self-reliant single woman who had successfully “worked on herself.” Feelings such as loneliness could consequently become difficult to acknowledge because they conflicted with the demand to remain positive.
For most participants, single positivity also had an expiry date. Although women generally viewed singlehood as acceptable or enjoyable in their twenties, many expected to feel mounting pressure as they approached 30 or their late thirties. Partnership remained the anticipated long-term destination, while singlehood was treated as a temporary period of preparation and personal growth. Women who remained happily and voluntarily single in their forties and fifties described having their contentment questioned or dismissed because others assumed that a relationship was necessary for happiness. Single positivity therefore appeared to broaden the identities available to younger single women without displacing the underlying couple norm; women could celebrate being single, but were still expected to settle down eventually.
Denby notes that the sample predominantly included White, cisgender, heterosexual, able-bodied women in their twenties and early thirties. Consequently, the study could not adequately determine how single-positive messages intersect with race, socioeconomic class, disability, or other identities.
This study shows that replacing negative stereotypes with upbeat messages about singlehood does not necessarily eliminate social pressure. It may simply make singlehood acceptable for a limited period before conventional expectations surrounding partnership re-emerge.
The study, “The Temporal Limits of Single Positivity: Single Women in Postfeminist Culture,” was authored by Alicia Denby.

British aircraft carrier deploying to deter Russia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:57:07 BST
00:57:07 KST

HMS Queen Elizabeth will sail from Portsmouth this weekend for a three-month deployment around the UK and northern Europe, with the Royal Navy saying the carrier will strengthen NATO deterrence, readiness and collective defence.
The 65,000-tonne aircraft carrier is due to begin leaving Portsmouth Naval Base at 6.20pm on Saturday 5 September with more than 800 sailors aboard. The deployment will combine advanced warfighting training with the ship’s new role as NATO’s afloat command platform for the Allied Response Force.
Over the next three months, Queen Elizabeth will operate around British and northern European waters alongside allied forces, developing the crew’s ability to conduct high-end naval operations and command a multinational force in a crisis. The Royal Navy stated that the deployment would see the carrier “conduct an intensive programme of training and operations, working alongside Allies to enhance collective security, deterrence and readiness.”
Queen Elizabeth assumed the NATO command ship role for the Allied Response Force in July, the first time either of the Queen Elizabeth-class carriers has performed the task. During the deployment, the ship will rehearse how an allied naval force would operate together if NATO was required to respond to a crisis.
Captain Claire Thompson, Commanding Officer of HMS Queen Elizabeth, said:
“We’ve returned from summer leave rested and ready for the next phase of our training. Sailing this autumn is a key milestone for both our NATO commitment, as the Afloat Command Platform and also on our journey back to the Royal Navy’s ‘very high readiness’ aircraft carrier, a duty we will resume from our sister ship HMS Prince of Wales in 2027. Sailing with an embarked battle staff, integration and training is essential whilst relearning the skills required to conduct safe and effective aviation as we ensure that we are prepared to deliver operational activity at the heart of NATO should it be required.”
The carrier will also undertake advanced training under the Royal Navy’s Fleet Operational Standards and Training organisation, covering the full range of modern naval warfare. The programme is intended to prepare Queen Elizabeth for higher readiness and eventual return to the UK’s principal carrier role. Training will continue into 2027, including participation in major NATO exercises, before Queen Elizabeth takes over from HMS Prince of Wales as the UK’s flagship and high-readiness strike carrier later that year.
The Royal Navy said British forces are already contributing to NATO deterrence across Europe, with more than 1,000 UK personnel serving in NATO command posts and Britain leading the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps from Gloucestershire.
UK forces also include an 800-strong battlegroup in Estonia, RAF Typhoon fighters deployed to defend NATO airspace over Romania, and P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and RC-135W Rivet Joint surveillance aircraft operating around the Baltic.
The UK also assigns its nuclear deterrent to the defence of the Alliance and, under plans confirmed in the Defence Investment Plan, intends to join NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft nuclear mission with F-35A fighters.
Queen Elizabeth’s autumn deployment will therefore combine NATO command duties with the process of returning the carrier and her crew to very high readiness, while maintaining a British carrier presence in northern European waters as NATO continues to strengthen deterrence and its ability to respond rapidly to a crisis.

What is Ukraine's SBU security agency?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:56:24 UTC
00:56:24 KST

What is Ukraine's SBU security agency?
LONDON, Sept 4 - Russia fired a drone into the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in central Kyiv on Friday, in what Ukrainian authorities condemned as the latest in a string of escalations in the war.
Here are some key facts about the organisation.
WHAT IS THE SBU?
The SBU is a powerful and shadowy organisation that emerged out of the Ukrainian branch of the Soviet-era KGB when Ukraine gained independence in 1991. It has a sprawling purview over domestic security and related matters. Since Russia's 2022 invasion, it has played an expansive role in the fighting, investigating war crimes, countering cyberattacks, conducting counterintelligence and catching Russian agents. It also has thousands of Alpha special forces which have conducted drone attacks on Russian military hardware on the battlefield as well as oil refineries and military facilities deep inside Russia. They have also used sea drones to attack tankers that transport Russian oil.
AUTHORS OF 'OPERATION SPIDERWEB'
The organisation has said it carried out some of the war's most spectacular operations against Russia, such as using a truck bomb to strike Russia's bridge to the occupied Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea in October 2022. Last year, it masterminded an elaborate 2025 drone attack, codenamed Spiderweb, that struck a slew of Russian strategic bombers at airbases deep inside Russia. It is also widely seen as a major player in a campaign of covert assassinations of senior Russian military and other figures blamed by Ukraine for carrying out war crimes. Russia has denounced those killings as terrorist attacks.
WHO IS IN CHARGE OF THE SBU?
The agency is run by acting head Oleksandr Poklad, whose office was directly targeted by the drone that hit the SBU's headquarters in Kyiv on Friday, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. Poklad, who was appointed in July, was not injured, the agency said.
HOW BIG IS THE SBU?
The SBU has expanded in size during the war. The number of people working in the SBU is classified, but legislation caps the maximum number of personnel it is permitted to have during wartime at 41,000. The figure is likely to be in that ballpark. The legislative cap was increased last year from the previous wartime threshold of 31,000 personnel.
BITTER RIVALRY WITH MILITARY INTELLIGENCE
The SBU has a long-running rivalry with the Main Intelligence Directorate, Ukraine's military intelligence agency. A dispute this week between members of the organisations spiralled into a shootout in which several military intelligence officers were injured in Kyiv. Zelenskiy has ordered an investigation into what happened. REUTERS

"The enemy continues to deliberately target facilities of the healthcare system. This time, three buildings involved in supplying Ukraine with medicines and medical supplies were targeted in a single day: Biokon warehouse, Teva warehouse, and the World Health Organization warehouse. It is clear that such actions are a blow to the ability to provide Ukrainian patients with the necessary treatment," he said on his Telegram channel on Friday.

Currently, Biokon Economic and Pharmaceutical Company has suspended all operations, including the receipt and shipment of medicines.
Another pharmaceutical warehouse destroyed by Russia was that of the pharmaceutical company Teva. As the company informed Interfax-Ukraine, an assessment of the damages is currently underway.
The WHO is also assessing the losses resulting from the aggressor’s destruction of a warehouse containing medical supplies and medicines in Dnipro. The organization noted that the destroyed warehouse held about 20% of the volume of goods that were stored there in 2025, as the WHO was able to reorganize its logistics to account for military risks.
As the Ministry of Health reminded the agency, at the end of August, the government simplified the conditions for storing medicines for the duration of martial law, enabling pharmaceutical companies to "more quickly secure additional warehouse space and distribute medicine stocks across various warehouses to reduce the risk of their loss due to Russian attacks".
"This decision became necessary due to systematic strikes on manufacturing, storage, and logistics facilities. After all, storing large stockpiles of medicines in a single location increases the risk of disruptions in their supply to pharmacies and patients," the Health Ministry said.
The ministry said that, according to the updated rules, during the period of martial law, pharmaceutical companies will be able to store medications not only in the warehouses listed in their license registry but also, if necessary, use additional storage facilities that are not included in their license registry.
"In the event of a security threat, stocks can be distributed more quickly across several locations, without being limited solely to the warehouses specified in advance in the license registry," the Health Ministry said.

Tesla launches Cybercab robotaxis: why this could become a challenge for the US
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

Tesla launches Cybercab robotaxis: why this could become a challenge for the US
Kyiv • UNN
Tesla has begun transporting passengers in driverless Cybercabs in Austin. The NHTSA is checking whether the vehicles comply with federal safety standards.
Tesla’s (TSLA.O) race to launch the Cybercab robotaxi will put existing regulatory rules to the test: the company is beginning to transport passengers in these sporty two-seater cars, which lack steering wheels, pedals and mirrors, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Several hours after the presentation in downtown Austin, Texas, the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) announced that it had begun examining approximately 1,000 Cybercab vehicles. The purpose of the investigation is to determine on what basis Tesla concluded that these cars comply with federal motor vehicle safety standards.
U.S. regulators restrict the commercial operation of vehicles that comply with federal safety standards adopted decades ago; those rules were designed for cars with drivers and require the presence of manual controls. However, according to industry experts, “gray areas” in the legislation and Elon Musk’s penchant for lawsuits could give Tesla a chance to nevertheless achieve the widespread deployment of the Cybercab.
Amid excitement among fans and bloggers in downtown Austin, Tesla’s robotaxi fleet, which had until now consisted of the popular Model Y crossovers, was expanded to include the Cybercab. The company said that rides in the Cybercab were available to everyone and presented pricing plans, but did not specify whether passengers had already begun to be charged for rides.
In addition,
The publication notes that the Cybercab — a gold-colored car with “butterfly-wing” doors — embodies Musk’s strategy of betting on self-driving technology and robotics. This bet has given the company a market capitalization of $1.4 trillion — a sum exceeding the value of several of the world’s largest automakers combined.
Unlike most countries, where new car models and technologies require regulatory approval before entering the market, in the United States automakers can put them on public roads by self-certifying their compliance with federal standards.
Musk left room for potential merger of SpaceX and Tesla23.07.26, 16:55 • 4959 views
"I don’t think there is a reasonable basis for finding that the Cybercab is capable of complying with federal motor vehicle safety standards," said Michael Brooks, executive director of the consumer advocacy organization Center for Auto Safety.
Although the NHTSA is making accelerated efforts to change safety standards and is simultaneously developing new rules for autonomous vehicles, experts note that implementing them will likely take more time than Musk promises.
However, it is known that Musk is not used to waiting for official approvals. "Tesla has historically tested the limits of what is permissible and challenged existing regulatory requirements," said Philip Koopman, a professor of engineering at Carnegie Mellon University and an expert in autonomous vehicle safety. "I fully expect Tesla to test those limits again this time."
According to Koopman, Musk may resort to a “creative interpretation” of the regulations: claim that the Cybercabs comply with federal standards and “flood the market with them.” It could take the NHTSA or state regulators years to sort out the situation. In the meantime, Tesla will be able to operate these vehicles on public roads.
Tesla did not respond to requests for comment.

The Italian delegation—composed of companies from various national production districts, specializing in a wide range of products (from Mediterranean and exotic plants to ornamental trees, citrus trees, olive trees, evergreen and deciduous trees, perennials, grasses, bonsai, cacti, succulents, and fruit crops)—participated in a program of meetings and visits with British industry operators, with a key highlight being their attendance at the Four Oaks Trade Show, a horticultural trade fair held in Macclesfield, Cheshire, England. The United Kingdom remains a strategic market for the sector. According to data from the UK government, in 2025, British ornamental plant production reached 1.62 billion pounds, of which 1.1 billion was attributable to the outdoor nursery segment; meanwhile, imports reached 1.55 billion, up 6.4%. In the first half of 2026, imports of live plants from Italy to the UK totaled 29.2 million pounds, representing a 2.8% increase year-over-year. The mission is part of an effort to consolidate Italy’s presence in a market characterized by significant demand and a high level of specialization. As part of the Four Oaks Trade Show, now in its 54th edition, Italian companies, gathered in the Italian Pavilion, presented their offerings and established valuable contacts with British operators, with the support of the Italian Embassy in London. The Embassy’s agricultural attaché, in collaboration with the ICE Office, organized, among other things, a discussion session with British institutional representatives. On the afternoon of September 2, a seminar titled “Climate Change: The Impact on Nursery Production” was also held, featuring presentations by Moreno Pinto, president of ANVE, and Luigi Pagliani, delegate of the European Nursery Stock Association (ENA), and moderated by Matt Appleby, editor and correspondent for HortWeek. The event focused on the impact of climate change on nursery production and, in particular, on the potential of water-wise Mediterranean species to contribute to the resilience of the British landscape in the face of increasing droughts.

Russia’s disappearance from the Mediterranean shows a navy stretched considerably thinner than its paper strength suggests, but the ships it does have remain dangerous and well handled, a naval analyst has told the UK Defence Journal.
Tom Sharpe, ex-navy Commander and Daily Telegraph columnist, who wrote about the Russian retreat from Tartus in December 2024, was responding to our report that a NATO official had confirmed Russia has had no sustained naval presence in the Mediterranean since June, the first time in ten years.
He told me: “Russia is clearly stretched thin. Their loss of the Med as a base shows this. But what they do have still has teeth, and some of it is well run. As their war in Ukraine goes from bad to worse, we are entering a worrying period, just at the time when our ability to counter or deter is equally low. Any sense that the new Prime Minister, Chancellor or Defence Secretary was going to inject funds to help reverse this are fading by the day.”
NATO outnumbers Russia at sea as Mediterranean presence ends
Terminal decline
On the Mediterranean itself, he said previously that the position had been in terminal decline since the loss of Tartus, and that while there had been talk of Russia using ports in Libya, he was not convinced any of them were suitable for long-term logistics support. Russia has recently been reduced to refuelling from a repair ship, a vessel built as a floating workshop rather than a tanker and carrying none of the equipment needed to pass fuel safely between two moving hulls.
NATO Maritime Command has meanwhile continued to draw attention to Russian movements through the region, making a distinction between vessels transiting the Mediterranean and the permanent or sustained presence Russia previously maintained there. WASHINGTON – The US has confirmed 3,134 measles cases so far in 2026, driven by a growing outbreak in Pennsylvania linked to two deaths that started a feud between the governor and the nation’s top health leader.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed 231 new cases in the week ending Sept 3.
The nation is already at the highest levels since 1991, the last year with more cases, which occurred prior to the formal elimination of the disease.
Pennsylvania has recorded 540 infections and 91 hospitalisations as at Sept 2, according to the state’s health department. Most of the infections are centred in Lancaster County.
In August, the state reported two measles-associated deaths, the first in the US in 2026.
On Aug 28, the CDC delayed its regular weekly update of case data. The agency’s site was then changed to say it was investigating the deaths, an unprecedented change that was ordered by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
The CDC update posted on Sept 4 still did not include the two deaths.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro blamed Kennedy for sowing distrust in vaccines that led to a decline in measles, mumps and rubella vaccination rates.
Kennedy – a longtime vaccine critic who has promoted debunked connections between shots and autism – responded by saying drops in MMR rates came before his time as the country’s top health official.
He also cited false information about the shot, saying incorrectly that it contains foetal tissue.
The social media jabs continued through the week, sparking confusion about the two deaths and raising questions about whether they were caused by the virus. Kennedy claimed the deaths may have been “fabricated” or from something other than measles.
But Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Debra Bogen pushed back on Kennedy’s assertion.
“I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County,” she said on social media.
The Lancaster County coroner told local news outlet WGAL that one of the deaths was an infant who died from a ruptured spleen and tested positive for measles. Paediatricians generally recommend children receive the first dose of the MMR vaccine after 12 months.
During the 2025 outbreak in Texas, when two unvaccinated children died, Kennedy touted unproven remedies, including vitamin A and cod liver oil, to curb infections.
Vaccine policy under Kennedy and President Donald Trump has been upended in the past year. In August, Trump signed an executive order that recommended the MMR combination vaccine be split into three shots, which would be costly and complicated for manufacturers and require more clinic visits to administer.
The CDC says 94 per cent of those with confirmed measles cases in 2026 are either unvaccinated or have an unknown vaccine status.

BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled two mandatory national standards to enhance safety and service quality in senior care institutions, as the country moves to professionalize and regulate a sector crucial to its rapidly growing elderly population.
The two standards -- the basic specification for senior care organization, and determination criteria for major accident hazards of senior care organization -- were jointly issued by the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) and the Ministry of Civil Affairs. They will take effect on Aug. 1, 2027.
The basic standard sets out 90 specific requirements across seven areas, including site selection, facilities and equipment, admission and discharge procedures, and safety management, drawing a baseline for compliant operations.
The criteria for determining major accident hazards establishes a systematic procedure for identifying safety risks, based on lessons learned from nationwide management practices, to help frontline managers detect and address risks precisely and in a timely manner.
"These mandatory standards will guide senior care facilities to focus on key safety and service elements and continuously enhance their risk‑prevention capabilities and operational quality," said Wang Yuhuan, an official with the SAMR.
China is racing to upgrade its elderly care system to meet the needs of an aging society. With more than 320 million people aged 60 and above, it has the largest elderly population in the world.
During the 15th Five‑Year Plan period (2026-2030), China aims to renovate and upgrade 2,000 public care facilities, and raise the share of nursing‑care beds in such institutions to over 73 percent, according to the National Development and Reform Commission. ■

Algeria’s wildfires show a state unprepared for climate chaos
A relentless series of fast-moving wildfires tore through northern Algeria last week, leaving many people dead, dozens injured, thousands displaced, and laying waste to vast tracts of forest and farmland.
The catastrophic blazes erupted amid an intense, persistent heatwave gripping the Maghreb region, pushing temperatures to dangerous extremes and creating prime conditions for rapid fire spread.
Between 26 and 30 August, the fires tore through several mountainous and coastal provinces, with the heaviest destruction concentrated in Jijel, Tizi-Ouzou, and the coastal region of Béjaïa.
Authorities recorded nearly 2,000 fires nationwide in July this year. The scale of the recent devastation echoes July 2023, when wildfires around Béjaïa killed more than 30 people and destroyed thousands of hectares of land, along with hundreds of homes.
Civil Protection teams, backed by army units, are continuing to battle 154 wildfires in the eastern provinces this week, with vast areas of forest scorched.
Fanned by powerful winds, the fast-moving wildfire advanced rapidly toward residential neighbourhoods, forcing dozens of families to evacuate and triggering a total shutdown of roads in the hard-hit areas.
The Interior Ministry initially reported 12 deaths in Jijel in one of its first statements at the start of the crisis in late August, when the government declared three days of national mourning.
No faith in the facts
And in a pure Stalinist tradition, private and public media outlets, operating under strict state control, have continued to report only a dozen deaths while highlighting the presence of government ministers on the ground, as well as the efforts of state institutions to help the victims.
However, the death toll is believed to be higher.
The Associated Press, for example, reported that twelve members of the same family were killed, and three others remain missing in the mountain village of Ouled Riyah. Lieutenant Djabri Said told AP: “I have worked in Civil Protection for 40 years. We have dealt with fires, but this is the first time we have faced such a human, environmental, and material catastrophe. There are hundreds of dead.”
Independent news outlets estimate that the wildfires, described as unprecedented in their intensity, have killed more than 200 people.
A municipal database has recorded more than 70 fire victims, offering a rare glimpse of the disaster’s scale amid the absence of an accurate official death toll. Clearly, local registries are filling gaps in government data as recovery efforts continue.
In fact, just last month, when a deadly blaze in an orphanage claimed the lives of 11 people, the authorities spent their time trying to keep the real causes of the tragedy and those responsible under wraps. Ordinary people were left to share the details on social media regarding the horrific event that killed mostly children.
Given the distrust of official information, many are understandably questioning whether the recent fires are due to the state’s failures or to deliberate arson, as authorities have claimed.
Independent journalists and opposition figures are also increasingly pointing fingers at public officials, alleging that institutional negligence and systemic poor planning have worsened the crisis.
Avoiding responsibility
For years, authorities have bypassed investing in an operational, state-owned fleet of Canadair water bombers, relying instead on a patchwork strategy of short-term aircraft leases and appeals for foreign intervention.
Following a diplomatic rift with Spain over the contested Western Sahara region, the decision-makers scrapped an agreement to purchase seven water bombers from a Spanish manufacturer.
It is undeniable that the Maghreb is warming at an accelerated rate of nearly 0.43°C per decade, according to global climate organisations. This rapid temperature spike has left Algeria bearing the brunt of global emissions, compounding the nation's climate vulnerability.
This has served as Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s primary argument and a rhetorical tool to deflect blame from his government’s neglect.
He cited the heatwave sweeping Mediterranean countries, including France, Italy, and Spain, arguing that climate change is contributing to increasingly dry conditions.
Whilst this is certainly true, what is missing from his rhetoric is the fact that a toxic mix of unmapped forestry tracts, archaic management, and bureaucratic silos are also hampering efforts to prevent the worst from happening.
It is obvious that the regime's failure is flagrant.
The wrong priorities
The priorities are also obviously elsewhere. For example, Algeria continues to drive a massive military buildup that is disproportionate to its regional security risks. This is further cemented by its status as the world’s fifth-largest weapons buyer and the top arms importer in Africa.
At the heart of this spending frenzy is the military’s historical central role in the country, and the regime’s survival helps explain the buildup, keeping defence spending a top domestic priority.
This, of course, is at the expense of urgent socioeconomic issues, including rampant public corruption, systemic tax evasion, embezzlement, kickbacks, and a severe youth unemployment crisis, while the country grapples with soaring inflation and inadequate critical infrastructure.
Nevertheless, public scrutiny is mounting regarding the Algerian government’s disaster readiness. Whilst the President has ordered compensation for affected families and the restoration of damaged homes and essential services, there is heavy focus on blaming arsonists and threatening tougher judicial action. Tebboune has gone as far as calling for the reinstatement of the death penalty for those convicted of starting the fires.
Rather than addressing long-term ecological management, the authorities are prioritising aggressive law enforcement measures. However, the government is either underestimating or ignoring the scale of public consciousness, which is calling out the deflection and pointing the finger at the state’s systemic failures in protecting the Algerian people and their land.
Dr Abd-el-Kader Cheref is a US-based Algerian scholar, freelance journalist, and former Fulbright grantee. He holds a PhD from the UK's University of Exeter and serves as an Assistant Professor of Africana and Multicultural Studies at Southern Illinois University. His research and writing focus heavily on African and MENA politics, democratization processes, postcolonial studies, Islam/Islamism, migration, and political violence.

Judge says he must declare mistrial in Lindsay Clancy trial over killing her children

Lindsay Clancy trial over killing her children ends in mistrial
- A mistrial was declared in Lindsay Clancy's murder case after jurors deadlocked over the killing of her three children amid claims of postpartum psychosis.
- Prosecutors argued Clancy planned the killings and was aware of her actions, while the defence claimed she was psychotic and not guilty by reason of insanity.
- Clancy's husband testified about her mental health struggles and described the tragic discovery of their children, highlighting the case's emotional and legal complexity.
AI generated
PLYMOUTH, Massachusetts - A judge declared a mistrial on Sept 4 in the US murder trial of Lindsay Clancy for killing her three young children, a tragedy her attorney said occurred while she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.
The nearly six-week-long televised trial revived longstanding debate about how postpartum mental health in women is treated in the US, and how the country’s legal system addresses cases when mothers kill their children.
Judge William Sullivan’s mistrial declaration came after jurors sent three notes this week indicating they had reached an impasse.
The mistrial paves the way for a potential second trial, which Sullivan said could take place later this year. Clancy is due in court for a follow-up hearing on Sept 29.
No one disputed that Clancy, 36, strangled her three children with exercise bands in January 2023 in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-storey window in an attempt to take her own life that left her paralysed.
Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, sought throughout the trial to convince jurors she should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, arguing she was a loving mother who had been in the midst of a psychotic episode when she killed Cora, five; Dawson, three and eight-month-old Callan.
Emergency appeal
The 12 jurors in Plymouth, Massachusetts, deliberated for seven days. Prosecutors supported the mistrial declaration.
In a dramatic sequence of events, Sullivan said on the morning of Sept 4 that he felt he had no choice but to declare a mistrial, after the jury sent its third note this week saying it was deadlocked. Clancy’s defence lawyers then filed an emergency appeal to Massachusetts’ highest court to stave off the mistrial declaration.
Clancy’s lawyers argued Sullivan should have inquired further into whether the holdout juror could heed the judge’s instructions to follow the law. The Supreme Judicial Court in Massachusetts’ Suffolk County denied the defence request, paving the way for the mistrial declaration.
Earlier on Sept 4, Sullivan rejected a defence request to remove the juror, who Reddington said was preventing the jury from returning a not-guilty verdict.
Reddington cited a note the jury foreperson sent on behalf of 11 jurors indicating that one juror had acknowledged doubt but refused to apply it to the verdict.
Jurors could only find Clancy guilty of first-degree murder if the prosecution proves its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
Prosecutors said Clancy planned killings
Prosecutors did not dispute that Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, had been dealing with mental health issues. But they argued she was able to appreciate the wrongfulness of killing her children and intentionally chose to do so anyway.
They presented testimony from a psychologist who, after examining Clancy, concluded that she had planned to take her own life and chose to kill her children because “she was convinced that they would suffer without her.”
Prosecutors focused on evidence showing how shortly before the killings, she sent her husband to pick up a food order and go to a pharmacy after mapping on her phone the time it would take for him to return home.
The trial drew comparisons to the case of Andrea Yates, a Texas woman who drowned her five children in a bathtub in 2001. After an appeals court overturned her initial murder conviction, she was found not guilty by reason of insanity in 2006. Her lawyers had said she suffered from severe postpartum psychosis.
Clancy struggled with mental health, husband says
Testimony from family members, including Clancy’s now ex-husband, Patrick, detailed how she had struggled with her mental health in the months following the birth of her third child, repeatedly seeking treatment from healthcare providers who prescribed a myriad of drugs.
Patrick Clancy testified that his wife had been discharged from a psychiatric hospital weeks earlier but showed no signs she planned to hurt herself or her children in the days that followed. She had a “normal” demeanour when he left to pick up dinner, he said.
He spoke on the phone briefly with his wife while at the pharmacy. Upon his return, he discovered her lying on the ground in the backyard with cuts on her wrists and neck. She told him she had tried to kill herself.
He said he asked where the children were, and she said they were in the basement. After he called 911 and first responders arrived, Patrick Clancy said he ran to the basement and discovered them with exercise bands tied around their necks.
Several witnesses, including Patrick Clancy, testified that later, while Lindsay Clancy was at a hospital, she spoke about having heard a man’s voice tell her that if she did not act, she would lose her chance. REUTERS

US sanctions Turkish bank accused of aiding Iran, says it 'severed the Iranian regime’s critical financial lifelines in Turkey'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:36:16 UTC
00:36:16 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- US sanctions Turkish bank accused of providing Iran access to global financial system
US sanctions Turkish bank accused of providing Iran access to global financial system
The Treasury says Golden Global Bank handled tens of millions of dollars in transactions for the IRGC-QF and helped move Iranian oil revenues from China to Turkey
The US Treasury imposed sanctions on Turkey-based Golden Global Bank and two of its subsidiaries, accusing the financial institution of providing Iran with access to the international banking system and facilitating tens of millions of dollars in transactions for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Quds Force.
The Treasury said Golden Global Bank was established to help a network serving Iran’s leadership transfer oil revenues from China to Turkey, where the funds could be converted into cash and gold by money exchangers.
According to the department, the bank knowingly offered correspondent banking services to Iranian financial institutions, allowing them to conduct international transactions through accounts controlled by the Quds Force and its proxies.
Those accounts included ones linked to Turkish businessman Sitki Ayan and his companies, the Treasury said. Ayan’s network was sanctioned by the US in 2022 over allegations that it moved hundreds of millions of dollars generated by Quds Force oil sales.
“Financial institutions continue to find out the hard way that we are serious about Operation Economic Outcast,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. “We know who you are, we know where you are, and we will continue to take action together with our allies and partners until we have buried the head of the Iranian snake.”
The sanctions also target Golden Global Varlik Kiralama and Golden Global Portfoy Yonetimi, two Istanbul-based subsidiaries controlled by the bank.
The move was taken under a presidential order authorizing sanctions against entities operating in Iran’s financial sector. Any assets belonging to the designated institutions that are held in the United States or controlled by US persons must now be frozen, while foreign financial institutions conducting significant transactions with them could face secondary sanctions.
The measures form part of Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign announced by Bessent on August 24 to target the financial networks Iran uses to sell oil, evade sanctions and fund its regional proxies. The Treasury last week took action against financial channels providing Iran with access to banks in the United Arab Emirates.

Palestine Action activists appeal against terrorism sentencing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:34:53 UTC
00:34:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Four UK Palestine Action activists appeal against terrorism sentencing
Fatima Zainab was arrested a day after she turned 20 for destroying and dismantling 40 quadcopter drones that were ready to be shipped to Israel.
Two years later, instead of completing her degree in Film and Media, she, along with three other comrades, was sentenced as a terrorist in a move described as setting a dangerous precedent.
Fatema Zainab Rajwani, Charlotte Head, Samuel Corner and Leona Kamio are all members of Palestine Action, a direct-action group that was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in 2025.
As the activists remain behind bars, almost two months after being sentenced as terrorists, they are calling for their sentences to be overturned.
"My experiences with the British legal system for the past 2 years in my struggle for justice for Fatema Zainab had prepared me to expect the worst at sentencing," Sukaina Rajwani, Fatema Zainab's mother, told The New Arab.
"However, this had not prepared me for the shock I felt when Justice Johnson announced my daughter and her co-defendants as terrorists and read off their lengthy sentences."
"The injustice of it all was so very blatant and obvious, that I was surprised the courts even allowed it to happen."
In a press conference held in London on Thursday, representatives of four of the six activists announced the appeal, arguing the conviction breaches Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), as Palestine Action was not a proscribed organisation at the time of the offence.
Speakers included the activists' mothers, including Sukaina, and their legal representatives.
The appeal challenges the evidence admitted, the finding of a terrorist connection, the compatibility and application of the relevant law, the fairness of the procedure, the severity of the sentences, and the judge's impartiality in one defendant's sentencing.
"To be honest, I am disillusioned with the British justice system and not really sure I hold a lot of faith in it anymore. That said, I would be very glad to be proved wrong on appeal," Rajwani said when asked for her thoughts on the appeal.
Charlotte Head, Samuel Corner, Leona Kamio, and Fatema Zainab Rajwani were found guilty of criminal damage "with a terrorist connection", the first time in British legal history that criminal damage convictions were sentenced as terrorism.
The terrorism sentencing increased the length of their sentences, meaning they would likely serve their full sentences in prison and would have to be registered as terrorists for up to 15 years.
Charlotte Head and Ellie Kamio were both sentenced to 5 years and 320 days. Fatema Zainab Rajwani was sentenced to 5 years and 200 days. Samuel Corner was sentenced to a combined eight years and eight months, including grievous bodily harm.
A further two activists, Zoe Rogers and Jordan Devlin, were acquitted.
Judge Justice Johnson's decision was based on the "serious property damage" clause of the Terrorism Act 2000", claiming that the damage to the weapons was done to "influence the government" and "intimidate a section of the public [Elbit Systems]".
The move to add "terror" charges was kept secret from the public and was done without the knowledge of the jurors, who only convicted the activists under criminal damage.
"The sentencing of Fatema Zainab and her co-defendants - direct actionists as terrorists is unprecedented in British history," Rajwani asserted. "It sets a horrific template for future protestors and actionists who could be convicted of criminal damage with no terror charges and then sentenced as terrorists."
"This should be a wake-up call for anyone that cares for free speech and democracy to fight tooth and nail to challenge this terror sentencing."
Johnson has been accused of bias against the activists, especially after the contempt-of-court action against Head's lawyer, Rajiv Menon KC.
The direct action caused damage to 40 weapons inside Elbit's Israeli weapons facility, including quadcopter drones.
The weapons manufacturer has been a constant target of the direct-action group over their ties with Israel, with its weapons being used in its genocidal war on Gaza.
Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in June 2025 after a group of activists spray-painted a Royal Air Force aircraft, making it now a crime to support the organisation.
The ban and the terrorism sentencing have been condemned by rights groups and the United Nations experts over the right to protest.

Rooney and Kate Mara Are Brilliant in Werner Herzog's Fractured Fairytale Bucking Fastard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:34:01 UTC
00:34:01 KST

Almost nothing in Werner Herzog’s fractured fairytale Bucking Fastards, playing in competition here at the Venice Film Festival, makes literal sense. But it all makes a kind of sideways sense, especially if, before watching, you can will yourself into a Herzogian brainspace, a place where possibly nonexistent elephants roam the Earth, where ancient cave drawings bear witness to the enduring creativity and wonder of humankind, where mad dreamers insist it’s possible to haul a multi-ton ship over a mountain. In that context, two inseparable sisters who speak only in unison, who are crazily lovesick over the man who has spurned them, and who believe they can dig a literal tunnel into a land of freedom, acceptance, and love: in a world where our deepest desires are so seldom met, how nuts does that really sound?
Real-life sisters Rooney Mara and Kate Mara play Joan and Jean Holbrooke, sisters living in Ireland—they are not, they adamantly insist, twins—who share every emotion, every thought, every waking moment as if they were a single entity. They dress exactly alike, in droopy trenchcoats and modest granny-style skirts; they both wear their long, silky hair parted neatly in the middle and tied partially back, like identical waterfalls. They don’t finish each other’s sentences; instead, they form their thoughts and words in unison and speak as one. It’s an eerie effect the first time you hear it. Even more unsettling, it comes to sound completely normal as the movie wears on.
Joan and Jean have fallen for a single man, their handsome rapscallion neighbor Gareth Mulroney (a saucy, salacious Orlando Bloom). It’s love at first sight—or is that sights?—when he bursts into their local church, a tankard of beer in hand, stirring up nothing but trouble. Afterward, they breathlessly wait for him to emerge through the church doors. Their eyes gleaming like double constellations, they proposition him: “I’d love to show you my inner cowgirl!” they tell him, the words tumbling out more like a song than a sentence. He’s charmed, intrigued; he’s horny. The trio land in bed, with Gareth in the middle flanked by his semi-nude cutie cowgirls, who ooh and ahh over him adoringly. They’re Goldilocks and he’s their just-right. This is how a sex scene, as imagined by Herzog, plays out.
But their bliss is short-lived. That meet-cute and its aftermath are relayed in flashback as the sisters huddle together in a courtroom, essentially defending themselves against charges of stalking. Gareth, after dallying with Joan and Jean for a time, has thrown them over and taken a wife. They can’t believe it—in their futile rage, they set the interior of his car on fire. (Their procurement of the gasoline they use to do so is a cracked mini-adventure by itself.) They also set the postbox outside his house aflame. Before the bewigged judge, Gareth’s lawyer tries to argue that the relationship was purely sexual. Joan and Jean justify their actions plaintively. “It was love!” they cry in unison, and later, “I am never going to stop loving him!”
But there’s no hope. Their linked hearts are broken, and the court case has brought them both fame and embarrassment. A kind villager (John Kavanagh) takes pity on them, knowing that the best thing for them is to get away. He offers them the use of a flat he doesn’t need, located in another town. He urges them not to open the door to strangers, people who want only to take advantage of them. From there, Bucking Fastard becomes a set of wriggly vignettes more than a linear story. There’s a sleazy neighbor (Malcolm Adams) who attempts to take, and post on the Internet, pictures of them undressing. (They put their heads together and cook up a giggly-devious plan to outwit him.) A kind social worker, played by Domhnall Gleeson, tries to show them how to collaborate in the task of opening a tin of sardines. But soon even their cozy flat comes to feel like a prison: they strike out on an adventure, going to live with an aunt who loves them (Marion O’Dwyer) and who encourages them to explore a mysterious cave near her country property, one whose twists and turns ignite their two-for-one imaginations. A fox named Cupid, with a perpetually alarmed-looking face, becomes their mascot. Through it all, they continue to mourn their lost love. But perhaps they can find a new one?
What does any of this mean? Though the story was inspired by real-life twins from York, England, Freda and Greta Chaplin—who spoke in unison and, like Jean and Joan, did everything together—the meandering storyline is pure, sweet, gaga Herzog. The picture’s most radiant sequences take place in the girls' beloved cave, where they toil for years to dig their way, admittedly nonsensically, to a better life. Herzog and his frequent cinematographer Peter Zeitlinger film the two of them, within a halo of light as they dutifully chip through a rocky passageway—their twin images are as luminous as a delicately carved shell cameo.
The Mara sisters are brilliant here, their eyes as hungry and haunted as those of an orphan in a Keane painting. You laugh with them, not at them, when they take revenge on that peeping tom. But there’s also something deeply touching about their refusal to give up on love. There’s a metaphorical idea shimmering beneath the surface of Bucking Fastard: it’s as if, through this strange and somewhat simple story, Herzog were trying to explore the things women want but don’t dare demand. Here, those longings are voiced in stereo. And yes, men can sometimes drive you crazy. What can you do?
The ending of Bucking Fastard might be considered a flaw; it’s hard to know exactly what has happened, or what it means. But then, an ambiguous ending is one we’re free to write ourselves. How can you not want the best for these dreamy, heartbroken girls, who at one point race through their cave in matching gauzy white gowns, like freedom-loving butterflies? You’ll want to believe that their hearts have at last found a home—a cave not of forgotten dreams, but of remembered ones, made sweeter with every recounting.

Civilian casualties reported after Houthi missile hit restaurant in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:32:27 UTC
00:32:27 KST

Civilian casualties have been reported after the Houthi group fired a ballistic missile at a restaurant west of Taiz province in southwestern Yemen, according to state media.
The Saba News Agency said on Friday that the Houthis “targeted a restaurant in the Mokha junction area west of Taiz with a ballistic missile.”
The strike caused civilian casualties, the agency said, without immediately giving their number or the nature of their injuries.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the report.
The attack came as Yemeni government forces retook a strategic position from the Houthis amid fierce fighting on several fronts west of Taiz, Saba reported.
Government forces regained control of Tabbat al-Khazan in the Jabal Habashi district following heavy clashes with Houthi forces, while fighting intensified on the Maqbanah and Al-Kadha fronts.
The latest fighting follows clashes Thursday in which the Yemeni army said 50 members of the Houthi group were killed or injured after they thwarted an attack aimed at seizing control of a road linking the cities of Taiz and Mocha in western Yemen.
The escalation is among the most significant rounds of fighting in Taiz since the UN-brokered truce in 2022, amid UN warnings over the risk of Yemen sliding back into a wider conflict.
Since September 2014, the Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa and other cities, while the internationally recognised government and allied forces control large areas in the south, east, and west of the country.

Aircraft refueling was restricted at Sochi airport after an attack on an oil depot
Kyiv • UNN
After a UAV attack and a fire at an oil depot, aircraft refueling was restricted at Sochi airport. The reception and departure of aircraft have also been temporarily restricted.
Airlines have been restricted from refueling aircraft at Sochi Airport following a Ukrainian Armed Forces attack on a local oil depot. This was reported by Russian media, citing a corresponding notice in the aeronautical information system, UNN writes.
Details
"Refueling at Sochi Airport is carried out exclusively by the fuel operator LUKOIL LLC for technical reasons; airlines must confirm that refueling will be provided by this operator," the NOTAM states.
The restriction was introduced today, from 13:35 Moscow time, until tomorrow, 13:30 Moscow time. This notice replaced the previous one, which was also issued today. It stated that refueling was generally restricted for all fuel operators.
Also, according to the Russian Federal Air Transport Agency, temporary restrictions have been introduced on the arrival and departure of aircraft at Sochi Airport to ensure flight safety.
Recall
During the night of September 4, drones attacked Sochi and "Sirius." Buildings were damaged, and an oil depot and an air defense division area caught fire.

Brazil's Supreme Court faces rare test as justices turn against each other
Unknown

Brazil's Supreme Court faces rare test as justices turn against each other
BRASÍLIA, Sept 4 - An open conflict between justices has engulfed Brazil’s Supreme Court, as it weighs whether to investigate two of its own in what may be the biggest test of its credibility since the country returned to democracy four decades ago.
One of the justices at the center of the conflict is Alexandre de Moraes, whose aggressive pursuit of former President Jair Bolsonaro and his far-right allies over a coup plot had already turned him into one of Brazil’s most polarizing figures, drawing even the ire of the Trump administration, which briefly sanctioned him last year, citing politicized prosecutions.
The other is Justice André Mendonça, who was appointed by Bolsonaro, and has made public a report that raised suspicions that Moraes made improper contact with a banker who allegedly led a multibillion-dollar fraud, prompting calls for an investigation. Moraes then asked the court to investigate Mendonça for abuse of authority Thursday evening.
"This may be the most dramatic moment in the history of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court," said Felipe Recondo, a journalist and researcher who has covered the court for decades.
The conflict has rattled campaigns weeks before Brazil's October 4 election, as parties push for judicial reform and try to tie opponents to the scandals.
"It is essential to investigate everyone, without shielding anyone, no matter who it hurts," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who holds a narrowing lead in polls, said in a social media post on Thursday.
Chief Justice Edson Fachin on Friday gave the attorney general five days to weigh in on Moraes' allegations against Mendonça. The court is also expected next week to decide whether to investigate Moraes.
What the court does next will have broad implications for a tribunal that has played an increasingly decisive and controversial role in government affairs in the past decade, including decriminalizing the possession of marijuana for personal use, barring laws to limit environmental protections, and – perhaps most importantly – arresting a president, Bolsonaro, who still, despite being convicted of threatening democracy, has the support of tens of millions of Brazilians.
Its moves may also resonate far beyond Brazil, as democracies around the world have struggled with a similar dilemma: how to protect courts from political intimidation in increasingly polarized societies while holding judges accountable.
"The Supreme Court can provide some balance in that game," said Recondo. "Remove the Court from that position, and all that remains is conflict. And that is a problem."
Neither Moraes nor Mendonça replied to a request for comment.
AN INCREASINGLY POLITICAL COURT
Allegations of misconduct involving two of the court's most high-profile judges have shaken up a previously calm campaign season a month before the general election.
Conservatives are calling on Brazilians to protest against Moraes during rallies scheduled to happen around Brazil on Monday, a holiday to commemorate the country's independence.
An investigation into a sitting member of the court would be a first and unthinkable a few years ago for a court that has long viewed criticism of its members as an attempt to undermine its authority.
The stakes are heightened amid falling public trust in the court, which polls show has eroded after years of polarizing decisions, as well as news reports about alleged wrongdoing affecting several justices.
Fachin, whose tenure started in January, has signaled a desire to strengthen the court's legitimacy by creating clearer rules for justices' conduct.
But his efforts became more relevant as the allegations against Moraes became more substantial. A federal police report unveiled this week showed text messages disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro allegedly sent to Moraes, which raise suspicions that the judge warned him of his impending arrest. The report also revealed a contract between the banker and Moraes' wife's law firm.
The court has little room to maneuver, Recondo says, because investigating Moraes risks weakening the institution, but failing to do so could also be damaging by creating the impression it is protecting one of its own.
"So for the court, whatever decision it makes is a bad one," Recondo said.
POLITICAL IMPACT
The clash between Mendonça and Moraes highlights how the court can no longer hide the internal political rifts that are weakening its standing from within, said Rubens Glezer, a law professor at the Getúlio Vargas Foundation.
One person with knowledge of the thinking of justices who are critics of Mendonça told Reuters that the justice may have a political goal. Moraes' scheduled presidency of the court is due for September 2027, but his removal would benefit Mendonça, who is next in line.
The most immediate impact of the crisis could be felt in the October election. Moraes critics frequently portray the judge as aligned with Lula. Moraes oversaw the case against Lula's 2022 opponent Bolsonaro but is formally independent of his government and was appointed by former President Michel Temer.
Lula is trying to create some political distance from Moraes to avoid being tied to the scandal, said two people close to the president, who requested anonymity.
A scandal could boost Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president and Lula's leading competitor, who has claimed his father, under house arrest and barred from running for office, is a victim of Moraes' persecution.
But the senator, for his part, has his own ties to Vorcaro, acknowledging in May that he met with the disgraced banker to secure funding for a film about his father, rattling the markets at the time that saw it as a risk for his own campaign.
Analysts say a Bolsonaro victory could also fuel a push to impeach Supreme Court justices in the Senate.
Still, it remains unclear if the court can gather enough support to start an investigation against any sitting member, as its politicization has made the outcome harder to predict, says Leonardo Barreto of political consultancy Think Policy.
"We're in a moment of great uncertainty." REUTERS
