Volkswagen plans 50,000 job cuts as analysts see ‘halo effect’ for German auto industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:04:49 UTC
22:04:49 KST

Volkswagen shares jumped on Friday after it announced plans to slash a further 50,000 jobs as part of a historic transformation plan amid intensifying tariff pressures and competition from China.
Europe's biggest carmaker said Thursday that its supervisory board had approved its Future Plan 2030, comprising 12 initiatives that would result in the "most strategically profound transformation program" in the group's 89-year history.
This includes cutting around 50,000 positions, including management roles, it said, citing global competition, changing demands, and technological shifts. It also said it plans to streamline its leadership with a flatter hierarchy. It adds to 50,000 job cuts that were already approved, bringing the total job reductions to 100,000.
Volkswagen topped the Stoxx 600 on Friday and was last seen up 8%. It's down 21% since the beginning of the year.
The company will also simplify its model portfolio by 50% by 2035, with a smaller product lineup as well as considering alternative uses for four of its German plants where future production had not yet been secured from 2031 to 2034.
"We are taking responsibility for our entire workforce, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide," Volkswagen's CEO Oliver Blume said. "Over the coming years, we will invest a three-figure billion sum to make our iconic brands even more attractive, stronger and more competitive."
Volkswagen has dealt with slumping profits over the past year with tariff pressures among the factors weighing on earnings. It reported tariff expenses of 2.9 billion euros ($3.4 billion) for the full year of 2025.
Two years ago, the German carmaker was paying 2.5% tariffs on vehicles from Europe, but that has since jumped to 15%, Blume said in August.
"Our cars are becoming more expensive and therefore increasingly difficult to sell – not because they have got worse, but because the rules of the game have changed," he said at the time.
Additionally, Volkswagen has faced fierce competition from Chinese rivals as domestic manufacturers such as BYD and Geely gained ground in electric vehicles and challenged its longstanding position in the market.
The car maker's restructuring plan reflects broader pressures facing Europe's auto sector, including Chinese overcapacity and much lower-priced imports, said Kevin Thozet, a member of the Investment Committee at Carmignac.
"Europe is therefore importing not only Chinese cars, but Chinese price deflation," Thozet said Friday.
Europe also has an "overcapacity problem of its own," he added, with Volkswagen particularly exposed because some of its German plants were built around first-generation electric sedans for which demand has weakened.
"China has too many cars. Europe has too many factories. And both problems are colliding," Thozet said.
'Better-than-feared outcome'
Analysts were expecting Volkswagen's shares to rise on the news. The announcement served as a "major surprise," but also represents that the company is capable of executing difficult decisions, Deutsche Bank analysts said on Friday.
"The unanimous approval of Volkswagen's Zukunftsplan 2030 last night is, in our view, a fundamental breakthrough and a much better-than-feared outcome," they said.
"Virtually every single one of the numerous investors we spoke to over the last few days continued to view Volkswagen as simply 'not fixable,' and scepticism around the likelihood of a comprehensive agreement remained extremely high," they added.
While the transformation does not solve Volkswagen's challenges overnight, it's a step in the right direction, marking a new phase for the company, they said.
They added that the outcome could have "broader implications" for the German auto industry, with other auto manufacturers taking similar steps to offset slower growth, excess capacity, international competition and pressure on returns.
"The December 2024 restructuring agreement arguably encouraged other manufacturers to pursue similarly difficult but necessary adjustments," they added. "Today's decision could create a similar halo effect."

There are common non-negotiables we look for in a prospective partner. They should be kind, caring and thoughtful. Having a shared interest helps. So does remembering important dates and anniversaries. But how much does it matter if they know how to pronounce the word “gnocchi”?

04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Germany has begun mass production of more than 5,000 medium- and long-range strike drones for Ukraine, defense company Auterion and its Ukrainian joint-venture partner Airlogix said.
The first units have already been manufactured in the greater Munich area under a German government order that industry sources estimate at about €300 million ($348 million).
The companies said the contract is due to be completed by mid-2027.
The drones are part of Germany’s military assistance to Ukraine, amid the conflict with Russia that began in February 2022.
The joint venture, founded in February, said it expects follow-on orders and a long-term commissioning.

“We will deliver already proven and tested systems this year -- at costs and at a manufacturing pace that actually make large stockpiles for deterrence possible,” Meier added.
Production is underway at an undisclosed site near Munich and is also planned at a second plant in eastern Germany, German news agency dpa reported.
Two models are being manufactured, according to company sources.
One has a medium range, while the other can fly up to 1,500 kilometers (about 930 miles), the sources said.
Auterion supplies the software and operating system, while Airlogix provides the hardware.
The one-way strike drones carry explosives and are designed to hit and destroy their targets rather than return.
Artificial intelligence is intended to keep the drones on course even when electronic warfare systems attempt to jam them.

====================================================================================================

Psychiatrists detail mother’s sudden descent into severe psychosis and delirious mania following childbirth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:00:38 UTC
22:00:38 KST

A recent case report published in Frontiers in Psychiatry details the experience of a 27-year-old woman who developed a rare and severe condition known as delirious mania shortly after giving birth. The case highlights how women with bipolar disorder may face an increased risk of complex manic episodes following multiple pregnancies and deliveries. The findings suggest that electroconvulsive therapy can be an effective and rapid treatment for this life-threatening psychiatric emergency.
Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition characterized by extreme mood swings, including emotional highs known as mania and lows known as depression. Following childbirth, women with bipolar disorder experience a heightened risk of recurrent psychiatric episodes. These postpartum episodes typically present as depression or standard mania. Postpartum psychosis is another related condition where mothers experience an abrupt onset of psychotic symptoms shortly following childbirth.
Delirious mania is an unusually severe neuropsychiatric condition that is rarely documented. It combines the hyperactive and erratic behaviors of mania with delirium, which is a state of profound confusion and disorientation. Patients may also experience psychosis, meaning they lose touch with reality through hallucinations or delusions.
Diagnosing delirious mania is challenging because doctors must first rule out a variety of physical illnesses that can cause similar symptoms. Infections, drug toxicity, and severe metabolic imbalances can all produce a state of delirium. Medical teams typically conduct extensive blood tests, brain imaging, and neurological exams to ensure the symptoms are not caused by an underlying physical disease.
Because delirious mania is poorly understood and infrequently documented, it often goes unrecognized in clinical settings. Lead author Bowen Song, a researcher at Sichuan University’s Mental Health Center in China, and a team of scientists documented this specific case to build a medical literature base that helps other doctors recognize the condition. By detailing the patient’s symptoms and treatment, the authors aim to provide evidence on how to identify and manage postpartum delirious mania before it escalates into a life-threatening situation.
The patient in this report was a 27-year-old Chinese woman with a documented history of bipolar disorder type I. She had previously experienced manic episodes characterized by excessive talking, a decreased need for sleep, and impulsive behavior. During her first pregnancy in 2020, she experienced a manic episode with psychotic symptoms following a routine amniocentesis. An amniocentesis is a medical procedure used to test amniotic fluid, and the physical stress of the event appeared to trigger her symptoms.
She was treated with medication and later delivered her first child via a cesarean section without further postpartum psychiatric issues. In 2024, she became pregnant again and delivered her second child, also via a cesarean section. Her mood had remained stable throughout the pregnancy on a low dose of an antipsychotic medication called quetiapine.
On the first day after her second surgery, her behavior changed drastically. She became highly excitable, talked excessively, and showed uncharacteristic aggression toward her family members. Over the next three days, she did not sleep and began experiencing auditory hallucinations, hearing voices mocking her. She also developed paranoid delusions, believing her husband had been unfaithful.
Her condition quickly deteriorated into a state of severe confusion and physical restlessness. She exhibited inappropriate behaviors, such as bedwetting, and became completely disoriented. She claimed to have lived for hundreds of years and could no longer recognize familiar people, places, or the current time.
Her family brought her to the emergency department, where doctors initially attempted to calm her using various medications. These initial treatments included sodium valproate, a mood stabilizer, and propofol, a strong sedative. These medications did not improve her symptoms. Her extreme agitation posed a risk to herself and the medical staff, requiring continuous sedation and physical restraints.
Given the severe and life-threatening nature of her symptoms, the medical team recommended electroconvulsive therapy, commonly known as ECT, on her seventh day of hospitalization. ECT is a medical procedure that involves passing small electric currents through the brain to intentionally trigger a brief seizure. This process appears to alter brain chemistry in a way that can quickly reverse symptoms of certain severe mental health conditions.
The patient received daily ECT sessions for the first three days, followed by treatments every other day. After the third session, her mood began to stabilize, and her consciousness returned to normal. She was once again able to recognize her surroundings and interact amicably with her family members.
Following the eighth ECT session, her emotional state stabilized entirely. Her hallucinations, delusions, and severe agitation resolved. She was discharged on the 19th day of her hospital stay and prescribed maintenance doses of oral psychiatric medications.
During a follow-up visit four weeks later, the patient remained alert and emotionally stable. She reported complete amnesia regarding the acute phase of her illness. She remembered nothing from the delivery until her third ECT treatment.
This single account cannot establish that multiple pregnancies or cesarean sections directly cause delirious mania in women with bipolar disorder. Biological changes during childbirth are complex, and individual medical events do not indicate a direct cause-and-effect relationship. The onset of psychiatric symptoms after delivery likely involves a combination of hormonal fluctuations, physical stress from surgery, and underlying genetic vulnerabilities.
These findings also do not imply that standard psychiatric medications are ineffective for postpartum psychiatric emergencies. For this specific patient, standard drugs did not stabilize her condition quickly enough, necessitating electroconvulsive therapy. Different individuals respond uniquely to treatments, and medications remain the standard initial approach for managing acute mania.
During the diagnostic process, the patient’s family declined a lumbar puncture, a routine procedure used to test the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. This meant doctors could not definitively test for autoimmune encephalitis, a condition where the immune system attacks the brain and produces similar psychiatric symptoms. The patient’s rapid recovery following ECT indicates an underlying psychiatric condition rather than an autoimmune disease, but the absence of this test leaves a small degree of diagnostic uncertainty.
Case reports describe the unique experiences of individual patients. They cannot be used to determine how common a condition is within the broader population or to create universal treatment guidelines. They are highly useful in medicine because they document rare clinical presentations, helping other doctors recognize unusual symptoms and consider alternative treatment options when standard therapies fail.
The report, “Postpartum delirious mania in a patient with diagnosis of bipolar disorder after cesarean delivery: a case report,” was authored by Bowen Song, Yiwen Yuan, Zhixiong Li, Zhongrui Ma, Xiufang Yang, and Zhe Li.

New island emerges in Norway’s Svalbard as glacier retreats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:59:45 UTC
21:59:45 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
A new island has emerged in Norway’s Svalbard archipelago after the Austfonna glacier retreated, Norwegian public broadcaster NRK reported Friday.
The island, covering roughly 0.45 square kilometers (0.17 square miles), was first identified in satellite images taken this summer, according to Geir Moholdt, a glaciologist at the Norwegian Polar Institute.
Radar images indicate that the landmass became separated from the glacier in late autumn last year. It now lies about 400 meters (1,312 feet) from the glacier front.
Austfonna, Norway’s largest glacier, has been melting at a record rate. Its glacier front stretches for more than 180 kilometers (112 miles), making it the longest in the Northern Hemisphere, according to the institute.
“In recent years, glaciers in Svalbard have lost more than one meter of ice on the surface on average per year,” Moholdt said, adding that the rate was far higher than previously observed.
He said Svalbard’s glaciers are retreating further onto land, causing fjords to lengthen while the ice becomes thinner because of warmer summers and extensive melting.
The rapidly changing terrain also makes updated maps increasingly important for researchers, local authorities, police, aircraft operators, and people traveling outdoors, said Anne Urset, a geodesist at the institute.
Moholdt warned that other landmasses could emerge as warming and glacial retreat continue.
“There are several candidates for new islands that could emerge with rapid warming and melting,” he said, adding that some glaciers could eventually disappear entirely.

WINDHOEK, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The United States will begin reducing financial assistance for Namibia's HIV response as the southern African country assumes greater responsibility for sustaining its epidemic-control programs, the two governments announced in a joint statement released Friday.
The reduction will be implemented in phases over the next year, with U.S. support shifting from financial assistance to technical cooperation as HIV programs are integrated into Namibia's national health system, according to the statement.
The transition marks a winding down of more than two decades of substantial U.S. financial support provided mainly through the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR.
The two governments attributed the shift to Namibia's progress in controlling the epidemic, noting that the country has achieved a 96-98-98 rate for HIV testing, treatment and viral suppression, exceeding the UNAIDS targets of 95-95-95.
The planned phase-down follows earlier disruptions to U.S. funding that affected parts of Namibia's HIV response.
UNAIDS previously reported that the disruptions affected community-based prevention services, services for key populations and community health worker programs.
UNAIDS also reported intermittent condom shortages, reduced access to some pre-exposure prophylaxis services and the termination of some staff contracts among U.S.-funded implementing partners.
Namibia launched a sustainability roadmap for HIV, viral hepatitis, tuberculosis and malaria control in November 2024, according to the joint statement. The roadmap is intended to strengthen the country's health systems and prepare them for a shift in international donor support toward technical assistance. ■

ROME, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Food Price Index averaged 133.3 points in August, up 1.9 percent from July and 2.5 percent from a year earlier, reaching its highest level since the end of 2022, the FAO said Friday.
The increase was broad-based, with all five commodity group indices rising. The FAO Sugar Price Index recorded the biggest increase, surging 11.9 percent month-on-month to its highest level since June 2025, amid growing concerns over global sugar supplies in the 2026/27 season. Hot and dry weather in the European Union and parts of Asia, lower sugar production in Brazil, and India's decision to allow duty-free raw sugar imports contributed to the rise.
The FAO Cereal Price Index rose 2.2 percent in August to its highest level since May 2024. Wheat prices increased 2.6 percent, supported by continued disruptions to Black Sea export logistics, lower production prospects in parts of Europe due to hot and dry weather, and a weaker U.S. dollar. Maize prices climbed 2.5 percent amid concerns over crop yields in parts of the United States and the European Union, strong demand from the ethanol and feed sectors, and disruptions to Ukrainian exports.
The Vegetable Oil Price Index rose 0.6 percent to its highest level since June 2022, marking its third consecutive monthly increase. The Meat Price Index increased 1.0 percent, driven by higher poultry, pig and ovine meat prices, while the Dairy Price Index rose 2.3 percent, its first increase in four months.
Despite the August rise, the FAO Food Price Index remained 16.8 percent below its record high reached in March 2022, the FAO said. ■

Following the listing, ICBC's cumulative issuance of renminbi-denominated bonds on Nasdaq Dubai has exceeded 10 billion yuan (about 1.49 billion dollars), the bank said. ■

====================================================================================================

South Korea’s military turns to AI as low birth rate shrinks pool of recruits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:57:44 UTC
21:57:44 KST

As South Korea's population rapidly ages and the pool of military recruits shrinks, Seoul is increasingly looking to artificial intelligence, robots and autonomous systems to help defend one of the world's most heavily militarized borders with fewer soldiers.
Earlier this month, President Lee Jae Myung called for selective conscription and a shift toward a smaller, technology-driven force, describing his goal as a “smart, elite and strong military centered on advanced equipment and technologies.”
The push is already moving beyond plans and policy.
In July, South Korea conducted its first test of a humanoid robot performing a ship's helmsman duties, with the robot successfully executing steering commands under simulated conditions including narrow waterways, bad weather and nighttime operations.
The Navy also carried out its first minesweeping trial using AI technology and unmanned vessels earlier this month.
The Army, meanwhile, has commissioned a study into automating key maintenance operations, including through AI-powered predictive maintenance, automated information management, maintenance robots and wearable strength-assist suits.
The push is part of South Korea's broader embrace of AI. In June, Lee unveiled investment plans worth more than $1 trillion for projects including semiconductors, physical AI and data centers.
But for the military, the technology is intended to address a particularly pressing problem – South Korea is running out of people to fill its ranks.
South Korean men are required to complete at least 18 months of military service, with some exempted or assigned alternative service.
But decades of falling birth rates are rapidly shrinking the population from which the military can draw its conscripts.
South Korea's total fertility rate stood at 0.8 in 2025, far below the 2.1 children per woman generally considered necessary to maintain a stable population without migration.
Around 1 million babies were born annually in South Korea in the early 1970s. By 2022, that number had fallen to just 249,000 and the fertility rate had dropped to 0.78, a level the government described as “unprecedented in world history.”
South Korea's population is projected to fall from around 52 million in 2024 to 36 million by 2072. Within the same time frame, the proportion of people aged 65 and older is projected to surge from 19.2% to 47.7% – meaning nearly half the population could be elderly.
“The demographic rationale is explicit and quantifiable,” Dongyoun Cho, a senior fellow for advanced technologies, national security and defense at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS-Europe), told Anadolu. “The active force has fallen to around 450,000, at just over 90% of required manning.”
But AI cannot simply replace every soldier who disappears from the ranks, she cautioned.
“AI substitutes selectively, not one-for-one – it is most credible in persistent surveillance, logistics and other manpower-intensive tasks,” Cho said. “The force will shrink regardless of AI. The question is what a smaller force can still do.”
South Korea is pursuing several programs aimed at building autonomous and AI capabilities across its armed forces, with the Future National Defense Strategy Committee putting AI and unmanned forces on the agenda, she said.
The Army aims to introduce more than 50,000 training drones by 2029, enough to provide one drone per squad, the Korea Herald reported in April, enabling service members to acquire basic drone operating skills and practical experience.
The Army's TIGER Plus program also envisions integrating AI, drones and other advanced technologies across the force by 2040.
In the air, South Korea is developing the LOWUS unmanned combat aircraft, envisioned as a “loyal wingman” that could operate alongside crewed fighters such as the country's KF-21.
At sea, the Navy's Sea Ghost concept is aimed at creating a force in which crewed warships operate alongside unmanned systems using AI.
But Cho argued that Seoul's technological ambitions are moving faster than its ability to put them into practice.
“Political will is running ahead of the ecosystem that has to deliver it,” she said, pointing to the reorganization of the Drone Operations Command after its initial creation was acknowledged as hasty.
And the biggest obstacles may not be the AI models themselves.
“The practical obstacles are less about algorithms than about integration – interoperability across platforms and services, test and certification bottlenecks, communications resilience under jamming, safety assurance and operator training,” Cho said.
Those challenges are compounded, she added, by military acquisition systems designed to purchase hardware rather than software that is continuously updated.
The gap between South Korea's ambitions and its ability to implement them will be “the defining feature of the next several years,” she said.
South Korea is hardly alone in racing to integrate AI and autonomous systems into its armed forces.
But Cho said Seoul differs from Washington and Beijing “less in scale than in motivation and structure.”
The US and China are investing in military AI on a much larger scale and across a wider range of applications.
South Korea, however, has an “unusually explicit demographic rationale,” Cho said, alongside an export-oriented defense industry and the need to ensure its systems remain interoperable with those of its US ally.
Japan has historically taken a more incremental approach, though that may now be changing, she added.
Tokyo is moving to revise its three major national security documents, with AI-enabled decision-making and unmanned systems reportedly among the issues under consideration.
According to media reports, Japan is also considering utilizing cutting-edge AI systems under its preemptive cyber defense policy such as US company Anthropic's Claude Mythos.
Rather than seeing the developments as a single race for AI military supremacy, Cho said each country is responding to its own strategic pressures.
“Rather than a race with a single scoreboard, these are programs shaped by quite different drivers and constraints – and (South) Korea's may prove one of the more instructive cases of adoption under demographic pressure,” she said.
Putting increasingly autonomous technology into military operations brings a different set of problems.
For Cho, three are particularly concerning: AI systems could misidentify targets or make errors in chaotic environments; human operators could place too much trust in machine-generated recommendations; and faster automated decision-making could increase the risk of military escalation.
All three carry particular weight on the Korean Peninsula.
Real-world conditions, Cho said, are “far harder than those in which systems are trained and tested.”
Under intense pressure, operators could also defer to recommendations generated by AI, weakening meaningful human control even when formal “human-in-the-loop” requirements remain in place.
Speed is another issue.
AI can process information and recommend action far more quickly than conventional military decision-making systems. While that can provide an advantage, it could also leave humans with less time to question what a system is telling them, Cho said.
That, Cho said, is “particularly consequential on a peninsula where warning times are already measured in minutes.”
Cho expects AI to move from an experimental capability to a structural part of South Korea's defense posture, shaping how the country designs its military rather than simply being added to existing forces.
The Army's TIGER Plus blueprint, which targets force-wide application by 2040, already points in that direction.
AI could help accelerate the process from detecting a potential target to deciding how to respond, including by integrating information from reconnaissance satellites. It could also support military command decisions and use predictive logistics to identify equipment problems before they occur, she said.
“The trajectory points toward a smaller but more automated force, and toward autonomy becoming a component of Korea's defense-export offer as well,” Cho added.
But whether that transformation succeeds, she argued, will depend on more than technological capability.
“The decisive variable will be whether governance keeps pace with adoption – assurance and safety cases, doctrine and interoperability with the United States and other partners.”
Countries that deploy military AI “responsibly and demonstrably will also be the ones trusted as suppliers and allies,” she predicted.

Brazilian exports of meat and other animal products to the European Union have been suspended following the introduction of updated EU animal health and food safety requirements, but shipments can resume once Brazilian authorities demonstrate compliance with the new rules, the European Commission said Friday.
"Once they can show compliance, exports to the European Union of these products from Brazil will be able to resume," European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told reporters in Brussels.
The EU suspended imports of Brazilian animals and animal-origin products intended for human consumption on Thursday, pending assurances that the country's exports comply with EU rules.
The measures affect products including beef, poultry, eggs, honey and animal casings.
EU rules require imports of animal-origin products for human consumption to meet the bloc's animal and public health standards, including requirements concerning residues from veterinary medicines.
Gill said the EU's rules on antimicrobial resistance apply equally and without discrimination to European producers and those from third countries seeking access to the bloc's single market.
He said the EU had engaged with its trading partners and provided support to help them meet the new requirements.

Netanyahu partners renew calls for removal of Gazans as Israeli election nears
JERUSALEM, Sept 4 - Two Israeli ministers floated proposals this week for the mass removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, resurfacing an idea voiced repeatedly by right-wing politicians over the past three years as they seek to rally supporters ahead of an election.
The calls by two of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political allies have revived Palestinian fears that Israel ultimately aims to forcibly expel them from Gaza despite U.S.-led diplomatic efforts to end the conflict there.
Far-right security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir laid out a seven-year plan for removing Gaza's population through "voluntary emigration" during a press conference on Thursday night. He said he would seek the creation of a "ministry in charge of emigration" in the next government.
"Instead of illusions of peace now, we need actions of emigration now," he said. "Instead of (them) digging tunnels, it’s time to pack suitcases," referring to tunnels dug under Gaza by Hamas before the war.
Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party said in a statement on Thursday that Turkey, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo were being considered as potential destinations.
Ismail Al-Thawabta, director of the Hamas government media office, said: "The Palestinian people are deeply rooted in their land and will not be intimidated by such threats."
Israel is due to hold a general election on October 27. It will be the first since Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, triggered an Israeli military campaign that laid waste to Gaza, which has a population of more than two million.
An October 2025, U.S.-backed, ceasefire halted large-scale fighting, but it has not ended Israeli strikes or produced progress on a plan for permanent peace.
FEARS OF A NEW 'NAKBA'
Ben-Gvir's comments followed those of Defence Minister Israel Katz, from Netanyahu's Likud party, who said on Wednesday there was "no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration".
“We are fully prepared to move them out if it becomes possible — by sea, by air, by every way possible. Egypt is not willing, so it won’t be through them," he said during an online conference hosted by Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.
Netanyahu's office did not immediately provide comment.
Polls suggest Netanyahu, who has led the most right-wing coalition in Israeli history, could lose power next month, his security credentials still shaken by the 2023 attack — though analysts say he can't be written off.
Israel's defence ministry in 2025 established an office tasked with overseeing “voluntary emigration” from Gaza, after comments by U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting Gazans could be permanently displaced.
Trump later backed away from the idea, which faced strong resistance from Arab states and was widely rejected internationally. Israel reportedly sounded out several African countries as potential resettlement sites.
Netanyahu has said he supports what his government has described as "voluntary emigration" from Gaza, but that far-right ministers' goals of re-establishing Jewish settlements in the territory are unrealistic. Israeli officials have denied intending to transfer Gaza's population out by force.
Calls for resettlement of Gazans have prompted fears among Palestinians of a new "Nakba" (catastrophe), the name given to the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians who fled or were driven from their homes in the wake of the 1948 war that accompanied the founding of the state of Israel.
The Gaza Strip is central to Palestinian hopes of statehood in territory captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
GENOCIDE ACCUSATIONS
The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies.
More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, according to Gaza health authorities.
A U.N. inquiry determined that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, arguing that its killings, siege and destruction were carried out with the intent to destroy Palestinian life in the enclave.
Israel, which is fighting a genocide case at the International Court of Justice, rejects genocide allegations as politically motivated and says that its military campaign targets Hamas, not Gaza’s civilian population.
This week, Ben-Gvir posted an AI-generated video depicting dozens of Palestinian prisoners on a conveyor belt, entering a prison facility. They emerge from the other side emaciated, distressed and in tears.
Ben-Gvir later deleted the video, after it had amassed millions of views on X. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a crowded Gaza City displacement camp, some Palestinians said that they believed the latest Israeli calls were an election ploy.
They also said Gaza was their land and they would never leave it.
"We will die on the land of Gaza," said one resident, 52-year-old Mohammed Abu Al-Qumbuz. "We were born on it, our children grew up on it, so it is very difficult to think of leaving." REUTERS

Valentyn Mondryivskyi, Deputy Head of the Kyiv City State Administration, emphasized that the format of schooling may continue to change. At the same time, the safety of children and employees of educational institutions remains the main criterion.

How the Chinese Government Has Controlled the Narrative on the Tibet Floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

As rescue efforts have continued on both sides of the border following the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, a fight over how the disaster is being reported has been growing in intensity on social media. The dispute centers on the claims and counterclaims following a story by the BBC’s China correspondent, Laura Bicker, about how China is censoring videos of the floods.
Bicker said videos of the landslide and flood surge sweeping through Gyirong Port on the border was scrubbed from the internet, in part, because Beijing fears instability in the politically sensitive region of Tibet.
Some social media users, however, have posted screenshots of the footage used by the BBC, pointing out it had actually been shown in the Chinese media. One Chinese journalist put it bluntly: “Never seen the BBC spread rumors so blatantly.” Another X user said the “middle ground often gets lost” in heated debates like this over Chinese censorship.
The Chinese government has long complained about what it sees as Western media “bias” in reporting on Tibet. Its supporters seem to have doubled down on this narrative this week on social media, zeroing in on the BBC.
But Chinese social media users, both inside and outside China, have long dealt with the authorities exercising control over information. This has certainly been the case in the aftermath of the floods, too.
As Bicker noted in her report, the most concrete example is the deletion of videos showing the massive wave of mud and water swallowing Gyirong Port. The footage was initially circulated on the platforms Weixin and RedNote, but users later could not access it.
Another form of control has been the restricted access for independent and foreign journalists. Allyson Horn of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation said she had made repeated requests to travel to Tibet, but was denied. Other foreign journalists have similarly been blocked. This makes it difficult, if not impossible, for foreign media to independently verify the Chinese government’s account of what happened there.
The absence of independent reporting, combined with the removal of footage from social media, has allowed the Chinese state media to dominate the narrative. This reflects a longstanding tendency in Chinese media to avoid material that could cause social instability or public panic.
Coverage of the Tibet floods by the state-controlled media has focused heavily on the People’s Liberation Army rescue operations, President Xi Jinping’s leadership during the crisis, and Premier Li Qiang’s visit to the disaster zone. There has also been some coverage of efforts to reopen roads and the delivery of disaster-relief supplies to affected residents.
But as the Guardian has noted, there has been much less reporting about how the disaster has affected local villagers, their homes, and communities. On the Nepali side of the border, meanwhile, foreign journalists have been able to interview survivors without restrictions.
Critics also say the Chinese government is hiding the true number of casualties. The problem with these contested claims is that no outsiders – whether they be critics or not – have been able to verify the death toll due to the restricted access to the disaster site.
China’s media environment has, at times, been less controlled than it is today.
On May 12, 2008, an earthquake measuring 8.0 on the Richter scale struck Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people and leaving millions homeless. Chinese state media provided extensive live coverage almost as soon as the quake struck. This continued for weeks, with China Central Television regularly updating the death toll and reporting extensively on rescue efforts.
Foreign media did raise questions about whether lives had been unnecessarily lost due to the collapse of poorly constructed school buildings. Foreign journalists also questioned whether justice would be served for the families of the victims. Chinese media reported on some of these controversies, including questioning whether the local government had done the proper quality control checks on school construction.
At the beginning, the coverage represented a major breakthrough in Chinese media reporting of emergencies and natural disasters. Its “unprecedented openness” was widely observed by Western media. But within weeks, the government had begun to clamp down on information about the schools for fear the issue could drive anti-government sentiment.
As a general practice, China’s state media outlets are instructed to emphasize “positive reporting” during times of crisis, while censors remove criticisms of government responses or culpability online.
The media coverage of a fatal train accident in the city of Wenzhou in 2011 was a good example.
Research shows that, unlike the Sichuan earthquake, the government kept a tight control on what was permissible in the media. The authorities ordered media outlets not to send reporters to the scene, limited the frequency of their reporting, and instructed them not to link the story to high-speed rail development. Journalists were also told not to investigate the accident’s causes or impact, or circulate personal microblogs on the incident.
Instead, they were urged to seek “moving” stories of bravery and sacrifice, such as local blood donations. The aim was to evoke love and compassion in the wake of the disaster.
When Xi came to power in 2012, the government’s concerns over potential challenges to its rule led to even more tightening on Chinese media and social media. The media’s handling of the Tibet floods is now following this pattern of restricted coverage and emphasizing positive news.
The disaster has also occurred at a time of growing distrust between China and the West. This seems to be adding to the perceptions of biased coverage. None of this is helped by the logistical difficulties in accessing both the disaster site and first-hand sources of information.
Chinese restrictions are making it harder for Western journalists to independently verify what is happening. The resulting information gap is raising suspicions in the West and criticism of censorship and biased coverage in Chinese media.
And that criticism, in turn, may reinforce Beijing’s belief that Western reporting on Tibet is inherently biased, giving it another reason to restrict information.
This article was originally published on The Conversation. Read the original article.

Ukraine must develop alternative routes to maintain access to global markets - experts

Ukraine must develop alternative export routes, including through Moldova, in order to fulfill contracts and avoid losing its position in global markets. Details
We have seen this initiative and closely followed the visit of the President of Ukraine to Moldova—it was a very interesting meeting. This initiative is officially called the Odesa Triangle. What is this Odesa Triangle? It means developing and further expanding logistics through Moldova—so, we have the Odesa region, Moldova, and the ports of Constanța
She noted that over the past seven months, 1.5 million tonnes of cargo have already been transported through Moldova, which is 35% more than during the same period last year. As part of the "Odesa Triangle," these volumes are planned to increase by at least 10%. In addition, the development of the route is of long-term significance.
So, the Moldovan route will not be shut down. If it is developed, it will remain in place for the future
Oleksii Buriachenko, President of the International Institute for Security Studies, said that the countries of the Black Sea region should be involved in such initiatives as much as possible.
Such projects should be scaled up not only to include Moldova, Romania, and Turkey, but also to involve all the countries of the Black Sea region as much as possible, as well as everything that follows the logistics routes we need—not only to Europe, but also to the Middle East and the countries of the South Caucasus, among others

Today, by the way, we have a state program to encourage the purchase of Ukrainian-made equipment. This is part of the broader framework, where there is cashback and similar measures. It is simply very small in scale and needs to be expanded

Palestinian sources initially suggested Israeli-backed militias were responsible, but Hamas sources later said an Israeli special forces unit had carried out the operation directly.
The two incidents have brought renewed attention to the activities of Palestinian armed groups reportedly operating with Israeli support.
Israel's Palestinian proxies
An investigation published by Haaretz in late August, based on testimonies from Israeli soldiers and officers, satellite imagery and conversations with Gaza residents, identified five-armed militias operating at six locations across the Strip and receiving Israeli financial and military support.
According to the investigation, the Israeli army and Shin Bet maintain close coordination with the groups, which are primarily hostile to Hamas.
An Israeli Air Force officer quoted by Haaretz said the government, army and Shin Bet send armed and trained militias into Gaza to carry out security missions, while the Air Force is instructed to protect them during their operations.
The groups are tasked with pursuing Hamas and other Palestinian faction members, conducting raids and kidnappings, gathering intelligence and operating in areas where Israeli forces face difficulties moving directly, according to Haaretz.
They have also been accused of attacking Palestinian civilians, looting property and burning homes, as well as participating in efforts to drive residents from certain areas.
The Yasser Abu Shabab group has emerged as one of the most prominent of these formations. It operated mainly in southern Gaza, particularly Rafah, and openly acknowledged cooperation with Israel.
In July 2025, Abu Shabab told an Israeli television channel that his group received support from the Israeli military.
Despite Abu Shabab's subsequent death under unclear circumstances, Haaretz reported that Israel's militia strategy continued to develop, particularly following the October 2025 ceasefire.
The groups do not appear capable of replacing the Israeli military or independently controlling Gaza. Instead, their role appears focused on specific security and intelligence operations, allowing Israel to use local Palestinian actors against its opponents.
'Tools of Israel'
Gaza-based political analyst Ahed Ferwana told TNA that Israel's reliance on the militias forms part of a strategy to create local Palestinian forces capable of carrying out operations inside Gaza.
"The militias cannot be regarded as independent Palestinian forces given their Israeli funding, weapons and operational coordination," he said.
He warned that their expansion could deepen Palestinian divisions by shifting confrontation towards armed clashes between Palestinian groups.
Akram Attallah, a political analyst in Gaza, told TNA that the militias are "tools of Israel […] Tel Aviv uses them when it wants to conduct operations indirectly but deploys its own forces when an operation exceeds their capabilities".
Attallah said the abduction of Moen al-Arabeed demonstrated the overlap between direct Israeli military operations and those carried out through locally backed armed groups.
He added that Israel can shift between using Palestinian proxies and deploying its own forces depending on an operation's nature and scale, making the distinction between the militias and the Israeli military increasingly difficult to separate.
For Attallah, the development of these groups reflects a broader Israeli effort to create Palestinian actors capable of performing security functions inside Gaza, potentially reshaping the Strip's security landscape and deepening divisions between Palestinian factions.

Civil society opposition to Sudan's Burhan-led dialogue mounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:43:35 UTC
21:43:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan's civil society 'stronger than credited' as opposition mounts to Burhan's dialogue, AU Commission endorsement
Sudan's civil society is "stronger than people give it credit for", analysts told The New Arab, after a Sudanese political coalition condemned the endorsement of a new intra-Sudanese dialogue led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan by the African Union's (AU) Commission.
The Sudanese Declaration of Principles coalition issued a formal complaint to the AU's Peace and Security Council on Wednesday over the commission's endorsement of Burhan's 'Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue.'
The coalition, made up of several political groups including the Somoud alliance and the Sudan Liberation Movement, accused the endorsement of contradicting previous AU statements on a humanitarian truce, effectively endorsing the partition of the country.
They also accused the commission of violating the 2021 suspension of Sudan from the AU that followed Burhan's coup against the civilian post-revolutionary government, and said the move gave political cover to Burhan's regime and neglected their own efforts to promote an alternative dialogue led by civil society.
Kholood Khair, founder and director of Confluence Advisory, a think-and-do-tank founded in Khartoum, told The New Arab: "The opposition believes it's important to register their lack of support for Burhan's process, but also register their discontent with the African Union because there have been concerns that the African Union would be pushing for recognition of Burhan's process as part of their efforts to bring about a national political process in Sudan."
The dialogue was announced by Burhan earlier in May with a stated intention of completing a transition to civilian rule.
The AU Commission said on Monday that it "welcomes" Burhan's initiative and that it "reinforces the African Union's roadmap and the track of the Quintet Mechanism within a coherent strategy led by Sudanese stakeholders."
The Quintet, which includes the AU, UN, Intergovernmental Authority on Development, EU and Arab League, was formed to bring about an end to the war that erupted in 2023 after fighting broke out between the Sudanese army and the rival Rapid Support Forces.
Khair explained that Burhan's initiative initially excluded most of Sudan's anti-military opposition, but later gave amnesty to groups and figures to participate in the dialogue.
"The problem with that is that, if some agreed and came and accepted temporary immunity, it would be like them accepting they had actually done wrong, that they had deserved the indictments in the first place, that they had been guilty of crimes, and that they were now coming to the talk in part so they would not be liable for prosecution."
Khair added that former dictator Omar al-Bashir, who was ousted in a revolution that preceded the 2021 coup and civil war, did a similar thing between 2014 and 2017: "we've seen this all before."
Leena Badri, a nonresident fellow for TIMEP, told The New Arab that the condemnation from the group was "no surprise", given the opposition's aversion to the Sudanese Armed Forces and the former National Congress Party that had for decades ruled the country.
"They envision that such efforts [by Burhan] carry a high risk of normalising the return of individuals formally affiliated with the party, in addition to normalising military rule and control over a political process."
African Union Commission endorsement 'win' for Burhan, but civilians needed for government
Badri added that the commission's endorsement was a "win for the SAF [Sudanese armed forces] because it offers legitimacy to their political efforts, and solidifies their position as being a party capable of developing and seeking out processes for dialogue and incorporating civilians into that process".
Sudan's armed forces have, in recent months, won a string of battlefield victories against the RSF, reconnecting a vital road between the semi-besieged city of El-Obeid in North Kordofan and Omdurman, the sister city of the capital Khartoum.
The army has also taken in a wave of defections from the RSF, despite the group's moves to form and solidify its own parallel government.
Despite the battlefield success, however, Khair said that the opposition's statement against the initiative and the AU Commission's endorsement show that "civil society has been stronger than people give it credit for, and that's what has changed since the revolution".
"The war, despite wanting to diminish the power of civilian actors, has not managed to do that," she said, adding, "even if Burhan makes territorial gains, he will not be able to rule without some kind of buy-in from civilian actors and politicians."
Further complicating the situation is the fact that the endorsement of the AU Commission of Burhan's dialogue reveals "a bit of schizophrenia within the AU", where one side of the body has moved against Burhan politically while the other endorses it.
Khair explained that the AU Commissioner, Mahmoud Ali Yousif, is pro-Burhan, but that his position runs against major concerns within the AU about legitimising coups and the formation of parallel governments in Africa, which has been rocked by several coups across the continent, in particular the Sahel, in recent years.
"The biggest danger is actually that the AU can undermine itself and it can undermine the quintet," in their efforts to push for a peace process.
The backlash to Burhan's initiative has also prompted rumours that those involved in the process may pull out on grounds that being involved with the military is becoming a huge liability.
Ultimately, Khair said that the opposition's condemnation of both processes has revealed that "It's very difficult for armed actors now in Sudan to rule by themselves as a result of the popular political movement that has been a key part of civilian Sudanese politics since the revolution".

U.S. Air Force’s EC-130H flies final mission alongside EA-37B
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:43:04 UTC
21:43:04 KST

- A U.S. Air Force EC-130H flew its final flight on September 3, in formation for the first time with its EA-37B replacement over Southern Arizona.
- The EC-130H has flown the Compass Call electronic attack mission since 1982, while the EA-37B has flown its own combat missions against Iran since March.
A U.S. Air Force EC-130H Compass Call aircraft flew in formation with an EA-37B Compass Call for the first time on September 3, in what the Air Force identified as the EC-130H’s final flight, marking the end of the propeller-driven aircraft’s role in the service’s electronic attack mission.
Both aircraft belong to the 55th Electronic Combat Group, flying together over Southern Arizona near the group’s base at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base. The formation flight represented the handoff between the two aircraft types: the EC-130H, a modified C-130 that has flown the Compass Call jamming mission since 1982, and the EA-37B, its Gulfstream G550-based successor.
The Compass Call mission disrupts, denies and degrades enemy command-and-control networks, using electronic attack to jam communications and radar systems that adversaries rely on to coordinate their forces. The 55th Electronic Combat Group, a geographically separated unit under the 55th Wing at Offutt Air Force Base, Nebraska, has been the Air Force’s only unit flying that mission.
The Air Force began retiring individual EC-130H aircraft years ago as EA-37Bs entered service. The 43rd Electronic Combat Squadron flew its last EC-130H mission in February 2024, becoming the first squadron under the 55th Electronic Combat Group to complete the switch. By this past spring, only a handful of EC-130H aircraft remained in the fleet, according to earlier reporting on the transition. The Air Force plans to field 10 EA-37Bs in total.
The EA-37B has already flown in combat. Two of the aircraft deployed from Davis-Monthan through RAF Mildenhall in the United Kingdom to Souda Bay, Crete, in late March, then entered the fight against Iran as part of Operation Epic Fury, which began February 28. Their mission there mirrored the EC-130H’s traditional role: jamming enemy communications and blinding air defense radar.
Over nearly four decades, EC-130H aircraft supported combat operations including Desert Storm, Iraqi Freedom, Enduring Freedom and Inherent Resolve. One of the type’s original aircraft, tail number 1587, flew close to 29,000 hours before its own retirement in 2020, including almost 11,000 hours in direct support of combat missions.

New Stryker brigade at Fort Carson receives first vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:40:09 UTC
21:40:09 KST

- The newly redesignated 3rd Stryker Brigade, 4th Infantry Division, began receiving Stryker vehicles at Fort Carson, Colorado, on September 2.
- The brigade, formerly an armored unit built around M1A2 Abrams tanks, completed its conversion after testing at Fort Irwin's Project Convergence Capstone 6 exercise.
Soldiers assigned to the newly redesignated 3rd Stryker Brigade, 4th Infantry Division, began receiving Stryker vehicles at Fort Carson, Colorado, on September 2, marking the next step in the unit’s conversion from a tank formation to a wheeled Stryker force.
The brigade, known as the Iron Brigade, previously operated as the 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team, built around M1A2 Abrams tanks and Bradley Fighting Vehicles. Its last Abrams tank left Fort Carson in mid-July, heading to Fort Irwin, California, for Project Convergence Capstone 6, an exercise where the brigade tested emerging technology including a new digital command-and-control system before completing its final conversion steps and taking on the Stryker Brigade designation.
The tanks the brigade gave up are headed to Army depots for overhaul, after which they will be redistributed to other armored units across the service, according to earlier Army reporting on the transition.
With Strykers now arriving at Fort Carson, soldiers will move into new equipment training, platform familiarization and leader development, covering vehicle capabilities, maintenance and digital systems. The Army has said the brigade will also see a personnel realignment as infantry soldiers arrive to fill out the battalions needed for a Stryker-based force structure, which relies more heavily on dismounted infantry than an armored formation built around tanks.
The Stryker is an eight-wheeled, armored combat vehicle that trades the heavier armor and firepower of a tank for greater speed and lower logistical demands, letting units move under their own power over longer distances instead of requiring the heavy-equipment transporters and rail movements that come with fielding tanks.
The conversion is tied to a larger organizational shift. The 4th Infantry Division has been reassigned to America’s First Corps, which supports U.S. Army Pacific, a headquarters focused on projecting land power across the Pacific and sustaining a regional military presence. Army officials have said the Iron Brigade’s move to Strykers is meant to give the division a more rapidly deployable, digitally connected force to support that mission.
“We absolutely honor the legacy of the 3rd Armored Brigade and their storied history,” said early Col. Nick Sinclair, the brigade’s commander, in July as the unit prepared for its final conversion steps. The brigade has spent decades as one of the Army’s principal armored formations, deploying to the Middle East and Europe and rotating repeatedly through the Army’s National Training Center.

Human Rights Are Essential to Australia’s Interests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:40:00 UTC
21:40:00 KST

World politics feels like it is in disarray. Rules intended to regulate the behavior of all countries and institutions seem not to matter. International human rights norms now appear decidedly unfashionable, even in Australia, a country that should be one of the staunchest defenders of global human rights, where I have just spent two weeks meeting with government officials and civil society.
Transactional power politics increasingly disregard internationally agreed rules, enabling powerful governments, from China and Russia to the United States and their allies, to accelerate violations of human rights with few consequences.
But the longing for human rights is not going away. Respecting them remains critical for so many people around the world, especially those facing the most severe repression. In recent years, protesters throughout Asia – often led by young people – have fought for rights and equality in Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and India, even at the cost of their lives.
Democracies that remain committed to human rights and a rules-based world order should recognize that. Instead of cowering to this geopolitical moment, they should seize the uncertainty by doubling down and recognizing that rights are central to their long-term national interests. Canberra should be first in line.
Instead, Australia and other democracies have become focused on military security, diminishing the focus on human rights. In the past year, Australia has prioritized signing new regional defense and security agreements while doing little to re-energize a rules-based world order.
To be sure, military and cyber threats pose real dangers in this new world disorder. But coercion from abroad can take many forms. It also works by intimidating exiled dissidents, silencing journalists, corrupting democratic institutions, and exporting surveillance. Defense pacts alone cannot address these tactics.
Governments such as Australia’s need to recognize that defending civil society and a free press throughout the region and beyond are not luxuries but central to a democratic resurgence. Doing so means weaving human rights into domestic and foreign policies.
Australia should establish an Asia Democracy Fund together with other democratic governments to support embattled independent journalists, human rights defenders, and civil society organizations, particularly those already endangered or in exile, and groups that cannot safely access funding otherwise. Australia, like Canada, could also provide a safe haven to threatened rights defenders by establishing a special immigration pathway for them.
Australia should also support independent groups documenting serious abuses, particularly important at a time when the United States and other governments are attacking the international justice system. The country should stand up for the embattled International Criminal Court. It should also advance international justice by taking on some of the world’s worst atrocities in its own court system, a practice known as universal jurisdiction. Unfortunately, few countries in the Asia-Pacific region have been willing to use universal jurisdiction to investigate and prosecute alleged war criminals.
Issue by issue – from international crimes to technology to labor rights – Australia and other governments need to push back against increasing global repression. A comprehensive foreign policy approach in multilateral and bilateral forums is crucial, but so is adopting effective domestic laws and practices. This can include continuing to strengthen laws to prevent importing goods made with forced labor and stronger laws on privacy that regulate technology.
When governments that care about rights come together on the international stage to promote and protect them, and at the same time create laws and policies that demonstrate their own state won’t become a refuge for rights abusers, there is a much greater chance that together they can fend off the pressure being placed on human rights protections.
Rights-respecting democracies and like-minded allies need to find strength in numbers. They should create diplomatic and economic cover, to coalesce around key norms and tools, and international law more generally, while containing – and reversing – the damage done. A global alliance in support of a rules and rights-based international order can act in concert to protect the International Criminal Court or the United Nations’ independent fact-finding mechanisms, or the integrity of human rights treaties under attack. Australia is well positioned to present itself as a reliable leader and partner in this pursuit.
The international system that has been built over decades to protect and promote human rights has never worked perfectly or consistently. It has at times failed, at great cost to many people. But it has constrained abusive governments, given smaller and middle powers like Australia leverage to promote reform, reduced risks to marginalized populations by providing some level of global and regional stability, and offered victims of atrocities an opportunity for justice.
The rules-based order will not be saved by post-Cold War nostalgia, nor by international law that goes unenforced. It will survive and flourish only if democracies make human rights practical, a shared pursuit, and costly for others to violate. Australia, I came away believing, still has the standing to lead that effort.

Body of King Oyo Nyimba, once world's youngest monarch, returns to Uganda for burial
KAMPALA, Sept 4 - The body of Uganda's King Oyo Nyimba, who became the world's youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne at the age of three in 1995, arrived back in the country on Friday after his death from cancer, and ahead of burial on September 12.
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV of Tooro Kingdom, one of many traditional monarchies in the country and located near the Rwenzori Mountains in Uganda's west, died on August 27 in the United States where he was receiving treatment.
He was 34.
Uganda is a constitutional republic and executive power is vested in an elected head of state. But the monarchies of the country's several ancient kingdoms that reigned before colonialism still exist and wield enormous cultural and social influence.
A video of his taking the throne in 1995 shows a little boy sitting in his chair playing with a toy, his small body almost disappearing underneath the huge royal crown and robes. Taking the role at such a young age endeared him to many.
Oyo Nyimba's body arrived aboard a chartered flight at the country's Entebbe international airport where President Yoweri Museveni was among a small crowd of dignitaries waiting to receive it.
"We don't really believe that his majesty is no longer with us, (it is) as if we are still dreaming and I wish it could really be a dream," said lawmaker Jennifer Mujungu, whose constituency lies in Oyo Nyimba's kingdom.
Museveni walked to the casket, draped in both the country's and the kingdom's flags, laid a wreath on it, and bowed.
The casket was then loaded onto a military helicopter and transported to Tooro Kingdom where official mourning ceremonies will begin, lasting up to burial on September 12.
"It is a painful moment for us...someone who went laughing, someone who had a whole life ahead of him," said Davis Mugenyi, a member of the royal family who was at the airport to receive his body.
The king was a U.N. ambassador championing the fight against HIV and AIDS, and the U.N. paid tribute to him.
The prime minister of the kingdom, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, said last week the king, who was unmarried, had left an heir and that "continuity of the Crown is assured." REUTERS

The suspect’s actions have been classified under Part 3 of Article 149, Part 2 of Article 156, Parts 2 and 3 of Article 301, and Parts 1, 3 and 4 of Article 301-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The prosecution will ask the court to impose pretrial detention without setting bail.

U.S. Marine Corps base runs active shooter drill in Jacksonville
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:34:51 UTC
21:34:51 KST

- Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island ran a four-hour active shooter and explosive threat exercise on September 3 with Jacksonville fire, police and federal agencies.
- The drill tested incident command, casualty response and interoperability, building on installation defense planning work done in January.
Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island in Jacksonville, Florida, ran a four-hour active shooter and explosive threat exercise on September 3, testing how the installation and local first responders would handle a complex security emergency inside an occupied office building.
The drill, called Exercise Urgent Response, combined Blount Island Command with Jacksonville fire and police, Florida state emergency managers and federal investigators. Simulated gunfire interrupted the workday as role players moved through stairwells, hallways and offices, forcing service members, civilian employees and contractors inside to decide in the moment whether to run, hide or fight.
Blount Island Command, a tenant command under Marine Corps Logistics Command, serves as the Marine Corps’ hub for maintaining and managing equipment stored aboard its Maritime Prepositioning Ships, vessels loaded with combat gear stationed around the world so Marine units can respond quickly during a crisis. The Jacksonville facility handles inspection, maintenance and distribution of that equipment when the ships return to port roughly every three years.
As the scenario unfolded, Marine Corps Police Department officers coordinated their response with the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office. People inside the building had to recognize the threat, find primary and alternate exits, report suspicious activity and respond appropriately once law enforcement arrived. Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department crews entered only after police secured the building, then triaged and treated simulated casualties before transport.
“It was a lot of great communication on all sides,” said Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department Capt. Shawn Hall. “By the time we arrived, the Marine Corps Police Department was already in place, already taking lifesaving steps and giving trauma care, so we could get in with medical treatment and transport.”
The scenario later expanded to include a simulated explosive device near the shoreline. The Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office Hazardous Devices Unit assessed the device and rendered it safe. Inside the installation’s emergency operations center, participants tracked the evolving situation and shared updates to maintain a common picture for decision-makers, with the Florida Division of Emergency Management providing state-level coordination and the Naval Criminal Investigative Service supporting intelligence sharing and exercise control.
The exercise built on operational planning work done in January, when the installation, Blount Island Command and local, state and federal partners examined how they would protect the facility and keep operations running during a major incident.
“The exercise successfully validated installation defense plans, mutual aid agreements and real-world interoperability with local, state and federal partners,” said Marine Corps Lt. Col. Beau Pillot, operations director for Blount Island Command. “Exercise Urgent Response bridged the gap between deliberate planning and real-world execution.”
The drill also tied into the Marine Corps’ 2026 National Preparedness Month theme, “Prepare Today. Protect Tomorrow,” part of the annual September observance encouraging emergency planning.
Evaluators from the participating agencies scored performance against the exercise’s objectives. Their findings will feed into a formal review process the Marine Corps will use to refine Blount Island’s response plans and shape future training exercises, though officials have not said when that review will be complete.

Russia Has Been Strapping FPV Drones to Shaheds for a Year, but the Trick Keeps Failing

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Has Been Strapping FPV Drones to Shaheds for a Year, but the Trick Keeps Failing
Russia has been experimenting for more than a year with Shahed-type drones as airborne carriers for smaller FPV drones, but the concept has proved unreliable and is rarely used, Ukrainian presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said on September 3.
According to Beskrestnov, Russian forces attach two FPV drones to a conventional Shahed or Gerbera drone, effectively using the larger aircraft to carry the smaller UAVs closer to their intended operating area.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The FPV drones are controlled through LTE modems using cellular networks and SIM cards once deployed.
“The effectiveness of this solution is very low, and the enemy uses it rarely—literally once a week or once every two weeks. The FPV often loses connection, control, and crashes,” Beskrestnov explained.
The concept could theoretically extend the operating range of short-range FPV drones by transporting them deep into Ukrainian territory before release. In practice, however, maintaining a reliable cellular connection while the smaller drone is in flight appears to be a significant limitation.
Beskrestnov also pointed to another constraint: the FPV drones can only be carried by conventional propeller-driven Shaheds.
“The FPV drones are attached to an ordinary Shahed. They would simply be blown off a jet-powered one,” he noted.
That distinction has become increasingly important as Russia shifts toward faster jet-powered Shahed variants in strikes against Kyiv, the surrounding region and other Ukrainian cities.
Moscow has increasingly relied on the faster models after Ukraine pushed interception rates against conventional Shahed-type drones above 90%, according to Beskrestnov.
Jet-powered variants are significantly harder to intercept because their higher speed leaves Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect, track, and engage them.
Earlier, reports emerged that a Ukrainian remotely operated machine-gun system originally designed for use across multiple combat platforms has now been adapted for aviation, with footage showing the Khyzhak module mounted aboard a helicopter and used to engage Russian Shahed-type drones.
