A computational model explains the sudden rise in societal division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:00:34 UTC
20:00:34 KST

As modern communication technology has doubled the number of close social ties people maintain, societies have fractured into deeply divided political camps. A computational model simulating human social behavior shows that simply having more connections past a certain threshold forces communities to splinter into polarized echo chambers. The research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Political polarization has risen sharply in the United States and other Western nations over the past two decades. During this same period, the average number of close friendships reported by individuals has nearly doubled, a trend coinciding with the public debut of smartphones and mass social media networks around 2008.
Stefan Thurner, Markus Hofer, and Jan Korbel, researchers at the Medical University of Vienna and the Complexity Science Hub Vienna, noticed the parallel timing of these two trends. They wanted to test whether the sheer volume of social connections might be driving the ideological divide.
To investigate this, the researchers focused on two well-documented features of human behavior: homophily and social balance. Homophily is the human tendency to seek out and befriend like-minded individuals. When people interact with those who share their views, they often reinforce each other’s beliefs, causing their opinions to align even more closely.
Social balance describes how groups of three people naturally seek comfortable, stable relationship dynamics. A balanced triad occurs when all three people are friends, or when two friends mutually dislike a third person.
Unbalanced triads cause psychological tension or social stress. This happens if one person tries to remain friends with two people who despise each other, or if three people all dislike one another. People naturally try to resolve this tension by either changing their opinions to match their friends or by distancing themselves from people who disagree with them.
To see how these basic social rules play out on a large scale, the research team built an agent-based computational model. In this virtual society, each simulated individual was assigned a mathematical profile representing a set of binary political stances on different topics.
Individuals in the simulation were connected in a network where relationships could be either positive or negative. A positive connection formed if two individuals shared a majority of their stances, acting as a virtual friendship. A negative connection formed if their stances opposed one another, acting as a rivalry or enmity.
The researchers used a mathematical algorithm to randomly select individuals and flip one of their political stances. After flipping an opinion, the model calculated the individual’s new level of cognitive dissonance, measured by how much they now agreed with their friends and disagreed with their enemies.
If the new opinion lowered their overall social stress, the individual kept the new stance. If the opinion increased their social stress, the individual rejected the change, though the model allowed a small probability of keeping it to represent occasional irrational behavior. As individuals updated their views, their positive and negative relationships shifted to maintain social balance.
The researchers ran this simulation multiple times, varying the average number of close connections each individual possessed. They tracked how the distribution of opinions across the entire population changed as the network became more interconnected.
The simulation revealed a sudden tipping point, which physicists call a phase transition. When the average number of close connections remained low, the virtual society maintained a diverse, cohesive blend of opinions. Small friend groups shared similar views, but these groups remained scattered and tolerant of the broader population.
Once the average number of connections surpassed a critical threshold of about five close friends, the societal structure abruptly collapsed into a highly polarized state. The numerous small, diverse clusters merged into two massive, opposing groups of roughly equal size.
Within each massive group, individuals held nearly identical opinions. Between the two groups, individuals held entirely opposite views and maintained strictly negative relationships with anyone on the other side.
Next, the researchers introduced radical influencers to the model. They assigned extreme, unchanging opinions to just two percent of the simulated population. These influencers never adjusted their stances to reduce social stress, but they still formed friendships and rivalries based on ideological alignment.
The presence of these rigid influencers changed the nature of the polarization tipping point. The transition from a cohesive society to a divided one became gradual rather than sudden. However, the splintering into opposing echo chambers began at an even lower threshold, occurring when individuals averaged just four and a half close connections.
To test if their model reflected reality, the research team compared their simulated results to real-world survey data. They analyzed data from large, multi-year surveys, including the Pew Research Center, which track both political ideology and the average number of close friendships among thousands of respondents.
The empirical data showed that ideological polarization in the United States remained relatively low and stable before 2010. Shortly after that time, the average number of close social ties increased, and polarization spiked rapidly.
The researchers found that their computational model accurately predicted both the timing and the magnitude of this real-world polarization spike. The model required no outside factors like economic changes or political campaigns to explain the divide. The mathematical rules of homophily and social balance, combined with an increasing number of social ties, were enough to produce the exact polarization trend seen in the survey data.
The study does present certain caveats. The computational model assumes every individual has the exact same sensitivity to cognitive dissonance and social stress. In reality, human beings display varied levels of tolerance for disagreement and differing levels of political engagement.
The simulation also uses a relatively fixed network structure. While relationships can switch between positive and negative, the underlying web of who knows whom does not fluidly dissolve and rewire over time. The authors note that real social media platforms use recommendation algorithms that constantly suggest new connections, which might amplify the clustering effect beyond what the current model captures.
One concerning finding from the model is a hysteresis effect, meaning the process is difficult to reverse. Once a society crosses the connectivity threshold and becomes highly polarized, simply reducing the number of connections back to the original level will not depolarize the population. A fractured society must drop its connectivity far below the initial tipping point to restore ideological cohesion.
Since reducing human connectivity is likely impossible in the digital age, the authors suggest alternative ways to raise the critical threshold. They suggest that educational efforts could train individuals to have a higher tolerance for opposing opinions, which mathematically prevents the phase transition. Disrupting the reach of radical influencers through content moderation could also delay the onset of extreme societal division.
The study, “Why more social interactions lead to more polarization in societies,” was authored by Stefan Thurner, Markus Hofer, and Jan Korbel.

How a Secret Orangutan Breeding Program Is Creating a Baby Boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

“It’s a girl!” Melissa Peterson exclaims.
Just outside the operating room, the hallway erupts in cheers. Joseph Dewane, an ob-gyn, has just delivered a healthy baby via C-section; Autumn Joi Goodwin-Samson, a neonatalist, tends to the newborn still slick with a waxy film.
It’s a successful delivery just like any other except for one, minor, difference: The patient is an orangutan.
Ruhana—or just “Ru” for short—is one of eight orangutan babies born in a collection of US zoos since the beginning of 2025. For these critically endangered primates, that’s a staggering figure. It’s also not random: The baby boom is the result of a meticulous breeding plan and decades of research to weave a conservation safety net, one birth at a time.
“It might seem like it was all a coincidence that everyone was born at the same time, but it was very carefully planned,” says Angie Selzer, a senior animal care specialist with the Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana and the Orangutan Species Survival Plan (SSP) program coordinator.
The SSP has been coordinating breeding recommendations since 1985; every two years, the program creates a breeding and transfer plan for animals at zoos accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA). Geneticists from the SSP consult a “studbook,” which contains the pedigree of all the animals in their system.
“We want to maintain a healthy and sustainable population that mimics the natural history of wild orangutans while ensuring successful mother-rearing of offspring,” Seltzer tells WIRED. Their recommendation accounts for a number of breeding factors, including underrepresented genetic lines, each animal’s unique personality, and group dynamics—always aiming for the lowest relation between breeding pairs.
“We’ve had a very good, happy outcome,” she says. It all started in February 2025 when the Indianapolis Zoo welcomed Edi, a healthy baby boy. After that, Weila was delivered at the Hogle Zoo in Utah in June; Bintang arrived at the Los Angeles Zoo, and in December, the Memphis Zoo welcomed Ruhana. Peterson, the associate primates curator at the Memphis Zoo says being present for that moment was a “remarkable experience.” The run of babies has continued this year, with baby girls born at the Cameron Park Zoo in Waco, Texas, Sedgwick County Zoo in Wichita, Kansas, and Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana. Just a few months ago, the Denver Zoo welcomed a baby boy named Rambutan.
Humans share over 90 percent of their DNA with orangutans, a figure well-evidenced in how they breed and give birth. Orangutans in the program are routinely given human birth control and human prenatal vitamins; they’re taught to pee on human pregnancy tests; they gestate for nearly nine months; and after humans, their offspring have the longest childhood of any mammal. While C-sections like Jahe’s are rare, some zoos keep ob-gyns on call for their orangutans and other primates.
“Looking at their eyes and their hands, it’s like a mirror,” says Matthew Lenyo, assistant curator of predators at Denver Zoo. “It’s humbling.”
As with humans, maternal behaviors are learned; training is a critical part of ensuring the health of orangutan babies. For first-time mom Hesty, the Sumatran orangutan at the Denver Zoo, training involved teaching her to pass the baby to and from keepers for essential health checks and nursing since Hesty’s mother had struggled with it.
For many zoos, prebirth training involves other orangutans in their care too. To be successful, this training requires a deep and hard-earned trust between keepers and these animals, and can prove invaluable if an orangutan cannot be cared for by their biological mother.
That happened at the Hogle Zoo, when Weila’s biological mom failed to bond with her. She was hand-reared by keepers while they prepared Acara—a proven foster who raised her younger brother—to take over as mom using a stuffed animal as a proxy. They slowly introduced the two to each other, rewarding Acara for properly handling Weila. “She also has a gentle behavior” and uses a very gentle touch, says Hannah Comstock, the animal care supervisor of primates at Hogle Zoo. The pair live together full-time now. Acara is a model parent, and Weila is thriving; she has even started adopting some of Acara’s mannerisms.
Still, zookeepers aim to be as hands-off as possible. “We do all this work, but then at the same time, the best outcome is when you’re not needed,” says Lenyo.
It’s estimated that there are around 100,000 Bornean orangutans and 11,000 Sumatran orangutans left in the wild. The population of Tapanuli orangutans is even more dire, with estimates indicating a few more than 700 are left in the wild. The rainforest habitat they rely on in their native Borneo and Sumatra is being razed to create palm oil plantations, and the great apes are also targeted by traffickers who kill orangutan mothers, kidnap their babies, and sell them on the black market as pets. Some estimates indicate that orangutans could go extinct in the wild within 50 years; some experts caution it could be even sooner, in the next 10 to 20 years.
While these new orangutan babies will not be released into the wild, they are a critical part of species conservation. Zookeepers call them ambassadors; when visitors can see the apes, abstract ideas like climate change and deforestation become more real.
But the captive population also has a direct impact on the well-being of wild and rehabilitated populations: Research conducted at AZA zoos on everything from disease management to quality of life is then relayed back to teams in Southeast Asia. Felicity Oram is a conservation practitioner and co-director of OrangJUGA, a Borneo-based conservation organization. Her research on orangutan’s teeth has been critical in the care of young orangutans rescued from the pet trade who live in rehabilitation and rescue centers. She quips that “captive orangutans can help their cousins in the wild and in rehabilitation centers just by opening their mouths.”
Before Oram’s research, estimating age was an imperfect science at best. “It’s very difficult with size,” Oram says. “It’s just like with human children—you go, ‘Isn’t that a cute 4-year-old!’ And then they tell you it’s 2.” She partnered with zoos, using data collected from captive orangutans to link tooth stages to behavioral and developmental stages. In turn, this research allowed rescuers to more accurately make critical decisions about nutrition, medical care, and socialization, giving these orangutans the best shot at having a successful life—and maybe one day having offspring of their own.

EXPLAINER: How a state election in Germany tests the far-right’s path to power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:59:50 UTC
19:59:50 KST

A state election in little-known Saxony-Anhalt is being watched across Europe for the shockwaves it could send through German national politics.
Voters on Sunday will elect a new state parliament in the mid-sized eastern region, home to less than 3% of Germany’s electorate.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) leads the polls and may form a state government, which would be the first far-right administration in a German state since 1949, after the Nazi regime fell and the Federal Republic was founded.
The political stakes far outweigh the state’s size. The AfD, which campaigns against immigration and is already the main opposition in the national parliament, is testing the “firewall” other parties have built to keep it from office.
A strong showing would hit Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s already-fragile coalition in Berlin, which has been weakened by a sluggish economy and infighting.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel has framed the contest as more than a state race. “We will form the government in Saxony-Anhalt,” she said. “We will also govern at the federal level.”
The far-right AfD has more than doubled its support in Saxony-Anhalt in five years. It took 20.8% in 2021. It now polls above 40%. 
 
Many observers credit lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund for driving the surge.
The 35-year-old lawmaker sells himself as a candidate of change and has already issued a “government program” plus a 100-day plan.
Immigration is the core of his pitch. He pledges to expel people without legal status “from the first minute,” expand deportation detention from dozens of places to hundreds and make asylum seekers work or lose benefits.
Weekly magazine Der Spiegel put him on its cover as “Germany’s most dangerous man.” Siegmund leaned into the label, signing copies for cameras and social media.
Critics say his moderate public image hides his ties to a tougher, more hardline network around him. The country’s domestic intelligence service has classified the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch as a “confirmed right-wing extremist” organization, citing anti-democratic goals and members’ ties to far-right groups.
Far-right candidate Siegmund’s closest rival is Premier Sven Schulze of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). 
 
The 47-year-old conservative took office only in January, after longtime leader Reiner Haseloff stepped down following nearly 15 years in power.
Schulze is less established than his predecessor and has struggled to turn name recognition into votes. The CDU presents itself as the responsible center-right choice and argues that an AfD government would scare off investors and isolate a state that lives from the European single market.
Schulze has repeatedly warned on the campaign trail that an AfD government would be an “economic catastrophe” for Saxony-Anhalt, since the far-right party is seeking to take Germany out of the euro and the visa-free Schengen area, causing alarm among investors.
“The AfD has no contacts whatsoever to make things better in Europe. It only wants out of the EU. That would be an economic catastrophe,” he said in a recent interview.
“I am the only one who, with the CDU, can keep the AfD from power and avert harm from Saxony-Anhalt.”
Polls from several institutes put the AfD at about 40% to 43%, well ahead of every other party. However, coming first is not the same as winning the state.
Seats are shared only among parties that clear the 5% threshold and enter the Landtag, so how many make it across that line can decide whether the poll leader also gets a majority.
The CDU, the center-right party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Premier Sven Schulze, is at about 22% to 23%, down from 37.1% in the 2021 state election. Of Schulze’s coalition partners, the Social Democrats are at about 7% to 9%. The pro-business Free Democrats are at about 3%, below the threshold.
The socialist Left Party is at about 11% to 13%. The Greens sit at about 5% to 6%, on the edge of the cutoff. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, a newer left-populist party that opposes military support for Ukraine, is at about 3% to 4%.
Sunday night will therefore turn as much on the small parties as on the AfD. If enough of them miss 5%, AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund could take a majority. If they squeeze in, he could finish first and still fall short.
Merz’s CDU has ruled out any coalition or cooperation with the AfD, citing the party’s record and intelligence findings that the Saxony-Anhalt branch is a confirmed far-right extremist organization. Other mainstream parties have taken the same stance.
Far-right candidate Siegmund is not seeking a partner and is running to govern alone. Estimates suggest he needs at least 45% to 48% to win a majority of seats in the state parliament.
The Landtag’s standard size is 83 seats. A party needs 42 to govern alone. If the AfD falls short of a majority of seats, Magdeburg could spend weeks arguing over who becomes premier.
The option raised most often is a CDU-led minority government with the Social Democrats and perhaps the Greens, surviving vote by vote.
Schulze has said he will not make himself dependent on the Left Party. Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the BSW, insisted that they want a “non-party” premier and will not serve as the majority-maker keeping the CDU in power.
German officials and analysts say Sunday’s result will echo in federal politics even if no one expects a snap election.
Calling early Bundestag elections would itself be read as an admission of failure by the co-ruling Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Social Democrats.
Pressure would fall first on Merz’s conservatives. A large AfD win and a weak night for the CDU would reopen debate over his future.
According to the latest opinion polls by public broadcaster ARD, 83% of eligible voters say they are dissatisfied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz - a historically poor rating. Only 13% say they are satisfied with his work, the lowest figure the poll has recorded for a sitting chancellor.
A leadership fight within the Christian Democrats would not automatically bring down the federal government. If party pressure forces Merz to resign, parliament could elect a new chancellor without dissolving the Bundestag.

A UN report published Friday said Israel forcibly displaced the entire Palestinian populations of three refugee camps in the occupied West Bank and continues to prevent their return, raising concerns of forcible transfer and “ethnic cleansing.”
The UN Human Rights Office report said Israeli forces displaced residents of the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarm refugee camps during Operation Iron Wall in January and February 2025.
Israeli forces killed civilians, destroyed homes and infrastructure, cut water and electricity, and restricted humanitarian access during the operation, according to the report.
More than 33,000 Palestinians were displaced from the three camps, with 33,362 still unable to return as of July, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

“The way Operation Iron Wall has been conducted suggests its aim was to expel as many Palestinians as possible and to make way for more illegal Israeli settlements, in further violation of international law,” UN rights chief Volker Turk said in the report.
According to the report, Israeli forces killed 102 Palestinians, including 21 children, during the period covered.
The fatalities accounted for 46% of all Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank during that period, it said.
By October 2025, 52% of structures in Jenin camp, 48% in Nur Shams and 36% in Tulkarm had been destroyed or damaged, according to the report.
Displaced Palestinians also told the UN office that Israeli officers said there would be “no more refugee camps” and that they should “all go to Jordan.”

In Cambodia, Floating Houses Are Stuck Aground as Climate Change Takes Hold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

Siem Reap province, Cambodia — A 63-year-old woman watched her two grandchildren play on dry ground beneath her high-stilted house in mid-July.
By this time of the year, Pou village in Siem Reap province is normally flooded as the nearby Tonle Sap lake rises and expands with the monsoon. Stilted houses would be perched over the water, while floating houses drift on the bloated river.
When Sok Rina was young, the water would begin rising in June, flooding the riverbank and surrounding forests by July. The floodwaters would become rich with fish, supporting the livelihoods of villages on the water.
Recently, however, the Tonle Sap has been low, year after year.
Researchers are seeing a change in Cambodian weather patterns as climate change takes hold across the world. The traditional monsoon season in June and July appears to be weakening, even as intense easterly storms return in September and October.
At the same time as weather patterns are changing, more than 200 large dams are planned, completed, or under construction in the lower Mekong basin. Together, climate change and hydropower dams are restricting the flow of water into the Tonle Sap.
And without water, there’s no fish. In Siem Reap province, residents of Pou, Me Chrey and Chong Khneas villages say they are facing severe challenges to their survival.
Collapsing Fisheries
Cheim Oeurn, 40, caught only about one kilogram of fish one July morning. It was all small climbing perch and moonlight gourami, which have almost no market value.
The Sangkae river is too low for fish to spawn in the flooded forests around Tonle Sap, he said. Rising water temperatures in shallow areas also threaten to destroy fish eggs.
“If there is a lot of water, there will be more fish; as the water rises, fish will breed. Less water means fewer fish,” Cheim Oeurn said.
In the past, fishers in Pou village could earn 50,000 to 100,000 riel ($12.50 to $25) daily with a 50- to 60-kilogram catch. Today, they often return with nothing of value.
In Chong Khneas village, Choum Chreb said her son had caught exactly five fish after fishing from 4 a.m. on July 23.
“He hasn’t caught any in the past three days, and today’s five fish aren’t even enough to cover the cost of gasoline,” Choum Chreb said.
The family has lived and fished on the Tonle Sap for 25 years, and this life is all they have.
“We lack land to move to,” she said. “We just earn enough to survive on the water.”
The Tonle Sap is Southeast Asia’s largest freshwater lake, and vital to millions of livelihoods. It is connected to the Mekong River, and its flow famously reverses direction twice a year.
In the wet season, the Mekong rises and pushes water into the Tonle Sap. The lake expands and floods nearby forests – creating a unique ecosystem around the lake that supports fish spawning and local livelihoods. In the dry season, the lake drains back into a lowered Mekong River.
“The reversal is the key driver of the Mekong’s robust fisheries, making the Tonle Sap the largest inland fishery in the world,” said the Stimson Center’s Mekong Dam Monitor.
Two Factors
The center has observed stark changes to the region’s river systems, and this year is no different: The Tonle Sap’s reversal started about six weeks late, and the flow is much weaker than average for this time of year. The reverse flow was measured at 4 billion cubic meters, below the average of 11 billion.
Both climate change and hydropower developments have combined to disrupt Tonle Sap water levels and livelihoods.
For the past five years, June and July have had less rain than normal, said Stimson Center Southeast Asia program director Brian Eyler.
“It seems like the traditional monsoon pattern that builds at the beginning of the wet season is weakening in strength,” he said.
At the same time, some recent September and October storms had been “extremely intense,” he said, explaining that the Mekong basin’s wet season was made up of two weather patterns: the early monsoon and the later easterly storms that come from the Pacific Ocean.
It’s during the early rains, however, that hydropower dams fill up their reservoirs. They produce electricity during the dry season by releasing stored-up water, and by the start of the wet season they are typically near-depleted.
“This all makes the expansion of the Tonle Sap Lake get off to a very weak start,” Eyler said.
This year was a case in point. “The Tonle Sap has hardly expanded and this will have a negative effect on fisheries. Just a few weeks ago, parts of the Mekong were recording all-time lows for that time of year.”
Both climate change and dam impacts play a role, but in the immediate term “there is opportunity to rethink the way upstream dams are operated,” he said, suggesting that dams could wait to fully fill up their reservoirs until late in the wet season when there is plenty of rain.
Data from the Mekong River Commission show that water levels on the Tonle Sap river in Prek Kdam, southeast of the lake, have been largely below the historical average during the early wet season for eight years in a row.
Damaged Livelihoods
In Siem Reap’s Me Chrey village, Pon Niem said her first daughter dropped out of school in grade 12 and has worked at a garment factory in Kampong Speu province since 2025. Her second son dropped out in grade 11 to start working at the same factory this year. They are now 21 and 19.
“They see the family’s hardships,” the 43-year-old said. “They told their two younger sisters to continue their school, not to worry.”
Preap Nakrei, 40, said her eldest daughter left school in grade eight to work in a restaurant in Siem Reap. Now 18, she works at a cigarette factory in Phnom Penh to help repay family debts.
While lower secondary school is available in the village, upper secondary students from ninth grade must relocate to the district center – a financial burden few families can afford.
“If we could earn 30,000 riel a day, we could support our children’s education,” she said, hoping her younger children will complete high school.
Declining catches have pushed many families into severe debt. Preap Nakrei’s family owes 10 million riel (about $2,500) to a private lender for fishing nets and 3 million riel ($750) to the microfinance institution AMK, requiring a monthly interest payment of 45,000 riel ($11.25).
“Under our contract, I was supposed to repay AMK 1.5 million in July, but I could not. I asked them to delay repayment until December, and they agreed,” she said.
Sorn Chavy, 28, a resident of Pou village, faces a similar struggle. Her family owes 2 million riel ($500) to microfinance institution Chamroeun and 3 million riel to AMK, while her husband struggles to catch fish.
In addition to microfinance loans, she owes a private lender approximately 17 million riel ($4,250) for fishing nets and fish-raising expenses. However, she has decided not to start raising fish yet because the water remains too low, which could kill the fish.
“It’s hard for us to move out of this area; I’m three months pregnant and my first son is just six years old,” Sorn Chavy said. “Since birth, we have known only fishing.”
A recent study by researchers from the Cambodia Development Resource Institute and Royal University of Phnom Penh observed wide-ranging impacts on communities around the Tonle Sap. The study highlighted a 50 percent drop in fish production between 2018 and 2020, from 291,260 to 144,635 tons, due to reduced water volumes and shorter flood durations.
“Fishing is no longer reliable, and fishing communities are shifting into farming by clearing the flooded forest areas,” the study said. Meanwhile, more young people are migrating to towns and overseas for employment.
It also noted physical changes in traditional floating villages: “Some floating communities are no longer floating.” Meanwhile, other communities that split their time on land and water “stay on land longer than on water throughout the year.”
Marks of Change
To reach Pou village, one travels down from the Puok district town along a red gravel road pocked with potholes, passing rice fields and dense forests.
The village reveals the changing climate at a glance: Traditional homes stand high on 5-meter wooden stilts marked by faint waterlines from past floods, but in mid-July the ground beneath them remained dry silt.
Along the Sangkae River, floating houses built on bamboo rafts and empty gasoline drums sat grounded on riverbanks, marooned above water levels that continue to arrive later and lower over time.
Sok Rina said her children – the parents of the grandchildren she kept an eye on – had moved away for work.
Her eldest son, 32, married in 2020 and moved with his wife to Sihanoukville last year. His wife works at a garment factory while he works at a plastic factory. Two other children moved to Sihanoukville for work in tourism, and another to Phnom Penh to work as a swiftlet nest cleaner.
“They dropped out of school because they witnessed our impoverished living conditions,” Sok Rina said. “They used to live with us, and fished, but they couldn’t earn a living. So they migrated for work.”
Living in the village was only getting harder. Last year, the area didn’t flood until August, and the floodwaters stayed just a few weeks until September.
“I’m not sure about this year,” she said.

Russian occupation court sentences captured Ukrainian journalist Levchenko to 15 years in prison
The ruling was published by occupation-linked channels, Ukrinform reports.
According to Russian sources, after the occupation of Melitopol, the journalist remained in the city and did not renounce her Ukrainian citizenship.
"After contacting a resident of Ukrainian-controlled territory via the Telegram messenger, the woman agreed to assist the Ukrainian special services by providing information about the locations of administrative buildings and employees of Russian authorities, as well as the routes used by Russian military personnel, military equipment, weapons and other troops and military formations in the Zaporizhzhia region," the Institute of Mass Information quoted the occupation-linked channels as saying.
According to information from the occupation court cited by the media, in February 2023, the woman allegedly provided information about Russian state ministries and agencies, including security and defense bodies, along with their addresses and lists of employees.
"The transfer of this information to the Ukrainian side could have resulted in strikes against the locations of these strategic facilities," the occupation court claimed.
The occupiers also alleged that Levchenko failed to delete the information from her phone.
The Russian authorities charged her with espionage under Article 276 of the Russian Criminal Code, which concerns the transfer, collection or storage, for the purpose of passing to the enemy, of information that can be used against the Russian Armed Forces.
The so-called "Zaporizhzhia Regional Court" found the former journalist guilty and sentenced her to 15 years in prison.
Russian forces abducted Iryna Levchenko and her husband, Oleksandr, in early May 2023 in temporarily occupied Melitopol and held them for some time in basements in the city. The couple were detained on the street and initially held together before being separated.
According to Levchenko's sister, Olena Rudenko, the journalist was held in a detention center in Donetsk in a cell measuring approximately 3 by 4 meters together with three other women.
In June 2026, it emerged that Iryna Levchenko had been transferred from a detention center in Simferopol to a detention center in Krasnodar, Russia.
According to RIA South, Oleksandr Levchenko was released in August 2024. He had been held in occupied Melitopol throughout his detention. Upon his release, he was given a document stating that he had allegedly served 21 days of administrative arrest for "violating the curfew."
His passport, bank cards and money seized during the search were not returned. During his entire period in detention, he saw his wife only once, while they were both out for a walk at the detention center, but they were not allowed to speak to each other.
According to the Institute of Mass Information, Iryna Levchenko has worked in journalism since 1981. She worked for factory newspapers, the Melitopol district newspaper Novyi Den, and served as a correspondent for regional and national print media outlets.

Crimea under attack: what the 2026 holiday season was like for Russians
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:50:07 EEST
19:50:07 KST

Crimea under attack: what the 2026 holiday season was like for Russians
Kyiv • UNN
Systematic strikes complicated logistics, weakened air defenses, and caused disruptions to energy and fuel supplies in Crimea. The 2026 holiday season has effectively been ruined.
Systematic strikes by the Defense Forces of Ukraine against the energy, fuel, transport, and military infrastructure of occupied Crimea throughout the spring and summer have significantly complicated Russia’s use of the peninsula as a military hub. Operation "Crimean Switch off" did not lead to the immediate collapse of the Russian grouping or the energy system of occupied Crimea, but it has had a cumulative effect: problems with logistics and fuel supplies, power outages, and reduced air defense capabilities. A collateral but tangible consequence was the effective disruption of the holiday season, on which a significant share of local small businesses depends. UNN discussed the consequences of the systematic Ukrainian strikes on facilities in the occupied peninsula with experts.
"Crimean Switch off": what kind of operation is it?
"Crimean Switch off" is the name of a campaign by the Unmanned Systems Forces aimed primarily at energy infrastructure in the occupied territories. It is being conducted in parallel with Operation "MoLoChKa," whose targets include tankers and other vessels providing Russian logistics in the Black and Azov Seas.
"Crimean Switch off" began on July 1, while "MoLoChKa" began on July 6. Both special operations fit into Kyiv’s strategy of coercing Russia into peace.
One of the first targets of Ukraine’s middle strikes was the "TES-Terminal-1" terminal in Kerch. It is a large facility for storing light petroleum products. Substations with voltages of 110–220 kV in Yalta, Kerch, Sudak, Feodosia, Alushta, and other populated areas were systematically targeted.
According to the Unmanned Systems Forces, by August 28, 315 energy facilities had been hit since the start of the operation. The targets included the Balaklava Thermal Power Plant in Sevastopol and gas-turbine stations in Karierne and Naumivka.
In parallel, Ukraine carried out strikes against maritime logistics. As of August 22, according to the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, 242 vessels in the Black and Azov Seas had been hit. It was separately reported that four of the five key ferries of the Kerch crossing had been disabled.
The Unmanned Systems Forces carried out the main strikes on tankers using attack UAVs manufactured by FirePoint
In addition, at the beginning of the summer, Ukrainian troops destroyed the main bridges connecting the peninsula with mainland Ukraine, which significantly complicated logistics for Russian occupation forces.
How strikes on Crimea affect the front
For Russia, Crimea remains primarily a major military and logistical hub through which, among other things, the occupying forces in southern Ukraine are supplied. That is why strikes by the Ukrainian military are not limited to the energy sector.
According to military expert Ivan Stupak, this summer Ukraine has been systematically targeting air defense, electronic warfare systems, warehouses, bases, fuel infrastructure, and Russian logistics.
This is important because Crimea is not simply territory for Russia, but a major military hub. And Ukraine is precisely trying to gradually undermine its capabilities. This concerns strikes on warehouses, bases, logistics, fuel infrastructure, and other military infrastructure. The goal here is absolutely clear—to reduce Russia’s ability to supply its grouping in southern Ukraine. In particular, this concerns Zaporizhzhia Oblast—the areas of Huliaipole, Orikhiv, and Stepnohirsk. We are trying to create conditions for Russia under which it will be more difficult for it to support its offensive operations
According to him, the fight against Russian road logistics has become a separate area.
And I would say that we have already significantly undermined their capabilities in Crimea. Over the past three months, according to the data I have seen and that can be verified, Ukraine has destroyed about 600 trucks every month. These are very large figures. In fact, this represents a serious reduction in the volumes that Russia can transport and supply
However, this does not yet mean the destruction of the entire Russian supply system on the southern front. Military expert Mykhailo Zhyrokhov draws attention to the key role of the Crimean Bridge and railway connections.
As long as such an important strategic structure as the Crimean Bridge exists, Russia has the ability to maintain more or less normal supplies for the troops stationed on the occupied peninsula. We understand that a single train can deliver more fuel than dozens of fuel trucks, which can then be destroyed on the road from Novorossiysk. Rail supply is the foundation
At the same time, experts identify the gradual weakening of Russian air defenses on the occupied peninsula as one of the most noticeable results of the Ukrainian campaign.
“Madyar” showed strikes by Ukrainian UAVs of the Fire Point company against Russian air defense systems
If we are talking specifically about military capabilities, I would say that Russia’s air defense capabilities have been severely undermined. Almost every day, reports emerged that either a radar station, an anti-aircraft missile system, or even some aircraft at an airfield had been destroyed. This is gradually reducing the Russians’ ability to shoot down our drones
But in his view, this is not yet a strategic turning point in this area.
Stupak also does not expect an immediate effect from the Crimean operations. In his assessment, this is rather a cumulative effect and a gradual reduction in the capabilities of Russia’s military machine in Crimea.
If this trend continues in the autumn and winter, I would not speak of some immediate collapse of Crimea. I am more inclined toward a different scenario - Russia may gradually reduce its presence on the peninsula
In his view, the Russians could potentially move some administrative and military structures to the mainland, change their basing locations, and reduce their use of airfields in Crimea.
Such a reduction in presence is quite likely. I think that Ukraine could potentially further reduce Crimea’s importance by 20–30%. And this, accordingly, could reduce the Russians’ ability to use the peninsula to launch attacks on Ukraine’s southern regions
Strikes on energy infrastructure: disruptions are already occurring, but the system is holding for now
Energy infrastructure became a separate area of the operation. Systematic attacks on substations, generation facilities, fuel terminals, and oil depots have caused disruptions both to civilian infrastructure and to the occupying forces. According to Zhirokhov, prolonged power outages in Crimea were reported in Russia.
Then a campaign of strikes on Crimea’s energy infrastructure began. What did this lead to? To certain shifts. Reports appeared on Russian public channels that individual districts had been left without electricity for one, two, or three days at a time
According to Zhirokhov, the key factor enabling Russia to compensate for some of its losses remains the energy bridge between Crimea and Krasnodar Krai.
Along with the construction of the Crimean Bridge, the Russians built what is known as an energy bridge, through which they transmit electricity from Krasnodar Krai. Therefore, without destroying this energy bridge, all these strikes are, you know, for now merely figures in the General Staff’s reports: so many electrical substations hit, some other facilities hit. This certainly creates problems, but it does not break the system
At the same time, fuel problems arising from strikes on tankers and oil depots could directly affect Russian units at the front. According to Stupak, internal Russian reports recorded a reduction in fuel supplies.
One separate and important issue is fuel and energy infrastructure. Strikes on oil depots, fuel terminals, and other facilities create problems for the Russians. I saw their internal reports and their response to Ukrainian strikes. At certain points, they acknowledged a reduction in fuel supplies to the front by approximately 20–25%
In modern warfare, fuel is needed not only for armored vehicles and automobiles, but also to operate generators, on which, among other things, the ability to charge FPV drone batteries, maintain communications, and so on depends.
And at certain moments, the Russians complained that they were short of fuel for their generators by approximately 20%. This means they have to conserve their batteries and launch fewer reconnaissance and strike drones. But I cannot say that this is already a widespread problem along the entire front line. Nevertheless, the local problems are noticeable
The situation in Crimea may become even more complicated in winter. Economist and former spokesperson for NJSC "Naftogaz of Ukraine" in the Lviv region Viktor Halchynskyi predicts problems with supplying the peninsula with gas as well.
If the gas issue is further addressed, it will be cold in Crimea. As far as I know, the storage facilities located there have also been damaged. If the Defense Forces take certain further actions, combined with the shortage of liquid fuel and electricity, this could lead to an extremely uncomfortable winter on the peninsula, even taking into account the fact that the climate there is warmer
Resort season under attack: Crimea has lost tourists and money
The disruption of the resort season was the most tangible consequence for the civilian population of occupied Crimea. Problems with fuel and electricity, constant strikes, disruptions to transport logistics, and the overall danger made vacationing in occupied Crimea almost impossible. At the end of June, Russians who had come to vacation on the occupied peninsula fled en masse. Even 15-kilometre queues to leave Crimea were recorded.
According to Halchynskyi's estimate, the 2026 resort season became the worst for the occupied peninsula since 2014.
It is difficult to assess the damage in absolute figures because we can see the situation in the temporarily occupied territory exclusively through media estimates and reports that leak onto the internet from individual users. But we can say with confidence that the damage from the 2026 resort season, which in fact did not take place, is probably the greatest since the occupation, that is, since 2014
In his opinion, the actual disruption of the resort season became the culmination of a process that began immediately after the occupation of Crimea, when Ukrainian and European tourists stopped visiting the peninsula.
Due to the lack of fuel and electricity, constant air attacks, and the blocking of transport connections, the season had effectively ended prematurely in June. Accordingly, the tourism sector failed to receive substantial funds
According to experts, the consequences are being felt primarily by local small businesses, whose earnings had been tied to the summer for decades. Mykhailo Zhyrokhov notes that the model was simple: the money earned in summer enabled many Crimeans to live through the rest of the year.
But psychologically and socially, this is undoubtedly a major blow for the residents of Crimea. Most small businesses in Crimea—both under Ukraine and under Russia—were built specifically around the resort season. People earned money in summer and then effectively lived on it in autumn and winter. Now this model has been disrupted. Certain economic problems have arisen, and people have failed to earn the expected amount of money
Halchynskyi also speaks of the gradual winding down of businesses and the possible outflow of the economically active population from the peninsula.
If we are talking about business in Crimea, it is obvious that a very large number of people earned their living specifically from tourism. Now businesses are closing. There are problems with energy and problems with security. And, judging indirectly from what we see, this process has gradually begun
According to him, there is no mass evacuation at present, but people may move their economic activity outside Crimea or leave the peninsula altogether.
At the same time, experts remind us that Crimea has always received subsidies from the state budget. For the occupation administration, a decline in tourist flows also means reduced revenues and greater dependence on Russia's federal budget.
Most likely, the Crimean authorities will once again have to appeal to Russia's federal budget and request more direct transfers for 2027. Crimea is already the most heavily subsidized region, and the reduction in tourist flows only increases this dependence
This, in his view, is one of the additional effects of the Ukrainian campaign of strikes on Crimea. After all, any additional Russian budget expenditures on Crimea reduce the possibilities for military spending.
It is beneficial for us if money from the Russian budget is spent not on military purposes. If Russia is forced to direct more funds toward supporting Crimea, compensating for losses in the tourism sector, restoring infrastructure, and making direct transfers, this already works to our advantage. Because Russia never has an excess of money. And the more the Russian budget is forced to spend on problems arising from Ukrainian strikes, the fewer resources potentially remain for the war
At the same time, Zhirokhov believes that losses suffered by small businesses due to the disrupted resort season will not be a problem for the Russian authorities, since the Kremlin will not consider the interests of Crimeans a priority.
Thus, the main effect of Ukrainian operations in Crimea lies in the gradual increase in the cost of occupying Crimea for Russia. Moscow is forced to simultaneously compensate for losses to military logistics, restore energy facilities, strengthen air defenses, support the subsidized economy of the peninsula, and respond to Crimea's growing unattractiveness to tourists.
And if the systematic nature of such strikes is maintained, occupied Crimea will become increasingly difficult to use simultaneously as a military bridgehead, a logistics center, and a symbolic "showcase" for Russians.

Israel hands Lebanon five civilians it had abducted, via ICRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

19:48:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel hands Lebanon five civilians it had abducted, via ICRC
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has confirmed that five people released from Israeli detention have been transferred to Lebanon, in a move that could provide fresh momentum to stalled negotiations between the two countries.
The ICRC said on Friday that it had facilitated the transfer at the request of the parties involved, with one detainee handed over on Thursday and four others on Friday.
"The ICRC's role in this process was strictly humanitarian," it said, adding that it had acted as a neutral intermediary between Israel and Lebanon and that the transfers were carried out with respect for the safety and dignity of those released.
The development marks a breakthrough in negotiations that had become deadlocked over Israel's continued military operations in Lebanon and its refusal to agree to a second trial area under the framework being discussed between the two sides.
The Lebanese army received Malik Ghazi through the ICRC at the Naqoura crossing on Thursday. The remaining four people, two of whom are Syrian, were transferred on Friday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had announced the release of the five detainees as part of the negotiations with Lebanon.
He also ordered efforts to locate the remains of members of Lebanon's Jewish community who were kidnapped and killed during the Lebanese civil war in the mid-1980s.
Lebanese official sources told The New Arab that the detainee issue had been a central focus of the third round of talks held in Rome in August.
They said the Lebanese delegation had pressed Israel to take a concrete step on the issue, amid growing frustration in Beirut over what officials saw as Israel's failure to meet its commitments.
"The Lebanese delegation insisted on the need for Israel to take a serious step on this issue, particularly as there was Lebanese discontent over Israel's failure to implement any of its commitments," one source said.
The sources said the release followed US diplomatic pressure, particularly from US Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa.
They said Issa raised the issue during a recent meeting with Mr Netanyahu, attended by US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, and urged Israel to make a gesture that would help preserve the negotiating process.
Washington is pushing for negotiations to continue and for both sides to implement a framework agreement reached on 26 June, according to the sources.
Lebanon has meanwhile pledged to provide information about the remains of missing members of the country's Jewish community, with work on the issue already under way.
The Lebanese sources said further detainee releases could follow as part of that process.
They described the transfer of the five detainees as an important development, but said Beirut would continue pressing for the release of all Lebanese prisoners, an end to Israeli military operations and Israel's withdrawal from territory it continues to occupy.
No date has yet been set for an eighth round of negotiations in Rome.
Several issues remain unresolved, including Israeli attacks, the establishment of a second trial area, arrangements for monitoring implementation and the mechanism expected to replace the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) after its mandate ends in 2026.
"We hope that the breakthrough on the prisoner file will have a positive impact on the process," one Lebanese source said.
However, the detainee release came as Israeli military operations in southern Lebanon continued.
Israeli forces abducted three civilians from the southern town of Halta on Thursday, according to Lebanese reports.
Israel also said it had completed an operation to clear what it described as Hezbollah underground infrastructure in the Ali al-Taher Heights in the Nabatieh district.
A series of Israeli attacks were reported across southern Lebanon overnight and on Friday morning, including in Qantara, Wadi al-Hujeir, Mansouri and Nabatieh al-Fawqa.
Hezbollah had not commented on the Israeli operation at the time of publication.
The Lebanese Association of Prisoners and Liberated Prisoners said Malik Ghazi had disappeared from the Ain Ata area in Rashaya district in eastern Lebanon but had not previously been registered on its list of detainees.
The association said the other four people released were also not on its lists and declined to identify them before an official announcement.
Its most recent list, published on 26 August, contains 36 people believed to be detained by Israel, including farmers, fishermen, civilians, volunteers and resistance fighters.
Three cases date from before October 2024, while 11 date from October 2024 and another 11 from after the ceasefire came into effect on 27 November 2024.
Ten people on the list were detained during the March 2026 war, while one was captured after the June framework agreement.
The issue of missing Lebanese Jews dates to a series of kidnappings in Beirut between 1984 and 1987, mainly in the Kantari and Wadi Abu Jamil areas.
Those abducted included Salim Murad Jamous, a former secretary-general of the Jewish community; community president Isaac Sasson; vice-president Dr Eli Hallaq; and businessman Eli Srour.
The kidnappings were attributed to a group calling itself the Organisation of the Oppressed on Earth, which announced that some of the captives had been executed.
The group demanded the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon following Israel's 1982 invasion and the release of Lebanese detainees held by Israel.
The fate of some of those abducted and the locations of their remains remain unknown.
In its statement on Friday, the ICRC said it remained in confidential dialogue with the authorities concerned over people detained, killed or missing as a result of the conflict.
It said many families in Lebanon were still waiting for information about relatives who may be detained, dead or missing.
The organisation said it was prepared to act as a neutral intermediary in further humanitarian operations if agreements were reached between the parties.
The ICRC also reiterated that it has been unable to visit detainees in Israeli detention facilities since October 2023, including Lebanese nationals.
It called for information on people detained in connection with the conflict and for access to detention centres, saying it remained in talks with the Israeli authorities about resuming visits.

Cyclosporiasis outbreak exposes a weakened US public health system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:46:43 UTC
19:46:43 KST

Cyclosporiasis outbreak exposes a weakened US public health system
YPSILANTI, Michigan, Sept 4 - During the height of the summer outbreak of cyclosporiasis, Dea Lancaster set aside her usual duties as nurse coordinator at Michigan's Washtenaw County Health Department to call patients, asking about their symptoms and tracing the contaminated food they ate.
The stress of handling one of the largest U.S. foodborne illness outbreaks in decades gave her an eye twitch as she called dozens of patients a day while commiserating with overwhelmed colleagues and cracking dark jokes to cope.
“It was a lot of exhaustion, phone calls and clicking of the keys,” said Lancaster, 44. “It was being busy at work and starving but taking food histories and being terrified of eating what they were eating. It was not a good time.”
The outbreak may represent a new — and risky — normal: a public-health system some experts say has been weakened by decades of underfunding, particularly for food safety, and further hollowed out by Trump administration cuts, leaving the country less able to detect and contain outbreaks. Cyclosporiasis is a parasitic disease that causes explosive diarrhea, abdominal pain and fatigue but is rarely fatal.
“What you're seeing this summer demonstrates the vulnerabilities in the system and what happens when they're put under stress," said Barbara Kowalcyk, a food safety expert at George Washington University.
"We used to have one hand tied behind our back and now we have both," Kowalcyk said.
CONTAMINATED LETTUCE
On July 16, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention linked an outbreak that the agencies now say has sickened over 11,000 people in 20 states to shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants. Two people died.
The next day, the agencies confirmed the lettuce came from the Mexico operations of U.S. produce company Taylor Farms. Taylor Farms issued a recall the same day.
Michigan public health officials said the government announcement came far too late. By then, Washtenaw County was swamped with cases. State officials have said lettuce is once again safe to eat, but the cyclosporiasis surge has raised questions about how well the U.S. is equipped to respond to the next outbreak.
As Michigan scrambled to contain the outbreak, some health workers dropped their usual duties. A nurse stopped giving vaccinations and some restaurant inspectors paused health inspections to call hundreds of sick patients.
In late June, weeks before the U.S. government outbreak announcement, Michigan health officials alerted the FDA and CDC about an unusually high number of cyclosporiasis cases. On July 4, as residents set up barbecues and picnics for the Independence Day holiday, Michigan advised residents to avoid lettuce and a handful of other fruits and vegetables. The state's chief medical executive said the move likely prevented more infections.
But in the weeks before the federal announcement, the illness spread rapidly across Michigan and the country. Washtenaw County, which logged a handful of cases per day in late June, was recording 80 cases a day by mid-July.
The FDA defended its response, saying it quickly conducted its analysis tracing the contaminated food.
"It wasn’t until the states received necessary information from suppliers on July 13 that the FDA could use that information to determine which commodity was the likely vehicle," an FDA spokesperson said.
Taco Bell has said it voluntarily removed Taylor Farms lettuce from its restaurants. A Taylor Farms spokesperson said the company quickly recalled the affected lettuce and hired independent experts to review its food-safety protocols.
"We are confident in our food and food safety systems and will continue to be transparent as more information becomes available," the spokesperson said.
STATE TOOK ON MORE WORK: HEALTH EXECUTIVE
Dr. Natasha Bagdasarian, Michigan's chief medical executive, said the state undertook work typically handled by the federal government, such as tracing contaminated produce and issuing food safety guidance.
"The state health department was taking on far more responsibility than is normally the case," she said. “I don’t think that this is sustainable. We simply don’t have the staffing; we don’t have the bandwidth."
A CDC spokesperson said the agency held weekly calls with states and met daily with the FDA and state health officials to share information and coordinate the response.
“CDC has made this response a priority, providing direct support and conducting outreach with states at least four times each week," the spokesperson said.
In Washtenaw County, the caseload climbed into late July.
Soon, the county had to reassign staff from its 108-person health department. Many of them were still exhausted after a recent measles outbreak. As many as eight county health staff were assigned daily to conduct time-consuming interviews with patients, questioning them about what food they ate, when they ate it and where they got it. Gathering that information was difficult, as it takes one week on average for cyclosporiasis symptoms to appear.
The county health department also took calls from baffled health providers seeking guidance on how to treat the cyclosporiasis patients filling doctors’ offices, urgent care centers and hospitals.
“I have never talked to so many people who have pooped their pants in adulthood,” said Adrienne Walling, a specialist in sexually transmitted disease prevention at the Washtenaw County Health Department. “It was overwhelming.”
Walling set aside her usual work to assist with the outbreak response. A colleague stopped performing blood draws and giving vaccinations at the department’s family health clinic to call cyclosporiasis patients.
‘I THOUGHT I WAS GOING TO DIE’ In neighboring Ingham County, the surge was similarly overwhelming. By late August, the county, home to about 290,000 people, had recorded 915 cases, though new cases had fallen to about three or four a day from 20 to 30 cases a day during the outbreak's peak.
Ingham's five communicable disease nurses struggled to manage the crush of case investigations, bringing in other county health workers. They included restaurant inspectors with little prior experience in disease investigations who had to be trained on the fly. Some Michigan labs ran out of cyclosporiasis tests, while others were so overwhelmed by the surge in samples that they were still working through backlogs in late August.
While health department employees made hundreds of calls, patients continued to fall ill.
“It was so scary. I literally thought I was going to die on more than one occasion. It’s been a nightmare,” said Kellye O’Hara, a 62-year-old retiree in Muskegon, Michigan, who became ill with cyclosporiasis in July and took more than a month to recover.
She was hospitalized for six days during her infection, which she said caused excruciating pain, fevers, countless trips to the bathroom and intense fatigue.
“It feels like you have pins passing through your colon,” she said.
O'Hara and hundreds of other cyclosporiasis patients are suing Taco Bell and Taylor Farms.
Taco Bell and Taylor Farms did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.
Bill Marler, a lawyer specializing in foodborne illness who is representing O'Hara and the other patients, said the scale of the outbreak is unlike anything he has seen.
“Had we had more boots on the ground doing investigations and interviewing people, my view is that this outbreak would have been caught earlier," he said. "We would have gotten product pulled off the market.” REUTERS

Rahul Gandhi vs C Joseph Vijay: Can TVK chief do what Arvind Kejriwal could not?

2026-09-04
10:43:51 UTC
19:43:51 KST

Rahul Gandhi vs C Joseph Vijay: Can TVK chief do what Arvind Kejriwal could not?
Pallavi / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Sep 04, 2026, 16:20 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Vijay's national ambitions: Can the TVK chief succeed where Kejriwal failed?
The honeymoon period between Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) and its coalition partner, the Congress, appears to be over. Barely months after the two parties came together to form the government, they are already sparring over a question that is ostensibly about the 2029 Lok Sabha election: Who should be the opposition's prime ministerial face - Rahul Gandhi or Vijay?What began as statements and counter-statements between the two party leaders has quickly acquired a sharper political edge.TVK PWD minister Aadhav Arjuna pitched Vijay as a potential national leader, arguing that the country's highest political office should go to a leader from Tamil Nadu. On the other hand, state minister S Rajesh Kumar said Congress ministers in the Tamil Nadu cabinet would resign if TVK did not support Rahul Gandhi as the PM candidate in 2029.
The confrontation spilled into the assembly as well. Congress Legislature Party leader and MLA Tharahai Cuthbert was shifted on August 31 from the section allotted to TVK legislators to the front row of the opposition benches.But beneath the immediate fight over Rahul versus Vijay lies a much bigger question: Does Vijay intend to remain a powerful Tamil Nadu leader, or does he see the state's 2026 mandate as the launchpad for a national political project?And if the latter is the plan, can he succeed where Arvind Kejriwal could not?
Vijay's extraordinary first step
The scale of Vijay's rise explains why the 2029 debate has surfaced so early.The April 2026 Tamil Nadu assembly election ended nearly six decades of dominance by the DMK and AIADMK.
TVK, only two years old, emerged as the largest party with 108 seats in the 234-member assembly. The DMK won 59 and AIADMK 47, while Congress secured five seats, with the remaining seats going to smaller allies.TVK was therefore not merely a new party that performed better than expected. It emerged as the central political force in an election that disrupted the state's traditional two-party equilibrium.There was, however, one problem: 108 seats were still short of the 118 required for a simple majority.That made Congress indispensable.Vijay eventually formed the government with the support of MLAs from Congress [5], VCK [2] and IUML [2], along with outside support from the Left parties [4]. The MDMK, which has two MLAs, later extended its support.Congress moved away from its long-standing association with the DMK and backed a TVK-led government along with smaller allies, taking the coalition's strength to 121. Vijay was sworn in as CM on May 10.Congress had submitted its letter of support after the election, making it clear that its support would be conditional on TVK keeping "communal forces" out of the alliance.
Vijay emerged as the disrupter-in-chief in Tamil Nadu elections.
The 234-member assembly currently has seven vacancies following the resignation of six AIADMK MLAs and Vijay vacating his second seat, Trichy East. The effective strength of the House is therefore 227, bringing the majority mark down to 114.The political equation is unusual. Congress is the junior partner, with only five seats, but its support helped Vijay cross the majority mark. At the same time, TVK's 108 seats give Vijay overwhelming dominance within the coalition.That inversion may be at the heart of the present tension.Congress had been with the DMK in the pre-poll alliance and had never secured a place in MK Stalin's cabinet. After the results, however, it quickly moved to TVK's side and helped Vijay form the government.The alliance therefore contains a built-in contradiction: the party that needs Vijay's government to survive does not want Vijay to emerge as the leader of the national opposition.
Congress leader on TVK's 'Vijay-for-PM' pitch.
The 'agnipath' of Vijay's path
Vijay's route to Delhi runs into a problem that no amount of success in Tamil Nadu can entirely solve: numbers.Tamil Nadu sends 39 MPs to the Lok Sabha. Even a TVK sweep in 2029 would leave Vijay nowhere close to the 272 seats needed for a majority in the 543-member House.History, however, offers a little hope.In the past, India has had PMs whose parties did not come close to a Lok Sabha majority. HD Deve Gowda became PM in 1996 after the Janata Dal won just 46 seats, emerging as the consensus choice of the United Front with Congress support. IK Gujral followed a year later under much the same arrangement, with the Janata Dal holding only around 45 seats. Chandra Shekhar became prime minister in 1990 after breaking away from the Janata Dal with just 64 MPs, relying on outside support from Congress.This may give Vijay some hope.But it is also where the historical comparison begins to fray. The coalition politics that made these leaders PMs belonged to a different national landscape where coalition governments were a norm. The BJP, however, has changed that equation, building the NDA into a durable national coalition rather than the loose, post-election arrangements that defined much of the 1990s.The opposition, meanwhile, has come together in the form of the INDIA bloc which Vijay's TVK is not part of yet.And yet, paradoxically, being outside the INDIA bloc may give Vijay an advantage over Rahul Gandhi.Rahul comes with the weight of the Congress's history: its national footprint, its alliances and rivalries, the Nehru-Gandhi legacy and the political resistance that the party can provoke among regional leaders. Vijay comes with much less baggage. He would enter a coalition conversation not as the leader of a decades-old national party, but as a new political force with a mass following built before he entered politics.
Rahul Gandhi's political journey.
That distinction could matter if the next Lok Sabha produces another fractured mandate. But that is a big if, and one that looks unlikely in the present circumstances.Congress MP Karti Chidambaram has already put the arithmetic bluntly: "Every party has dreams, ambitions, and desires ... but we know what the political reality is. There are 543 constituencies."Thus, for Vijay, even if his party manages to sweep all 39 Tamil Nadu seats, the real test would be in finding enough allies to make Delhi possible.
Can Tamil Nadu be Vijay’s launchpad?
There is, however, one route Vijay could attempt that would give his national project a distinct political identity.He could build around Tamil Nadu's distinctive relationship with the Centre and a broader southern assertion in national politics — the argument that Delhi needs a stronger voice from a region that has historically resisted political and cultural centralisation.That could give TVK's national project a political argument beyond Vijay's celebrity and the anti-incumbency against established parties.But it comes with its own problem.
BJP has used the opportunity to question TVK-Congress alliance.
A political identity rooted in Tamil pride and southern assertion may work strongly in Tamil Nadu, but it does not automatically translate into votes in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, West Bengal or other states.Vijay would therefore have to balance two identities: the Tamil leader whose legitimacy comes from Tamil Nadu and the national leader who must persuade voters elsewhere that his politics is not confined to the state.
Why Congress cannot simply step aside
For Congress, the dispute is not simply about Rahul Gandhi's personal ambitions or the future of the Gandhi family. It is about whether the party can retain its position as the principal national pole of the opposition after years of organisational and electoral decline.Rahul has spent years positioning himself as the principal challenger to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP. Congress's improved performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha election and Rahul's emergence as leader of opposition strengthened that claim.The subsequent assembly elections, however, have weakened the party's position against the BJP.A recent survey placing Rahul as the second-most preferred PM choice and Vijay next is nevertheless significant. Vijay's position is remarkable for a leader whose party has contested only one assembly election, even though such surveys are hardly a substitute for actual elections.For Congress, conceding the national leadership question to Vijay now would risk allowing another regional leader to occupy the political space the party is trying to reclaim, especially after the weakened positioning of Mamata Banerjee, MK Stalin and Kejriwal.
The Kejriwal test
Kejriwal also began with an extraordinary political breakthrough in a single territory before attempting to turn his party into a national alternative.When he launched the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) in November 2012, his political project was built around challenging established parties, particularly Congress, which had governed Delhi for 15 years under Sheila Dikshit.AAP's breakthrough came almost immediately. Kejriwal became CM in December 2013, resigned after 49 days and returned in February 2015 with one of the most emphatic mandates in Indian electoral politics: AAP won 67 of Delhi's 70 assembly seats, reducing Congress to zero.But Kejriwal did not intend to stop at Delhi.The 2014 Lok Sabha election was his first major attempt to build a national footprint. AAP contested 432 seats and won four, all in Punjab. Kejriwal himself challenged Narendra Modi in Varanasi, while Kumar Vishwas contested Amethi against Rahul Gandhi. Neither challenge produced the national breakthrough AAP was seeking.The party then entered the Punjab and Goa assembly elections in 2017. Punjab became a second political laboratory, with AAP winning 20 of 117 seats and emerging as the principal opposition force behind Congress. Goa, however, exposed the limits of the expansion strategy, with AAP failing to win a single assembly seat.Punjab eventually provided the big breakthrough. In the 2022 election, AAP won 92 of 117 seats and formed a government under Bhagwant Mann.Kejriwal had therefore achieved something genuinely difficult: he had built governments in two states and turned AAP into a recognisable political force beyond Delhi.Yet the national leap remained elusive.AAP's electoral strength outside its core states never matched the scale of its Delhi and Punjab victories. In Gujarat, where it tried to establish itself as a third force, the party won five assembly seats in 2022, while Goa remained marginal. Its Lok Sabha presence also remained modest.
Vijay's one-point lead on Kejriwal
The Tamil Nadu CM has one advantage over Kejriwal though that their starting points are different.Kejriwal had to build a mass political identity almost from scratch. Vijay, however, spent decades building one through cinema before entering politics. He then converted that popularity into 108 assembly seats in his very first election, which was dubbed as an extraordinary political conversion.But it can also become a weakness.The question is no longer whether millions of people know Vijay. They do.The question is whether voters who know him as an actor and Tamil Nadu CM will vote for TVK in states where the party has no political history, local leadership or cadre network.To go national, Vijay would need candidates, local leaders, a cadre network and alliances. Most importantly, he would need a political proposition that resonates with voters who do not know him primarily as a Tamil film star.This is where Kejriwal's experience matters most.AAP's success in Delhi could not simply be reproduced across the country. Punjab offered a favourable political opening, but Goa and Gujarat demonstrated that national visibility and electoral organisation are very different things.Vijay's task could be even harder because many of the states he would need to enter already have powerful regional leaders with their own political ambitions.For now, the 2029 PM debate may therefore be premature, but the political conflict it has exposed is not. Vijay may need Congress to consolidate the power he has won in Tamil Nadu even as he seeks to challenge Congress's claim to national opposition leadership.
That is the paradox at the heart of his political project.If Vijay can use the Congress alliance to build a durable organisation without becoming politically dependent on it, he may have found a route Kejriwal could not. But if TVK's national ambitions remain ahead of its organisational reach, the 2029 debate could end up looking less like the beginning of a national challenge and more like the first sign of a regional party reaching beyond its electoral weight.

Brazil's richest captured record income share despite Lula's effort to prioritize the poor
