Taiwan Cabinet defends use of frozen funds in 2025 budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:43:14 UTC
18:43:14 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) defended Thursday the Cabinet's decision to use NT$500 million (US$15.7 million) in funds frozen in its 2025 budget, stressing that the action was lawful.
During the review of the 2025 budget, opposition lawmakers, angered by then-Cabinet Secretary-General Kung Ming-hsin's (龔明鑫) decision to leave a legislative committee meeting without approval from the meeting's convener, proposed freezing NT$500 million from the Cabinet’s budget, per UDN. While the funds could have been unfrozen if Kung apologized, he never did, and the proposal was approved by the committee.
However, the financial statement for the Cabinet's 2025 budget year revealed it spent nearly all of its NT$1.5 billion budget despite the freeze. When questioned by KMT lawmakers about the situation, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics explained that the Cabinet had decided that the frozen funds, which were not attached to any specific budget item, would be used for personnel expenses, a mandatory spending item.
Lee explained the Cabinet's reasoning, saying that to maintain basic operations and minimize the impact on contractors, the Cabinet had decided to designate the frozen funds as personnel expenses, per CNA. She said civil servants' pay is a mandatory expense under the law, so the Cabinet was required to issue the payments, stressing that its spending had undergone scrutiny by the National Audit Office.
KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chair Chen I-hsin (陳以信) criticized the move, arguing that the frozen funds were for operational expenses rather than personnel expenses, per Z.Media. He noted that under the Budget Act, operational expenses should not be used for personnel expenses, alleging that the Cabinet had bypassed legislative oversight to access the funds.
Chen argued that Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) should be impeached for this. Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) echoed Chen's criticisms, noting that the Cabinet had previously refused to countersign legislation passed by the legislature, per Liberty Times.
TPP Legislative Caucus Convener Chen Ching-lung (陳清龍) noted that the Cabinet had unilaterally decided to use the frozen funds despite not meeting the conditions for unfreezing them. He called on the National Audit Office to review the action immediately.
TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) argued that the audit office should not allow the Cabinet to pass its financial statement review, per FTNN. He also suggested that the legislature should only propose budget cuts in the future, since the Cabinet might seek a workaround to access frozen funds.
DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) defended the action, saying that the situation was the result of political maneuvering by the opposition, per RTI. He said the Cabinet had reasons to justify the move, adding that the legislature should be more precise in its budgetary oversight.

Belgium condemns honors for convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:43:11 UTC
18:43:11 KST

Melike Pala
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot on Friday condemned the honoring of convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic at his funeral, warning that the act further distances Serbia from the European Union’s fundamental values.
“I condemn that act in the strongest terms, and have passed this message to my Serbian counterpart in charge of European affairs this morning,” Prevot said on US social media platform X.
He said honoring Mladic, who was convicted of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, was “shameful and disrespectful” to the victims and their families.
Prevot said the act represents “a step distancing Serbia from the EU’s fundamental values of respect for human dignity, human rights and the fight against impunity.”
He warned that it was “going in the opposite direction of what is expected from an EU candidate country.”
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos also said on X that she had decided to cancel her planned visit to Serbia, citing the glorification of Mladic following his death.
“The glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built. That path requires confronting the past, genuine reconciliation and respecting the victims of war crimes,” she wrote.
“The values that underpin our common future are not negotiable. In this context, I have decided not to proceed with my planned visit to Serbia at this time,” she added.
Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012 and has been engaged in accession negotiations with the bloc since 2014.
Mladic, known as the “Butcher of Bosnia,” was found guilty by the UN tribunal of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, including for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica genocide.
Mladic died on Aug. 27 while serving his sentence in prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic offered to organize the burial in Serbia for him.

Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte faces arrest warrant over threats charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:42:03 UTC
18:42:03 KST

A Philippine court on Friday issued an arrest warrant for Vice President Sara Duterte over an alleged death threat against the country's president, with her defence team saying she would "exercise all her legal remedies".
Duterte was charged last month with "grave threats" stemming from remarks in November 2024 that she had spoken with an assassin and instructed him to kill President Ferdinand Marcos, his wife and his cousin, who at the time was speaker of the Philippine House.
Duterte made the remarks during an online news conference, saying they would be assassinated if she were killed. She has denied threatening them.
The alleged assassination threat also forms a crucial element of her ongoing Senate impeachment trial, where a guilty verdict would see her removed from office and permanently banned from politics.
Under the Philippine legal code, a criminal conviction on the charge would carry a jail term of up to six months.
Justice department spokesperson Polo Martinez confirmed the warrant had been issued, noting that a court in Metro Manila's Quezon City had quashed a motion to defer it.
But the warrant seemed unlikely to result in Duterte being taken into custody.
Duterte appeal options
Paolo Tamase, associate dean at the University of the Philippines College of Law, told AFP that Duterte's lawyers could now be expected to file for bail, perhaps before day's end.
"The easiest thing for VP Sara to do is to file for bail with the regional trial court," Tamase said in a phone interview, noting Duterte would likely not need to be present.
He added that the warrant could yet be challenged at a higher court.
"She can potentially question the issuance of the warrant of arrest, which means she would go up to the Court of Appeals or potentially the Supreme Court," he said.
The vice president's legal team issued a statement saying she had "no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies".
Justice department officials have rejected arguments by the vice president's legal team that she cannot be prosecuted for offences that are also tied to her impeachment.
Duterte was impeached in May by the House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament, on charges that also included graft and corruption.
A guilty verdict in the Senate — where her trial recently concluded its ninth week — would spell an end to a planned run for president in 2028. Duterte first announced her candidacy in February.
She is the daughter of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte. She previously served as the co-concurrent Secretary of Education and as the longtime mayor of Davao City before stepping onto the national stage.

WHO warehouse storing medical supplies attacked overnight in Kyiv region, WHO says
GENEVA, Sept 4 - One of the World Health Organization's main warehouses storing humanitarian medical supplies in Ukraine was struck during an air attack overnight on Wednesday in the region surrounding Kyiv, the WHO said on Friday.
"Access to the site remains restricted due to heavy smoke and safety concerns, while assessments of possible damage and stock losses are ongoing. No WHO personnel were affected," WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said.
The attack overnight on Wednesday into Thursday morning follows a strike in August on a WHO humanitarian warehouse in the southern city of Dnipro, resulting in the loss of half of the medical supplies and equipment intended to support an estimated 225,000 people living in front-line and hard-to-reach areas, according to the WHO.
Another warehouse used by the WHO near Kyiv was damaged during a large-scale wave of attacks on the capital and surrounding region in July, Lindmeier said.
"The attacks are part of a broader pattern affecting humanitarian operations across the country. In 2026, at least 20 attacks have affected warehouses storing humanitarian supplies, including 15 attacks on warehouses holding health-related humanitarian supplies," Lindmeier told reporters in Geneva.
Alternative storage arrangements have already been identified following the latest incidents, the WHO said. REUTERS

Exiled in Denmark, United by Rugby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

Because you can have a job, an apartment, a gym membership and 500 people on Instagram and still feel like you haven’t quite found your place. For a lot of us, rugby changed that.
Although, to be fair, rugby doesn’t exactly look like the easiest way to make friends at first. In the beginning, it’s chaos. You don’t know the rules, you don’t understand half the phrases, and you’re mostly trying not to get run over.
Then, somehow, the person who just tackled you is the same person you’re having a beer with an hour later. And then you come back the next week.
You start recognising people. You slowly begin to understand the weird phrases (because what the hell is an inner shoulder?). 
Someone asks if you’re staying for a beer after training, then you get invited to a game, a party, a weekend trip. And without really noticing when it happened, you suddenly have people here.
People you see every week, who notice when you’re not there, and who gradually become part of your life.
Exiles Ladies, 2026. Credit Nicolo Magistris
But there’s something else that keeps you coming back: the rugby itself.
It’s physical, messy and loud. You run, tackle, push, fall over, get back up and do it again. For two hours, you’re not thinking about exams, your boss or whether your love life is going anywhere. You just play.
Exiles Men vs Frederiksberg RK, 2026 Credit – Daniel Storch
And one of the beautiful things about rugby is that there’s no single “rugby body.” Small and agile? We’ve got a winger. Fast and fearless? Scrum-half. Strong and sturdy and not particularly interested in running 80 metres? Guys, we’ve got a new prop.
Rugby doesn’t ask you to fit a certain body type. It gives you a position where the body you have can be an advantage.
You run until you’re exhausted, put some frustration into a tackle, laugh when
everything goes completely wrong, and leave training feeling like you’ve actually let something out.
Exiles Ladies vs CSR, 2026. Credit – Renata Lima
And somewhere along the way, all of that creates a bond that stays even after the game is over. That’s where rugby becomes more than rugby.
At DTU Exiles, people come together for all sorts of reasons. Some work, some
study, some are figuring out what comes next. Some have played rugby for years; others have never held a rugby ball. It doesn’t matter.
What matters is that you become part of it.
Schietwetter cup, Kiel 2026.
And once you do, the club becomes a place where cultures naturally mix. As an
international, you might find yourself discovering Danish traditions and getting invited to your first julefrokost. 
As a Dane, you might be trying Polish dumplings your teammate brought to training. You pick up new traditions, new friendships and, somehow, strong opinions about a New Zealand vs Argentina match.
That mix of people is nothing new. In 1968, rugby players from different parts of the world came together in Denmark to form the Copenhagen Exiles Rugby Union Football Club.
Their aim was to develop what they called “The Spirit of the Game.”
More than 50 years later, that spirit is still at the heart of the club. You don’t need to know anyone. You don’t need to know rugby. You just need to show up.
Exiles Men, 2026. Credit Nicolo Magistris
Maybe that’s what being an Exile is really about: finding somewhere you
belong and eventually becoming the person who makes someone else feel
they belong too.
We’re the Exiles, an inclusive and international rugby team based at DTU, Lyngby.
We train every Tuesday and Thursday from 18:00 to 20:00, and we’re always looking for new players to join our squad.
Next Tuesday, 8 th of September at 18:00, we’re having an open Rookie Practice and a team BBQ on our home pitch in Lyngby.
Never played? Come try it. Played before? Come meet the team.
Copenhagen 7s, Kastrup 2025
Follow us on Instagram and Facebook for more information and latest update or send us a message if you have any questions.
Come for the rugby. Stay for the socials.
See you on the pitch! DTU Exiles RUFC

Far-right AfD eyes win in east German state vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

Election posters for Ulrich Siegmund, the top candidate for the Afd in the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, are seen fixed on a fence in Osterwieck, Germany. (AFP Photo)
Germany faces a landmark regional election on Sept. 6 in the ex-communist east where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to win and has its sights on heading its first state government.
While it is far from assured that the AfD will win enough votes to rule the state alone, topping the polls in Saxony-Anhalt state would heap pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz and spell another boost for the anti-immigration party.
For months the AfD has polled at 40 percent or higher in the state, led by its top candidate Ulrich Siegmund, a telegenic 35-year-old who is feted like a rock star at campaign events and by his legions of TikTok followers.
His campaign promises include an immediate “remigration and deportation” offensive targeting irregular migrants, a ban on LGBT pride rainbow flags at public schools, and an end to new wind farms.
The Moscow-friendly party has also tapped into a sense of nostalgia for the bygone days of communist East Germany and resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
Siegmund has vowed to “make history” on Sept. 6 and lead a political revolution from the small state of 2.1 million people that he hopes will propel his anti-establishment party to national victory in 2029.
The incumbent state premier, 47-year-old Sven Schulze of Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party who leads a multi-party coalition, has put up large billboards beside highways that warn voters that the “far right leads into the ditch”.
While many AfD voters pine for dramatic change, the scenario of an AfD victory scares much of Germany, a country long at pains to atone for its dark history of World War II and the Holocaust.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency BfV categorizes the AfD’s state branch as a “right-wing extremist” organization.
In its latest report, the BfV documents that many AfD politicians in Saxony-Anhalt “employ language that demonizes migrants” and routinely brand Muslim refugees as criminals, a collective disparagement that violates “the principle of human dignity.”
All other major parties have so far maintained a “firewall” of non-cooperation with the AfD, although the tiny BSW party, which is economically on the left but veers right on immigration, has now signaled it may support the AfD forming a government.
Merz has vowed to halt the decade-long rise of the AfD by rebooting the stagnant economy and restricting irregular immigration, but so far without success as the former fringe party keeps coming first in nationwide polls.
“If the AfD wins the Saxony-Anhalt election, it would represent a personal defeat for Friedrich Merz,” said Oliver Lembcke of Ruhr University in Bochum.
“He had aimed to cut the AfD’s vote share in half. Instead, the AfD has overtaken the CDU as the strongest party, even at the federal level. He bears personal responsibility for this outcome.”

Romanian prosecutors indict Andrew Tate for trafficking minors, money laundering
BUCHAREST - Romanian prosecutors officially indicted social media influencer Andrew Tate on Sept 4 for trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering and his brother Tristan for complicity, years after they began investigating them.
The Tate brothers, former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship, were arrested in Miami in late July after Britain requested their extradition.
Mainly based in Romania since 2017, they have been under criminal investigation in the country on charges including human trafficking since December 2022. They have denied all wrongdoing.
Romanian prosecutors said the Tates recruited their victims by seducing them and falsely claiming to want a relationship or marriage, before forcing them to produce pornographic content for a webcam business.
“We will examine every aspect of (the indictment) with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process,” a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, Eugen Vidineac, said in a statement.
“Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them.”
The Tate brothers remain in jail in the US while a judge decides on the request for their extradition to Britain, where they are wanted on rape charges.
The spokesperson for the Romanian anti-organised crime prosecuting unit DIICOT — which is investigating the Tates — said it was not immediately clear whether the unit will seek their extradition from the United States.
The Tates can be tried in absentia in Romania, but the trial will not start immediately. Under Romanian law, the indictment gets sent to a preliminary court chamber, where a judge will inspect the case files to ensure legality.
While the law states that the preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalise the report, indictments routinely take significantly longer.
Andrew Tate, a self-described misogynist, previously said he moved to Romania because law enforcement was more lax there.
Both brothers have grown their following of mainly young men by building a lavish, hyper-macho image of driving fast cars and dating beautiful women. REUTERS

Interview: "Shanghai Spirit" offers valuable insights for South Caucasus in transition, says Armenian scholar
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:32:17 CST
18:32:17 KST

YEREVAN, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The South Caucasus has entered a period of structural and geopolitical adjustments, and the principles of the "Shanghai Spirit" are highly relevant to regional stability and development, Armenian scholar Johnny Melikyan has said.
In a recent written interview with Xinhua, Melikyan, a senior analyst at Armenia's Orbeli Center, said the expansion of cross-regional connectivity, shifting regional balances, and evolving security dynamics require the countries of the South Caucasus, including Armenia, to pursue foreign policies that are highly pragmatic, flexible and multidimensional.
Melikyan said the core principles of the "Shanghai Spirit" -- mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations, and pursuit of common development -- align closely with Armenia's foreign policy priorities. Armenia's institutional engagement with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) should be viewed within the framework of its active efforts to pursue a diversified foreign policy, he added.
Against the backdrop of today's fragmented international landscape, countries in the South Caucasus should play a constructive role in promoting regional connectivity, he said.
He said the SCO has evolved from a primarily security-focused organization into a comprehensive platform for economic and digital cooperation, demonstrating that modern security extends far beyond military might.
"Lasting regional stability requires deep economic interdependence, climate resilience, digital cooperation, and joint disaster-response mechanisms," he said.
Melikyan said the SCO's role as a bridge between civilizational spaces is invaluable as global politics becomes increasingly dominated by narratives of division.
Melikyan said that as the SCO enters its second quarter-century, challenges confronting Eurasia will only grow more complex. He stressed that no single nation or exclusive military-political bloc can resolve these challenges in isolation, adding that the future belongs to flexible, pragmatic networks of inclusive cooperation.
"I hope that the countries of the South Caucasus, with the support of our SCO partners, can transition from a zone of geopolitical competition into a secure, predictable, and prosperous continental hub connecting East and West, North and South," Melikyan said. ■

China's long-term care insurance covers over 320 million people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:31:49 CST
18:31:49 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on advancing the high-quality development of healthcare security to better serve Chinese modernization in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Xiaoyu)
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China's long-term care insurance system now covers more than 320 million people, with the fund's cumulative spending reaching 114.2 billion yuan (16.85 billion U.S. dollars), a health insurance official said on Friday.
More than 4.6 million people have received care services under the program, said Wang Wenjun, deputy head of the National Healthcare Security Administration, at a news conference held by the State Council Information Office.
To date, 22 provincial-level regions have issued implementation plans for the program, Wang said.
The number of localities where the scheme has been established reached 121, and the figure is expected to rise to 247 nationwide by the end of this year, he said.
As an important part of China's social security system, long-term care insurance provides care services or financial support to people who have partially or completely lost the ability to care for themselves. The scheme helps cover their basic daily needs and related medical care, easing the burden on both them and their families.
The program is also a priority under China's five-year plan for improving medical security as the country responds to its rapidly aging population. At the end of 2025, China had 323.38 million people aged 60 or older, accounting for 23 percent of the population. That figure is projected to exceed 400 million by around 2035.
China aims to have the long-term care insurance system in place nationwide by the end of 2028, according to a national plan to implement the program.
Provisions on long-term care insurance were added to the recently adopted law on healthcare security by Chinese lawmakers at a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress.
The law specifies that a long-term care insurance system should be established and improved. It also stipulates that the relevant authorities under the State Council shall formulate specific measures for the financing, benefits, fund use, and supervision of long-term care insurance. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Chief scientist of China's Tianwen-3 mission says search for signs of life on Mars is top goal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:31:38 CST
18:31:38 KST

HEFEI, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China's Tianwen-3 mission is seeking evidence of whether life has ever existed on Mars, aiming to collect high-value Martian samples and conduct detailed analyses after bringing them to Earth, the mission's chief scientist Hou Zengqian told Xinhua in an interview Thursday.
Searching for potential signs of life on Mars is the top scientific goal of the Tianwen-3 mission, Hou said on the sidelines of the 2026 International Deep Space Exploration Conference, which opened on Thursday in Hefei, capital of east China's Anhui Province.
As a key step in China's planetary exploration program, Tianwen-3, planned for launch around 2028, is expected to become the first Mars sample-return mission in human history. Previously, NASA's Perseverance rover collected shallow surface samples, and will rely on a follow-up mission to return them to Earth. In contrast, Tianwen-3 aims to accomplish both sampling and return in a single mission.
Hou, also an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said China expects to finalize the landing site for the mission by the end of 2026, while Chinese scientists are advancing work on a new-generation geological map of the entire Mars.
Mars is one of the terrestrial planets in the solar system most similar to Earth and is widely considered a celestial body that may have once harbored life beyond Earth. Although Mars has evolved into a cold and arid planet with a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field, its past habitability and the possibility that life once existed there remain among the most important frontier questions in planetary science.
Over the past half-century, 47 Mars exploration missions have been conducted worldwide. However, more challenging endeavors, including sample-return and crewed missions to Mars, have yet to achieve a decisive breakthrough.
"The Tianwen-3 mission will look for microbial traces potentially similar to early forms of life on Earth, while also taking into consideration the possibility of unknown forms of life that may have emerged through Mars' unique evolutionary history, providing crucial evidence to answer this major scientific question," Hou said.
The mission could also deepen scientific understanding of the planet's climate evolution and geological processes and advance research in comparative planetology and the origins of life, the scientist said.
According to Hou, Mars sample return is an extremely complex project, with landing-site selection, planetary protection and contamination control, and the identification of potential signs of life among its key challenges.
Chinese scientists are selecting candidate landing sites for the mission based on factors that include geological age, history of water activity, habitability and the potential for preserving biosignatures.
China will also build the world's first planetary protection laboratory to prevent terrestrial microorganisms from contaminating Mars while ensuring the safe isolation of returned samples, according to Hou.
To address the challenge of detecting potentially tiny amounts of life-related materials in Martian samples, Chinese scientists are conducting dedicated research to establish a high-fidelity methodology covering the entire process for identifying biosignatures in returned samples.
"Regardless of whether signs of life are found, the returned Martian samples will have irreplaceable scientific value," Hou said.
He said analyses of the samples at microscopic, molecular and isotopic scales could deepen understanding of Mars' geology, environment, evolution of habitability and the conditions under which life may originate.
The mission has now entered the stage of developing engineering prototypes, Hou said.
He added that the Mars sample-return mission will not only provide a comprehensive test of China's engineering capabilities, but also serve as a major driver of planetary science.
Chinese scientists are advancing work on a new-generation geological map of the entire Mars by making full use of data from the Tianwen-1 mission and multiple international sources. The project integrates information from imagery, spectroscopy, radar and gravity measurements, and applies artificial intelligence to geological interpretation. Version 1.0 of the 1:5 million scale geological map of the entire Mars is scheduled for completion by the end of 2028.
Tianwen-3 will uphold the principle of open cooperation and work with scientists around the world to explore the mysteries of Mars, contributing China's expertise and solutions to expanding humanity's scientific frontier and advancing planetary science, Hou added. ■

Ferdi Uzun and Merve Berker
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
The husband of Turkish American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, killed by Israeli soldiers in the occupied West Bank two years ago, criticized Friday the lack of progress in the US legal process over her death.
Speaking to Anadolu at Eygi's graveside in the Didim district of Türkiye’s southwestern Aydin province, Hamid Mazhar Ali said: “The legal process in the US is at exactly the same point as the day she was killed.”
“There has been absolutely no progress,” he said during a memorial ceremony marking the second anniversary of her death.
“Despite our persistent requests over the past two years, no investigation has been launched.”
Ali said the pain of losing his wife remains as intense as it was when she died.
“It is just as difficult now as it was on the day she died,” he said. “It has not become any easier.”
“I think about her all the time. But it is also something a person has to learn to live with over time,” he added.
Ali said he misses hearing her laugh and joking with her.
Describing Eygi as someone who supported struggles for justice in different parts of the world from her youth, Ali said she “passionately advocated for peace and justice not only in Palestine but everywhere in the world.”
“Throughout her youth, she took part in many different struggles for peace and justice,” he added.
Ali said the situation in Palestine had deeply affected her.
“I think she was profoundly affected, especially by the events that began in 2023 and by the genocide,” he said.
“That is why she felt she had to go there. Seeing that all of this is still continuing today after such atrocities would have made her, like all of us, very angry and deeply disappointed.”
'Extremely hypocritical stance' by US
Ali said the family's pursuit of justice in the US has so far produced no results.
“I think this is an extremely hypocritical stance. But it is not surprising. We have seen this for the past 20 years, ever since Rachel Corrie,” he said.
Corrie was an American peace activist killed by an Israeli bulldozer in Gaza in 2003 while trying to prevent the demolition of a Palestinian family's home.
“She was an American, born and raised in the US, and her parents were American too. Yet justice was not delivered for her either,” Ali said.
“This is disappointing and it makes me angry. But when it comes to Israel, this double standard is not surprising,” he added.
“Looking at America's approach toward Israel and its record of not holding it accountable, its talk about justice seems extremely hypocritical.”
Ali said they would continue seeking justice at both the state level in Washington and the federal level.
“We will continue doing this because we know the issue is not only Aysenur. It is everyone who has been unjustly killed around the world, including by Israel,” he said.
Incident
Israeli soldiers opened fire during a peaceful demonstration in the occupied West Bank, seriously wounding Eygi, who had joined the protest in support of Palestinians and also held US citizenship.
Eygi was taken to a Palestinian hospital after being shot in the head and died on Sept. 6, 2024.
She was laid to rest in Didim, Aydin, on Sept. 14.
Eygi was a human rights activist and volunteer with the International Solidarity Movement, which supports Palestinians through peaceful and civilian means against Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories.
The occupied Palestinian territories have periodically witnessed shootings, stabbings and car-ramming attacks targeting Israeli soldiers or occupiers amid Israel’s attacks on the Gaza Strip and occupied West Bank.
Israel has killed more than 73,000 people and injured over 174,000 others in Gaza since Oct. 8, 2023.
Israeli army and settler attacks in the occupied West Bank since the start of the Gaza offensive have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians and injured over 12,000 others, while around 24,000 have been arrested.

====================================================================================================

What the Heck? Another Perfect Geometric Shape Has Been Detected on Saturn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

A team of astronomers discovered a strange polygonal atmospheric structure on Saturn near the planet’s south pole. This 10-sided shape, known as a decagon, joins one of the gas giant’s most famous features: a hexagon near the north pole that was first observed 44 years ago. Images of the new decagon were captured by the Hubble Space Telescope, and the discovery was recently published in the journal Science Advances.
The formations at both the north and south poles aren’t solid structures, like a wall or a rock formation. Saturn doesn’t even have a defined solid surface like Earth’s crust. If you were to descend through the atmosphere of the ringed planet, the pressure and density would progressively increase, but you would never reach a “ground” on which to land. Instead, what astronomers have witnessed are patterns formed by clouds, albeit very unusual ones.
Each side of the decagon measures approximately 16,800 kilometers, which is a few thousand miles longer than the diameter of Earth. Near the feature is a jet stream reaching speeds of 116 meters per second, or nearly 260 miles per hour. By way of comparison, a Category 5 hurricane—the most intense storm level possible on Earth—is defined by winds above 157 miles per hour. Interestingly, although the jet stream circulates at tremendous speed, the decagon pattern shifts at a mere 2.5 meters per second—less than 6 miles per hour.
The south pole feature appears to have formed recently. For decades, scientists have been searching for a counterpart to the famous northern hexagon. However, major missions that observed the planet have previously not been able to find an equivalent, long-lasting structure in the south. The search was further complicated because, due to Saturn’s tilt, its southern hemisphere was not clearly visible from Earth for many years.
The first clues of the decagon came from ground-based observations, some by amateur astronomers. As the images accumulated, it became evident that something strange was happening in Saturn’s southern cloud bands. Data from the Hubble Space Telescope made it possible to trace the pattern back to images taken in 2023. Monitoring continued, and by 2025 its 10 vertices had become much more clearly defined, confirming the presence of a new polygonal feature in the ringed planet’s atmosphere. Science, however, hasn’t settled on an explanation for how these structures came to be.
Various hypotheses have been proposed since the discovery of the north polar hexagon. One is that the polygons are the visible manifestations of enormous atmospheric waves confined by powerful jet streams. You can think of these as similar to ocean waves, which are not simply objects traveling across the ocean but rather disturbances propagating through the water.
A wave’s behavior changes depending on the space in which it moves and the boundaries it encounters. On Saturn, waves of atmospheric gases may be encountering jet streams that confine them, in a sense, like the edge of a beach. Except in this case, the “beach” wraps all the way around the planet.
Various other factors, such as Saturn’s rapid rotation, exact wind speeds, and variations in the currents, could all contribute to the distinct geometries of the shapes. A current that coils around the planet six times can form a hexagon; one that does so 10 times, a decagon. This is one of the more likely explanations for how an atmosphere without any solid structure can end up forming something that looks like a gigantic polygon, but there are still many unanswered questions.
We don’t know how deep these geometric figures extend, how long the new decagon might last, whether its appearance is related to Saturn’s seasons, and—most importantly—what sparked its formation in the first place. Researchers hope to find some answers by tracking the decagon’s evolution. To do so, they plan to continue observations with the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes and use more advanced atmospheric models to reconstruct possible conditions that could give rise to such a structure.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

“We are grateful to everyone who is trying to contribute to resolving this issue. Are there chances? In my view, yes, there are,” Putin said.

The Russian president separately criticised attacks on civilian vessels and threats against civilian aircraft, calling such actions “state terrorism” and saying they complicated prospects for bilateral peace talks.
Strikes on energy infrastructure
Meanwhile, the conflict between the two countries continues to escalate.
Overnight, Russia attacked energy infrastructure facilities in Ukraine’s southern Odessa region, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said on Friday, warning of possible restrictions on the electricity network.
Odessa Governor Oleh Kiper said one person was killed and at least five others wounded in the attack, which also damaged civilian infrastructure.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Friday that its forces had struck two cargo vessels in the Black Sea that were transporting weapons, ammunition and military equipment for Ukraine. The claim could not be independently verified.
A Ukrainian drone strike, meanwhile, caused a fire at an oil depot in the Russian Black Sea port city of Sochi, authorities in the Krasnodar region said. No casualties were immediately reported.
Tensions inside Ukraine
Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said an investigation would determine how a dispute between two Ukrainian security agencies escalated into a shootout in Kiev that left three members of the Defence Ministry’s HUR Military Intelligence Directorate injured.
The confrontation occurred on Tuesday after the home of a Russian nationalist activist fighting alongside Ukrainian forces was searched. The activist said he had been detained by the SBU Security Service and forced to sign a confession saying he had collaborated with Russian intelligence, a statement he later retracted.
The SBU said its officers had acted to prevent what it described as a Moscow-backed plot to assassinate Russian anti-Kremlin activists in Kiev.
“It is important that the truth come out. And that situations like this do not recur,” Zelenskyy said.
He said the heads of the SBU and HUR would be assessed following an internal investigation, adding that both sides should be held accountable for actions that “should not have happened”.
Two servicemen from the agencies have been issued notices of suspicion in connection with the incident. Zelenskyy also dismissed Oleh Khramov, head of the SBU department responsible for protecting state secrets.
Shooting targets Russian serviceman
In Russia, a serviceman was hospitalised on Thursday after being shot in the city of Engels in Saratov region, according to the regional branch of the Investigative Committee.
Authorities said bullets and shell casings were found at the scene and a criminal investigation was opened on charges of attempted murder and illegal arms trafficking. They did not identify the serviceman or say who carried out the attack.
Last week, a serviceman was killed and his wife injured in a car bombing near St Petersburg, while three weeks earlier a factory director supplying drones to the Russian military was seriously injured and his driver killed when their vehicle exploded near Yekaterinburg.
Kiev has claimed responsibility for some attacks inside Russia. Ukraine’s SBU said in December 2024 that it had organised the killing of Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, who headed Russia’s military nuclear, biological and chemical protection forces. Kirillov was killed by a bomb hidden in a scooter outside his Moscow apartment building.
The latest developments underscore the widening security risks surrounding the conflict, even as Putin says there remains a chance for a diplomatic settlement.

Find contracts in technology and research and development with the Ministry of Defence
A list of places to find Defence contracts and funding in the technology and innovative research and development (R&D) space.
Every year the Ministry of Defence (MOD) works with companies and researchers to develop next-generation innovation, technology and digital solutions to support our frontline troops. You can find some of the places we advertise those opportunities on this page. This is not an exhaustive list.
Opportunities outside the technology and innovation space can be found at Procurement at MOD.
To get notified every time this page gets updated sign up for email updates.
To give feedback on this page, please contact the Commercial X team at defcomrcl-comrclx@mod.gov.uk.
Guidance for new suppliers
A common way for suppliers to bid for contracts is via online platforms known as frameworks. These are usually set up to help government buy a specific type of product or service, and have standard terms and processes which make it easier to contract with us. Once you are on a framework you can apply for any advertised opportunities until the framework ends.
Some frameworks are ‘open’, which means they can be joined at any time, while others are only open during certain periods. There also dynamic markets which are similar to frameworks and are always open to join.

Ivan Fedorov is leaving the post of head of the Zaporizhzhia RMA - where he will work next
Kyiv • UNN
The head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration and former mayor of Melitopol will head the State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine. Serhii Sukhomlyn, who had previously been mayor of Zhytomyr, was dismissed from this position at his own request.
Ivan Fedorov has been appointed Head of the State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine. Prior to that, since February 2, 2024, he had served as head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration. UNN reports this with reference to the resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated September 3 of this year, No. 870-р.
Details
To appoint Fedorov Ivan Serhiiovych Head of the State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine from the date he actually begins performing his official duties, for a term of no more than 12 months from the day martial law is terminated or canceled, with remuneration in accordance with the law, establishing a three-month probationary period
In another resolution dated September 3, 2026 (No. 868-р), the government dismissed Serhii Sukhomlyn from the position of Head of the State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine at his own request.
Additionally
Ivan Fedorov was mayor of Melitopol from December 2020 to February 2024. In 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion, he refused to cooperate with the occupiers and was abducted. He was exchanged after six days in captivity for nine captured Russian conscript soldiers.
Serhii Sukhomlyn was mayor of Zhytomyr from 2015 to 2024.

Earlier, UNN reported that Ruslan Oliinyk had been appointed Deputy Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine.

Iceland’s rejection of accession talks ‘a blow to EU’: Expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:25:25 UTC
18:25:25 KST

Icelanders have rejected reopening accession negotiations with the EU, voting to preserve a relationship that gives them extensive access to the bloc while keeping the country outside it.
In an Aug. 29 referendum, 52.8% voted against restarting the talks, while 47.2% supported the proposal.
Turnout reached 82.5%, the highest since 2009, with 118,040 voting “no” and 105,399 voting “yes.”
The ballot was not a direct vote on EU membership. It asked whether negotiations suspended more than a decade ago should continue. Any resulting accession agreement would have required a second referendum.
“It is a blow to the EU,” Marianne Riddervold, a research professor at the ARENA Centre for European Studies at the University of Oslo, told Anadolu.
“Enlarging to democratically stable and relatively wealthy countries would help balance Eastern enlargement. And the EU has a strong interest in developments in the Arctic,” Riddervold said.
Riddervold said the “no” campaign succeeded in transforming a procedural vote on negotiations into a wider debate over membership.
“The no campaign made this into a discussion about membership more than whether or not to start negotiations,” she said.
“The yes campaign wasn’t really prepared for this, and the no campaign had more resources and support by the main newspaper, which is partly owned by strong fishing interests.”
The final Gallup poll before the referendum showed 51.6% opposing renewed talks and 48.4% supporting them.
However, an earlier survey by Icelandic pollster Maskina had placed the “yes” side narrowly ahead at 51.3%, indicating a shift during the closing stages of the campaign.
Riddervold said the opposition was driven by both economic interests and identity-based concerns.
“The main arguments against were linked to national control over national resources, not least fisheries, and there was a strong ideational component to the opposition, linked to the idea of sovereignty and independence,” she said.
The fishing industry accounts for about 8% of Iceland’s gross domestic product and nearly 40% of exports. A pre-referendum Gallup survey found that 90% of companies connected to the sector opposed EU membership.
“The no campaign had more resources, and support by the main newspaper, which is partly owned by strong fishing interests,” Riddervold said.
Membership would bring Iceland under the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy, although quotas, access and possible exemptions would have been negotiated. Icelanders decided there was no need to open the talks before arguing over how they might end.
The result also exposed an urban-rural divide. Reykjavik North backed negotiations by 57.5%, while Reykjavik South voted 54.5% in favor.
The “no” vote reached 62.9% in the Northwest, 61.2% in the Northeast and 60.5% in the South.
The referendum took place amid Russia’s war on Ukraine, growing strategic competition in the Arctic and uncertainty over the future of transatlantic relations.
Iceland was a founding member of NATO but has no standing armed forces. It relies primarily on the alliance and a bilateral defense agreement signed with the US in 1951.
Despite this dependence, Riddervold said security played a smaller part in the referendum debate than expected.
“Security played less of a role in the debate than I had assumed,” she said.
The country signed a Security and Defence Partnership with the EU on March 18, providing a framework for closer cooperation in areas including maritime security, cyber and hybrid threats, space, crisis management and support for Ukraine.
The partnership is not a collective defense agreement.
Riddervold said Iceland would nevertheless continue trying to deepen practical security cooperation with the bloc.
“This is already an ongoing process. Iceland recently signed a security and defense partnership with the EU, but this is not a binding agreement,” she said.
“Like Norway, it wants to connect more closely in this domain, and I think this cooperation will continue. But like Norway, it is struggling to be included in everything it wants.”
She said the EU could take a pragmatic approach in areas such as Arctic security, while Nordic and Nordic-Baltic defense cooperation would also continue to strengthen.
“European security is a patchwork of different security cooperation agreements,” she said.
Iceland already participates in the EU single market through the European Economic Area (EEA). It is also part of Schengen, the EU Emissions Trading System, and programs including Erasmus and Horizon Europe.
The EU accounts for 53.6% of Iceland’s total trade and receives about 66.5% of its exports, according to European Commission figures.
The EEA largely excludes fisheries and agriculture, conveniently leaving two of Iceland’s most sensitive industries outside the Brussels package.
“I think that the fact that Iceland already is integrated in the single market through the EEA agreement, is part of Schengen and has a lot of other agreements with the EU played a role,” Riddervold said.
“Like in Norway, many people feel that this already gives the country what it needs,” she further added.
Iceland initially applied for EU membership in 2009, after its banking system collapsed during the global financial crisis. Negotiations began in 2010 and were put on hold in 2013 after a change of government. By then, 11 of 35 negotiating chapters had been provisionally closed.
The EU kept a low profile during the campaign, partly because Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir’s government asked it not to interfere in a domestic decision, according to reports.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos gave several interviews to Icelandic media, including public broadcaster RUV, explaining the accession process and what negotiations would involve in practice.
Senior EU officials, however, largely refrained from actively campaigning for a “yes” vote.
After the result, European Council President Antonio Costa said through a spokesperson that the EU “fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic people.”
“Iceland remains one of the EU’s closest and most trusted partners,” he added.
Several European lawmakers, however, said on US social media company X that the result should prompt reflection in Brussels.
French Renew Europe lawmaker Sandro Gozi called the vote “a warning for Europe,” saying fears over fishing and emotional arguments had defeated the case for “yes.”
“The EU must change, overcome vetoes and become more effective and sovereign,” he said.
Finnish center-right lawmaker Mika Aaltola said Icelanders had assessed what full membership would add to their current arrangements and concluded it was “not enough.”
“A nation weighed what membership would add to what it already has, and answered: not enough,” said Aaltola, who is also an MEP.
“If we cannot charm a small North Atlantic democracy with Trump in the White House and Putin waging war on our continent, then the conditions for charming will not get better than this,” Aaltola said.
Nicola Procaccini, co-chairman of the European Conservatives and Reformists Group, said Iceland’s decision should not be “dismissed lightly.”
“The fact that the Icelandic people nevertheless chose not to take even that first step should give Brussels pause,” he said.

Live: Rabbitohs thrash Roosters reserves as Jai Arrow makes tearful 100th Souths appearance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:15:40 UTC
18:15:40 KST

Jai Arrow makes his 100th Rabbitohs appearance, South Sydney beat Roosters 50-22 to secure home NRL final
Tears flowed as Jai Arrow made his 100th Rabbitohs appearance, with his Souths teammates helping crush the reserve team of their arch rivals, the Roosters.
Arrow choked back tears when he was hugged by Wayne Bennett as the forward was given a hero's reception at a sold out Sydney Football Stadium.
The 31-year-old father of one was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) this year and, until two weeks ago, was stranded on 98 NRL games for the Bunnies.
At Bennett's initiative, the NRL allowed Souths an extra interchange against the Gold Coast last week for game number 99 and again on Friday against the Roosters.
"It was pretty emotional," Cam Murray told Channel 9.
"I'm just so happy that everyone was able to get around him and he's been able to feel all the love.
"I know he really appreciates it and we love to see it.
"We all love him and happy he was able to notch up 100 games."
Arrow led his teammates out to the sound of the Gerry and the Pacemakers rendition of You'll Never Walk Alone, with 14th Immortal and dual-club legend Ron Coote ringing the Rabbitohs' bell.
The former Queensland State of Origin forward was given a guard of honour by more than 100 Souths old boys, including members of the 2021 grand final squad Arrow was a member of and his family, who all sobbed along with him and plenty of others in the stands.
"It was emotional," Roosters captain Connor Watson said in his post-match press conference.
"It was very touching. Things like that are bigger than rugby league."
In the subsequent match, the Rabbitohs ran in 10 tries to pummel the Roosters 50-20, who had rested 10 of their star players with a top four spot secure.
But in completing the win, Souths have themselves earned a home finals spot, and will face Newcastle at either the Olympic Stadium or Sydney Football Stadium next week.
Campbell Graham scored twice for the Rabbitohs, who had nine different try scorers on the night, including Alex Johnston, who crossed for the 30th time this season.
Latrell Mitchell was one of them, scoring on his return to the starting line up while mixing his sublime skill with fearsome physicality, most notably when he flattened Toby Rodwell in the closing stages, standing over the stricken half like Mohammed Ali over Sonny Liston in their 1965 rematch.
If Mitchell's performance was heartening — a poor 5/10 kicking rate aside — Roosters firebrand Spencer Leniu will have raised concerns from coach Trent Robinson in the first half.
Leniu squared up to Keaon Koloamatangi after the Rabbitohs prop smashed him in a tackle twice in the same set, the second time tossing the ball away and giving away a penalty.
Titans fume over questionable calls
Earlier, the Dolphins hung on to beat the Titans 24-20 on the Gold Coast.
It was the Dolphins' seventh-consecutive win, but almost didn't happen as the Titans fought back late on and were unfortunate not to come away with the win.
The Titans were left fuming when, while leading 14-0, they had Keano Kini sin-binned in the 23rd minute for a very soft push on Dolphins winger Tevita Naufahu.
Josh Hannay was fuming after that call, and a trio of others in the closing minutes, went against his side.
"I thought it was incredibly harsh and not long after that they get a try from a knock-on," Hannay said.
"You talk about momentum swings — they don't get much bigger than that. Moe [Moeaki Fotuaika] got smacked in the face at the end and ends up in the bin for retaliating.
"[Jamayne Isaako] throws a leg out to trip [AJ Brimson] in the act of a potential try-scoring play and it is just a penalty.
"It was probably more sin-binnable than Keano's play.
"You stack all those things up and you lose by four points, you have got to be proud of your team's effort."

More bodies recovered from wreckage of Kyrenia ferry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:15:35 UTC
18:15:35 KST

AA photo.
Two more bodies have been recovered from the wreckage of a ferry that sank off the coast of Turkish Cyprus’ Kyrenia, bringing the confirmed death toll to 12, Turkish Cypriot Prime Minister Ünal Üstel announced on Sept. 4.
Üstel said the bodies, both of which were identified as women, were found during deep-sea search operations carried out by the Turkish naval vessels TCG Işın and TCG Alemdar. Authorities have launched procedures to establish the identities of the victims.
The high-speed passenger vessel Filo Jet, which operates between Kyrenia Port in Turkish Cyprus and Taşucu Port in Türkiye’s southern Mersin province, began taking on water from its bow shortly after departing around noon on Aug. 30.
The vessel carrying 267 people capsized while attempting to return to the port.
Search efforts are continuing around the clock for the 16 people still missing, Üstel said, stressing that the operation is being conducted with the support of Türkiye and the involvement of all relevant units.
“All teams involved in the search operations will continue their work with the same determination and diligence to locate the missing individuals,” he said.
Late on Sept. 3, the premier said that additional bodies were spotted in the wreckage. He expressed hope that further recoveries could be made during the Sept. 4 operations.
Meanwhile, Turkish Defense Ministry spokesman Rear Admiral Zeki Aktürk said seven ships and 11 aircraft from the Turkish Navy were taking part in the search-and-rescue operation off Kyrenia.
Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, who visited Turkish Cyprus on Sept. 3, said that only two of the 133 people who were hospitalized after being rescued alive from the sea following the accident remain in hospital.
Neither of the two patients is in critical condition, Yılmaz said.
Expert reports prepared as part of the investigation indicated that the disaster could have been averted had the vessel returned to port slowly, immediately after it began taking on water.

Haiti mourners bury 47 victims of Kenscoff gang massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

More than 100 mourners gathered Wednesday at a church in Haiti’s Kenscoff community, where gangs recently carried out a deadly attack that killed dozens and shook the troubled country.
The funerals were held for two brothers and three of their cousins at the church in Kenscoff, a mountain farming community overlooking Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.
Gangs stormed the once-peaceful community on the night of Aug. 23, killing 47 people and abducting more than 50 others in one of Haiti’s largest mass kidnappings in recent years.
The attack left residents fearful and grieving as violence continues to spread across the country.
Days after the abductions, a gang leader agreed to free six children and seven women following intervention by community leaders and UNICEF.
Marta Hurtado, a spokesperson for the U.N. Human Rights Office, said about 150 heavily armed gang members participated in the attack. She said they first killed 13 people who tried to flee and then pursued 50 others who had sought refuge inside the church where the funerals were held Thursday.
Gang members executed 22 Haitians in the church courtyard and 12 others behind the church, she said.
Patrique Saint-Hilaire, an official with Haiti’s Civil Protection Agency in Kenscoff, told The Associated Press that the government plans to support the families who lost loved ones.
So far, 17 of the 47 people killed have been buried.
"Kenscoff is still under red alert," he said. "People are very traumatized."
Friends and family of those killed have organized protests and vigils, blaming police for the attack. Haiti’s National Police has said it is investigating the attack and whether it was "due to complicity or negligence."
Mourners declined to speak to journalists Thursday as anger over the killings persisted. After the service, some people attacked a couple of journalists, including an AP photographer who received medical care.
The latest attack comes as Haiti prepares for its first general elections in more than a decade.
Gangs control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swaths of land in Haiti’s central region and beyond. They are also seeking to seize territory in Kenscoff.
Gang violence has displaced a record nearly 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,050 people were reported killed between January and June, according to the U.N.

In a striking statement at the first hearing for an April school shooting in the southern province of Kahramanmaraş, the assailant’s father on Sept. 4 said he plans to file a criminal complaint against his son for stealing the firearms used in the attack.
The court began the trial on Sept. 4 of the parents of the attacker responsible for the deadly school shooting that sent shockwaves across Türkiye.
In April, a student opened fire at his school, killing nine students and a teacher. The attack prompted the Education Ministry to introduce a broad range of security measures, including tighter controls at school entrances and psychological risk assessments for children.
The attacker, who died at the scene, used firearms belonging to his father, a senior police officer, to carry out the assault.
The father, Uğur Mersinli, and mother, Peyman Pınar Mersinli, appeared before the court on Sept. 4 over alleged negligence that contributed to the attack.
Uğur Mersinli said his son had found the firearms, arguing that his access to the weapons did not amount to parental negligence.
He said he had no knowledge that his son was planning to carry out a shooting at his school, arguing that it was wrong to place the entire responsibility for the incident on him.
“It is wrong to attribute the entire risk of the incident to me. The firearms were stolen. Bedrooms are places in homes that are kept locked,” he said.
Arguing that there was a perpetrator if a crime had been committed, Mersinli said: “The perpetrator is İsa Aras Mersinli, and no public case has been brought against him. The prosecution prepared a mixed indictment under public pressure in order to accuse the mother and father.”
Mersinli also announced that he intends to file a criminal complaint against his son and was seeking to have him prosecuted for theft over the firearms.
The father is facing 10 aggravated life sentences for “intentional killing with possible intent” and up to 30 years in prison for “causing injury with possible intent.”
The mother is also being prosecuted and faces up to 22.5 years in prison for “causing the deaths and injuries of multiple people through conscious negligence.”
Ahead of the hearing, lawyer of the families of the victims Özcan Kara said the ruling in the case will constitute an important legal precedent concerning parents’ responsibilities in educating and supervising their children and would help shape society’s approach to the issue.
Kara said the indictment was primarily based on the presence of firearms in the home, including seven handguns with loaded magazines and two shotguns.

Analyst ties drone surge to CIA chief’s Moscow warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:14:10 UTC
18:14:10 KST

- CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on August 25 and 26 to warn Russia against attacking a NATO member, as Russian drones repeatedly entered Romanian airspace that month.
- Moldova closed at least three border crossings in August due to nearby drone strikes, including one around its August 27 Independence Day.
Civilians and infrastructure on NATO’s eastern flank faced near-daily Russian drone incidents through August, even as the CIA director made a rare visit to Moscow to warn Russia against attacking a NATO member state, according to Cristian Vlas, an Eastern Europe analyst at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED).
CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on August 25 and 26 for meetings with Russian intelligence officials, a trip first reported by the Wall Street Journal and CBS News, which said Ratcliffe’s goal was to discourage Russia from testing NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense commitment. President Donald Trump later called the visit “semi-routine.” The Kremlin confirmed contacts took place but said Ratcliffe did not meet with President Vladimir Putin.
Romania recorded repeated Russian drone incursions into its airspace through August, according to Vlas, most of which Romanian and NATO aircraft intercepted. Drone debris landed in both uninhabited and residential areas along Romania’s southeastern coast, near Black Sea tourist sites and oil infrastructure, he said.
On August 20, a Romanian Air Force F-16 destroyed a drone laden with explosives roughly 80 nautical miles (148 kilometers) off Constanța, near the Neptun Deep gas platform operated by OMV Petrom and Romgaz, after a commercial ship spotted the device drifting toward the site, according to Romania’s Defence Ministry. Ukraine’s military told Romanian officials the drone was not one of theirs; Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia, though authorities have not formally identified who built it.
Vlas said Moldova has also been affected by spillover from Russian strikes on Ukrainian territory near its border, with at least three crossing points temporarily closed during August because of nearby drone strikes. A Russian strike on August 21 damaged the Tabaky crossing, and a Ukrainian border crossing near Vulkaneshty-Vinogradovka closed on August 25, two days before Moldova marked its Independence Day on August 27.
“Moldova has also been affected by the spillovers from Russian attacks on Ukrainian grain routes, with three border checkpoints having been closed temporarily amid daily drone incidents, including on its Independence Day, highlighting Chisinau’s air defense vulnerability,” Vlas said.
Vlas said the recurring drone incidents are straining air defense resources across Eastern Europe, and that they may be compounding “possibly renewed Russian-linked sabotage attempts” in Germany, Estonia and Slovakia, which he said could be intended to divert investigative and prosecutorial resources while testing European Union resolve to continue backing Ukraine.
“Calling these increasingly regular security incidents hybrid warfare threats undermines efforts to define the deteriorating security environment, develop EU-wide and local solutions, and call out Russia’s systematic use of openly military or covert violence against Europe,” Vlas said.

Russian Speaking Forum Leaks 153 Million US and Canadian Driver’s Licenses Online
An online service listed on the Russian-speaking cybercrime forum Exploit offered access to more than 153 million driver’s licenses belonging to US and Canadian citizens, according to cybersecurity expert Brian Krebs
The Nexus service posted online in August also contained 10 million identity cards, 3 million passports, and nearly 580,000 medical records. The database even included special cards used for purchasing legal marijuana.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The compromised records included the driver’s license of US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. The operator of the Nexus platform offered to provide a copy of the official's document as proof to Krebs.
Federal law enforcement authorities in the United States, including the FBI, are investigating the breach, while the landing page for the Nexus service now indicates that it is no longer active.
The creators of the service claimed they gathered the document scans by breaching a major identity verification IT platform used by numerous Fortune 500 companies. Between August 31, 2025, and September 1, 2026, the database expanded by another 400,000 entries.
Scans of documents belonging to Krebs and his mother appeared on the platform on the exact day they rented a vehicle from Hertz and provided their personal information.
Security researcher Zach Edwards discovered his own driver’s license in the database after presenting it at a Planet 13 cannabis dispensary. In 2022, identity verification provider IDScan secured a service agreement with Planet 13 in the United States.
IDScan states on its website that its services are utilized by major brands including Hertz, Target, FedEx, Motorola Solutions, and casino operator Caesars Entertainment. The company’s verification systems carry out over 21 million checks across more than 20,000 locations worldwide. Headquartered in New Orleans, Louisiana, IDScan stated that an internal investigation is currently underway.
In the United States, driver’s licenses serve as the primary form of national identification, frequently used to verify identity when applying for loans or opening bank accounts.
The physical cards are required for various daily functions, including proving age for purchasing alcohol or entering night venues, renting property, passing airport security checks, and securing entry into government facilities.
Russian state-backed hackers compromised internet-connected cameras across NATO countries, including the Netherlands, to collect intelligence on military shipments destined for Ukraine, according to Dutch intelligence services.
The operation targeted IP cameras positioned along military logistics routes, allowing Russian actors to monitor transportation movements and gather information about the types of weapons and equipment being delivered to Kyiv, according to an investigation by the Netherlands' General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD).

China bans enforcement of U.S. oil sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:13:47 UTC
18:13:47 KST

China’s Ministry of Commerce announced on Saturday, May 2, 2026, that the U.S. sanctions against the five Chinese companies restrict their normal economic and commercial activities with third countries and constitute what Beijing described as the “extraterritorial application” of U.S. law, according to Xinhua.
The companies targeted by the sanctions are Hengli Petrochemical (Dalian), Shandong Shouguang Luqing Petrochemical, Shandong Jincheng Petrochemical Group, Hebei Xinhai Chemical Group, and Shandong Shengxing Chemical.
The United States has placed the companies under sanctions over what it described as their involvement in oil transactions with Iran, imposing measures including the blocking of assets and a ban on transactions with them.
China’s Ministry of Commerce said the U.S. sanctions violate international law and the norms governing international relations. Beijing stressed that the blocking order was issued under Chinese laws designed to counter the extraterritorial application of foreign laws.
China said the measure is aimed at protecting its sovereignty, security and development interests, as well as the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies and citizens.
The decision is significant because China’s independent “teapot” refineries are major buyers of Iranian oil, and the United States has imposed sanctions on a number of these refineries and other entities involved in Iran’s oil trade in recent years.
The latest move by China’s Ministry of Commerce also marks Beijing’s first official use of a “blocking order” to directly counter specific U.S. sanctions targeting Chinese companies linked to trade with Iran. The move could open a new chapter in tensions between Beijing and Washington over the extraterritorial enforcement of U.S. sanctions.

Wars, droughts, trade disruptions push world food prices to four-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:05:50 UTC
18:05:50 KST

Wars, droughts, trade rows push world food prices to four-year high
- World food prices rose 1.9 per cent in August to the highest since November 2022 amid geopolitical tensions and extreme weather.
- Climate shocks, conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, and disrupted trade are tightening food supply expectations and pushing grain prices to three-year highs.
- The threat of a strong El Nino and poor European harvests may cause ongoing market volatility and inflationary risks in global food markets.
AI generated
PARIS – World food prices climbed in August to the highest since the end of 2022, as escalating geopolitical tensions and extreme weather deepen concerns over supplies from key producing regions.
The United Nations’ index of food-commodity prices climbed 1.9 per cent from July, led by grains, sugar and dairy, according to a report from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) on Sept 4.
The FAO food price index, which tracks monthly changes in a basket of internationally traded food commodities, averaged 133.3 points in August, up from July’s revised reading of 130.8.
That was the highest score since November 2022, though nearly 17 per cent below a record peak from March 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Extreme heat and drought in Europe, the threat of a severe El Nino weather pattern and trade upheaval caused by the Ukraine and Iran wars have unsettled agricultural markets, pushing grain prices to three-year highs and sugar to a one-year peak.
“August’s increase in global food prices is a warning that the risk premium is returning to food markets. Climate shocks, geopolitical tensions and disrupted trade logistics are converging to tighten supply expectations,” FAO chief economist Maximo Torero said in a statement.
Tensions in the Black Sea breadbasket have escalated since mid-July, with Russia preparing to step up attacks on Ukraine, where farmers are struggling to export grain.
Hopes are also dimming for a peace deal between the United States and Iran, while poor harvests in Europe could leave the continent more reliant on imports, potentially intensifying competition for supplies.
Global wheat prices rose 2.6 per cent in August, while sugar jumped 11.9 per cent.
The FAO index tracks internationally traded food commodities, meaning it can take time for price changes to reach supermarket shelves.
Other warning signs are also emerging.
Futures of key crop staples like wheat and corn have climbed to multi-year highs. The Bloomberg Agriculture Spot Index, which tracks 10 major products, rose more than 13 per cent in August, its steepest gain since July 2012.
The threat of an unusually powerful El Nino means weather risks are unlikely to fade any time soon, keeping global food markets vulnerable to another inflationary shock. BLOOMBERG, REUTERS

Britten-Norman flies first fully UK-built Islander aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:05:46 UTC
18:05:46 KST

- Britten-Norman flew its first fully UK-built Islander aircraft on September 3 from Bembridge Airport, bound for the Falkland Islands Government Air Service.
- The company aims to build eight Islanders a year at Bembridge, with a second airframe already in production and components ordered for a third.
Britten-Norman flew its first Islander aircraft built entirely in the UK on Thursday, marking the return of complete airframe manufacturing to Britain after years of assembling major sections built overseas.
The BN2B-26 Islander took off from Bembridge Airport on the Isle of Wight at 2:25 p.m. and has now entered flight testing, the company said. The aircraft is destined for the Falkland Islands Government Air Service, known as FIGAS, which has flown Islanders to connect remote settlements across the Falklands since 1948.
Until now, Britten-Norman built major sections of the Islander overseas and shipped them to Bembridge for final assembly. The company says it now builds the entire airframe on-site from individual components, giving it direct control over the build schedule, tooling and quality checks rather than depending on parts arriving from abroad.
“Operators want to know two things. Will the aircraft do the job, and will it arrive when we said it would,” said Richard Milne, Chief Operating Officer at Britten-Norman. “The first has been settled for a long time. Assembling the airframe here is how we settle the second, because it puts the sequence, the tooling and the quality standard in our own hands.”
The aircraft reached 75% structural completion in June, had power applied for the first time on July 29, and rolled out of the factory the following day, according to the company. A second airframe is already under construction at Bembridge, and Britten-Norman says components for the aircraft after that are already on order. The company is aiming for a steady production rate of eight aircraft a year.
Britten-Norman says roughly 350 Islanders are currently flying in more than 70 countries, together logging about 20 million flight hours. The twin-engine aircraft can continue flying safely if one engine fails, runs on Lycoming piston engines with Hartzell variable-pitch propellers, and holds design approvals from UK, European and Ministry of Defence aviation authorities. Britten-Norman describes itself as the UK’s only approved civil aircraft manufacturer under the country’s A2 production certification.
Building the workforce for the new line has relied heavily on passing down decades of hands-on experience. Peter Dowers, who joined Britten-Norman as a fitter in September 1978, completed his 500th Islander build this year while training newer staff on the Bembridge line. Callum Trueman, who began his apprenticeship under Dowers in 2006, is now a production manager at the facility.
“This aircraft is Pete’s 500th and my first, and the next one is already on the line,” Trueman said.
FIGAS currently operates five Islanders across the Falklands for air ambulance flights, mail and freight delivery, and scenic tours, relying on the aircraft’s ability to operate from short runways. Britten-Norman has previously said FIGAS signed a letter of intent for four additional Islanders worth £7.97 million ($10.1 million), on top of the two aircraft it already has under contract, of which Thursday’s aircraft is the first.
Britten-Norman has not disclosed a target delivery date for the aircraft to reach the Falklands, saying only that delivery will follow completion of its flight test program.

At least 37 dead in Nigeria pipeline incident, group says
LAGOS, Sept 4 - At least 37 people died after inhaling fumes as they tried to tap an oil pipeline in southern Nigeria, an environmental group said on Friday, though authorities have not confirmed the toll.
The Youths and Environmental Advocacy Centre said the incident happened at around midnight on Thursday at Okrika in Rivers State. Police said the victims died while attempting to steal crude oil.
"Investigation is ongoing to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident and ascertain the facts," said Rivers police spokesperson ASP Blessing Kaborlo Agabe.
The incident, the worst known death toll since at least October 2023, highlights the persistent problem of crude oil theft and pipeline vandalism in the Niger Delta, where illegal tapping has caused deaths, pollution and losses to Nigeria’s oil industry.
The environmental group said the incident occurred at Okari Jetty while a vessel was loading and suspected thieves were siphoning a petroleum product under high pressure into boats. It said others were missing and bodies had been seen floating in the river.
Reuters was not able to independently confirm what happened and the death toll.
The Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps said circulating casualty figures remained unverified and the substance involved required technical confirmation.
It said it was working with security agencies to determine the number of dead, injured and missing, and investigate possible negligence, collusion or criminal facilitation. REUTERS
