Theresa Long, who also serves as an adviser to US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., reportedly gave the testimony during an August 14 deposition in a federal court case in Virginia. Neither her testimony nor her role at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) had previously been reported.
Long allegedly said that the 2,544 unverified deaths were reported to the department’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS).
Former US President Joe Biden ordered all US military staff to be vaccinated or be discharged from service, resulting in over 9,000 dismissals. After returning to office, President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to offer reinstatement to those who had been discharged for refusing a vaccine.
Mass-produced Covid-19 vaccines using mRNA technology were fast-tracked for deployment. Pharma giants that made billions in profit – Pfizer and Moderna – later acknowledged that their vaccines could, in rare cases, increase the risk of inflammation of the heart muscle.
Long testified for the defense in a lawsuit being heard by District Court Judge Michael Nachmanoff over the dismissal of Terry Adirim as director of the CIA’s Center for Global Health Services. Adirim alleges that the intelligence agency fired her for political reasons, specifically because of her advocacy for Covid-19 vaccination.
Adirim served as acting assistant secretary for health affairs at the Department of Defense during the pandemic. The CIA fired her in April 2025, a move highlighted at the time by several conservative political commentators, including Ivan Raiklin, who is a defendant in the lawsuit. Her termination came about a month before she would have qualified for full federal retirement benefits.
In May 2025, Nachmanoff expressed skepticism about Adirim’s chances of prevailing in the case when he declined to issue an injunction reversing her termination. The CIA has argued that the matter is an ordinary contract dispute.
Kennedy has repeatedly argued that some vaccines have been insufficiently studied and may carry serious side effects. Critics have accused him of promoting anti-vaccine views and argued that they make him unsuitable to serve as health secretary.

Far-right AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund said Friday he will become premier of Saxony-Anhalt only if his party wins an absolute majority and can govern alone.
Siegmund told ZDF’s Morgenmagazin that the AfD is not seeking a coalition in Sunday’s closely watched election in the eastern German state. He said he would take the top job only if he can carry out the program he put before voters.
“If someone wants to tackle the basic problems in the state such as migration, crazy energy policy, all the gender nonsense and so on — then I will gladly do that. But is there this partner? There isn’t in this state.”
He said other parties have shut the AfD out for a decade. “For 10 years people have wanted to ban us, for 10 years they have excluded us, for 10 years they vote our committee chairs out and deny us deputy speakers of the state parliament.”
“And we have accepted the realities and say: Fine, if no one wants to do it with us, then we just have to do it alone.”
Public broadcaster ZDF put the AfD at 41% in its latest poll, well ahead of its rivals. The current premier, Sven Schulze of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), was second at 23%.
In the same poll, the socialist Left Party stood at 11.5%, the Social Democratic Party (SPD) at 8.5% and the Greens at 6%. The newer left-populist BSW was at 4%, and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) at 3%.
The state parliament normally has 83 seats, meaning 42 are needed to govern alone. If the AfD falls short, Magdeburg could face weeks of negotiations over who becomes premier.
Saxony-Anhalt’s domestic intelligence service has classified the AfD’s state branch as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization, citing anti-democratic aims and members’ ties to far-right groups. Mainstream parties have ruled out coalition talks with the AfD.
Speaking on the same program, CDU lead candidate Schulze ruled out formal coalitions not only with the AfD but also with the Left Party.
“There will be no coalition with the Left Party, there will be no coalition with the AfD. I would ideally like to lead the state from the centre,” he said. “I know the poll numbers. So please let us wait for the election result.”
If the AfD falls short, the scenario most often discussed is a CDU-led minority government with the SPD and possibly the Greens, surviving vote by vote. Even then, such an arrangement would likely still need Left Party support to command a majority in the state parliament called Landtag.

Why the Falklands Is a Pressure Point For the U.K.—and How Milei, Trump Are Stoking Tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:13:05 UTC
05:13:05 KST

Argentina’s President Javier Milei has escalated his country’s claim over the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory, warning he will place economic pressure by sanctioning oil companies with operations in the area.
The Falkland Islands are "Argentine, by history and by right, there is no debate about it,” he said in a nationally televised address Thursday evening.
Milei argued the “winds of change blowing around the world” are favorable to Argentina’s long-claimed sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago, citing remarks made by his ally, U.S. President Donald Trump, who recently suggested the U.S. would be reviewing its neutrality on the dispute.
The Argentine President flagged a planned oil project in the area as a cause for concern. Within the next 18 months, two companies—one British and the other Israeli—are set to start extractions from the Sea Lion oilfield, which lies north of the islands and holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
Milei described the project as an urgent threat to Argentina’s sovereignty. "If we do not act swiftly, in a few months they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea—something that has never happened before,” he said.
The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as “Islas Malvinas,” sit roughly 300 miles from the Argentine coast, and have been a British territory for almost two centuries, but Argentina has never accepted British sovereignty over the area.
Vowing to take action, Milei said he plans to send a bill to Congress to strengthen Argentina’s response to what he views as attacks on its sovereignty.
Responding to the economic threats, the U.K. government reasserted its “unshakeable” commitment to the archipelago on Friday, with British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting insisting: “Milei’s statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands.”
“The U.K. supports the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources for their own economic benefit, and this is an integral part of their right to self-determination,” a spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham told TIME. “We continue to have a diplomatic relationship with Argentina, and from our perspective we want to continue to strengthen that.”
Here’s what to know about the contentious history of the Falkland Islands and why Milei and Trump’s remarks have sparked concern amid mounting geopolitical tensions.
Do the Falklands belong to Britain or Argentina?
The Falklands' defense and foreign policy is handled by the U.K., but otherwise it has an internal government of its own. The territory has its own constitution and as of 1983, residents of the islands have been British citizens.
In a 2013 referendum, Falkland residents voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining under British rule. The referendum saw 92% of all eligible voters turn out, with 99.8% of votes being “yes.”
“The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” Streeting said Friday, pointing to the will of the voters.
The first recorded landing on the island was made in 1690 by English naval captain John Strong. Britain took possession of West Falkland in 1765. France and Spain each had settlements on the islands at different times, but Britain re-established control in 1833 and has since administered the islands.
“Argentina claims the U.K. took the islands as an act of imperialism in the 1830s, but the remedy to colonial acquisition would be self-determination,” says Marc Weller, programme director of the international law programme at U.K.-based think tank Chatham House.
Given the British government’s insistence on Falklanders deciding their future, “it is therefore acting in accordance with the principle of self-determination,” he tells TIME.
Under the rule of military dictator Leopoldo Galtieri, Argentine forces attempted to stake a territorial claim in April 1982, sparking a 74-day war that Britain won.
Argentina has since continued to claim sovereignty over the islands and the rhetoric has become a unifying issue in the country, experts tell TIME.
The issue recently reared its head during Argentina’s victory over England in the semi-finals of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with some Argentine players holding up a banner reading "Las Malvinas son Argentinas,” which translates to "The Falklands are Argentine.”
“The Argentinian nation is easily united behind this claim through the Falkland Islands. It's a rallying point, and it's perhaps no accident that as the present Argentinean government is in a little bit of trouble, that they have rediscovered the issue,” says Weller, pointing towards Milei’s controversial fiscal policies and falling popularity among the public.
Milei steps up claim over British territory with sanctions threat
Milei has previously ruled out using force to claim the islands, instead pushing for a diplomatic resolution. Still, his newly-announced plans to impose sanctions against oil companies with operations in the area pose an economic threat.
The two petroleum firms heading the Sea Lion oil drilling project have already felt the impact of Milei’s proposed sanctions.
British company Rockhopper Exploration’s stock value fell by around 10% on Friday morning, with Israeli firm Navitas Petroleum stock value falling by at least 4.5%.
“It's an attempt to add some uncertainty, perhaps to inhibit investment,” suggests Weller, adding he’s doubtful any such threats will impact Downing Street’s position on the sovereignty dispute.
Trump says U.S. position on Falklands is under review
The dispute over sovereignty remains a tense geopolitical issue. China, for example, has been vocal in its support of Argentina’s claim, encouraging negotiations to take place on the matter.
The U.S., meanwhile, has historically recognized the U.K.’s “administration of the islands,” but has maintained a neutral position regarding sovereignty.
However, Trump has indicated that the U.S. may be open to reversing that position.
The Falklands sovereignty became a talking point in April as the U.S. and Europe drifted on account of Trump lambasting European leaders for refusing to get actively involved in the Iran war.
A leaked Pentagon email, which reportedly suggested various ways the Administration could punish NATO allies it believes let the U.S. down, suggested a review of the U.S. position on Britain’s claim to the Falkland Islands, according to Reuters.
Earlier this week, when asked if the U.S. position on the islands was under review, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: “I always review every position. That's just one of many."
In an interview with a British broadcast channel that aired on Thursday, Trump did not directly respond when asked if the U.S. would come to the U.K’s aid if Argentina claimed the Falklands.
Trump instead pivoted to discuss the Iran war, repeating his claims that the U.K. let him down. “Your country was not there to help me,” he insisted.
When approached by TIME, a spokesperson for Burnham said such comments “are a matter for the U.S. President.”
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Andrew Gawthorpe, a lecturer at Leiden University and an expert in the foreign policy of the U.S., tells TIME a Washington reversal on the issue “would be an enormous defeat for the U.K. diplomatically and a huge blow” to the special U.K.-U.S. relationship.
Weller agrees, adding that if any U.S. policy were to go against the territorial integrity of the U.K., then “Britain would have to respond quite strongly.”
Trump’s remarks on the Falklands this week could prove difficult for Burnham, who inherited a splintered Washington-London relationship upon replacing Keir Starmer as Prime Minister in July.
“On the one hand, Burnham needs to appear like a strong leader,” says Gawthorpe. “But on the other hand, I think he's very aware that he needs to not annoy Trump any more than is strictly necessary.”

SC awards pension to Mumbai engineer who forged ST certificate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:09:18 UTC
05:09:18 KST

SC allowed him to superannuate in peace with retirement benefits
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court has rewarded a wrongdoer - a man who got appointed as a junior civil engineer in Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM) by producing a forged ST certificate, and, subsequently, stalled the scrutiny of his eligibility for quota for more than a decade - by allowing him to superannuate in peace with retirement benefits.Shirish P Patil got a certificate in 1984 by identifying himself as belonging to the 'Tokre Koli' Scheduled Tribe community. Based on the certificate, he was appointed a junior civil engineer in MCGM in 1994. He misplaced the original ST certificate but managed to secure a fresh one from the sub-divisional magistrate, Bhusawal division, in Oct 2000.Following scrutiny initiated by MCGM, the Police Vigilance Cell traced Patil's family history and found that his ancestors had been recorded as 'Koli', 'Hindu Koli' and 'Hindu Suryawanshi Koli', none of which belonged to the ST category. In July 2009, MCGM issued a show cause notice to Patil.He successfully dodged and delayed proceedings before the scrutiny committee until Jan 2020, when the panel rejected his plea that his lawyer and elderly family members were not available, and invalidated the ST certificate. HC dismissed his appeal against cancellation of ST status.
SC, however, stayed Patil's dismissal from service through an interim order on Nov 18, 2021.
As a result, the engineer continued to serve until June 30, 2025, when he retired after being employed with MCGM for more than three decades based on a forged ST certificate.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi Thursday upheld the cancellation of Patil's ST certificate and Bombay HC order. However, it took a lenient view given his undertaking that he or any of his family members "shall (not) be entitled to claim any future benefit on the basis of the invalidated ST certificate".The ruling contrasts with SC's consistent rulings against benefits accruing to people who forge SC or ST certificates to gain admission or employment.

In Gdańsk, a train crashed into a truck at a railway crossing; no passengers were injured. The accident delayed 279 trains and caused losses of 140,000 zlotys.
In Gdańsk, a train traveling from Gdynia Główna to Zielona Góra collided with a truck that had become stuck between the barriers at a railway crossing. There were approximately 250–300 people on the train; none of the passengers were injured. RMF24 reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to PKP Polskie Linie Kolejowe, a 42-year-old citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina drove onto the crossing when the barriers had already begun to descend. Witnesses signaled to the driver to break through the barrier and leave the tracks, but the man did not do so. The train collided with the truck’s trailer.
Two passenger trains collided in Poland, there are casualties25.06.26, 23:59 • 8945 views
The driver was charged with creating an immediate risk of a disaster in land transport. He pleaded not guilty and gave testimony. The man faces up to 3 years in prison.
Hundreds of trains arrived late
The accident seriously disrupted traffic on the Tczew–Gdańsk route. A total of 279 trains were delayed, with the combined delay exceeding 17,500 minutes. Another 30 services were canceled on part of the route, while 45 were diverted.
The cost of repairing the damaged infrastructure, locomotive, and crossing equipment was estimated at approximately 140,000 zlotys. PKP PLK plans to seek compensation for these costs from the person responsible for the accident through the courts.

PMLA court: Cheques, drugs constitute proceeds of crime

PMLA court: Cheques, drugs constitute proceeds of crime
TNN / Sep 05, 2026, 01:11 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
The judge convicted two accused and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for three years
NEW DELHI: Broadening the definition of "property" under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, a special PMLA court in Mohali has ruled that seized bank cheques, even if not encashed, and narcotics both fall under the definition of "property" and constitute proceeds of crime under the money laundering Act.The judgement came Thursday, when ED launched a massive search operation at 30 premises across all zones of the southern region in different narcotics-related cases. The searches are being conducted under the mandate of Centre's 'Nasha Mukt Bharat' campaign with targets in the first phase spread across Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Telangana.The judge convicted two accused and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for three years, while rejecting the contention of the defence that their property and bank accounts were not attached and the seized contraband could not be considered proceeds of crime as no money trail had been brought on the record.Special judge Hardip Singh also rejected the defence's argument that the cheques recovered from the accused were not encashed and thus could not constitute proceeds of crime. The judge noted that the cheques were exchanged for the purpose of purchasing the contraband and the accused could not provide any explanation to the contrary.Starting with the four southern states, ED Thursday began a crackdown on major drug syndicates operating across the country.
The drive has been launched as part of Centre's "drug-free India" campaign to attach properties of all those engaged in drug dealing and generation of "proceeds of crime". The ED's search covered targets involved in trafficking of illicit drugs like methamphetamine, marijuana, and MDMA. Over 20 foreign nationals are under scanner, an official said.Searches were conducted at premises in Chennai, Tirunelveli, Nagapattinam, Velankanni and Ramanathapuram in Tamil Nadu; Kolar, Malur (Kolar district) and Hoskote (Bengaluru North district); Serilingampally and Nanakramguda (Hyderabad) and Ranga Reddy district in Telangana; Kozhikode, Kannur, Malappuram and Thrissur in Kerala.ED is coordinating with other central agencies and state police forces that have registered cases of drug trafficking in the past few years to further investigate the money trail and track the proceeds of crime."The investigation prima facie discloses not merely trafficking of methamphetamine, but also the generation, receipt and movement of money arising out of this," a senior official said, adding that syndicates were using hawala and crypto currency dealers to further transfer the proceeds of crime outside the country to tax havens.
The money trail to uncover cash-based hawala settlements revealed "account details, transaction records, diaries, slips or tokens, mobile phones, electronic communications and digital devices, property documents and other financial records". Based on these findings, the agency ascertained the complete quantum and trail of the proceeds of crime, and the persons who received, possessed, transferred, concealed, utilised or invested such proceeds.Further these details help in identifying movable and immovable properties acquired and that leads to their attachments.

What the latest flare-up between the U.S and Iran means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:41:34 UTC
04:41:34 KST

The past few days have seen a flare-up of the war of choice that the United States launched against Iran. American forces launched a series of attacks against Iran, killing both military personnel and civilians. The latter included five people at a wedding, two of them children.
Iran responded by attacking American military locations in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and, later, the United Arab Emirates.
While the mutual attacks, including the probable war crime by the U.S., represented a break in what had been a relative lull in fighting, they were also calibrated to maintain each side’s control over escalation. Neither side seeks an immediate escalation back to the all-out fighting of the spring months.
That, however, should not imply that both sides are equally reluctant to reignite greater fighting. Although Iran has much more at risk by a return to all-out war, it also has a greater incentive than the United States to end the current state of tension, which is primarily characterized by less firepower and more economic warfare.
The American strategy, to the extent that the administration of Donald Trump has one, is currently to focus on enacting ever-tighter sanctions on Iran, closing off alternative revenue streams, and hoping that the economic collapse does today what it has not done for forty-seven years and brings down the Islamic Republic.
Iran, conversely, is trying to hold on to control of the Strait of Hormuz while continuing to push the United States’ military farther away from the Persian Gulf region. Their increased focus on attacking the remaining American bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, and the UAE is coupled with their growing focus on American positions in Jordan. But they seem, at least for the moment, to have decided to refrain from further attacks on Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
That indicates that Iran is trying to promote a new regional security regime, diminishing the American role, thereby shifting the defense focus from Iran to Israel.
That reflects a more careful long-term strategy, which is sensible for Tehran as the United States is simultaneously making other moves that threaten to entrench this conflict for the long term, bringing a new “forever war.”
How does Trump intend to sell that war to his MAGA followers, who backed him based on “no forever wars”? The same way he always does: he’ll lie to them.
Media blackouts and disinformation
From the beginning of this war, both the United States and Iran have worked to hide information on the damage they have suffered. Iran has more incentive than the United States to broadcast damage, however, so we have had somewhat better views of some American actions, such as this week’s bombing of a wedding in the town of Sirik.
A Reuters investigation confirmed what was initially clear: the United States had directly attacked the wedding site. Obviously, Iran wants to let the world know about such crimes, and the United States, which does not risk its own civilians in this war, has no such temptation.
Of course, Iran has other reasons to conceal some data, such as the extent of the damage the U.S. has done to its missile and drone manufacturing capabilities. Whether those are as greatly diminished as the U.S. dubiously claims or remain largely intact, keeping that knowledge secret is advantageous to Tehran.
This week’s attacks illustrate that advantage. The American attacks, though the largest in many weeks, mostly targeted sites they had hit before, so they were not likely to have caused much more damage, given the mobility of Iran’s defensive systems.
On the other hand, the United States claimed that the Iranian strikes in response were all intercepted or landed in uninhabited areas. Other reporting disputes that, supporting Iranian claims of having hit American communication, radar, and hangar sites as well as the headquarters of an American commander.
There is no way to be certain where the truth lies, but earlier similar American claims have been shown weeks later to be false. The clampdown on reporting has only stiffened since then.
Damage assessments are not the only arena of disinformation. Both sides have an interest in giving the impression of total control of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran insists that the Strait is closed, but some ships are getting through, even without Iran’s permission. They are moving stealthily, often at night, and with their transponders turned off to avoid detection. They are accompanied by American naval and air forces, an expensive, provocative, and unsustainable operation, but one that has temporarily eased the global shortage of oil that has resulted from this war to some degree.
But this week’s claim from U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright that the United States was able to bring 17 million barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday — a figure nearly on par with pre-war traffic through the Strait — was met with widespread skepticism.
Commercial tracking agencies detected only a handful of ships transiting the Strait that day, nothing like the more than one hundred that would be required to match Wright’s claim. Those companies rely not only on transponder signals but also on satellite imagery to count traffic.
The oil market also does not seem convinced by the Trump administration’s claims.
It would take several weeks for shipments of crude oil leaving the Gulf now to hit the market, so we wouldn’t expect to see crude oil prices fall yet.
But if oil buyers believed these figures, we would expect to see an effect on the price of crude oil futures, which is based on the expected market, not the current one. But those prices, too, have not come down.
High oil prices hurt Trump’s claims of victory and of controlling the Strait. But he might still be able to deceive parts of the public if the shooting war does not heat up again.
Trump’s first attacks this week seem to have been intended to deter Iran from exercising more control over the Strait by laying more mines and positioning more launchers. It is unclear whether the American strikes were successful in doing that.
What is clear is that Iran is not likely to allow Trump to strangle the Iranian economy without a response. That was the message sent by Iran when they continued attacking American sites even after they had responded to the first American strikes.
That strategy is becoming even more imperative as the Trump administration, consciously or not, takes steps to prolong this war.
Entrenching the war in Lebanon and Saudi Arabia
There are two matters, beyond the direct confrontation between Iran and the United States in the Persian Gulf, that must be resolved for this war to end. Those are the Israeli invasion and occupation of Lebanon and the issue of Iran’s nuclear program.
The Israeli invasion of Lebanon must end for there to be negotiations with any hope of success. The nuclear issue will upend any deal that might be made if it is not resolved, and the future is currently very hard to see.
Events this week made both of those areas tougher to confront.
Iran had warned the United States not to allow Israel to attack the Ali Taher Ridge, which was a key Hezbollah outpost. The warning should not have been necessary since there is supposed to be a ceasefire, and both Israel and Hezbollah are supposed to be holding their positions until there is a resolution.
Even that unjust arrangement was not good enough for Israel, which, given the impunity it continues to enjoy, went ahead and took out the Hezbollah headquarters, without provocation. As always, a ceasefire means the other side ceases, while Israel fires.
Initial reports stated that IRGC personnel were also in Ali Taher Ridge, but reports after the operation claimed there were none. It is possible the Iranians evacuated to avoid the Israeli assault.
In any case, it remains to be seen if Iran will retaliate, but even if they don’t, there is little hope that Israel will withdraw from Lebanon in the foreseeable future. Talks in Washington between Israel and the Lebanese government, always a meaningless sideshow, have paused as even the Lebanese president has been unable to maintain credibility while engaging Israel.
The looming midterm elections certainly mean Trump will be even more reluctant to press Israel on Lebanon, and after them, it is entirely possible that a thoroughly lame duck Trump will embark on even more radical paths. That, of course, would free Israel even more to act as it wants. Israeli Prime Minister’s precarious position only makes him more inclined to naked aggression.
Even in the unlikely event that the Lebanon issue can be resolved and that terms for ending the war in the Gulf could be found and agreed to, neither Iran nor the U.S. can end the war without a deal on Iran’s nuclear program that lifts the economic sanctions on the Islamic Republic.
As if that wasn’t already difficult enough, the announcement this week was that the United States and Saudi Arabia had signed an agreement for the U.S. to help Saudi Arabia develop a nuclear energy program.
The deal will certainly make it harder for the U.S. to reach an agreement with Iran, and that difficulty is likely to persist beyond Trump’s administration.
The nuclear deal would allow Saudi Arabia to enrich up to 20%, a level the U.S. had cried foul about when Iran enriched to that figure more than fifteen years ago. Moreover, the deal would not require Riyadh to sign on to the Additional Protocol, which allows for much more intrusive inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency, and which Iran did sign on to as part of the JCPOA.
It’s a clear double standard and one that will make Iran even more reluctant than it already is to find common ground with the U.S. on the nuclear issue. This comes on top of the fact that the war itself increased the impetus for Iran to develop a nuclear weapon.
All these factors are coming together and pointing the conflict in a hopeless direction. The way out, however, is still clear: a negotiated settlement along the lines of the Memorandum of Understanding reached in June, combined with elements of the JCPOA and international guarantees for all of it.
Does that mean the United States would have to admit defeat? Yes. But that defeat is manifest already, and Iran is not going to allow the U.S. to prolong this war and the economic strangulation of the Islamic Republic indefinitely. There will, eventually, be blows in the region and possibly beyond that which dwarf what we’ve seen already.
This war has been calamitous enough. The longer it goes on, the harder it will be to end, and the more likely it becomes that a certain global disaster will result.

Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist's murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:31:00 UTC
04:31:00 KST

Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist's murder
September 4, 2026
"Murderer!" — "Scum!" — "Mafia!"
As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The 44-year-old Maltese businessman pushed through, flanked by his security guards. Just minutes earlier, a jury had acquitted him of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
The verdict came as a shock to her family. Her son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, said it was a "terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from." He later doubled down on his criticism, describing the verdict in a post on Facebook as "obscene" and saying: "Their decision flies in the face of all evidence, of all logic, of the truth."
Almost nine years after Caruana Galizia's murder, Malta is again confronted with the crucial question: Who was responsible for her death on October 16, 2017? The men who procured the bomb, placed it under the driver's seat and detonated it remotely have already been convicted. But the person who contracted them to do it has still not been legally identified.
A difficult trial
For years, Fenech was considered to be the central figure in the investigations. His arrest on the morning of November 20, 2019, was like something out of a movie. His luxury yacht, Gio, had just left harbor when it was stopped by a Maltese military patrol boat. Fenech was arrested on board and subsequently interrogated by the police.
Fenech's arrest, and suspicion that people in government circles were involved in the crime, sparked protests all across the country. Joseph Muscat, prime minister at the time, was accused of protecting political allies and stepped down in January 2020. Fenech spent more than five years in detention before being released on bail, under strict conditions, in early 2025.
His trial only began this summer, and the final verdict was decisive. Eight of the nine jurors rejected the prosecution's argument that it was Fenech who had ordered the journalist's murder.
Who was responsible?
The prosecution case relied above all on the testimony of Melvin Theuma, who confessed to being the middleman and testified that Fenech had contracted him to organize the murder. Theuma received a pardon in exchange for his cooperation.
But Fenech's defense called Theuma's credibility into question, highlighting contradictions in his testimony and false statements he had made previously.
Fenech's lawyers also sought to prove that evidence pointing to Keith Schembri, chief of staff to Muscat at the time, was not properly followed up. Schembri has denied any involvement in the murder, and the investigators did not charge him as a suspect in this case.
The public prosecutors' argument was that Caruana Galizia had been investigating Fenech, specifically his company 17 Black and the energy consortium ElectroGas, on suspicion of corruption. This, they said, meant Fenech had a motive for silencing her. She had not, however, been on the point of publishing anything that could have threatened him.
Open questions
Many in Malta are outraged by the not-guilty verdict. But there is no indication to date that Fenech did not receive a fair trial, or that the process was manipulated. For him to be convicted, Fenech's guilt had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Caruana Galizia's family are therefore also focusing on institutional failures that they believe facilitated the murder. They complain that these have not been addressed, and necessary reforms not implemented. An official investigation already established, in 2021, that an "atmosphere of impunity" in Malta created conditions that made the murder possible.
Reforms in Malta
Since then, Malta has made progress with a series of reforms, but many say they do not go far enough. This is especially the case with regard to press freedom. In 2021, the committee of inquiry recommended that journalists be better protected against political and economic pressure and their role institutionally strengthened, yet the country is still waiting for comprehensive media reform.
Following years of discussion and a public consultation, the Maltese government brought the relevant bill before parliament in March 2026, but the legislation was not passed before early parliamentary elections in May.
In its latest Rule of Law Report, the European Commission only certifies limited progress made by Malta. It acknowledges that it has introduced some specific protection measures for journalists, but says core recommendations from the investigation into the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia remain unfulfilled.
Government sees progress
But the government paints a different picture. It has highlighted changes to the judiciary and anti-corruption measures, as well as better protection of journalistic sources, and additional measures to protect media professionals. This is what the EU Commission referred to as progress in specific areas.
The case has also shone a spotlight on the slow pace of the Maltese justice system. According to a report by the Daphne Caruana Galizia Foundation, 46% of homicide cases brought to trial between 2010 and 2020 had still not been concluded in mid-2025. The foundation regards this as a structural problem, and warns that when proceedings go on for so long, it compromises the chances of an effective prosecution.
Fresh investigation?
No decision has yet been made as to what will happen now, following Fenech's acquittal. Judge Edwina Grima has ordered that the evidence presented at trial be passed on to the chief of police, who will decide whether criminal proceedings should be brought against anyone else.
On Thursday, former PM Muscat said that, according to the public prosecutors, further investigations were ongoing.
The Institute of Maltese Journalists (IGM) has called on the authorities to pursue every line of inquiry that came to light during the trial — including, explicitly, those that lead to former high-ranking politicians. The acquittal must be respected as the outcome of the constitutional process, the IGM said, but it does not close the case.
The demonstrators outside the courthouse in Valletta are in no doubt. Someone must have issued a contract for the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia. And almost nine years after her death, still no one has been held responsible.
This article was originally written in German.

Adelaide returns to scene of finals flop to face biggest test of growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:02:34 UTC
04:02:34 KST

analysis
Adelaide's elimination final against Western Bulldogs looms as its biggest test of growth
Every week it seems like there is history being written in the AFL.
Some of this is welcomed, memorable and celebrated, such as when Scott Pendlebury broke the games record earlier this year, or when Lance Franklin notched the 1,000-goal mark in 2022.
Moments like these are cherished throughout each club's fanbase and reflects the long history of the league and sport.
Other slices of history are far more trivial. Last week, Sam Walsh set the record for the most disposals in the Wildcard Finals round. While the stat is interesting, it is not necessarily illustrative of a feat of great importance.
Nonetheless, it provides colour to the rich tapestry that is Australian football.
And there are some feats that players and coaches avoid like the plague.
Many football fans know the tale of Kevin Murray. The former Roys stalwart managed to play 333 games, all without winning a single final — a league record.
While his career was rich and storied, eventually earning him Legend status in the Hall of Fame, the achievement underscored the futility of playing for Fitzroy through most of the second half of the 20th century.
Though never winning a VFL final, Murray did manage to play in a finals win during a lucrative mid-career stint at East Perth in 1966 on the way to a losing Grand Final against Perth.
This Saturday night Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks is set to, at least temporarily, claim his own slice of footballing ignominy.
Nicks will join Alec Hall as the coaches to steer their sides through the most VFL/AFL games without winning a final.
For those who don't immediately recognise the name Alec Hall, his last game as coach came more than a century ago.
Over the last two years Nicks's Crows have won the second most regular season games. Last year's minor premiership season was cut short with a straight sets exit.
This year the Crows are already on their last chance with a rampaging Bulldogs ahead of them.
Nicks has quietly rebuilt his side's biggest question mark. But in the Bulldogs, the Crows face a test designed to test this weakness in full.
Mayhem in the middle
Fresh in the mind of Nicks, and all Crows fans, is how their 2025 season came to an end.
Like all sides who fall short of their end goal, reflection on their failings quickly sets in.
For Nicks, the message on what went wrong was clear, and last year's disappointment has put them in a stronger place for this year.
"I think we're ahead of last year," Nicks said after their round 24 win over the Giants, despite being "a little lower on the ladder."
"We've been doing a lot of work around what it was we didn't get right last year. Under that immense pressure that Collingwood and Hawthorn brought last year we weren't able to execute and deliver our game on our game plan."
That pressure around the contest is arguably what brought their once-promising 2025 season undone. Against Hawthorn, the Crows struggled both at contests both at stoppage and in general play, with the Hawks midfield unit gaining control of the game.
Starved of opportunity with ball in hand, the Crows' defence could only do so much to hold the wave of Hawks back.
The Hawks ended that final with a six-clearance advantage and 20 more post-clearance ground ball gets. Starved of the ball, the Crows were left passengers in a finals series that they were meant to drive from the front.
At the most basic level, only part of the contest game needed adjustment from the outside. The Crows finished the 2025 season leading for post-clearance ground ball gets and contested possessions.
They were relatively weak at stoppage, however, with a negative clearance differential across the year.
But that hid a slide against the best of the best.
The Crows struggled more against good opposition midfields than most other contenders, perhaps the canary in the coalmine for their finals struggles.
This is despite their units at either end of the ground largely holding up their ends of the bargain.
The Crows defence in 2025 and 2026 has actually gotten stronger against the best sides in the league. They conceded just 1.47 points per inside 50 this year — better than any team's full season record.
The figures were even starker last year. While the Crows concede more in games against good sides, this has largely been down to an increased volume of inside 50s their defence has to protect against.
It's yet another mark of honour for the severely underrated Adelaide backline. Over the past two years the Crows defence has arguably been the strongest defensive unit in the league, despite the lack of individual acknowledgement.
Only one Crows defender, Wayne Milera, has made the All-Australian team in this time despite the depth and strength of their taller options.
While their forward line has had a rotating list of players contribute it has been a little stronger when it matters most.
The territory battle at the contest, particularly up the ground and at stoppage, is so important for one of the Crows' other weaknesses.
Despite their defensive miserliness, their backline has struggled to transition the ball from defensive 50 and the defensive half to create scoring opportunities.
It means the Crows can absorb the pressure of opposition attacks, but sometimes struggle to get the game back on their terms in this way.
Without the benefit of winning the territory battle, or control of the footy at the contest, it can make a spellbinding side look pedestrian at best.
The shift
This has spurred the Adelaide brains trust into action. Throughout this year Nicks has experimented with different looks up the ground.
Bodies have floated through the middle and up forward to try to execute when it matters most.
The highest profile change through the year was one involving a player who missed last year's finals altogether.
Since he entered the league with Gold Coast, Izak Rankine has long been viewed as one of the game's most damaging attacking players. He is the type of player that makes the hair stand up on the back of your neck, or your eyes quickly dart back to the TV if the commentator mentions his name in excited tones.
His 2025 season ended not due to form or injury, but rather as a consequence of using a homophobic slur towards a Collingwood player in round 23. Suspended for four matches, Rankine admitted his mistake and apologised publicly and privately.
It is always difficult to judge atonement and sincerity from a distance, but Rankine has made further efforts to build a relationship with the Rainbow Crows supporter group, which has in turn praised the progress made.
Some fans, both of Adelaide and the sport more broadly, may need more time to evaluate his response to the incident.
Others, particularly a large cohort of Crows fans, believed the punishment to be too severe from the outset.
Regardless of your stance, Rankine appears to be choosing his own course in making amends for his grave misstep.
Rankine's on field evolution in 2026 is far easier to evaluate than anything off field.
This year Rankine has been deployed full time in the middle of the ground for the first time in his career. The results have been dramatic.
Since the shift, Rankine has been about the most damaging player in the competition, with his previous skill in limited opportunities scaling up when foisted around the ball more often.
The tipping point for Nicks to throw Rankine through the middle more was making sure the young Crow fit with the defence first mindset of the side.
"I've always wanted to play midfield." Rankine told AFC.com.au earlier this month.
"I just had to fix up my two-way running, understanding the game, and when the opposition gets momentum against us how to mentally stay in the game and not get frustrated.
"I've found that the way I can get more of those opportunities is really delving into the defensive side of the game, getting back and helping the defenders, and being an option for them when they get stuck."
It's hard to overstate the growth in Rankine's game. Rankine has moved his predominantly front-half game to impact across the ground.
Defensively, Rankine has increasingly involved himself at contest and tracked his opponent while retaining that attacking flair that makes his game so appealing.
In that time, Adelaide has become even stronger at the contest without suffering on the defensive side. Rankine provides an explosive attacking strength that few other sides can boast, and his improved defensive effort has cost the Crows little the other way.
Rankine is not the only adjustment the Crows have made in the middle through the year.
The Crows have exposed players like Jake Soligo and Brayden Cook at the contest, with other experiments along the way. Instead of direct results on a week to week basis, it appears that Nicks is attempting to expose a wider group to action in the middle in order to maximise his options come September.
Perhaps the last shift might be their biggest, as over the past month the Crows have shifted recent draftee Dan Curtin to the guts in order to provide a vastly different look.
At 197cm and with the build of a key position player, Curtin may be the league's biggest full-time midfielder.
If it sticks, Curtin might provide a midfield option that few other sides have seen before.
"He's still got so much upside in his game. We haven't really scratched the surface there yet," Nicks said.
"I think we see Dan as a midfielder moving forward. We feel like he's got the football intelligence, the execution and the awareness that you need to be a midfielder.
"He's unique in that he's such a big body, so he's a tough match-up. He's still a very young player that's still learning a fair bit about the game. But it's exciting for us."
Curtin presents opponents a rare challenge of raw size alongside unquestioned footballing ability, similar to Patrick Cripps and experiments with ruck-mids such as Mark Blicavs and Luke Jackson.
Curtin's exposure to different roles across his short professional career has also gifted him with a sense of defensive responsibility when running through the middle — key to executing the Crows' game plan.
A meeting with the biggest midfield test
Given how much of their focus has been on building their game at the contest, it is somewhat fitting that their first finals test comes against arguably the league's most damaging contested side on their day.
While the Bulldogs are entering September with a depleted forward line and a defence with more questions than answers, few can question the raw ability and system of their midfield unit.
For a side entrenched in the mid-table hustle over the last two years the Dogs are a side few want to see when the footy starts to get serious.
It's that ability in the middle of the ground, led by All-Australian duo Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards, that is set to stress test Nicks's personnel changes.
While the Crows have improved their work at the contest as the year has progressed, the results across the whole year paint a similar picture to that of 2025.
Looking at the entire season likely undersells where they sit right now. While they lost the clearance battle to Fremantle in round 23, they dominated the post-clearance contested battle — crucial to maintaining field position.
Despite Adelaide's strong performances over the last two years, rumbling from Victoria has suggested that Nicks must steer the Crows to victory to retain his job.
"I understand the narrative, it's part of this industry, [but] it's probably not something I could talk to," Nicks said.
If, for whatever reason, the Crows do the unthinkable and remove Nicks from his post after the season, it would be a move without little recent precedent.
The most recent coach to lead his side to at least 33 wins over his last two seasons in charge before leaving his role was Mick Malthouse in his "negotiated handover" to Nathan Buckley at Collingwood.
Few, if any, coaches have been legitimately sacked in league history with so many home and away wins immediately prior to their removal.
While it is likely just a rumour spread wild, the game on Saturday night presents a chance to silence the speculation of the doubters.

Air Force Speeding Up New Low-Cost Drone Program after Heavy MQ-9 Losses Against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:01:33 UTC
04:01:33 KST

The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft.
Back in July, the Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit announced plans to develop a low-cost drone to do all the missions that an MQ-9 can do today, and when necessary fly in groups to overwhelm an enemy’s anti-drone capabilities and force them to expend large numbers of munitions. They called the effort Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA.
At the time, officials said they wanted to have a prototype to test fly within 21 months of a contract, and then 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031 to achieve initial operating capability.
Now, though, officials are targeting a more ambitious timeline. During a media roundtable at the Pentagon, DIU military deputy Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel said the MMA program will try to follow DIU’s typical timeframe of prototyping a system within a year of a contract, and then fielding it at scale within three years—as soon as 2029.
Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said those goals changed “fairly recently,” when Air Force Secretary Troy Meink “called us in and said ‘You need to move faster.’”
That urgency, Niemi acknowledged, came at least partly in response to the significant losses the MQ-9 fleet has taken in the past year or so during operations against Iran and Iranian-backed militias. Since the start of the Iran war, the Air Force has lost at least 45 MQ-9s, roughly a quarter of its fleet. The service was already thinking about what it needed to succeed the MQ-9 as a medium-altitude intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance platform, but Niemi said the combat losses pushed it to move faster.
“Although we have plenty of MQ-9As today, we are going through them at a rate that is concerning to us,” Niemi said.
Replacing, Not Reinventing, the MQ-9
The MQ-9 has long been a workhorse of the Air Force fleet, valued by combatant commanders for its long endurance, loitering ability, and ability to combine strike and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach called the Reaper the “most valuable player” of Operation Epic Fury in a May congressional hearing.
Unsurprisingly, then, officials said they were eager to replace the ones lost in combat. Niemi said the Air Force has “spent a lot of time and energy” in recent months trying to figure out how to do so and found “there’s not a lot of good options to immediately replace those aircraft.”
The Air Force considered General Atomics’ MQ-9B, a larger and more complex—and more expensive—version of the MQ-9A, Niemi said. Ultimately, officials concluded the MQ-9B was not the right choice because the Air Force needed something more “attritable,” or inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.
“If you don’t like losing an MQ-9A that cost on the order of $50 million, with the sensors, you’re probably not going to like losing an MQ-9B at a higher price point,” Niemi said.
For that reason, the Air Force decided to go all-in on the MMA concept. The Air Force plans to field at least 180 of the drones, Niemi said, but probably more than that.
In order to move fast and keep costs down, Niemi said the Air Force plans to “accept prudent risk” on the MMA program. Kunkel also said the Air Force wants “significantly increased levels of competition” to keep costs down.
As the Air Force wrote out what attributes MMA drones would need, Niemi added, it tried to allow as much flexibility as possible and not include hyper-specific requirements that “push technology to the very edge.”
“When that happens, you’re going to pay a lot for it, because it’s hard to do,” Niemi said. “It takes a lot of engineering, cutting-edge science, emergent technologies, things like that. So we’re trying to be more aligned with sort of an ‘80 percent is good enough,’ [using] mature technologies” approach.
That means MMA won’t have the latest and greatest flight control systems, engines, or manufacturing processes, he said—and they’ll actually resemble the MQ-9 in some key ways: they’ll likely have long-aspect wings and will likely be powered by turboprop engines.
One way officials are looking to differ from the MQ-9, though, are higher levels of autonomy and automation than the MQ-9A has today, Niemi said—“more mouse clicks and keyboard strokes instead of a stick and throttle.” That will reduce the number of Airmen needed to operate MMA drones and allow a single Airman to operate multiple drones simultaneously.
At the same time, Niemi said MMAs won’t have the same level of autonomy as the Air Force’s flagship autonomous drone program, Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
“It’s not going out and autonomously finding targets and employing weapons,” Niemi said of the MMA drone. “It’s more like a truck that’s carrying packages, whether it’s a sensor package or whether it’s a weapon, to a point where it can be employed.”
CCAs and MMAs
While CCAs and MMAs will both be unmanned and have some kind of autonomy software, Niemi was quick to note there will be major differences between the two.
“They’re going to look very different,” Niemi said. The MMA is “going to look like an MQ-9, and [CCA is] going to look more like a fighter, like you’ve seen in the current too CCAs that we’re flying.”
The Air Force wants MMA drones to be able to fly about 4,000 miles—more than twice the expected range of autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft drones—and carry a heavy payload, although they will be slower than CCAs, Niemi said.
Those differences extend to price, too—while the Air Force is targeting $10 million for an MMA drone, it’s hoping for $20 million per CCA once they reach full production. Those costs are for just the base aircraft, excluding sensors, weapons or other equipment that might be loaded onto them.
From an acquisition perspective, the Air Force is hoping to use the same methods across the CCA and MMA programs to keep costs down and production simple.
That includes moving quickly to award contracts and keeping several vendors on contract to provide a variety of drones. Like CCAs, MMA drones will also use open architecture, Niemi said. That will ensure the drones have standardized interfaces and could be easily upgraded with newer sensor packages or weapons capabilities, even from different vendors, he said. This would also allow MMAs to be tailored with the gear needed for a particular mission.
“If you want to build a package that’s going to go on this new aircraft, as long as it conforms to this [standardized interface], we can do it very speedily and very readily,” Niemi said. “That’s something we struggle with at the opposite end of the spectrum, something like the F-35, where it’s very very hard to incorporate new things onto it, because of the construct and the architecture of that system.”
The Air Force also wants manufacturers to be able to produce MMA drones in large numbers, Niemi said, but also be able to ramp production up or down as needed, such as if the Air Force started losing large numbers in a heated conflict. Keeping MMAs simple is the best way to ensure that production flexibility, he said.
“If you wanted to suddenly ramp up production of something like an F-35, it’s not a limiting factor so much as money, as the ability to build out your production capacity and actually crank more of those things out,” Niemi said. “And the more complex the aircraft, the harder that problem is. … In major combat operations, depending on who you’re fighting, we could be losing dozens [of MMA drones] a day, and so you have to figure out how do you adjust the industrial capacity in order to make [necessary production levels] happen.”
General Atomics, which also makes the MQ-9, is planning to pitch a newly designed drone it calls Wildfire for the MMA program.
“Our new Wildfire aircraft addresses all of the concerns posed by the MMA solicitation,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement to reporters. “We can deliver years earlier and maintain the same high quality. You can have everything that makes Reaper special, plus more, at a price that doesn’t break the bank.”

Fresh US Fighter Jets Rotate into Middle East as Trump Tries to Up Pressure on Iran

The U.S. is rotating fresh fighter squadrons to the Middle East to support the Trump administration’s open-ended pressure campaign against Iran.
The move will free up units that have been based in the region far beyond the Air Force’s usual six-month deployments. More fighter unit rotations are expected in the coming weeks.
Units on their way home include the 158th Fighter Wing of the Vermont Air National Guard, which flies F-35 Lightning II aircraft. F-16 Fighting Falcons from the 555th Fighter Squadron based at Aviano Air Base, Italy, are also returning, according to people familiar with the matter and data collected by the open-source group the Military Air Tracking Alliance.
The departing units have been deployed overseas since last year. The Vermont F-35s first deployed to Puerto Rico in December 2025 and supported the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, before deploying to the Middle East ahead of the U.S. air war against Iran. The Vermont ANG’s F-35s were spotted transiting through RAF Lakenheath, U.K., on their way back home. The F-16s from the 555th Fighter Squadron had been deployed to the Middle East since November.
Arriving in CENTCOM are F-16s from the Ohio Air National Guard’s 180th Fighter Wing. Twelve F-16s from the Ohio ANG departed Lajes in the Azores on Sept. 4, according to local aircraft spotters. The planes, which arrived on the Portuguese island on Aug. 29, are due to head to the Middle East.
A spokesman for U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last month that the U.S. is stepping up its economic sanctions campaign to try to stop Iran from interfering with oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz while pressing Tehran to make concessions on its nuclear program. That is in addition to the ongoing American maritime blockade.
“If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart,” Bessent told CNBC last month.
But U.S. officials also say that the increased economic pressure might lead Iran to retaliate militarily. Fighting in the region flared up late last month when the U.S. struck Iranian launchers that were preparing to launch rockets with mines into the strait, and Iran retaliated by firing ballistic missiles at American forces in Jordan.
The new U.S. pressure campaign is likely to reduce the need for defensive and offensive munitions in the near term. But it still requires an ongoing military presence in the region and efforts to manage operational demands on the force.
The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Thailand earlier this week after spending nine months at sea. The Lincoln took part in Operation Epic Fury—which officially lasted from Feb. 28 to early April—and then helped enforce a U.S. military blockade of Iranian ports and partook in tit-for-tat clashes against the Iranians for months.

Germany’s Suspected Power Grid Attack Devices Found, but Timers Never Triggered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:00:43 KST

- Category
- World
Germany’s Suspected Power Grid Attack Devices Found, but Timers Never Triggered
German police are treating the discovery of suspected launch devices near an electrical substation as a suspected sabotage attempt against the regional power grid, BILD reported on September 4.
The discovery was made on Thursday around 6:15 p.m., when a passerby spotted suspicious objects in a field in the Gohr district of Dormagen and immediately alerted authorities, prompting several patrol cars to race to the scene.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to BILD, the items were again launch apparatuses for homemade rockets, fitted with timers and copper wires, resembling devices found earlier in Bergheim, also in North Rhine-Westphalia, and in Jänschwalde, Brandenburg.
"Someone apparently tried to deliberately cause a short circuit," the Cologne police spokesman stated, describing the suspected intent behind the find. Investigators added that a letter claiming responsibility referencing the Bergheim and Jänschwalde incidents had reached them, though a police spokeswoman cautioned that the devices had not activated.
"Nothing happened," she noted, adding that whether the object was capable of causing damage had not yet been established.
Investigators indicated it remained unclear whether a technical defect was involved or whether the timers were set to trigger later. Officers assembled a large contingent to cordon off the area, illuminating the fields with searchlights as they combed for further devices. Firefighters assisted, a helicopter circled overhead, and police checked additional substations in surrounding regions for suspicious objects.
The Dormagen substation lies just 13 kilometers from the site of the attack on the substation at the lignite-fired power plant in Bergheim.
A separate attack had targeted the substation near the Jänschwalde lignite plant in Brandenburg, with both of those incidents occurring on Tuesday. All three cases are being investigated on suspicion of attacks on critical infrastructure, and investigators are examining possible connections without treating any link as established.
The left-leaning daily taz, cited by BILD, reported that it had received a letter of responsibility relating to the Brandenburg incident, apparently mailed from within North Rhine-Westphalia according to its postmark.
The paper noted that the sender presents himself as a lone actor who describes the rockets in detail, citing a motive of "immeasurable suffering" caused by the use of fossil fuels, while stressing that it is unclear whether the author is, in fact, the perpetrator.
The Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs weighed in, with a spokesman telling the Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland that the incidents underscored "how important it is to consistently strengthen the resilience of the power system."
The spokesman pointed to "the Russian war of aggression, increased acts of sabotage against the economy, but also increasing extreme weather events" as reasons the country and its economy must "better arm" themselves, describing sabotage against critical infrastructure as "a serious threat."
Such trial attacks have prompted sharp warnings from regional leaders, with the frequency of the incidents cited as evidence that infrastructure protection must be decisively reinforced. Emergency services and substation personnel were credited with preventing worse outcomes through timely action, and no injuries were reported in the Brandenburg case.
Concern over deliberate interference with the power grid extends well beyond Germany's borders, as Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia have been coordinating to protect dams, power plants, and gas infrastructure against possible sabotage, reinforcing security around key sites amid warnings that hostile actors could stage incidents to test alliance responses.
