Everyone but Australia reconsiders relationship with America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Australia appears confused about its place in the global world order
If there has been an underlying theme in global politics in the past 18 months it has surrounded the lack of reliability of the United States as an alliance partner or, more recently, the cost of having such an alliance with the US.
As Donald Trump has led his country away from its alliances and into a war that has made the majority of its allies in the Middle East vulnerable Iranian targets, countries around the world have been left scurrying to re-evaluate their needs and their friendships.
Except Australia.
No-one inside federal politics seems particularly interested in discussing the large orange elephant in the room and how it is materially changing every other country's views of the world.
Two major conflicts merge
There is an increasing unease in the Northern Hemisphere about how the Ukraine and Gulf conflicts seem to be slowly melding into each other, particularly as the links between Iran and Russia seem to expand, and stories of their deep technological cooperation on weapons continue to appear.
In Europe, there is growing consternation about Russian incursions into European airspace, into drone attacks in Germany and Poland, and into European political campaigns.
This weekend, the German state of Saxony-Anhalt goes to the polls, amid allegations of heavy Russian interference in an area that was once part of East Germany and where the far right AfD party is predicted to win a huge majority.
The implications of this result for the government led by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and for the balance of policies in Germany, is significant.
The AfD is hostile to Ukraine and supportive of Russia. The result will intensify pressure on Merz to back away from Germany's current support for Ukraine, which of course wouldn't matter so much if European states weren't already trying to make up for the withdrawal of US support for Ukraine.
Europe, the Middle East, the Baltics, the subcontinent, South East Asia, North Asia — they are all pragmatically reorganising themselves to deal with the growing absence of the US.
But not Australia.
Instead, our Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister, Richard Marles, turned up in Washington this week, beaming like a kid in a lolly shop next to Defence Secretary Peter Hegseth, announcing that the US was going to be escalating even further its military presence in Australia.
Marles' spin on AUKUS
Australia and the US, along with the United Kingdom are now operating under the AUKUS alliance. The most notable aspect of that alliance agreement was supposed to be the transfer from the US to Australia of (initially) some US nuclear-powered submarines and (later) the technology to build a new nuclear-powered submarine class, the SSN AUKUS, in Australia in conjunction with building in the UK.
But in Washington this week, Marles put a different spin on what "making real progress in relation to AUKUS" now means.
That is, AUKUS is — not altogether surprisingly — morphing into an arrangement where the US has a base in Australia, as opposed to Australia having its own capabilities.
The Perth submarine presence is in addition to the annual rotation of US Marines through Darwin, and the significant US presence at the Tindall air base in the Northern Territory, which is speculated to host nuclear-armed B52 bombers.
Marles was asked why any US president would agree to give Australia a valuable asset like a submarine when "America simply can't produce as many as it wants to".
"Because what AUKUS is doing is providing more sea days for the Virginia class fleet for the United States Navy, and more sea days' worth than a single submarine," Marles replied. (Emphasis added.)
"The establishment of the Submarine Rotation Force West at HMAS Stirling, as well as the establishment of the Henderson Defence Precinct offers the opportunity for US Navy submarines to undergo maintenance much closer to their critical area of operation, which creates sea days for the United States Navy, and that's ultimately why this is such an important agreement from the United States point of view."
Australia, Marles said, was facing "as significant a sovereignty moment" as it has faced since the end of the Second World War.
But the threat to our sovereignty, according to Marles, doesn't come from passively agreeing to become an even bigger military base for another country, but from the country perceived to be the greatest threat to us: China.
A three-way split on China in the US
At the global level, with all the noise being generated by the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, analysts occasionally look aside to mutter with uncertainty about what role China is playing in either of these conflicts, or what it may win or lose from them.
One thing it has "lost" is a significant slab of the US military presence off its coastline as the US has had to move an aircraft carrier and significant personnel and armaments from the region to the Middle East.
That's certainly made Taiwan, Japan and South Korea nervous.
But there seems to currently be a three-way split in the assessment of China in the US, a point highlighted by former prime minister Paul Keating this week in an appearance in Sydney with the author of a new book about Keating and foreign policy, Professor James Curran.
The split breaks between the Trump view of the world, the US intelligence community's view of the world, and the US defence establishment's view of the world.
Keating describes Trump's view of the world (the US, China and Russia) as basically being akin to that of the American mafia. The New York mafia doesn't interfere with the Chicago mafia and neither interfere with the Florida mafia.
Trump's mafia view lines up with Keating's continuing belief in the "great powers" view of the world. This in turn is partly driven by a pragmatic assessment about numbers: numbers of weapons, armed forces, and manufacturing capabilities.
But, according to Keating, the important point of it is that Trump does not want to go to war with China.
Chinese leaders seek to reduce tension
Keating sees the US push for bases in Australia as one that comes primarily from the US defence establishment, rather than its political establishment, and argues the history of this goes back to the time when in a Eurocentric US, "policy in the Pacific was run by the Navy out of Honolulu".
But the former PM highlighted another, and very different, China assessment: that the US intelligence community doesn't see China as a risk.
Keating pointed to the 2026 Annual Threat Assessment of the US Intelligence Community, published in March this year.
In its China Strategic Overview, the assessment says: "President Xi and his government aim to achieve 'the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation' by 2049.
"China will seek to increase its power and influence to shape its region and world events; create an environment favourable to Chinese interests; overcome perceived containment efforts by the US; secure its freedom of movement at sea; reduce US military presence and operations on its periphery; and fend off challenges to its reputation, legitimacy, and capabilities at home and abroad."
But, significantly, the review, which summarises the views of 18 US intelligence agencies, including the CIA, defence intelligence and national security agencies, says: "China also sees benefits to and is prioritising a productive, stable economic relationship with the US, as evinced by its approach to the Busan Agreement with the Trump administration.
"Beijing has been deeply suspicious of Washington's intentions and has long viewed the US as pursuing a coordinated effort to contain China's development and rise, undermine Chinese Communist Party (CCP) rule, and prevent the country from achieving its aims.
"[But] at the same time, Chinese leaders will seek to reduce tension with Washington when they believe that such efforts benefit Beijing, protect China's core interests, and buy time to strengthen its position."
Loading
Australia confused about its place
Keating observed: "Now, this doesn't sound like a wartime power. This is the US time view of them, right? This is the official US view for the Congress this year.
"Of course, the absurdity of the American position is, they are a naval power," he continued.
"It's 10,000 kilometres from San Diego to the Chinese coast. There they meet a continental power with four times the population and a bigger economy and a bigger navy.
"But, don't worry, you're gonna dust them off and put them in their place. And we're going along.
"They're gonna show the Chinese who's in charge, you see?
"What we want to see is an Asia where the two great powers coexist. The United States as the balancing power: we can all support that.
"But what we can't support is the American trying to contain China … with their base, 10,000 kilometres away in San Diego … A military exchange between the Chinese and the Americans and East Asia would last about five days. It'll be all over."
Given Taiwan has always been seen as the flashpoint for such a conflict, it's worth highlighting that the US intelligence community assessment notes that China "prefers to achieve unification without the use of force, if possible".
"The IC assesses that Chinese leaders do not currently plan to execute an invasion of Taiwan in 2027, nor do they have a fixed timeline for achieving unification.
"Chinese officials recognise that an amphibious invasion of Taiwan would be extremely challenging and carry a high risk of failure, especially in the event of US intervention."
The world is a particularly confusing place just now. But no-one seems more confused about their place in it than Australia.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

====================================================================================================

Why political optimism has become scarce in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
'Afraid of change': political optimism now a rare commodity in Australia
What a despairing mob we've become.
This week's national accounts confirmed how stuck we are in a foul and pestilent congregation of vapours … to steal from English literature's greatest melancholy wobbler.
It's doubtful Hamlet ever dwelt on the state of Denmark's real net national disposable income (RNNDI) per capita.
But if he had he might have embraced what a downer it is.
RNNDI is one of those measures that helps explain why voters look desperate to try new and "dangerous" things, as the prime minister put it this week. He was referring to One Nation and its quickening political momentum around the country, where Pauline Hanson is eagerly harvesting the dark mood.
Prosperity heading in wrong direction
The Australian Bureau of Statistics says RNNDI estimates the income a person derives from the economy that they can spend and save after the pernicious impact of inflation is taken into account.
It renders what's left in people's pockets after cost-of-living increases.
"This is a broader measure of prosperity than the commonly cited measure of real GDP," the bureau explains on its website.
"It more accurately reflects the average lived experience and prosperity of Australians."
In the June quarter, it shrank by 0.4 per cent from the previous three months. And from the same period a year earlier it was unchanged.
Over the last two years it has been either falling outright or pretty much flat.
By contrast for most of the last half century this measure has enjoyed steady gains with brief exceptions such as the early 1990s recession and the post GFC "secular stagnation" of the early and mid-2010s.
In the real world, this reflects how pretty much every generation since federation has secured a better quality of life, greater opportunity and choice than their parents.
But now, living standards and prosperity are headed in the wrong direction.
Which is where a majority of Australians think the country is going.
Albanese government's performance judged harshly
Perceptions of the national economy, as well as state and territory economies, are at their lowest level, according to a nationwide poll in August by JWS Research that began testing views on this question in 2013 during the dying days of the Rudd-Gillard-Rudd turmoil.
And to the degree that governments are responsible for the gloomy sense of national direction, the JWS survey shows they're getting a good slab of blame.
Views of state and territory governments are at their lowest ebb since early 2017.
For the federal government it's particularly acute.
Judgements on the Albanese government's performance have never been this harsh.
It's worse, according to JWS, than at any time during Scott Morrison's oft-derided prime ministership.
And is now on par with levels of disillusionment that accompanied Malcolm Turnbull's time in office not long before his colleagues rolled him out the door.
War, bond markets and AI
These may turn out to be temporary miasmas of the public's mood.
But there was a creeping sense this week that the federal government hasn't yet figured out how to flip the script. And that time is starting to run out.
To be sure, some of what ails people and the economy that dictates their fortunes is externally driven.
There's a lengthening war in the Middle East.
Loading...
Bond market klaxon horns are blaring about the dangers of ballooning government debt and persistent global inflation. And AI is giving many the jitters.
Yet Labor is already well into its fifth year in office.
By the standards of Australian governments this is early middle age.
Well before the autumn of life, so to speak, but also when things start to get tired.
The old sparkle doesn't come so easy. There's no blaming youthful indiscretions when things go wrong. The last lot is long gone.
The buck is firmly in hand. And consequences from mistakes or omissions of the past begin to accrue.
While much of what ails people can be linked to a crazy world, voters often respond to two big drivers: a sense the government has a positive plan and knows where it wants to go.
And a belief that it's fighting for people rather than its own preservation.
The government claims it is embarking on the most thorough economic reform program in a generation with its changes to capital gains taxation of assets and overhaul of trusts.
Promoted as "fairness measures" they're mainly about collecting more tax.
For many critics in the business community — and voters more generally — they're a drag rather than an inspiration.
For economists they fall short of producing what used to be called a "growth agenda".
And Labor's opponents accuse it of running a redistributionist program rather than an expansionist platform.
At the same time, the progressive left is frustrated that the government isn't targeting the honey pots of billionaires and "greedy" foreign corporations.
Loading
A reminder that leadership matters
Paul Keating this week told an audience in Sydney that governments are "afraid of change".
And not-withstanding the adjustments to negative gearing and capital gains on housing that have been legislated to boost affordability, he warned the country needs to "manage capital accretion … more ambitiously than we have in recent times".
"We've gone 26 years without any structural change. And of course it shows [in] the lag in productivity and the lagging growth numbers."
A new history of Keating's prime ministership by historian James Curran published this week makes the case for boldness and bravery.
Keating's legacy — as recognised by both sides of fair-minded elements of the political divide — is that he delivered that in spades when it came to economic reform.
But Curran's book, Grand Ambition, is a reminder that he can flourish in other realms.
Keating became prime minister within days of the end of the Cold War and the collapse of the Soviet Union in late 1991, a geopolitical rupture that compares surely to anything happening today.
Grand Ambition details how the new prime minister didn't retreat into passivity in the face of that new global reality — the moment, in Keating's words, when the "electromagnets of the Cold War were switched off".
Others might have been content to merely describe the new world for Australian voters.
Keating, according to Curran, saw the juncture as an opening.
He pressed George HW Bush — just arrived in Sydney — to engage in the region, setting the stage for Keating to win support for turning APEC into a leaders' forum.
One that endures to this day.
Keating noted this week that the November APEC leaders meeting will allow Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to meet and "discuss their real matters".
"That's been going on now for 34 years. This was a gift to the West by Australian foreign policy and it made a very big difference," Keating said on Wednesday.
"And because we invented the show, we were in charge."
Whether you bought into Keating's story — one that fused foreign policy and domestic reform into one big "ball of wax" (as Keating's advisor Allan Gyngell told Curran) — or not, that's not the point.
It was a time when Australia aspired to be more than history's passenger. Or a fixed South Pacific aircraft carrier for a powerful friend.
A reminder that leadership matters.
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

Germany calls on the EU to restrict the issuance of tourist visas to Russians following acts of sabotage
Kyiv • UNN
Berlin links the suspected attack on Leipzig Airport to Russian special services. Germany demands tougher visa restrictions for Russians.
Germany is calling on its European partners to tighten restrictions on the entry of Russian citizens into the EU for tourist visas following recent acts of sabotage, for which Berlin holds Moscow responsible, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
German authorities are investigating a Belarusian citizen who also holds a Russian passport in connection with an alleged attempt to attack Leipzig Airport using drones and explosives.
According to available information, the person entered the Schengen Area on a tourist visa issued by the Italian Embassy in Minsk (Belarus). Sources in the security services note that, apparently, he did not visit Italy.
Germany's Foreign Ministry has expressed dissatisfaction that too many visas are being issued to Russians.
"The number of visas issued to Russian citizens for holidays in the European Union is excessively high," a ministry representative said.
Sources close to the government claim that the significant number of visas issued to Russians contradicts the spirit of the sanctions imposed in connection with the war in Ukraine and makes it impossible to determine who is entering the EU and for what purpose.
Statistical data show that in 2025 Italy issued more Schengen visas than any other country in the bloc; according to Euractiv, Italy, France and Spain accounted for three-quarters of all visa applications from Russians.
Last year, Italy issued more visas to Belarusian citizens than any other EU country, with the number rising sharply after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to European Commission statistics analyzed by the Italian news outlet Linkiesta, in 2021 Italy issued Belarusian citizens only 2,968 visas, whereas last year the figure was 50,709.
A similar trend can be observed with regard to Russia. The number of Italian visas issued to Russian citizens rose from 63,894 in 2021 to more than 165,000 in 2025 — nearly a threefold increase despite the war.
This week, the German government announced measures in response to the Kremlin's actions, stating that Russian intelligence services were likely behind the alleged plot to attack Leipzig Airport. These measures include closing the Russian consulate in Bonn, summoning the Russian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry, and tightening controls on Russia's "shadow fleet" — illegal vessels transporting oil to the Baltic Sea. The EU also announced its 22nd package of sanctions and said it was expanding the list of Russians banned from entering the union's territory.
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani ordered an investigation into the visa issued to the Belarusian citizen suspected in the Leipzig sabotage case.
"There is a specific procedure for issuing visas, since established requirements must be observed," Tajani said. "If applicants meet these requirements and there are no particular concerns regarding them, the visa is issued. If that was indeed the situation, we will try to determine why this visa was issued."
Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and the Czech Republic have virtually stopped issuing visas to Russian citizens, introducing national restrictions that go beyond the pan-European measures. However, a number of other EU member states continue to issue visas in large numbers, and in some cases have even increased their numbers.

UN adopts new map: Africa bigger, North America and Europe smaller

UN adopts new map: Africa bigger, North America and Europe smaller
The US was the only vote against the resolution for a shift to the Equal Earth cartographic projection over the traditional Mercator map
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe.
Aimed at “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the US voted against it and six other states abstained.
The new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world”, the resolution said.
It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.
Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which drove the resolution, said maps “guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions”.
“They are therefore never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation.”

How to keep your kids safe at petting zoos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

A three-year-old girl has died from a rare illness after visiting a petting zoo in Victoria. She had developed brain damage and kidney failure after spending weeks in intensive care.
The girl is confirmed to have had haemolytic uraemic syndrome, a rare but serious serious condition, caused by infection with a specific type of Escherichia coli bacteria (or E. coli for short). This can be transmitted in a variety of ways, including after contact with animals on a farm or at a petting zoo.
Fortunately, such tragic cases are rare. But they do shed light on bacterial infections harboured by some animals and the need to take hygiene precautions when visiting petting zoos.
I'm a microbiology lecturer, and I'm planning to visit a petting zoo next weekend with my family.
Here's what we know about the infection risk at petting zoos, and what parents can do to help keep their children safe.
What is haemolytic uraemic syndrome?
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome most commonly results from infection with types of E. coli that produce a specific toxin called the Shiga toxin.
Early symptomsof infection are nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea, which can contain blood.
Warning signs that need urgent medical assessment include bloody diarrhoea, markedly reduced urination, lethargy, pallor (looking pale), unexplained bruising or red-purple spots on the skin.
If a doctor suspects someone has haemolytic uraemic syndrome, they will ask about symptoms and examine the person. Hospitalisation as soon as possible will be necessary. Blood, stool and sometimes urine tests confirm the diagnosis.
The Shiga toxin can damage the lining of blood vessels, which leads to circulatory and kidney problems. This can progress to haemolytic uraemic syndrome, leading to kidney failure, high blood pressure, seizures and in some cases death.
So emergency medical treatment is essential, in a hospital intensive care unit, with dialysis and blood transfusions often needed.
The disease is more common in children.
How is it spread?
These bacteria can can spread to humans by contaminated food and water. Humans can also spread the bacteria to other humans, via faeces, such as when changing nappies.
But the situation most relevant here is the spread via some animals. Bacteria are present on animal fur and wool, so children can come into contact with it when patting or cuddling an animal. But that's not the only way.
Bacteria are also present on manure, bedding, soil, feed, enclosure floors and fences.
The risk lies when people's contaminated hands come into contact with their mouth.
Toddlers are particularly difficult to protect because they often put fingers, toys, food and dummies in their mouths and need help to wash their hands thoroughly.
Are some animals riskier than others?
Cattle and other ruminants, including sheep and goats, are recognised animal reservoirs for Shiga-producing E. coli, as well as some other pathogens.
For example, animal contact can also expose children to Salmonella, Campylobacter and Cryptosporidium, all of which can cause gastroenteritis.
While exposure to these can occur on farms, petting zoos and open zoos specifically have been identified as a risk for these microorganisms. Animals may not always show symptoms.
But petting zoos are great for kids, aren't they?
Petting zoos and farm experiences can provide children with educational experiences involving animals, farming, food production and animal welfare. They're also such a great family activity and educational resource.
The Australian Veterinary Association supports petting zoos where animal health, welfare, public safety and disease-transmission risks are appropriately managed.
Hygiene plans include clear communication about the risks of infection, readily accessible handwashing facilities, and physical separation between animal-contact and food areas.
Parents need to ensure their children are supervised. Most importantly, they need to ensure their children's hands are washed before coming into contact with anything that might go into a child's mouth — a dummy, or food, for instance. Hand sanitiser is not as effective as washing with soap and water for 20 seconds or more.
So when choosing a petting zoo, favour venues with handwashing stations immediately outside animal areas, with running water, soap, disposable towels and signs reminding visitors to wash before eating or drinking.
Thomas Jeffries is a senior lecturer in microbiology at Western Sydney University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

Women’s football also set new transfer records, with spending more than doubling compared with 2025 to reach $28.6 million, while more than 1,400 transfers were registered.
Beyond World Cup players, more than 12,500 international transfers in men’s football reached a cumulative value of over $9.89 billion.
- Record growth in women’s football
Women’s professional football continued its growth, setting records for both the number of international transfers and transfer fees.
A total of 1,406 international transfers were registered in women’s professional football, the highest number ever recorded and a 19.2% increase from the previous record, according to FIFA.
Transfer fees also reached an all-time high, with $28.6 million spent on international transfers, more than double the amount recorded during the previous mid-year window.
English clubs led spending with $8 million, followed by clubs in Spain with $6.6 million, Germany with $4.9 million, the US with $2.9 million and Italy with $2.1 million.
Swedish clubs were the biggest recipients of transfer fees, receiving $4.2 million, ahead of clubs in England with $4 million, France and Germany with $3.6 million each, and the Netherlands with $2.9 million.
 
- Men’s market continues to grow
The men’s transfer market also recorded a significant window, with more than $9.89 billion spent on transfer fees across more than 12,500 international transfers, the highest amount ever recorded, according to FIFA.
English clubs led global spending with more than $3.02 billion in transfer fees, followed by clubs in Italy with $1.1 billion, Spain with $940 million, Germany with $904 million and France with $641 million.
English clubs also completed the highest number of incoming transfers, followed by clubs from Spain and Portugal.
French clubs received the highest total in transfer fees at $1.7 billion, followed by clubs in England with $1.43 billion, Germany with $1.02 billion, Spain with $773 million and Portugal with $642 million.

DRC Health Minister Roger Kamba said containing the outbreak required efforts beyond the health sector, involving communities, government agencies, partners and donors. "The government is fully mobilized to protect every Congolese," Kamba said.
According to the WHO, full implementation of the revised plan would require an estimated 1.3 billion U.S. dollars.
Damien Mama, United Nations resident coordinator in the DRC, said the Ebola response needed to be integrated into the broader humanitarian effort and supported by sufficient, flexible and predictable funding.

"It would obviously be very good for national security if it were about pursuing a common objective against transnational crime, transnational drug trafficking, transnational terrorism," Fernandez told Reuters in an interview, when asked about the possibility of U.S. ground operations on Costa Rican soil.
Costa Rica and the U.S. have cooperated for years on security matters, including through joint maritime patrols. U.S. President Donald Trump invited Costa Rica to join his Shield of the Americas coalition, which is aimed at combating drug cartels.
A right-wing populist who took office in May, Fernandez campaigned on a tough anti-crime platform, vowing to restore order in Costa Rica, a country that has seen a spike in drug trafficking and violence in recent years. The homicide rate hit a record 17.2 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023, double the rate of a decade ago.
Fernandez said she is not considering requesting from Congress a state of emergency or suspending constitutional guarantees in order to address the wave of violence, noting that homicides are declining.
Court data shows that in the first half of 2026 homicides fell 14% compared to the same period in 2025.
Fernandez has been in a tense standoff with Costa Rica's courts, accusing the judiciary of being infiltrated by organized crime and blocking her tough-on-crime security policies.
"I've been very critical of how slow the courts are, very critical in specific cases where judges release convicted criminals long before their sentences are complete, and I've also been very critical of administrative failures and potential corruption in the judiciary," Fernandez said.
The dispute has increasingly centered on the judiciary's role and funding. Fernandez has backed significant budget cuts to the judicial branch and supports a legislative proposal to have Congress, rather than the Supreme Court, appoint the attorney general.
Judicial officials have denied corruption allegations, challenging Fernandez to provide evidence. They argue that budget cuts planned for 2026 and 2027 would weaken democratic checks and balances and undermine efforts to fight crime. REUTERS

Treatment-resistant depression linked to reduced brain entropy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:00:48 UTC
03:00:48 KST

People who suffer from depression that does not respond to standard treatments may experience a loss of complexity in their resting brain activity. A recent brain imaging study found that patients with treatment-resistant depression display reduced neural entropy, meaning their brain signals are more rigid and less unpredictable than those of healthy individuals. The research, published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, suggests that system-wide reductions in brain flexibility could serve as a biological marker for this severe form of the illness.
Major depressive disorder is a chronic condition that ranks among the leading causes of disability worldwide. While many patients find relief through standard medications, a substantial portion do not. Treatment-resistant depression is typically diagnosed when a patient fails to achieve remission after at least two adequate trials of antidepressant therapy.
Individuals dealing with this form of depression often experience severe symptoms, including persistent low mood, an inability to feel pleasure, and cognitive difficulties. They also face a higher risk of relapse and suicidal thoughts. Understanding the biological mechanisms behind this resistance to treatment is a major goal for psychiatric research.
To explore these underlying mechanisms, researchers often look at brain entropy. In the context of neuroscience, entropy refers to the level of complexity, irregularity, and unpredictability in spontaneous brain signals. A healthy brain exhibits high entropy, which allows it to flexibly adapt to new information, process emotions, and perform cognitive tasks.
Conversely, lower brain entropy indicates a more constrained and stereotyped pattern of brain activity. Previous imaging studies have linked lower entropy to poorer emotional regulation and cognitive rigidity. However, the concept had not been extensively mapped in individuals specifically diagnosed with treatment-resistant depression.
A team of scientists based at Taipei Veterans General Hospital and National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University in Taiwan conducted the recent investigation. The study was led by researchers Wei-Chen Lin and Li-Kai Cheng, alongside senior author Mu-Hong Chen. They wanted to see if the severe clinical features of treatment-resistant depression were reflected in a loss of neural complexity across specific brain networks.
The researchers recruited 48 adults diagnosed with treatment-resistant depression and 38 healthy adults with no history of psychiatric disorders. The patients with depression had all failed to respond to at least three adequate courses of antidepressants, classifying their condition as moderately treatment-resistant. Both groups were matched in terms of age and sex distribution.
To measure brain entropy, all participants underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. This type of brain scan tracks blood oxygenation levels in the brain over time. Because active brain regions require more oxygen, these fluctuating blood oxygen levels serve as a proxy for neural activity.
During the scans, participants were instructed to simply rest with their eyes closed, stay awake, and let their minds wander. This allowed the researchers to capture the brain’s spontaneous, baseline activity rather than its response to a specific task. The team then calculated the sample entropy of these brain signals across 166 distinct anatomical regions.
Sample entropy is a mathematical formula that quantifies how unpredictable a time series is. The researchers applied two different mathematical thresholds to their entropy calculations. One threshold was more permissive, designed to catch the most robust and pronounced drops in brain complexity. The other was more stringent, designed to detect subtle, widespread reductions in signal irregularity.
Using the more permissive threshold, the researchers found that patients with treatment-resistant depression exhibited lower brain entropy in three specific areas. These included the right angular gyrus, the left cerebellar Crus II, and the median raphe nucleus. The median raphe nucleus is located in the brainstem and serves as a major source of serotonin, a chemical messenger heavily involved in mood regulation. The right angular gyrus and cerebellar Crus II help integrate sensory information and support social and emotional processing.
When the researchers applied the more stringent threshold, they observed a much broader pattern of reduced entropy. The patients displayed lower neural complexity across 24 distinct brain regions compared to the healthy adults. This widespread reduction affected several large-scale brain systems, including the default mode network, the salience network, and the reward network. These systems collectively govern how humans process emotions, assign value to external stimuli, and navigate social environments.
Affected regions within these networks included the prefrontal cortex, which is associated with decision making and cognitive control. The researchers also saw reduced entropy in the thalamus, a central hub that relays sensory signals, and the nucleus accumbens, a key node in the brain’s reward circuitry. This extensive pattern suggests that treatment-resistant depression involves a global disruption of neural flexibility rather than an isolated defect in a single anatomical structure.
The researchers also looked for relationships between entropy levels and the severity of a patient’s treatment resistance. They noticed a preliminary trend in a specific part of the cerebellum where higher entropy correlated with more severe treatment resistance. The researchers suspect this might represent the brain attempting to compensate for dysfunction elsewhere, though the finding was not statistically significant after adjusting for multiple mathematical comparisons.
The study relied on a cross-sectional design, meaning the researchers observed the participants at a single point in time. Because of this, it is impossible to determine whether reduced brain entropy contributes to the development of treatment-resistant depression or if the prolonged illness causes the brain to lose its complexity. Tracking patients over several years could help clarify the direction of this relationship.
Another detail to consider is the use of medication among the study participants. All the patients with depression were taking antidepressants during the brain scans, and many were taking additional medications such as mood stabilizers or atypical antipsychotics. While this reflects the reality of treating severe depression, it leaves open the possibility that the medications themselves might influence the complexity of resting brain signals.
The research team also did not include a control group of patients whose depression responds well to standard treatments. Without this group, it is difficult to isolate which entropy reductions are unique to treatment resistance versus those that are common to depression in general. Future studies comparing treatment-resistant patients directly with treatment-responsive patients could highlight the specific biological signatures of treatment failure.
Finally, the researchers noted the need for accompanying cognitive and behavioral tests in future work. Incorporating detailed psychological assessments alongside brain scans would help connect the observed reductions in brain entropy to specific real-world challenges, such as memory deficits or emotional blunting.
The study, “Treatment-resistant depression is associated with reduced brain entropy,” was authored by Wei-Chen Lin, Li-Kai Cheng, Tung-Ping Su, Li-Fen Chen, Pei-Chi Tu, Cheng-Ta Li, Ya-Mei Bai, Shih-Jen Tsai, and Mu-Hong Chen.

UN urges restraint in Yemen, warns of civilian risks in Gaza, West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:00:29 UTC
03:00:29 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
The UN on Friday urged Yemen’s warring parties to exercise restraint amid a sharp escalation in fighting, while expressing deep concern over the safety of civilians in Gaza and the West Bank.
UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said the UN was “deeply concerned by the ongoing military clashes across multiple front lines in Yemen, including Ta’izz.”
“We call on the Yemeni parties to exercise restraint, de-escalate tensions, and refrain from actions that could lead to further military escalation,” Dujarric told reporters at the UN headquarters in New York.
He warned that further escalation could have “devastating political, economic, and security ramifications for Yemen and all of its people.”
“The parties must prioritize dialogue and engage constructively with the United Nations-led efforts towards a negotiated political settlement,” he added.
On Lebanon, Dujarric said UN Humanitarian Coordinator Imran Riza visited Nabatieh in southern Lebanon, where he met communities receiving people returning to their homes as well as displaced residents.
Authorities highlighted damage to vital infrastructure, including water and sanitation systems, he said.
In the village of Mayfadoun, damage to a water well station, including solar panels and pumping equipment, has affected water supplies, according to Dujarric.
He stressed the importance of “early recovery efforts to restore these essential services” and support municipalities and communities seeking to recover.
Dujarric said the UN’s 2026 Lebanon flash appeal ended last month after receiving less than 52% of the requested funding, with $330 million received.
Despite the funding shortfall, humanitarian partners have reached more than 1.2 million people with at least one form of critical assistance since the latest escalation began, including more than 900,000 people who received cash assistance.
“Yet, as Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher stressed, the needs continue, access remains constrained, and many families in Lebanon still cannot return home safely,” he said.
Regarding the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Dujarric said the UN remains “very concerned about the safety of civilians both in the Gaza Strip and in the West Bank.”
He said UN agencies and humanitarian partners in Gaza were helping communities prepare for the rainy season, but “more funding and access are urgently needed.”
Citing World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Dujarric warned that public health risks are growing as winter approaches, with many people still displaced in overcrowded tented sites.
“Gaza’s already overwhelmed health system cannot withstand additional surges in diseases and illness,” Tedros said, according to Dujarric.
In the West Bank, UN humanitarian colleagues reported that more than 6,400 Palestinians have been displaced from 130 communities by occupiers' violence since 2023. More than 2,500 were displaced this year alone, over half of them children.
Dujarric said the UN’s humanitarian concerns were being compounded by repeated attacks, damage to homes and infrastructure and restrictions on access to land and essential services.

====================================================================================================

UN backs Africa-led push for a fairer world map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:31:56 UTC
02:31:56 KST

The United Nations General Assembly has backed an Africa-led campaign to replace the widely used Mercator world map with a projection that more accurately represents the relative size of countries and continents.
The resolution, sponsored by African states and led by Togo, passed on Friday by a vote of 164-1, with six abstentions. The United States was the only country to vote against it.
Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey said the initiative was aimed at challenging perceptions created by a map that significantly distorts the size of land masses, particularly those near the poles.
“A fair world begins with a fair map,” Dussey told Reuters ahead of the vote.
Why Africa is challenging the Mercator map
Created in the 16th century, the Mercator projection expands the apparent size of land masses as they move towards the poles. As a result, Greenland can appear roughly comparable in size to Africa on many maps, even though Africa is about 14 times larger.
The UN resolution promotes the Equal Earth projection, which is designed to represent continents’ relative areas more accurately.
The measure is not legally binding and does not seek to eliminate Mercator for navigation. Togo’s Foreign Ministry said the projection remains appropriate for maritime and aerial navigation.
The campaign reflects broader African efforts to address what Togo describes as the lingering influence of colonial-era representations.
“This is not against Europe, it is not against any other civilisation,” Dussey said, arguing that the widespread use of Mercator is linked in part to the legacy of colonisation.
Togo plans classroom overhaul
Togo plans to become the first country to replace Mercator-based geography materials in its schools, with Dussey saying the government aims to update its textbooks by the end of the year.
“In the classroom, we need to change it to give an example to all the countries in the world,” he said.
Togo also plans to encourage other governments, schools, international organisations and technology companies to adopt Equal Earth and other more accurate alternatives.
Over the next six months, the country intends to engage African Union members and supporters from other regions on ways to expand adoption, including discussions with companies involved in mapping, GPS and other location-based technologies.
The United States opposed the resolution, describing it as promoting an “ideological agenda” and distracting from what it called more pressing issues involving international peace, prosperity and relations.
For Togo, however, the debate is about more than cartography.
“The world is changing. Africa also is changing,” Dussey said.

Five European nations aim to sign deals this year to send irregular asylum seekers without legal residency to countries outside the European Union, they have said at a meeting hosted by Denmark.
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands said on Friday that they had agreed on concrete steps towards a deal with a non-European Union country on return facilities, the latest effort by European nations to reduce immigration.
The countries, known as the Group of Five, did not name the nations they expect to host return centres.
"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year that will enable the establishment of return hubs," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters at a press conference in Copenhagen.
The group, which has held a series of meetings this year, plans to reconvene in Munich, Germany, at the end of September.
The European Parliament in June approved an overhaul of migration policy aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to set up centres abroad, in what critics say could weaken safeguards for irregular asylum seekers.
Human rights concerns
The Council of Europe, a non-EU body that promotes human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the continent, said in July that return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks", and several other groups have also criticised the plan.
Danish Refugee Council Secretary General Charlotte Slente said it would be better to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which focuses on stricter border screening, faster asylum and return procedures, and expanded digital systems for managing asylum claims.
"Return hubs focus on a small number of returns; they will not stop people from taking even more dangerous routes, and they could violate basic human rights," Slente said.
Denmark expects to be ready to send irregular asylum seekers to the return hub by the end of 2027, Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov said.
"It's a new chance to have a life in a partner country," he said, adding that the five nations would be in dialogue with the UN body, the International Organization for Migration, and the UN Refugee Agency for their next steps.
A UNHCR spokesperson said the agency had not been approached with details of a proposal and could not comment on the arrangements being discussed.

China Focus: China to build international constellation for exploring Earth-moon space
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:25:37 CST
02:25:37 KST

HEFEI, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China has officially launched a scientific program to construct a satellite constellation in the Earth-moon space in collaboration with multiple countries, filling gaps in systematic observation of the region.
According to experts attending the 2026 International Deep Space Exploration Conference held in Hefei, capital of east China's Anhui Province, which runs from Thursday to Friday, the Cislunar CubeSat Constellation (C3) Program will be open to scientists and institutions worldwide, providing opportunities for developing countries to take part in deep-space exploration missions.
The cislunar space spans from low Earth orbits to about 2 million kilometers from Earth. It represents a new frontier for expanding human activity and will be a key operational area for future crewed lunar missions and the construction of lunar research stations.
Yet human understanding of this region has long relied primarily on isolated, point-based observations, leaving gaps in spatial and temporal coverage and insufficient data from key areas. A systematic and continuous observation network is therefore urgently needed, experts said.
According to Hu Zhaobin, vice chairman of International Deep Space Exploration Association (IDSEA), 30 CubeSats, each weighing no more than 30 kilograms, will form a constellation for space environment monitoring and gamma-ray burst detection. All satellites are scheduled for launch and deployment before 2030.
Through synchronized observations from multiple satellites and multiple locations, the constellation will enable comprehensive tracking of the evolution of space weather events and achieve sub-arcsecond positioning accuracy for gamma-ray bursts.
Once completed, the project will transform cislunar exploration from intermittent, point-based observations to networked and continuous monitoring, providing core data support for crewed lunar landing life safety and frontier scientific research on the cislunar space environment.
"We look forward to working with partners around the world to push the boundaries of human knowledge of deep space," Hu said.
The initiative was jointly launched by the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory (DSEL) and IDSEA, with support from the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization.
The program will also provide technical training and establish unified interface standards to enable developing countries to participate more deeply in deep-space exploration.
Research institutions from countries including Thailand, Serbia, Egypt, Senegal and Indonesia have already joined the initiative.
The first phase of engineering development has begun, with overall design studies for the satellites, payloads, tracking and control systems and other major components nearing completion.
The DSEL was officially inaugurated in February 2022. It has since established partnerships with more than 60 international research institutions.
In July 2025, the laboratory and several other institutions jointly proposed the establishment of IDSEA, the first China-based international academic organization for deep space exploration. ■

Economic Watch: Cross-Strait semiconductor firms eye cooperation, new opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:25:19 CST
02:25:19 KST

TAIPEI, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Chinese mainland and Taiwan semiconductor companies taking part in SEMICON Taiwan 2026 -- a world-leading specialized semiconductor exhibition -- expressed their willingness to pool complementary strengths and embrace new opportunities.
The three-day exhibition concluded on Friday at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center. Organized by the global semiconductor industry association SEMI, the annual event was first held in September 1996, covering the entire semiconductor supply chain, including equipment, materials, packaging and testing. This year it brought together more than 1,300 exhibitors and hosted over 4,300 booths.
A number of mainland companies attended the exhibition and presented their latest products, offering a glimpse of the potential to share new opportunities in the rapidly evolving semiconductor industry on both sides of the Taiwan Strait.
At the booth of Huangshan Juxin New Material Co., Ltd., samples of materials in various sizes and colors were neatly displayed, drawing inquiries from Taiwan industry professionals.
"Many Taiwan companies have shown strong interest in our products, and some visitors are friends we met at last year's exhibition," said Qu Chao, the company's sales director.
The high-tech company, which specializes in high-performance polyimide materials, was attending the exhibition for the second time.
"Polyimide materials are used throughout the semiconductor industry, from front-end chip manufacturing to back-end packaging," Qu said, adding that Juxin's products offer competitive prices, customized services and full traceability.
"There is considerable room for greater cross-Strait industrial cooperation," Qu said, adding that with Taiwan possessing a well-developed semiconductor supply chain, materials from mainland suppliers could be further processed by local companies and applied across a wider range of fields.
At the booth of Taiwan-based Veego Corporation, anti-reflective optical windows and gold-coated quartz panels were displayed under bright lights. The products were manufactured by Lianyungang Huide Quartz Glass Co., Ltd., and were being exhibited in Taiwan for the first time through Veego Corporation.
"We are optimistic about the quality and potential of mainland quartz products," said Chuang Ya-hui of Veego Corporation, noting that the two companies established their partnership last year, hoping to introduce the products to more Taiwan customers and explore additional applications.
Other mainland exhibitors also used the event to explore more advanced forms of industrial cooperation.
Anchu Technology Co., Ltd., based in the eastern Chinese city of Zhangjiagang, specializes in formulated functional electronic chemicals and the safe storage of electronic specialty gases for semiconductor manufacturing.
The company brought its flagship product -- a negative-pressure gas cylinder designed for the safe storage of high-purity electronic gases -- to this year's exhibition.
"We believe the product has strong competitiveness in the Taiwan market," said Jing Shaoqing, the company's marketing director.
Anchu Technology has participated in the exhibition for three consecutive years and consistently received enthusiastic inquiries from Taiwan businesses, Jing said.
The exhibition came as Taiwan's semiconductor industry faces growing pressure to expand production overseas, particularly in the United States, as industrial insiders warned of a broader U.S. strategy to establish a whole supply chain that increasingly sidelines Taiwan.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), the world's leading contract chipmaker and a cornerstone of Taiwan's technology industry, has become a central focus of those efforts. The company has announced massive investments in Arizona, while its suppliers in Taiwan are also facing increasing pressure to expand operations in the United States.
Against this backdrop, industry observers are calling for diversifying markets and strengthening industrial links.
"The two sides of the Strait have strong complementarities in terms of semiconductor applications and markets," said Lo Huai-jia, secretary-general of the Taiwan R&D Managers Association.
Noting that the mainland is one of the world's most important manufacturing bases, Lo said as its manufacturing sector continues to develop, demand for semiconductor products and the range of their applications are also expected to expand.
"The complementary strengths of industries on both sides of the Strait could create much broader room for cooperation," Lo added. ■

Economic Watch: Asia-Pacific SMEs seek new growth through AI, deeper connectivity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:25:07 CST
02:25:07 KST

GUANGZHOU, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- On a production line at Seng Fong Holdings Berhad in Malaysia, a robotic arm grips a 35-kilogram block of rubber, with 3D cameras, laser scanners and AI algorithms serving as its "eyes" and "brain."
The setup is designed to tackle a longstanding challenge in the traditionally labor-intensive rubber processing industry. Rubber blocks coming out of drying ovens vary in shape, making them difficult for conventional robotic systems to handle.
Developed by an AI company in China's southern Guangdong Province, the solution has enabled the Malaysian rubber processor to automate more of the handling process, cutting labor costs by 20 to 30 percent while improving management efficiency, according to the company's chairman.
The case points to a broader shift taking place across the Asia-Pacific. AI is creating new opportunities for SMEs to innovate, while deeper regional connectivity is helping them turn technological advances into new sources of growth.
That trend was reflected at the 32nd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Small and Medium Enterprises Ministerial Meeting, held on Friday in Guangzhou, capital of Guangdong, as officials from APEC economies gathered to explore how technological innovation can empower SMEs and drive their further development.
SMEs are a major pillar of the regional economy. As technological and industrial transformation accelerates and global supply chains undergo profound changes, AI and other emerging technologies are creating both new opportunities and new challenges for SMEs across the Asia-Pacific.
AI-powered robotics are opening up new pathways for the digital transformation of SMEs, while open-source technologies are further lowering the barriers to technology access and application, enabling more businesses to participate in technological innovation, said Yang Qian, co-founder and chief operating officer of the Shenzhen-based embodied AI startup X Square Robot, at a parallel forum held alongside the ministerial meeting.
"What once required six months, costly computing power and a professional team can now be done in three days with a workstation and an idea," she said. "This gives SMEs, for the first time, a more level playing field with industry giants in innovation."
Yet SMEs across the region still face challenges, such as high digital transformation costs and talent shortages, highlighting the need for greater regional cooperation.
Kwon Jong-hyun, vice chairman of the Beijing Chapter of the World-OKTA, cited embodied intelligence as an example, saying China's strengths lie in scale and speed, while those of the Republic of Korea lie in precision and reliability.
Such cooperation, he said, is not simply about adding strengths together, but about multiplying their impact by combining complementary capabilities.
China's experience in supporting SMEs' digital transformation offers one example. The latest move came on Friday, when the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released an action plan to support AI entrepreneurship among SMEs for 2026-2028. The plan aims to foster more than 10,000 technology-based and innovative SMEs, more than 2,000 "little giant" firms, as well as a number of gazelle companies and unicorns.
Beyond domestic efforts, China is also seeking to extend AI cooperation through technology sharing and practical collaboration. It has announced that it will provide 5,000 opportunities for AI training and seminars for developing countries over the next five years.
It is also advancing the establishment of AI application cooperation centers with ASEAN countries, with overseas branches in Laos, Malaysia and Vietnam already operational. These centers promote cross-border cooperation in large models, the data industry, and smart agriculture, bringing Chinese solutions together with local partners.
China stands ready to work with all parties to help more SMEs thrive and grow, Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing said in a speech delivered at the opening ceremony of the meeting.
The country is enhancing its policy support for SMEs and strengthening practical cooperation with APEC economies to jointly boost the high-quality development of SMEs, Zhang added. ■

BEIJING, September 4. / TASS/. It will take decades to eliminate the remaining chemical weapons arsenals of the Imperial Japanese Army from World War II on the territory of Chinese provinces bordering Russia, Russia's Permanent Representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, Vladimir Tarabrin, who is on a visit to China, told TASS.
"There are mainly shells with pepper gas, chlorine, and sulfur-based agents. <…> The gases that were used during World War II," he said. The diplomat noted that each shell must be carefully extracted, transported to a special facility, cleaned, and after several technological stages, they are moved to a special chamber where they are destroyed by explosion.
"This is every shell. And there are hundreds of thousands of them. <…> They are all in the ground. They extract several hundred [per year]," Tarabrin said. According to him, this work has been ongoing since 2007, and each year the deadlines for its completion are pushed back. "The current plan is supposed to end in 2027. It is absolutely clear that it will not be fulfilled," Tarabrin emphasized. He also agreed with the view that, at the current pace, this work will take many years. "This is a matter of decades," the Russian permanent representative to the OPCW stated.
"The Chinese side has legitimate claims against the Japanese side. Primarily, that insufficient funds and personnel are being allocated," he emphasized.
"Everything works very slowly. The Japanese also complain that this is very dangerous work. Incidentally, in May of this year, two Japanese experts suffered burns," the diplomat said.
Earlier, Tarabrin stated that some of the remaining Japanese chemical weapons arsenals are located 20 km from the border with Russia in the Chinese city of Hunchun (Jilin province, bordering Primorsky Region). In his assessment, these chemical weapons stockpiles pose a threat to the population and the environment, including due to the risk of leakage and contamination of groundwater.

====================================================================================================

Guard F-16s Kept Pace on Kadena Deployment, but Edge Wears Thin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:54:40 UTC
01:54:40 KST

An F-16 Air National Guard unit’s six-month deployment to Kadena Air Base, Japan, this year illustrated the capabilities the Guard’s oldest fighter units can still offer—but also the challenges they face, officials told reporters this week.
On one hand, leaders said the Colorado ANG’s 120th Fighter Squadron was largely able to keep pace with its fifth-generation teammates and hone its Agile Combat Employment skills throughout the Pacific.
But on the other, the squadron’s 1980s-era F-16s are starting to show their age and lack at least some of the high-end capabilities the Air Force has said it wants to prioritize for a high-end fight.
“We’re able to keep up, with the exception of obviously being a fourth‑gen airplane,” Lt. Col. Frank “Chester” Prokop, squadron commander and detachment commander during the deployment, said. “We can’t get nearly as close to surface‑to‑air threats or air‑to‑air threats posed by China over there as some of the newer models. So, we’re kind of getting to the end of our capability. We’ve maxed it out. We played the perfect game.”
The January-to-June deployment, part of a rotation of fighters through Kadena as the base waits for its new F-15EX Eagle IIs, is a signpost of things to come for both the Air Force’s total fighter fleet, but more specifically for challenges faced inside the Air National Guard. The fleet is getting older while replacements are slowly ordered and delivered, and with the Active-Duty force being prioritized, the Guard is pushing the envelope with its legacy aircraft.
“The first piece is that any aging airframe is going to negatively impact operational availability and daily ops tempo,” Heather Penney, a former F-16 fighter pilot who now serves as the director of studies and research at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “I mean, you could talk about taking your 35‑year‑old car to an F1 race. Is that really what you want to do?”
Six Months at Kadena
Originally, the 120th was supposed to deploy a dozen of its F-16C Block 30 jets to Kadena from January to May. But that stay was extended six weeks due to demands across the Air Force related to Operation Epic Fury and the conflict with Iran. The conflict also impacted plans to join exercises in Thailand.
Still, the Guardsmen and their jets got to put into practice the Agile Combat Employment training they—with the rest of the Air Force—have been putting in for years now. ACE envisions small teams of Airmen dispersing from large central hubs to operate from remote or austere airfields, and the 120th implemented that through “small-package movements,” shuffling two to six jets around the region.
Prokop and 140th Wing Command Col. Christopher “KojaCk” Melka said the unit can now generate detailed ACE deployment packages, including personnel, aircraft load, and ground equipment needs, in 10-15 minutes, rather than the weeklong planning cycles common only a few years ago.
For a Philippines deployment, the squadron took four F-16s with a C-130 and worked with Marine Corps units. For Exercise Beverly Midnight at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, Japan, the unit conducted hot-pit refueling and rearming work alongside F-35s.
The unit also employed the “Multi-Capable Airman” approach to shrink its maintenance manpower footprint, Melka said. Operating mostly out of Kadena, a smaller package of cross-trained airmen handled various maintenance tasks for the squadron, rather than relying on a larger footprint with specialized technicians.
“We’ve actually exposed some of our Airmen to other career fields to give them a little bit more background on both, so that if, for whatever reason, they found themselves in a more austere environment where we could only send a certain package of maintainers and support personnel, maybe one person covered the duties of two,” Melka said.
Recap Ripple Effects
While the 120th was able to practice concepts like Agile Combat Employment and Multi-Capable Airmen during its deployment, the unit also had to stretch to keep its F-16s going, Melka and Prokop said.
“When these F-16s were first produced, it was roughly about six to eight maintenance man-hours per flight hour,” Prokop said. “Now, our maintainers are averaging 15 to 20 maintenance man-hours for every hour of flight.”
That’s because issues that require more in-depth maintenance, such as structural failures such as cracks on the airframe, “are happening at a much increasing rate right now,” Prokop said. “And that is probably the biggest challenge that we face is our maintenance unit has not received any increase in manpower commensurate with the level of increased requirements for maintenance time on the aircraft.”
The unit has been fortunate, the lieutenant colonel said, to have experienced, veteran maintainers working those airframes. But the increased maintenance needs are pushing leadership to make adjustments, like using more simulator flight time rather than flying hours to keep pilots sharp.
“The capacity of our maintainers to keep them safe and keep them combat effective is still working very well,” Melka said.
The jets themselves have also been upgraded many times over the years to stay effective with things like new AESA radars, Link 16 data links, and ongoing software upgrades; Prokop noted the F-16 has an unofficial nickname of the “Burger King jet” as a reference to the fast-food chain’s “Have It Your Way” slogan.
Nevertheless, the decades-old aircraft, while competent now, are closer to the end of their service lives—and the 120th is one of around a dozen Guard squadrons that have not been officially selected to recapitalize their fleets with newer aircraft such as the F-35A or F-15EX, leaving the unit’s future in doubt.
For now, Penney said, units like the 120th can keep flying their F-16s. But the Air Force has yet to signal its long-term plan for them and currently isn’t buying new jets fast enough to replace the older jets anytime soon.
“The Air Force has got to recapitalize at a meaningful rate, because they have deferred and delayed increasing their recapitalization rate,” Penney said. “If you want to be recapitalized by 2035, you’ve got to buy more than 100 fighters a year.”
Service leaders have said they need to procure at least 72 fighters per year to keep the fleet’s age from increasing. But the last time the service managed to budget for that was in fiscal 2024.
In fiscal 2025, the budget request was for 60 fighters. In 2026, it dropped to a low of 45. The fiscal 2027 request, still pending, is for just 62 fighters.
And even then, these new fighters—the F-35 and F-15EX—are mostly going to the Active-Duty force, leaving the Guard to wait. That could have a ripple effect, as the Guard deploys in nearly any major contingency or large-scale operation as a need, not an add-on, Penney said.
“If the Air Force does not recapitalize the Guard in a concurrent and proportional manner, they risk not only losing a key element of the total force, but they risk leaving the Guard with operationally irrelevant airframes,” Penney said.

“It may sound like a small thing, but to me it's way beyond a shoe. It is the desire that the world we live in would sometimes adjust itself to us, and not always that we will have to adjust ourselves to it,” Biton wrote in a post on Instagram, promoting Adidas and his collaboration with the brand.
Biton has posted photos and videos of himself and other Israeli soldiers on Instagram in Gaza, singing and dancing. His social media profile also has images of him carrying arms.
Pro-Palestine organisations and activists have called for a boycott of the brand, noting that Biton should not have been used in the campaign, due to his involvement in the bombardment of Gaza.

“Gaza has the highest per capita rate of child amputees in the world. More than 5,000 traumatic limb amputations have been estimated since October 2023, as a result of Israeli attacks carried out by soldiers like the one Adidas chose to model for them,” she wrote on X.

“The German sportswear brand Adidas is using Zionist war criminals from the "Israel" army, who lost a foot while invading Gaza, to promote their new single-foot sneakers. More than 4,000 Palestinian children have been amputated by "Israel's" bombs, but Adidas and other millionaire multinationals ignore them,” another activist wrote on X.
Others said that Adidas had now associated itself with genocide and apartheid.
Earlier this year, the NGO Humanity & Inclusion reported that 70 to 80 percent of those being admitted to the 12 hospitals which were still partially functioning in Gaza had lost limbs or suffered spinal cord injuries.

US midterm elections begin with chaos over mail-in voting crackdown
- US midterm elections began amid confusion over mail-in voting as Trump seeks court approval for new Postal Service restrictions affecting ballot handling.
- States face uncertainty with federal rules in flux and whistleblower warnings about a flawed USPS verification system risking ballot delays or rejection.
- The election's outcome will decide Congressional control, with Democrats favoured to gain the House amid narrow Republican majorities and voter dissatisfaction.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - America’s midterm elections opened on Sept 4 in a fog of confusion over mail-in voting, with ballots already going out as President Donald Trump presses courts to let him impose sweeping new restrictions on how they are handled.
North Carolina became the first state authorised to begin sending out ballots, formally launching an election season that culminates on Nov 3 and will determine control of Congress for the final two years of Trump’s term.
Yet voters and election officials still do not know what rules may govern millions of mail-in ballots, as Trump asks the Supreme Court to revive curbs blocked by a federal judge and as states scramble to prepare for changes that could come after voting has begun.
The dispute has been compounded by whistleblower allegations that a new Postal Service verification system was rushed, inadequately tested, and could delay or even disqualify entire batches of ballots because of a single barcode problem.
A federal judge weighing whether to extend the temporary block on Trump’s plan warned on Sept 4 that hurried changes could cause widespread disruption.
“We’re not playing an intellectual puzzle game,” Judge Indira Talwani reportedly told a lawyer defending the restrictions, in remarks widely picked up by US media.
“We’re talking about people’s right to vote.”
Trump’s March executive order would require states to provide the US Postal Service with lists of eligible mail voters through a new federal portal.
Rules in limbo
Ballot envelopes would also need individual barcodes and other design features, with USPS empowered to refuse mailings that fail to meet its requirements.
The administration says the rules are to protect election integrity, although it has produced no evidence of significant fraud through mail voting.
Trump has repeatedly denounced the practice as corrupt while using it himself – including to vote in Florida’s Republican primary in August.
The uncertainty comes on top of a voting system that already differs dramatically from state to state.
Some automatically send ballots to registered voters, others require voters to request them, while identification requirements, return deadlines and rules for counting late-arriving ballots vary across the country.
Election officials now face the additional prospect of federal requirements changing while voting is already under way.
“The states set the time, place and manner of elections in this country, not the president,” Marc Elias, the founder of voting rights platform Democracy Docket, said on his YouTube show.
“In fact, the Congress can override the states in many instances, but in no instance can the president. The president is given no power over federal elections.”
North Carolina officials said mailings on Sept 4 would proceed normally and that the state has no plans to use the federal portal at the centre of the dispute.
But time is rapidly running out for any nationwide overhaul.
‘Rushed, chaotic’
Sept 4 marks 60 days before Election Day – the deadline Trump’s order itself envisioned for states to submit voter information – while another 18 states are expected to begin distributing ballots roughly 45 days before Nov 3.
That leaves little room for officials to redesign envelopes, update computer systems, train workers and upload voter data if the courts suddenly allow the restrictions to take effect.
Concerns intensified this week after an anonymous USPS whistleblower alleged that the ballot portal had been developed through a “rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed” process.
The official warned that under a proposed “zero-per-cent failure” policy, one barcode that fails to scan or match could result in an entire batch containing thousands of ballots being rejected until it is checked again.
USPS told AFP no mandatory verification procedures were being performed and that election officials would initially use its portal only voluntarily.
The fight – alongside disputes over partisan redistricting in around a dozen states – come with high political stakes.
Republicans hold narrow congressional majorities, but Democrats are favoured to capture the House as Trump’s approval ratings remain weak and voters voice frustration over living costs and the continuing war with Iran.
A new Cornell University forecast gives Democrats an eight-in-10 chance of taking the chamber, projecting a roughly 226-209 majority. AFP

Volkswagen board backs 50,000 further job cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:58 UTC
01:38:58 KST

Volkswagen AG’s supervisory board backed a sweeping restructuring that calls for 50,000 additional job cuts, far fewer models and a smaller industrial footprint, giving chief executive officer Oliver Blume his clearest mandate yet to overhaul Europe’s biggest carmaker.
The measures approved on Thursday at a meeting in Wolfsburg double workforce reductions across Volkswagen Group brands since late 2024, while also paving the way for the company to slim its vehicle lineup by as much as half by 2035. The new staff cuts represent about 8 percent of Volkswagen’s global workforce as of the end of last year.
Management is pursuing the reductions in response to declining sales in China, high costs in Germany and underused factories. It is also tightening investment, planning 135 billion euros (US$157 billion) of capital expenditure and research and development spending over next year through 2031, about 16 percent less than the investment round agreed on last year.
Photo: AFP
The spending reductions come as Chinese rivals led by BYD Co (比亞迪) expand in Europe, adding to pressure direct investment toward its strongest businesses.
Volkswagen’s works council, which represents the company’s employees, sought to temper the potential for job losses, saying the 50,000 figure is a planning assumption derived from Volkswagen’s target to achieve a 9 percent margin by 2030 rather than a fixed headcount goal.
That distinction reflects the broader compromise behind Thursday’s unanimous board vote, reached a day earlier than expected after weeks of increasingly bitter rhetoric. Labor representatives had accepted that Volkswagen needed further cost reductions, but they fiercely opposed plant closures, moves to weaken co-determination — Germany’s system of worker representation in corporate decisions — and plans to separate parts of the core Volkswagen business.
In the final package, dubbed “Future Plan 2030,” Blume won backing for the extra job cuts and broad efficiency measures. The overhaul targets an operating margin of 9 percent by 2030 on annual sales of about 9 million vehicles.
Workers secured assurances that no factory would be immediately abandoned and that contentious site decisions would be worked through over the coming months.
The deal stops short of closing factories right away. Volkswagen acknowledged that it has about 500,000 vehicles-worth of excess annual capacity in Europe. The company said its factories in Emden, Hannover, Neckarsulm and Zwickau lack competitive future production plans once existing models phase out between 2031 and 2034.
The Porsche-Piech family, which controls a majority of Volkswagen’s voting rights through Porsche SE, has pushed for faster action as returns and dividend flows come under pressure. Blume has argued that Volkswagen can no longer afford to carry the same sprawling cost base and industrial footprint while funding investments in electric vehicles, batteries and software.
